Seahorse flux analysis showed diminished oxygen consumption rate (OCR), indicating reduced mitochondrial oxidative phosphorylation in TAA-mutant VSMCs compared to control VSMCs.
TAA-mutant VSMCs (ACTA2 R179H, TGFBR2 G357W) produced increased extracellular lactate, indicating a metabolic shift toward glycolysis in the presence of TAAD mutations.
Treatment with nicotinamide riboside (NR) reversed the metabolic deficits (reduced OCR and increased lactate) caused by ACTA2 R179H and TGFBR2 G357W mutations in VSMCs.
NR increased F-actin polymerization, indicative of a restored contractile VSMC phenotype, in FBN1-silenced (Marfan model) VSMCs as well as in ACTA2 R179H and TGFBR2 G357W mutant VSMCs.
NR treatment reduced the expression and gelatinolytic activity of matrix metalloproteinases and other secretory/synthetic markers in TAA-mutant VSMCs.

The authors conclude that reduced Tfam expression and mtDNA levels drive a metabolic shift from oxidative phosphorylation to glycolysis in VSMCs affected by familial thoracic aortic aneurysms, a metabolic reprogramming increasingly recognized as a hallmark of aneurysm pathogenesis.

The study concludes that mitochondrial dysfunction is a common pathological mechanism across hereditary thoracic aortic aneurysm syndromes, including Marfan syndrome, FTAAD, and Loeys-Dietz syndrome, supporting mitochondrial-boosting therapies (e.g., NR) as a promising therapeutic avenue.

The literature reports that congenital radial head dislocation (CRHD) can be associated with genetic connective tissue and syndromic conditions including Ehlers-Danlos syndrome, Turner syndrome, and hereditary multiple exostoses.

In this specific patient, genetic testing for syndromic connective tissue disorders such as Ehlers-Danlos or Turner syndrome was not performed because the patient lacked systemic signs or phenotypic features typical of these syndromes.
Prior literature (Smith et al.) emphasizes autosomal dominant inheritance in familial cases of congenital radial head dislocation, suggesting a genetic basis for the condition.

The patient presented with bilateral cubitus valgus, asymmetric elbow range of motion (left 170° extension/60° flexion; right full extension/45° flexion), and bilaterally reduced supination (10°) and pronation (15°), with carrying angles of 33° (left) and 31° (right).

Radiological and 3D CT imaging revealed bilateral radial head anterior luxation with capitellum hypoplasia, an ovoid-shaped radial head, an elongated radial neck, and a shallower-than-normal incisura trochlearis.
Conservative treatment (clinical observation) was successfully used to manage this patient's asymptomatic bilateral CRHD for approximately 6 months without worsening of symptoms or function loss.

Surgical removal of the radial head (radial head excision) has been reported in the literature to potentially cause deterioration of elbow stability and arthropathy, so surgery is generally reserved for symptomatic or unstable cases.
Mutations in COL12A1 (collagen XII) cause myopathic Ehlers-Danlos syndrome, presenting with early-onset myopathy and joint disorder.
COL12A1 expression correlates with LDL levels and is increased in patients with obesity.
In a Col12a1 null mouse model, collagen XII deficiency reduced the volume of subcutaneous, visceral, and brown adipose tissue compared with wild-type mice.
Adipocytes were smaller in Col12a1 null subcutaneous and visceral adipose tissue but not in brown adipose tissue compared with wild-type controls.
Real-time PCR analysis revealed that Col12a1 mRNA is expressed in both visceral and subcutaneous adipose tissue.

Microarray analysis of subcutaneous adipose tissue from Col12a1 null mice identified 1243 upregulated genes, of which 167 were implicated in cytoskeletal muscle structure and 153 in muscle development.
Immunohistochemistry showed myostatin-positive cells were clearly detected in Col12a1 null subcutaneous adipose tissue but not in wild-type tissue.
Joint hyperlaxity patients comprised 6% of new hand clinic patients, roughly twice the expected rate in the general population.
Patients diagnosed with joint hypermobility in the hand clinic had Beighton scores above 6 out of 9.
The hand clinic was the first musculoskeletal specialist evaluation for 46% of the hyperlaxity patients in the cohort.
Pain was reported in 90% of hyperlaxity patients presenting to the hand clinic.
Hyperlaxity patients most commonly had multiple, bilateral, and recurrent wrist disorders as their previous diagnoses, without prior recognition of hyperlaxity.
Nerve compression syndromes and trigger fingers were uncommon among hyperlaxity patients in the hand clinic.
Hyperlaxity patients were on average younger (37.1 years) than typical hand surgery patients and most lacked an inciting traumatic event.

Across all 11 examined neurodivergent, neurological, and mental health groups, participants reported enhanced sensitivity on all four visual hypersensitivity factors compared to the general pattern, indicating a transdiagnostic phenomenon.
Sensitivity to Intense Visual Environments was especially pronounced in Autism, ADHD, Dyslexia, and Dyspraxia, forming a shared cross-condition pattern.
The heightened Intense Visual Environments sensitivity pattern seen in autism/ADHD/dyslexia/dyspraxia was also shared by fibromyalgia and PPPD, and to a lesser extent by Eating Pathology and Fear.

Migraine and synaesthesia showed a different pattern of visual hypersensitivity subtypes compared to the shared Intense Visual Environments-dominant pattern seen in autism, ADHD, dyslexia, dyspraxia, fibromyalgia, and PPPD.

In regression analyses controlling for comorbidities, 9 of 11 neurodivergence/condition labels each significantly and uniquely predicted visual hypersensitivity, with autism, fibromyalgia, migraine, and PPPD being the strongest predictors.
Serum IL-8 levels were significantly higher in patients with chronic low back pain than in healthy controls.
Serum IL-6 levels did not differ significantly between chronic LBP patients and healthy controls.
Serum IL-10 levels did not differ significantly between chronic LBP patients and healthy controls.
Serum TNF-α levels did not differ significantly between chronic LBP patients and healthy controls.
IL-1β was undetectable (<5 pg/mL) in both LBP patients and healthy controls.
Serum IL-8 levels showed a weak positive correlation with anxiety severity as measured by the HADS anxiety subscale, though this did not survive Bonferroni correction.
Serum IL-8 levels showed a weak positive correlation with functional disability measured by the EIFEL (Roland-Morris) score, not surviving Bonferroni correction.
Serum IL-6 levels showed a weak positive correlation with BMI among LBP patients, not surviving Bonferroni correction.

Serum IL-6 levels were negatively correlated with lumbar spine mobility (Schober's test), suggesting IL-6-mediated inflammation may contribute to reduced spinal mobility, though not significant after correction.
No significant correlations were found between serum cytokine levels (IL-6, IL-8, IL-10, TNF-α) and pain intensity, neuropathic pain characteristics, or radiological findings.
Serum IL-8 levels did not differ significantly between chronic LBP patients who screened positive for fibromyalgia (via FiRST) and those who did not.
Fibromyalgia, screened using the validated Arabic FiRST tool, was present in 12% of chronic LBP patients, comorbid with anxiety (38%) and depression (36%).
The paper reports a rapid increase in the use of an unspecified mast cell activation diagnosis code in the United States over time.
Transglutaminase-catalyzed glycosylation (TGcG) induced measurable structural alterations in shrimp tropomyosin as shown by SDS-PAGE, CD, fluorescence, and surface hydrophobicity analyses.
TG-catalyzed glycosylation enhanced the resistance of shrimp tropomyosin to simulated gastrointestinal digestion compared to native TM.
In a mouse allergy model, serum histamine levels were 30% lower after TGcG-treated tropomyosin exposure compared to native TM.
Serum mMCP-1 levels were 23% lower in mice exposed to TGcG-treated tropomyosin compared to native TM.
Mast cell activation markers c-Kit+/FcεRI+ were downregulated by 64% in mice exposed to TGcG-treated tropomyosin versus native TM.
Duodenal tissue damage in the mouse allergy model was reduced by 45% following TGcG-treated tropomyosin exposure compared to native TM.
Transglutaminase-catalyzed glycosylation of tropomyosin was associated with an improved Th1/Th2 immune balance compared to native tropomyosin.

Overall, enzyme-mediated glycosylation (TGcG) of shrimp tropomyosin reduced its allergenicity in a mouse model while preserving protein functionality, suggesting a strategy for hypoallergenic seafood product development.

In an adjuvant-induced arthritis rat model, acupuncture with a 180° rotation angle and 1.0 Hz frequency produced the strongest analgesic effect, correlating with increased pain threshold recovery ratio and elevated mast cell degranulation rate.
Local injection of histamine replicated the analgesic effects of acupuncture in the AA rat model, indicating histamine release mediates the analgesic mechanism.
Administration of an H1 receptor antagonist reduced the analgesic effects of acupuncture, implicating histamine H1 receptor signaling in the mechanism.

Local lidocaine administration (nerve conduction blockade) reduced the analgesic effects of acupuncture, indicating a requirement for intact local nerve conduction in the mast cell-mediated analgesic pathway.
24 h of 5 mM butyrate treatment altered the mast cell transcriptome, downregulating 864 genes and upregulating 551 genes.
BTK, a key FcεRI-signaling kinase, was downregulated ~3.97-fold in mast cells after 24 h butyrate treatment.
SYK, an essential FcεRI-signaling kinase, was downregulated ~3.89-fold in mast cells after 24 h butyrate treatment.
MRGPRX2, the receptor mediating IgE-independent (pseudoallergic) mast cell activation, was downregulated ~4.86-fold by butyrate.
KIT, the mast cell growth factor receptor and identity gene, was downregulated ~2.45-fold with hypoacetylation at its TSS after butyrate treatment.
F2RL1 (PAR2) expression was strongly upregulated (~1500-fold) accompanied by hyperacetylation at its TSS after butyrate treatment.
CLGN expression was strongly upregulated (~675-fold) with hyperacetylation at its TSS after butyrate treatment.
Genome-wide H3K27Ac histone acetylation coverage was markedly increased (up to ~2.6-fold) by butyrate treatment, evident by 3 h and sustained to 24 h.
Butyrate treatment did not significantly alter overall genome-wide H3K4Me2 coverage, indicating selective effects on HDAC-targeted acetylation rather than other histone marks.
Most super-enhancers (~84%) in human mast cells overlapped with non-TSS regions that became hypoacetylated after 24 h of butyrate treatment.
Genes associated with hypoacetylated super-enhancers were particularly enriched for cell activation, FCERI-mediated Ca2+ mobilization, and mast cell-mediated immunity pathways.

Super-enhancer hypoacetylation was the strongest predictor of transcriptional downregulation (~19-24% of associated genes downregulated), compared with only 6-13% for typical enhancers and TSS regions.
The BRD4/bromodomain inhibitor JQ-1 potently and dose-dependently inhibited IgE-mediated primary human mast cell degranulation without affecting cell viability.
Combining suboptimal doses of JQ-1 and butyrate did not further increase inhibition of mast cell degranulation beyond butyrate alone, suggesting both act on the same super-enhancer-driven mechanism.

Both JQ-1 and butyrate independently repressed expression of the super-enhancer-associated mast cell activation genes LAIR, LCP2, LAT, and LAT2, supporting a shared super-enhancer targeting mechanism.
A single 1 mM dose of butyrate substantially suppressed mast cell degranulation and IL-8 production for up to 7 days, but this inhibitory effect was transient and had subsided by 14 days.
Genes downregulated by butyrate, particularly canonical mast cell genes, had substantially higher basal (pre-treatment) expression levels than unaffected or upregulated genes.

608 reproducible super-enhancers linked to 588 unique genes were identified in vehicle-treated primary human mast cells, strongly enriched for immune effector processes including cell activation, exocytosis, and secretion (e.g., CD9, LAIR1, COTL1, LAT, KIT, MS4A2, LYN).

Hereditary alpha-tryptasemia (HαT), defined by tandem duplication/triplication of the TPSAB1 alpha allele, is the most common cause of elevated basal serum tryptase in the general population, more common than systemic mastocytosis.
In the original 2016 study of 98 individuals, 8.2% had both elevated BST values and HαT.
A UK study of 423 individuals found that 5% had HαT.
Modeled reference range data showed that each additional tandem TPSAB1 alpha allele contributes approximately 10 ng/ml to basal serum tryptase on average.
Greater than 90% of patients with systemic mastocytosis harbor the activating KIT p.D816V mutation.
Approximately 20% of the population may carry a frameshifted, functionally null TPSB2 βIII allele (βIIIFS).
A targeted amplicon next-generation sequencing assay using machine learning accurately estimated 96% of alpha and βIIIFS tryptase alleles and 94% of extra alpha alleles on TPSAB1.
Systemic mastocytosis has an estimated prevalence of 0.9-1.7 per 10,000 individuals, with indolent SM being the most common subtype.
Patients with smoldering SM have a higher risk of progression to advanced SM (9.4%-15%) compared to ISM (4.9%) and BMM (1.7%) over a median follow-up of 2.0-4.3 years.

A large cohort study with median 62-month follow-up demonstrated 10-year progression-free survival rates of 100% for BMM, 98.1% for ISM with skin lesions, 87.4% for SM-AHN, 62.5% for SSM, and 55.6% for ASM.
Median survival in advanced SM subtypes is significantly reduced: 3-5 years for SM-AHN, 3-4 years for ASM, and 0.5-1.6 years for MCL, compared to near-normal life expectancy in ISM.
The median time to SM diagnosis is 7 years across all subtypes, with the greatest delays occurring in non-advanced SM.
Around half of SM patients report a history of one or more anaphylaxis episodes, typically severe, triggered by Hymenoptera venom, foods, drugs, or idiopathic causes.
Osteoporosis occurs in up to 30% and fragility fractures in up to 50% of SM patients, with osteoporosis/fractures more prevalent in ISM and osteosclerosis more prevalent in AdvSM.
Nearly half of patients with non-advanced SM may present with basal serum tryptase values below the 20 ng/ml WHO diagnostic threshold, risking diagnostic delay.

The REMA score, derived from multivariate analysis of 83 anaphylaxis patients without skin mastocytosis, identified male sex, BST >25 ng/ml, syncope/presyncope during anaphylaxis, and absence of urticaria/angioedema as predictive of SM, with syncope/presyncope being most tightly linked.

The REMA score has a specificity of 74%; its sensitivity is 87% among SM patients with anaphylaxis but no skin involvement, but only 34% among all SM patients regardless of anaphylaxis or skin involvement history.
A 2014 analysis of 59 patients with adult-onset maculopapular cutaneous mastocytosis found that 97% had systemic mastocytosis, indicating adult-onset MPCM is highly specific for systemic disease.
A 2024 study demonstrated that monomorphic maculopapular cutaneous mastocytosis is tightly linked to systemic mastocytosis with a specificity of 97%.

In a 2022 study of 58 patients with elevated BST (>=11.5 ng/ml) and no HαT, 20% had myeloid neoplasms and 12% had CKD, while 63% of the elevated-BST group overall had HαT, suggesting myeloid neoplasms are much more likely when HαT is absent.
In a 2023 study of 409 patients with elevated BST screened for HαT and myeloid neoplasms, 74% had HαT and 29% had SM or another myeloid neoplasm.

Elevated BST based on tryptase genotype was the single most accurate screening test for SM (Youden's index), with sensitivity of 84% and specificity of 90%, outperforming BST≥11.5, BST≥20, and REMA score alone.

A 2024 osteoporosis-focused scoring system for SM prediction had sensitivity 71% and specificity 67%; replacing the raw BST>19 ng/ml cutoff with genotype-adjusted elevated BST improved sensitivity to 87% and specificity to 76%.
Among urinary mast cell mediators tested for SM screening, N-methylhistamine (NMH) was found to be the most specific, with a specificity of 88%.
Preliminary PIONEER study data show a similar percentage reduction in mast cell burden (serum tryptase and KIT p.D816V VAF) with low-dose avapritinib in patients with and without HαT.
Based on the authors' clinical experience, avapritinib 25 mg daily does not lead to normalization of BST values (to <11.5 ng/ml) in SM patients with HαT.

BST values in SM patients without HαT (excluding SM-AHN) would be expected to fully normalize on disease-modifying TKI therapy, whereas BST values in SM patients with HαT may not normalize despite effective treatment.
Han et al. observed significant reductions in intraepidermal nerve fiber density in patients with neuronal intranuclear inclusion disease, consistent with the original study's findings.
Impaired sudomotor innervation was observed in NIID patients, supporting widespread small fiber loss alongside reduced epidermal nerve fiber density.
Marked perivascular nerve fiber loss was observed in NIID patients, extending the anatomical characterization of small fiber pathology to vascular innervation.

The authors agree that although IENFD is a valuable and diagnostically useful biomarker, it can be disease non-specific and should be interpreted together with other clinical, pathological, and genetic findings.
Genetic testing for NOTCH2NLC expansion is highlighted as an important complementary diagnostic tool alongside skin biopsy findings and intranuclear inclusions for confirming NIID.
NIID patients showed significantly reduced density and length of vascular pan-neural (PGP 9.5+) nerve fibers compared to healthy controls.
Vascular noradrenergic (TH+) nerve fiber density and length were significantly reduced in NIID patients compared to healthy controls.
Vascular adrenergic (DβH+) nerve fiber density, length, and positivity rate were significantly reduced in NIID patients compared to healthy controls.
Vascular cholinergic (VIP+) nerve fiber density, length, and positivity rate were significantly reduced in NIID patients compared to healthy controls.
NIID patients showed reduced sudomotor pan-neural nerve fiber density in the distal forearm skin, consistent with prior findings of impaired sudomotor innervation by Liu et al.
Sudomotor noradrenergic (TH+) nerve fiber density was significantly reduced in NIID patients compared to controls.
Sudomotor cholinergic (VIP+) nerve fiber density and positivity rate were significantly decreased in NIID patients relative to healthy controls.
Intranuclear inclusion frequency correlated negatively with sudomotor noradrenergic nerve fiber density, suggesting selective noradrenergic vulnerability in NIID.
Intranuclear inclusion frequency also correlated negatively with sudomotor noradrenergic nerve fiber length.
Automated quantification of sudomotor innervation correlated well with stereological assessment, supporting the validity of the automated method used in this study.
The estimated prevalence of small fiber neuropathy is at least 53 cases per 100,000 inhabitants.
The most frequent symptoms of small fiber neuropathy are neuropathic pain and dysautonomic dysfunction.
Diagnosis of small fiber neuropathy relies on symptoms, clinical examination, neurophysiologic testing, and skin biopsy.
New genetic causes of small fiber neuropathy have recently been described, including mutations in sodium channels.
Immune causes of small fiber neuropathy have been described, including autoantibodies against trisulfated heparan disaccharide (TS-HDS).
Immune causes of small fiber neuropathy have been described, including autoantibodies against FGFR-3.
Immune causes of small fiber neuropathy have been described, including autoantibodies against plexin D1.
Current treatment of small fiber neuropathy is mainly symptomatic, using antidepressants and antiepileptics in a trial-and-error approach.
Neuromuscular and non-neuromuscular specialists did not differ significantly in the mean number of tests ordered for an initial evaluation of distal symmetric small fiber neuropathy.
Complete blood count, vitamin B12, basic metabolic panel, thyroid stimulating hormone, and hemoglobin A1c were the five most commonly ordered tests for initial evaluation of small fiber neuropathy.
Non-neuromuscular specialists were more likely than neuromuscular specialists to order a paraneoplastic panel for secondary evaluation of small fiber neuropathy etiology.
Neuromuscular specialists were significantly more likely than non-neuromuscular specialists to order skin biopsy for intraepidermal nerve fiber density testing in small fiber neuropathy evaluation.

Recommended high-yield studies for diagnosing the cause of distal symmetric polyneuropathy, including small fiber neuropathy, were not universally ordered by surveyed neurologists, indicating variability in diagnostic approach.
Pooled mean IENFD in the thigh among healthy subjects was 23.2 fibers/mm, the highest value among all anatomical sites, with significant between-study heterogeneity.
Pooled mean IENFD in the forearm among healthy subjects was 17.3 fibers/mm based on only three studies with no significant heterogeneity.
Pooled mean IENFD in fingers of healthy subjects was 11.3 fibers/mm, derived from a single study.
Pooled mean IENFD in the distal leg among healthy subjects was 12.9 fibers/mm with very high heterogeneity across studies.
Pooled mean IENFD in toes of healthy subjects was 14.5 fibers/mm, based on only two studies.
In neuropathic patients, pooled mean IENFD in the forearm was 5.7 fibers/mm, markedly lower than healthy subjects.
In neuropathic patients, pooled mean IENFD in the thigh was 17.2 fibers/mm with high heterogeneity, lower than healthy subjects but relatively preserved compared to distal sites.
Pooled mean IENFD in the distal leg of neuropathic patients was 5.1 fibers/mm, substantially lower than in healthy subjects.
Pooled mean IENFD in toes of neuropathic patients was 2.5 fibers/mm, based on only two studies, with the highest coefficient of variation of all sites.
Across anatomical regions, neuropathic patients showed an overall IENFD reduction of about 8.0 fibers/mm compared to healthy individuals, with similar patterns across regions.
In healthy individuals, IENFD decreased significantly with age, by an estimated 1.35 fibers/mm every 5 years.
In neuropathic patients, age was not significantly associated with IENFD, showing a much slower, non-significant decline compared to healthy subjects.
Among healthy subjects, a higher percentage of females in a study was associated with significantly higher leg IENFD values (groups with 50-74% and 75-100% female).
In neuropathic patients, no consistent systematic trend of IENFD with percentage of female participants was found, unlike in healthy subjects.
Gender dimorphism was observed in distal leg IENFD, with females exhibiting consistently higher values than males across studies.
In Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease type 1A, duplication of the PMP22 gene causes Schwann cell dysfunction and impaired axonal support contributing to small fiber loss.
Mitochondrial dysfunction in Friedreich ataxia impairs energy metabolism, rendering small nerve fibers susceptible to oxidative stress and loss.
Chronic HIV infection worsens small fiber loss through ongoing immune activation and neurotoxic cytokines including TNF-α and IL-6.

The thigh had the lowest coefficient of variation among tested sites (23.8% in healthy, 40.8% in neuropathic subjects), supporting its use as the preferred reference biopsy site for standardized IENFD assessment.
A 50-year-old male with Loeys-Dietz syndrome due to a pathogenic TGFBR2 variant developed a direct carotid-cavernous fistula without preceding trauma.
Transarterial embolization with coils and Onyx liquid embolic agent achieved complete occlusion of the arterio-venous shunt and resolved the patient's tinnitus and exophthalmos.
Direct carotid-cavernous fistula is frequently reported in association with Ehlers-Danlos syndrome but not with Marfan syndrome.

In EDS, increased carotid circumferential wall stress, higher carotid distensibility, and lower carotid intima-media thickness are proposed mechanisms increasing risk of direct carotid-cavernous fistula.

Loeys-Dietz syndrome is caused by pathogenic variants in genes of the TGF-β signaling pathway leading to excess TGF-β activity, which may cause vascular wall fragility predisposing to arterial rupture and fistula formation.
Endovascular embolization is reported as first-line therapy for carotid-cavernous fistula, with over 80% of patients achieving complete cure.

The authors suggest that endovascular treatment is more feasible in LDS than in vascular EDS, as LDS arteries generally tolerate catheter manipulation without complication, based on this and other reported cases.
Three weeks of dark-phase melatonin administration at any of three doses did not reduce systolic blood pressure or heart rate compared with placebo at the end of the experiment.
In the placebo group, systolic blood pressure increased significantly from the control week to the third experimental week in both light and dark phases.
In the Mel10 (9-10 mg/kg/12h) melatonin group, systolic blood pressure showed a borderline significant increase in the dark phase from control to M3 week.

Heart rate was significantly reduced from the control week to the third experimental week in the light and dark phases across all groups including placebo, suggesting a general time effect rather than a melatonin-specific effect.

Melatonin produced dose-dependent changes in the maximum rate of pressure rise (dP/dtmax, decreased) and the percent recovery point (increased) between control and M3 weeks, seen in Mel10 (light only) and Mel45 (both phases).
Locomotor activity decreased significantly in the Mel10 group in the light phase from control to M3 week.
The LF/HF ratio decreased significantly from control to M3 week in the placebo group (dark phase) and Mel10 group (light phase).

Time-domain HRV parameters (SDNN, RMSSD, NN9, pNN9) increased significantly from control to M3 week in the placebo group in both phases, with partial replication of some parameters in the Mel10 and Mel45 groups.
Spontaneous baroreflex sensitivity (sBRS) increased significantly in the dark phase from control to M3 week in both the placebo and Mel45 groups.
Melatonin administration did not affect the systolic pressor response to subcutaneous norepinephrine challenge.
The pressor response to exogenous norepinephrine was higher when given at the beginning (ZT02) than at the end (ZT10) of the light phase, regardless of group.
Melatonin dose-dependently increased the 24-h amplitude of systolic blood pressure, gradually in Mel10 and immediately in Mel45, with no effect in Mel2.
The percent rhythm (circadian robustness) of systolic blood pressure changed significantly in the Mel2 and Mel45 groups.
Melatonin affected heart rate circadian amplitude (increased in Mel45) and percent rhythm (increased in Mel10, decreased in Mel45).
Adrenal tyrosine hydroxylase (TH) expression was decreased in SHR compared to normotensive Wistar rats (borderline significance).
Low-dose melatonin (Mel2) increased adrenal TH expression compared to placebo and the high-dose Mel45 group.
Melatonin did not affect adrenal monoamine oxidase A (MAO-A) expression at any dose.
Baseline kidney expression of eNOS, CD68, ENaC and TGF-β1 did not differ between SHR and normotensive Wistar rats.
High-dose melatonin (Mel45) reduced renal CD68 (macrophage marker) expression compared to placebo, suggesting an anti-inflammatory effect.
Low-dose melatonin (Mel2) increased renal eNOS expression compared to placebo.
AVP expression was significantly decreased in the suprachiasmatic nucleus (SCN) and paraventricular nucleus (PVN), but not the supraoptic nucleus (SON), in SHR compared to Wistar rats.
Melatonin decreased AVP density in the SON in a dose-dependent manner in SHR, with no effect on SCN or PVN AVP expression.
The 24-hour percent rhythm of pulse pressure changed significantly only in the low-dose (Mel2) melatonin group.
Spontaneously hypertensive rats showed reduced tyrosine hydroxylase expression in the adrenal gland compared to normotensive Wistar rats.
Low-dose melatonin (Mel2) increased adrenal tyrosine hydroxylase expression compared to both placebo and high-dose (Mel45) groups.
Adrenal MAO-A expression did not differ between spontaneously hypertensive and Wistar rats, and was not affected by melatonin treatment.
Kidney protein expression of eNOS, CD68, ENaC and TGF-β1 did not differ between Wistar and spontaneously hypertensive rats.
High-dose melatonin (Mel45) decreased renal CD68 (macrophage marker) expression compared to placebo, suggesting a possible anti-inflammatory effect.
Low-dose melatonin (Mel2) increased renal eNOS expression compared to placebo.
Spontaneously hypertensive rats showed significantly decreased AVP mRNA expression in the suprachiasmatic and paraventricular nuclei, but not in the supraoptic nucleus, compared to Wistar rats.
Melatonin did not change AVP expression in the SCN or PVN of SHR but decreased AVP density in the supraoptic nucleus in a dose-dependent manner.
The density of GAD65 and GAD67 mRNA in the nucleus tractus solitarii was significantly decreased in spontaneously hypertensive rats compared with Wistar rats.
Melatonin administration did not affect GAD65 and GAD67 density in the NTS of spontaneously hypertensive rats.
GAT1 and GABAAR mRNA density in the NTS did not differ between spontaneously hypertensive and Wistar rats and was not affected by melatonin treatment.
Renal ENaC expression showed a non-significant increasing trend in spontaneously hypertensive rats compared to Wistar rats, and was not changed by melatonin.
Among 2406 patients with documented NF1, gastrointestinal manifestations (obstruction or dysmotility) were seen in about 2% of the cohort.

Thirteen NF1 patients had small bowel or colonic obstructions caused by tumors including gastrointestinal stromal tumors, malignant peripheral nerve sheath tumors, neurofibromas, diffuse ganglioneuromatosis, schwannoma, and inflammatory fibroid polyp.
38 NF1 patients had abnormal gut motility including esophageal achalasia or spasm, delayed gastric emptying, slow colonic transit, and dyssynergic defecation.
Gastric, small bowel, and colonic manometry in NF1 patients showed normal amplitude but incoordinated contractions, suggestive of an underlying neuropathic process.
Histological examination of resected specimens from some NF1 patients identified myenteric plexus proliferation or diffuse ganglioneuromatosis underlying the dysmotility.
In healthy control rats, insulin-immunoreactive myenteric neurons were proportionally fewer in the duodenum than in the ileum and colon.
In acute (1-week) hyperglycemic rats, the proportion of insulin-immunoreactive myenteric neurons markedly increased in the ileum and colon but was unchanged in the duodenum compared to controls.

In chronic (10-week) diabetic rats, the proportion of insulin-immunoreactive myenteric neurons was significantly decreased in the colon (with no change in duodenum/ileum), and insulin treatment failed to prevent this colonic decrease.
In acute hyperglycemic rats, the proportion of nitrergic (nNOS-expressing) myenteric neurons co-containing insulin was significantly increased in the ileum and colon compared to controls.

In chronic diabetic rats, the proportion of insulin-nNOS-immunoreactive neurons did not change relative to controls in any gut segment, but insulin treatment increased this ratio specifically in the ileum.

Immunogold electron microscopy showed markedly decreased insulin labelling density in both endocrine and exocrine pancreas of chronic diabetic rats compared to controls, confirming loss of pancreatic insulin production.

Immunogold quantification showed segment-specific changes in myenteric ganglion insulin content in chronic diabetics: increased in duodenum, unchanged in ileum, decreased in colon; insulin treatment only partially normalized the colon and paradoxically reduced duodenal levels below control.
In control rats, ELISA-measured tissue insulin concentration in the intestinal smooth muscle/myenteric plexus decreased distally along the gut, being highest in the duodenum.
Chronic diabetic rats showed a significant decrease in tissue insulin concentration specifically in the duodenum, with no change in ileum or colon.

PCR analysis detected insulin mRNA only in pancreatic tissue of controls and not in the duodenum, ileum, or colon of control or diabetic rats, and diabetic pancreas also lacked insulin mRNA, indicating that intestinal insulin protein is not locally synthesized by myenteric neurons but likely uptaken from the environment.
Twice-daily subcutaneous insulin treatment in chronic diabetic rats markedly lowered blood glucose from severely hyperglycemic levels but did not fully normalize it to control values.

A woman with refractory idiopathic gastroparesis developed late dumping syndrome, characterized by postprandial hypoglycemia and autonomic symptoms, following gastric peroral endoscopic myotomy (G-POEM).
The patient's late dumping syndrome improved favorably with dietary management alone, without requiring pharmacological treatment.

Broad-spectrum antibiotic treatment induced significant taxonomic changes in gut microbiota of both sexes compared to untreated controls, appearing earlier and involving more potentially harmful taxa in females.
LGG supplementation effectively prevented antibiotic-induced alterations in microbial communities in both sexes, with a more pronounced protective effect in males.
Antibiotic-induced dysbiosis reduced intestinal transit efficiency only in female mice.
Antibiotic-induced dysbiosis reduced nitrergic (nitric oxide-mediated) relaxations in the gut only in female mice.
Antibiotic-induced dysbiosis reduced tachykinergic contractions in the gut only in female mice.
LGG had no significant effect on dysbiosis-induced reductions in transit efficiency, nitrergic relaxations, or tachykinergic contractions in female mice.
Antibiotic-induced dysbiosis decreased cholinergic contractions in the gut in both female and male mice.
LGG restored cholinergic excitatory contractions to control levels only in male mice, not in females.
LGG treatment restored dysbiosis-induced reductions in cholinergic contractile responses to control levels, but only in male mice, not females.
In female mice, LGG treatment did not significantly reverse the dysbiosis-induced deficits in intestinal transit efficiency, nitrergic relaxations, or tachykinergic contractions.
Intracisternal administration of carnosine improved LPS-induced colonic hyperpermeability in rats, measured by the Evans blue dye method.
The barrier-improving effect of central carnosine administration was abolished by brain H1 receptor antagonism, indicating H1 receptor signaling mediates carnosine's action.
Inhibition of basal forebrain cholinergic neurons abolished carnosine's improvement of colonic hyperpermeability, indicating these neurons are required for the effect.
Inhibition of adenosine A2B receptor signaling abolished carnosine's improvement of colonic hyperpermeability, indicating A2B receptor signaling is required for the effect.
Vagotomy abolished carnosine's improvement of colonic hyperpermeability, indicating vagal signaling is required for the effect.

High-dose intraperitoneal carnosine also alleviated LPS-induced colonic hyperpermeability, and this peripheral effect was similarly blocked by brain H1 receptor antagonism, vagotomy, and inhibition of BFCNs or adenosine A2B signaling.
Exercise reduced LPS-induced colonic hyperpermeability in rats, an effect eliminated by brain histamine H1 receptor blockade, implicating muscle-derived carnosine in central barrier regulation.
Functional dyspepsia patients showed lower vagal tone than healthy participants, implicating autonomic imbalance in GI dysmotility.
Among type 1 diabetic patients with peripheral neuropathy, those with lower cardiac vagal tone had more severe impairment of gastric motility and colonic transit.

In 10 gastroparetic patients refractory to medical therapy, gastric electrical stimulation activated vagal afferent pathways, increased vagal efferent tone, mitigated gastric sensitivity, and improved postprandial gastric accommodation.
Acupuncture at the Neiguan (P6) acupoint improved nausea and vomiting in healthy subjects, associated with increased vagal tone measured by HRV.
Gentle (2 Hz) manual acupuncture increased gastric motility amplitude via the vagal nerve in an animal study, whereas strong (4 Hz) stimulation did not.
Electroacupuncture at ST36 restored rectal distension-induced motor impairment by enhancing vagal activity in a canine gastroparesis model.
Electroacupuncture improved gastric dysrhythmia, delayed GI transit, and impaired accommodation mainly through the vagal nerve in diabetic rats.
2 Hz stimulation at ST36 partly shortened recovery time in postoperative ileus mice by directly activating the vagal nerve, but did not regulate local gastrointestinal inflammation.
Acupuncture promoted vagal efferent activity and increased gastric motility by inhibiting GABA transmission in the dorsal motor nucleus of the vagus (DMV).

Electroacupuncture activated the α7nAChR-mediated JAK2/STAT3 signaling pathway in macrophages, reducing TNF-α and IL-6 production and promoting gastrointestinal motility in a postoperative ileus mouse model; the protective effect was abolished by vagotomy or GABAA receptor agonist injection into the DMV.

Low-frequency (1 Hz) electroacupuncture at ST36 restrained zymosan-induced leukocyte migration by activating the sympathetic nervous system, an effect blocked by sympathetic denervation or propranolol but not by adrenalectomy.
High-intensity (3 mA) electroacupuncture at abdominal ST25, via a spinal-sympathetic axis, inhibited splenic inflammation for systemic inflammation prevention.
A 4-week course of acupuncture increased serum ghrelin concentration, which positively correlated with improvement in functional dyspepsia symptoms.

A 2013 meta-analysis of 14 RCTs (948 diabetic gastroparesis patients) found acupuncture more effective than domperidone for improving dyspeptic symptoms (nausea, vomiting, loss of appetite, bloating), with no heterogeneity.

A 2014 meta-analysis of 7 RCTs (730 postoperative gastroparesis patients) found neither acupuncture alone nor acupuncture plus medication had a significantly greater total effective rate than standard care or medication alone.
A 2018 meta-analysis of 32 studies (2601 participants) found acupuncture might improve gastroparesis symptoms, but the quality of evidence was very low.
The FDA issued a black-box warning for metoclopramide, the only FDA-approved gastroparesis drug, due to risk of tardive dyskinesia, and limited it to a maximum 12-week duration.

A meta-analysis of 15 high-quality RCTs (965 participants) found acupuncture shortened time to first flatus, defecation, bowel sound recovery, and oral feeding, and decreased hospital stay in postoperative ileus.

In a prospective RCT with 165 postoperative ileus patients, electroacupuncture (postoperative days 1-4) resulted in shorter time to defecation/ambulation and reduced analgesic requirement compared with no or sham acupuncture.
Compared with sham acupuncture, real acupuncture resulted in fewer residual Sitz markers in the small intestine on postoperative days 3 and 5, suggesting shortened postoperative ileus.
A meta-analysis of 31 studies (3,234 patients) found acupuncture more effective than medication for weekly bowel movements, total symptom score, and IBS-D symptom severity.
A review of 5 RCTs (449 participants) found 84% of acupuncture recipients had reduced IBS symptom severity versus 63% receiving pharmacological treatment.
Despite benefits versus standard medical treatment, acupuncture showed no evidence of superiority over sham acupuncture for IBS symptom severity or quality of life.

A 2013 meta-analysis of 14 RCTs with 948 diabetic gastroparesis patients found acupuncture more effective than domperidone at improving dyspeptic symptoms such as nausea, vomiting, loss of appetite, and bloating, with no heterogeneity.

A 2014 meta-analysis of 7 RCTs with 730 postoperative gastroparesis patients found that neither acupuncture alone nor acupuncture combined with medication showed a significantly greater total effective rate than standard care or medication alone.
A 2018 meta-analysis of 32 studies and 2601 participants found acupuncture might improve gastroparesis symptoms but the evidence was of very low quality, so no definitive conclusions could be drawn.

A single-blinded randomized pilot study found that short-term electroacupuncture, compared with sham EA, reduced dyspeptic symptoms and accelerated solid gastric emptying in diabetic gastroparesis, with improvement maintained 2 weeks post-trial.

A multi-center RCT of 99 gastroparesis patients found acupuncture at Zhongwan (CV12) plus Zusanli (ST36) was more effective in decreasing GCSI scores and symptom scores than PC6 plus ST36 or ST36 plus non-acupoint stimulation.

A meta-analysis of 15 high-quality RCTs with 965 participants found acupuncture shortened time to first flatus, defecation, bowel sound recovery, and oral feeding initiation, and decreased hospital stay length in postoperative ileus patients.

A prospective study of 165 postoperative ileus patients found electroacupuncture, versus sham or no acupuncture, produced shorter time to defecation and ambulation and reduced postoperative analgesic requirement.

A systematic review and meta-analysis of 31 studies with 3,234 patients found acupuncture more efficacious than medication for weekly bowel movements, total symptom score, and IBS-D symptom severity, improving global clinical effectiveness in IBS-D.

A review of five RCTs (449 participants) found 84% of acupuncture recipients experienced reduced IBS symptom severity versus 63% with pharmacological treatment, indicating acupuncture was significantly more efficacious than drugs or no targeted intervention.
Multiple reviews found no evidence that acupuncture improved IBS symptom severity or quality of life compared with sham acupuncture.

A pragmatic RCT with 233 IBS patients (average 13-year symptom duration) found acupuncture significantly reduced IBS Symptom Severity Score at 3 months compared to usual care, with benefit persisting at 6, 9, and 12 months but disappearing by 24 months.

A multicenter RCT in China with 531 IBS patients found IBS-SSS decreased by 123.51 points after acupuncture versus 94.73 points after pharmacological treatment (polyethylene glycol for IBS-C, pinaverium bromide for IBS-D), with effects lasting up to 12 weeks.
None of the sham-controlled trials demonstrated advantages of true acupuncture over sham acupuncture for IBS symptoms, quality of life, or sleep quality.

A systematic review and meta-analysis of 9 RCTs found electroacupuncture significantly improved frequency of spontaneous bowel movements, total response rates, and reduced symptom scores compared to medication in chronic functional constipation, and was safer.

A meta-analysis of 33 trials with 4342 participants found acupuncture had a larger therapeutic effect on stool frequency, response rate, and lower adverse-event rate than placebo, probiotics, and other non-pharmacological treatments for chronic functional constipation.

A multicenter trial of 1,075 participants found electroacupuncture, versus sham acupuncture, significantly increased weekly complete spontaneous bowel movements and improved quality of life in severe chronic functional constipation over an 8-week treatment, with benefits continuing through a 12-week follow-up.

A multicenter noninferiority RCT of 560 participants found electroacupuncture noninferior to prucalopride for improving weekly complete spontaneous bowel movements in severe chronic constipation from weeks 3-8, with effects persisting 24 weeks post-treatment and a favorable safety profile.

A study comparing electroacupuncture and mosapride found both significantly enhanced weekly complete spontaneous bowel movements, stool consistency, and defecation difficulty, but acupuncture was more effective at improving quality of life and reducing depression and anxiety.

The authors note that acupuncture cannot currently be recommended for clinical practice in IBS, gastroparesis, FD and other GI dysmotility conditions due to high risk of bias in most trials and challenges from placebo effects on subjective endpoints.
At baseline, 73% of all study participants (COVID+ and COVID− combined) fell into one of three latent classes characterized by poor health-related quality of life (HRQoL).

Substantial shifting among HRQoL latent classes occurred between baseline and 3-month follow-up, with 58% of participants in a poor-HRQoL class at 3 months, after which class membership stabilized through 12 months.

Compared with symptomatic COVID− controls, COVID+ participants had a higher adjusted probability of being in the optimal HRQoL class and a lower probability of being in the poor overall HRQoL class at baseline and at all follow-up timepoints through 12 months.

Recovery from poor physical HRQoL to optimal HRQoL occurred predominantly early, with 50.8% of COVID+ individuals in the poor physical HRQoL class transitioning to the optimal HRQoL class between baseline and 3-month follow-up.

Recovery from poor mental HRQoL to optimal HRQoL was slower and more pronounced later, with 20.6% of COVID+ individuals in the poor mental HRQoL class transitioning to the optimal HRQoL class between 6 and 9 months.
Recovery from the poor overall HRQoL class to the optimal HRQoL class was similar between COVID+ and COVID− groups and remained low throughout follow-up, ranging from 1.4% to 5.2%.

Self-reported long COVID at final follow-up was substantially more prevalent among participants in the poor overall HRQoL class (42.4%) than among those in the poor physical (24.2%), poor mental (17.8%), or optimal HRQoL (9.7%) classes.

Participants classified into the poor physical HRQoL and poor overall HRQoL latent classes had significantly higher acute illness symptom severity scores, higher prevalence of comorbid conditions, and more baseline symptoms than those in other classes.

The probability of poor mental HRQoL increased from baseline to 3 months and then gradually decreased from 3 through 12 months, in contrast to poor physical HRQoL which decreased early and remained stable.
A genome-wide significant SNP cluster within the intronic region of ARHGEF28 on chromosome 5q13.2 was newly associated with widespread pain in the UK Biobank primary GWAS.
A suggestive (marginally genome-wide significant) locus in FAF1 on chromosome 1 was associated with widespread pain.
SNP-based heritability of widespread pain in the UK Biobank was estimated at 0.18.
Weak replication of one discovery SNP (rs761429057, TMCC1) was found in the TwinsUK chronic widespread pain cohort.
None of the 14 discovery SNPs replicated in fibromyalgia cohorts from FibroGene or FinnGen.
The male-specific GWAS found no locus reaching genome-wide significance for widespread pain.
A novel female-specific locus within LRMDA on chromosome 10 was significantly associated with widespread pain.
Gene-based analysis mapping SNPs to 18,115 protein-coding genes found no gene meeting genome-wide significance for widespread pain.
Gene-set enrichment analysis of 17,109 gene sets found none significantly associated with widespread pain.
ARHGEF28 showed higher tissue expression in nerve, oral, and adrenal gland tissues compared to other tissue types, though overall tissue-specificity testing was not significant.
Widespread pain showed the strongest genetic correlation with 'other joint disorders, not elsewhere classified' among 1396 UK Biobank phenotypes tested.
Widespread pain showed strong genetic correlation with spondylosis.
Widespread pain showed strong genetic correlation with other diseases of the anus and rectum.
The genetic correlation of widespread pain between females and males was 0.80, suggesting partly distinct genetic underpinnings by sex.
Two SNPs near the widespread pain locus showed significant cis-eQTL associations with gene expression in cultured fibroblasts.
PheWAS of the top widespread pain SNP (rs34691025) revealed associations with psychological tenseness/restlessness, brain white matter microstructure, and long-standing illness/disability.
PheWAS showed ARHGEF28 was associated with hearing difficulty, high blood pressure, and hypertension.
PheWAS showed FAF1 was associated with standing height, headache, and stomachache.
Two-sample Mendelian randomization found no significant causal effect of hearing loss on widespread pain, nor evidence of reverse causation.

PI-ME/CFS patients showed significantly higher axial diffusivity than healthy controls across multiple association fibre tracts (right superior longitudinal fasciculus, right uncinate fasciculus, right external capsule) and projection fibre tracts (cerebellar peduncles, corona radiata, sagittal stratum, corticospinal tract, medial lemniscus).
No significant group differences were found in FA, MD, or RD between PI-ME/CFS patients and healthy controls.
GO-ME/CFS patients showed significantly lower axial diffusivity than healthy controls in the body and genu of the corpus callosum.
No significant group differences were found in FA, MD, or RD between GO-ME/CFS patients and healthy controls.

Across all PI-ME/CFS-group participants (patients and HCs combined), higher AD in association and projection fibre tracts was significantly negatively correlated with SF-36 physical component summary (PCS) scores, indicating higher AD relates to worse physical health.
Within the PI-ME/CFS patient group only, AD in the right external capsule was significantly negatively correlated with disease duration.

Across all GO-ME/CFS-group participants (patients and HCs combined), lower AD in the corpus callosum and corona radiata was significantly positively correlated with SF-36 mental component summary (MCS) scores, indicating lower AD relates to worse mental health.

PI-ME/CFS and GO-ME/CFS patient subgroups did not differ significantly in demographic characteristics or clinical/behavioural scores, suggesting conventional clinical instruments cannot distinguish the two onset-based subtypes despite their distinct white matter findings.
PI-ME/CFS patients had significantly worse anxiety, depression, mental and physical health, sleep quality, and disability levels compared to matched healthy controls.
GO-ME/CFS patients had significantly worse anxiety, depression, mental and physical health, sleep quality, and disability levels compared to matched healthy controls.
ME/CFS donor lymphocytes (CD4 T, CD8 T, and B cells) show significantly higher total ROS (DCFDA) levels than healthy controls.
LC donor lymphocytes show elevated total ROS compared to HCs, reaching significance in CD8 T cells but not CD4 T or B cells.
Total ROS elevation in ME/CFS and LC is female-specific; males show no significant ROS differences from control males.
Mitochondrial ATP levels were decreased on average 1.6-fold in ME/CFS lymphocytes compared to controls.
Mitochondrial ATP levels were decreased on average 2.8-fold in LC lymphocytes compared to controls.
No differences in mitochondrial mass or membrane potential were detected between ME/CFS, LC and HC lymphocytes.
No association was found between patient-reported fatigue severity and total ROS levels in ME/CFS and LC donors.
Female LC subjects showed a weak positive association between symptom duration and total ROS levels, while males showed a weak negative association.
Among LC donors, BMI positively correlated with total ROS levels in B cells.
Mitochondrial calcium levels, measured by Rhod-2 AM, are significantly elevated in ME/CFS and LC female donor lymphocytes but not in males.
LC donor CD4 and CD8 T cells show significantly lower SOD2 protein levels compared to HCs, with similar reductions across both sexes.
ME/CFS lymphocytes show significantly higher glutathione levels than HCs in both females and males.
Total ROS levels positively correlate with GSH levels across lymphocyte populations in both sexes, consistent with an antioxidant compensatory response.

Reanalysis of published scRNA-seq data shows GPX4 transcript levels are uniquely elevated in female LC central memory T cells across 4, 8, and 24 months post-infection, compared to recovered controls.
Male ME/CFS and LC donor lymphocytes show significantly higher lipid peroxidation compared to controls, more pronounced than in females.
Mitochondrial-targeted lipid peroxidation is elevated in ME/CFS T cells, particularly in males.
Reanalysis of published bulk RNA-seq data shows PLA2G6 transcript is significantly suppressed in LC male donors, with no significant change in females.
Lipid droplet levels are significantly lower in ME/CFS and LC donor lymphocytes across both males and females compared to HCs.
Lipid droplet levels are inversely correlated with glutathione levels across both males and females.

Mass spectrometry and systems chemistry analysis identified phospholipid synthesis (lysoPE metabolite) reactions as the most significantly up-regulated metabolic pathway in ME/CFS T cells compared to HCs.
Reanalysis of external whole-blood RNA-seq data showed significantly higher PLA2G4A transcript levels in ME/CFS donors compared to sedentary controls.
Immunofluorescence staining of CD3 T cells showed significantly higher GPX4 protein levels in ME/CFS and LC donors compared to HC.

Extreme-value (95th percentile) GSH distributions differ by disease group: HC CD4 T cells decay quickly (light-tailed), LC show heavy-tailed decay, and ME/CFS show a shifted, bounded tail; this heterogeneity is concentrated in memory, not naive, CD4 T cells.
Female ME/CFS CD4 and CD8 T cells hyperproliferate after anti-CD3/CD28+IL-2 stimulation compared to female controls, and show a flatter dependence on ROS levels.
Female LC CD4 and CD8 T cells hyperproliferate compared to female controls after stimulation.
ME/CFS male T cells show no average increase in proliferation compared to controls and exhibit relative insensitivity to ROS levels during activation, unlike females.
In-vitro metformin treatment significantly reduced CD4 T cell hyperproliferation in ME/CFS female donors but had no effect in HC donors.
N-acetylcysteine at micromolar concentrations did not significantly reduce T cell hyperproliferation in ME/CFS or LC female donors.
No differences in mitochondrial mass or membrane potential were detected between ME/CFS, LC, and HC lymphocytes.
No association was found between total ROS levels and patient-reported fatigue severity in ME/CFS and LC donors.
No association was detected between total ROS levels and donor age.
T cell surface activation markers CD69 and CD137 showed no differences after stimulation between ME/CFS, LC, and HC samples.
ME/CFS male T cells show relative insensitivity to ROS levels during proliferation compared to control males, unlike the hyperproliferative response seen in females.

A separate study cited by the authors found significantly higher intracellular IL-2 levels in stimulated CD4 T cells from LC donors, produced via ROS-NFAT signaling, externally supporting the paper's proliferation/activation model.
An influenza vaccination study cited by the authors found T cell hyperproliferation in the ME/CFS group versus controls, externally corroborating the hyperproliferation finding in this paper.
A cited double-blinded phase III clinical trial of over 1,300 patients found that prophylactic metformin reduced Long COVID incidence by 41%, especially among females and those with higher BMI.

The authors hypothesize that sex hormones such as estradiol, which regulate serum antioxidant enzyme levels and T cell activation, may partially explain the distinct redox biology observed in ME/CFS and LC females.

The authors propose that androgens modulate PPARα levels in CD4 T cells, and that differences in PPARα-regulated fatty acid oxidation may explain the sex-specific lipid metabolism differences observed.

The authors interpret the heavy-tailed oxidative stress distribution in LC T cells as reflecting an intermediate disease state between healthy controls and the shifted/bounded distribution seen in ME/CFS.
Comparing only the extreme (95th percentile) GSH fluorescence values, rather than medians, revealed statistically significant elevation of GSH in LC and ME/CFS CD4 T cells compared to HCs.

This study and a separate deep phenotyping study on ME/CFS patients both report sex-specific differences in fatty acid oxidation between ME/CFS males and females, with this study additionally identifying larger changes in lipid peroxidation.
Healthy controls were 1.65 times more likely than PI-ME/CFS patients to choose the hard task on the EEfRT (the Proportion of Hard Task Choices measure).
Once choosing the hard EEfRT task, controls were 27.23 times more likely than PI-ME/CFS patients to successfully complete it, a much larger effect than the difference in task choice.
PI-ME/CFS patients completed only 65% of hard EEfRT tasks they chose versus 96% for controls, a statistically significant difference.
Both PI-ME/CFS patients and controls completed the easy EEfRT task at near-ceiling rates with no significant difference between groups.

Proportion of hard task choices (the measure Walitt et al. termed 'effort preference') was positively correlated with hard task completion rate across participants, suggesting ability confounded the preference measure.
Seven of 15 PI-ME/CFS patients had lower hard-task completion rates than any healthy control, completing only about 30% of chosen hard tasks on average.
PI-ME/CFS patients had markedly lower SF-36 physical function scores than healthy controls, indicating severe physical limitations relevant to their inability to complete the hard EEfRT task.
Walitt et al. found no significant group difference on the Grooved Pegboard Test of psychomotor ability, but the analysis was underpowered to detect even large effects.
Prior studies using other measures indicate motor speed impairments in ME/CFS patients, paralleling reported cognitive processing speed deficits.
Plasma SMPDL3B protein levels were significantly higher in ME patients than in healthy controls in the Canadian cohort.
A plasma SMPDL3B threshold of 30 ng/mL, derived via Random Forest and ROC analysis, discriminated ME severity with high accuracy in the Canadian cohort.
The association between elevated SMPDL3B and increased symptom severity was replicated in an independent Norwegian cohort, and SMPDL3B was higher in severe versus mild ME.
Women with ME had significantly higher circulating SMPDL3B levels than men with ME in both Canadian and Norwegian cohorts.
Plasma SMPDL3B concentrations declined progressively with age, with the highest levels in patients aged 18-30 years.

Multivariate logistic regression showed each 50 ng/mL increase in plasma SMPDL3B was associated with three-fold higher odds of greater disease severity, an association driven primarily by female patients; age was not a significant predictor.
Women with ME using oral contraceptives had higher plasma SMPDL3B than non-users in both cohorts, while menopausal women showed reduced levels, implicating estrogen as a regulator.
Dose-dependent estradiol treatment of Jurkat T cells increased total SMPDL3B protein levels in vitro, supporting an estrogen-driven regulatory mechanism.
Membrane-bound SMPDL3B on monocytes was significantly reduced in ME patients compared to HC, with a more pronounced reduction in patients with high circulating (soluble) SMPDL3B.
Women with ME showed higher membrane-bound SMPDL3B on monocytes than men with ME, potentially reflecting sex-based differences in gene expression and hormonal regulation.
SMPDL3B gene expression was elevated in ME patients relative to HC, suggesting the reduction in membrane-bound protein is not due to reduced transcription.
PLCXD1 (encoding PI-PLC) gene expression was upregulated in ME patients and positively correlated with SMPDL3B expression and plasma SMPDL3B, but negatively correlated with membrane-bound SMPDL3B.
PBMCs from ME patients produced more IL-6 in response to LPS (TLR4 agonist) stimulation than PBMCs from healthy controls.

Adding recombinant soluble SMPDL3B to LPS-stimulated PBMCs did not inhibit TLR4 activation or reduce IL-6 expression, indicating the soluble form lacks the regulatory function of the membrane-anchored form.
LPS stimulation upregulated PLCXD1 expression in ME patient PBMCs, which correlated with reduced membrane-bound SMPDL3B, supporting an inflammation-driven cleavage amplification loop.

In healthy-donor PBMCs, vildagliptin (100 µM) increased membrane-bound SMPDL3B on monocytes and decreased soluble SMPDL3B and PI-PLC levels, consistent with PI-PLC inhibition stabilizing membrane anchoring.
Saxagliptin (100 µM) similarly increased membrane-bound SMPDL3B and reduced soluble SMPDL3B and PI-PLC in healthy-donor PBMCs, though it did not reduce PLCXD1 expression as vildagliptin did.

Linagliptin, structurally distinct DPP-4 inhibitor used as negative control, did not stabilize membrane-bound SMPDL3B; instead it increased soluble SMPDL3B/PI-PLC and reduced membrane-bound SMPDL3B, confirming the effect is independent of DPP-4 inhibition.

In ME patient PBMCs, vildagliptin and saxagliptin (100 µM) reduced SMPDL3B/PLCXD1 gene expression and increased membrane-bound SMPDL3B, with effects more pronounced in patients with high baseline plasma SMPDL3B; linagliptin had no significant effect.
Vildagliptin reduced soluble PI-PLC in all treated ME patient PBMCs, whereas saxagliptin reduced it only in patients with initially low plasma SMPDL3B; linagliptin showed no such effect.
Fibromyalgia was a highly prevalent comorbidity (35.7%) in the Canadian ME cohort and was entirely absent among healthy controls.
Dysarthria/word-finding difficulty had the highest odds of new onset post-COVID compared to pre-COVID among the 29 neurologic symptoms assessed.
Concentration and memory difficulties showed markedly increased odds post-COVID compared to pre-COVID.
General weakness, focal weakness, delirium, and fatigue were all highly associated with COVID-19 onset compared to pre-COVID prevalence.
Pre-existing neurologic conditions did not substantially alter the prevalence of post-COVID neurologic symptoms compared to those without such conditions.

Pre-existing psychiatric conditions did not substantially impact post-COVID neurologic symptom prevalence, with arthralgia being the only symptom showing a significant difference in the post-COVID period.

Headache prevalence pattern differed by pre-existing neurologic condition status: those with pre-existing neurologic disease reported more headaches pre-COVID (83.6%) than post-COVID (63.24%), whereas those without pre-existing neurologic disease reported 0% pre-COVID headaches rising to 57.2% post-COVID.
Fatigue, concentration/memory issues, unrefreshed sleep, and trouble sleeping were significantly more likely to be rated as severe post-COVID compared to pre-COVID.

Elapsed time since SARS-CoV-2 infection significantly increased the prevalence of 20 of the 29 queried neurologic symptoms, with fatigue, word-finding difficulty, unrefreshed sleep, general weakness, and pain symptoms most impacted.
Meeting 2016 fibromyalgia criteria and having moderate-to-severe post-exertional malaise both became more prevalent with greater elapsed time since SARS-CoV-2 infection.
Using PROMIS scales, nearly half of the cohort met criteria for anxiety and/or depression post-COVID, with moderate-to-severe anxiety in 34% and moderate-to-severe depression in 27%.

Having a pre-existing psychiatric condition increased the odds of meeting criteria for moderate-to-severe anxiety, depression, or both after COVID-19, while pre-existing neurologic conditions had no such effect.

Participants with moderate-to-severe post-COVID depression were significantly more likely to report fatigue, general/focal weakness, loss of appetite, concentration/memory difficulty, dizziness, noise/touch sensitivity, visual disturbances, myalgia, and unrefreshed sleep.

Participants with moderate-to-severe post-COVID anxiety were significantly more likely to report fatigue, loss of appetite, general/focal weakness, nausea, balance difficulty, numbness/tingling, touch/visual sensitivity, myalgia, delirium, and unrefreshed sleep.
Hospitalization for acute SARS-CoV-2 infection had negligible impact on post-COVID neurologic symptoms, with the exception of reduced noise sensitivity in hospitalized participants.
The Long-COVID cohort was over-represented for female sex relative to the general population, consistent with the known female predominance in fibromyalgia and ME/CFS.
Pre-existing migraine or headache diagnosis was over-represented in the Long-COVID cohort compared to the general US population.
Pre-existing depression and anxiety were substantially over-represented in the Long-COVID cohort compared to the general US population.

Applying BIO-INSIGHT to gene expression data from fibromyalgia, ME/CFS, and comorbid patients produced gene regulatory networks with condition-specific regulatory interactions, suggesting distinct disease-relevant gene regulation for each group.

On an academic benchmark of 106 gene regulatory networks, BIO-INSIGHT achieved statistically significant improvements in AUROC and AUPR compared to MO-GENECI and other consensus GRN inference strategies.

Across all chronic physical health conditions studied, children and adolescents showed higher anxiety symptoms than peers without such conditions or test norms, with a small-to-moderate overall effect size.
Among the chronic physical health condition subgroups analyzed, young people with chronic fatigue syndrome showed one of the highest anxiety effect sizes relative to controls.
The magnitude of the anxiety-CPHC association was moderated by rating method, comparison type, sample sex composition, ethnic composition, and country development status.
Serum neuronal and astroglial damage markers (NSE, S100B, pTau217, GFAP) were significantly elevated in Parkinson's disease patients compared with healthy controls.
HOMA2IR was elevated while calcium and HOMA2%S (insulin sensitivity) were reduced in both Parkinson's disease subgroups compared to controls.
Serum NSE, S100B, and IL-10 rose progressively from healthy controls to low MOOD+CFS to high MOOD+CFS symptom subgroups of Parkinson's disease patients.
Composite indices reflecting glial projection toxicity (Comp_GPT) and immune-inflammatory activation (Comp_IRS) showed an upward trend from controls to low to high MOOD+CFS subgroups.
In the whole sample, calcium (inversely) plus NSE, IL-10 and HOMA2IR (positively) explained 55.5% of variance in the non-motor Experiences of Daily Living (nM-EDL) score.
NSE, IL-10, HOMA2IR (positively) and calcium (inversely) accounted for 54.8% of the variance in the CFS symptom score in Parkinson's disease patients.
NSE, IL-10, HOMA2IR, S100B (positively) and calcium (inversely) accounted for 52.5% of the variance in the combined MOOD+CFS score.
Immune-inflammatory activation (Comp_IRS) and glial projection toxicity (Comp_GPT) composite indices together accounted for 31.0% of the variance in MOOD+CFS score.
In the restricted patient-only analysis, IL-10 and NSE together accounted for 31.9% of the variance in the CFS score and 26.3% in the combined MOOD+CFS score.
In patients only, GFAP and HOMA2IR together accounted for 26.3% of the variance in the motor Experiences of Daily Living (m-EDL) score.
In the full study sample, Comp_IRS (immune-inflammatory composite) was significantly correlated with NSE, S100B, pTau217, GFAP, and the composite glial damage score Comp_GPT.
HOMA2IR (insulin resistance) was significantly correlated with all four neuronal/glial damage biomarkers (NSE, S100B, pTau217, GFAP) in the full sample.
The combined effects of Comp_IRS and HOMA2IR explained 37.0% of variance in the glial projection toxicity composite (Comp_GPT) in the full study sample.

Protein-protein interaction network analysis of MAPT (tau), S100B, ENO2 (NSE), and GFAP showed a tight gene network enriched in glial cell projections, neuronal cell bodies, neurofilament, and type III intermediate filament components.

The MOOD symptom score correlated significantly with the MDS-UPDRS motor examination (Part III) score in Parkinson's disease patients, but no significant correlations were found between CFS scores and any MDS-UPDRS domain.
Serum magnesium, copper, zinc, and IL-6 concentrations did not differ significantly among controls and the two Parkinson's disease MOOD+CFS subgroups.
In the design-phase focus groups, 40% of patient participants reported a diagnosis of Ehlers-Danlos syndrome, and half of those also reported a comorbid fibromyalgia diagnosis.

Patients piloting the digital intervention (phase 2) presented with a heterogeneous set of diagnoses, including hypermobile Ehlers-Danlos syndrome and chronic fatigue syndrome alongside migraine, herniated disc, arthritis, fibromyalgia, and complex regional pain syndrome, with one participant unaware of their pain diagnosis.
Focus group patients with chronic pain reported moderate-to-high pain intensity, averaging 5.8 currently and 6.6 over the previous week on a 0-10 scale.
Pilot-phase patients reported baseline current pain levels averaging 5.1 and previous-week pain averaging 5.6 on a 0-10 scale.
Patients piloting the DAHLIA digital behavioral intervention rated weekly modules as very helpful, moderately enjoyable, and very understandable on 7-point scales.
Most patients completed the full digital intervention program, with a minority discontinuing before completion.
Therapists delivering the pilot intervention perceived it as very beneficial for patients, reported satisfaction with delivery, and expressed interest in continuing to use the intervention.

Patients and therapists differed in preferred communication mode for weekly contact, with patients generally favoring video calls and therapists viewing phone calls as similarly useful and suggesting patient choice.

Three fictional patient personas representing heterogeneous chronic pain characteristics (including varying age, gender, and pain conditions) were used to guide initial treatment design before recruiting real patients.
Adolescents with HSD/hEDS spent significantly more time in sedentary behavior during the day than healthy controls.
Adolescents with HSD/hEDS spent significantly less time in moderate-to-vigorous physical activity (MVPA) during the day than healthy controls.
There was no significant difference between HSD/hEDS and control groups in daytime light intensity physical activity (LIPA).
Adolescents with HSD/hEDS exhibited significantly more nighttime sleep movements (percentage of nighttime spent in sedentary-intensity movement) than controls.
Total nighttime sleep duration differed significantly between groups, adjusted for age and sex.
Adolescents with HSD/hEDS reported significantly higher levels of fatigue (lower PedsQL-F scores) across total and all subscale scores compared to controls.
Adolescents with HSD/hEDS reported significantly higher pain catastrophizing (PCS-C) total and subscale scores than controls.

Pain over the past week was significantly more common in adolescents with HSD/hEDS, with all patients reporting pain duration over 3 months and most reporting widespread pain, versus mostly no pain in controls.
There was no statistically significant association between perceived fatigue and daily sedentary behavior or MVPA in the HSD/hEDS group or in all participants combined.
There was no statistically significant association between sleep movements and perceived fatigue in the HSD/hEDS group or in all participants combined.
There was a statistically significant association between perceived fatigue and pain catastrophizing (PCS-C), both in the HSD/hEDS group and across all participants.
Adolescents with HSD/hEDS had significantly higher Beighton hypermobility scores than controls, as expected for the diagnostic criteria.
Vulvodynia patients with comorbid Ehlers-Danlos syndrome were significantly younger (mean age 39) than vulvodynia patients without Ehlers-Danlos syndrome (mean age 48).
Patients with comorbid vulvodynia and Ehlers-Danlos syndrome had a higher prevalence of chronic pain conditions than vulvodynia patients without Ehlers-Danlos syndrome.
Vulvodynia-Ehlers-Danlos comorbid patients had a higher prevalence of musculoskeletal conditions compared to vulvodynia patients without Ehlers-Danlos syndrome.
Vulvodynia-Ehlers-Danlos comorbid patients had a higher prevalence of neurologic conditions compared to vulvodynia patients without Ehlers-Danlos syndrome.
Vulvodynia-Ehlers-Danlos comorbid patients had a higher prevalence of gynecologic conditions compared to vulvodynia patients without Ehlers-Danlos syndrome.
Vulvodynia-Ehlers-Danlos comorbid patients had a higher prevalence of immune conditions compared to vulvodynia patients without Ehlers-Danlos syndrome.
Patients with comorbid vulvodynia and Ehlers-Danlos syndrome had a higher prevalence of psychiatric conditions compared to vulvodynia patients without Ehlers-Danlos syndrome.
Vulvodynia-Ehlers-Danlos comorbid patients had higher rates of most nonsurgical interventions compared to vulvodynia patients without Ehlers-Danlos syndrome.

Rates of vaginal estrogen use were similar between vulvodynia-Ehlers-Danlos comorbid patients and vulvodynia patients without Ehlers-Danlos syndrome, not reaching the Bonferroni-corrected significance threshold.
Rates of vulvar surgery were similar between vulvodynia-Ehlers-Danlos comorbid patients and vulvodynia patients without Ehlers-Danlos syndrome.

Vulvodynia-Ehlers-Danlos comorbid patients showed signs of more frequent medical contact, including more postoperative visits, vaccinations, and inpatient admissions, than vulvodynia patients without Ehlers-Danlos syndrome.
hEDS patients reported significantly higher pain scores (worst, least, average, current pain, pain severity) than OI type I and IV patients, and higher pain interference than OI type I patients.
hEDS patients reported significantly higher pain severity and worst pain than XLH patients.
On the EQ-5D-5L, hEDS patients reported more problems with usual activities and more pain/discomfort than OI type I patients.
OI type III patients reported more mobility problems than most other disease groups (except OI type IV), and OI type IV patients reported more mobility problems than OI type I.
OI type IV patients reported more self-care problems than OI type I patients.
No significant differences in anxiety/depression were found between any of the disease groups (EQ-5D-5L).
Global subjective quality of life (VAS) was significantly lower in hEDS patients than in OI type I patients.
SF-36v2 scores for general health, social functioning, and vitality were significantly lower in hEDS patients compared to OI type I patients.
OI type III patients reported lower physical functioning QoL compared to all subgroups except OI type IV.
hEDS patients reported lower physical role functioning and pain-domain QoL on SF-36v2 compared to OI type I and XLH patients.

Multivariate regression (Model 1) showed that diagnosis of XLH, OI type I, or OI type IV (vs hEDS reference) was associated with higher QoL in general health, physical role functioning, social functioning, physical functioning, vitality, and mental health subscales.
Higher BMI was associated with lower physical functioning QoL in regression Model 1.
Higher pain severity was the strongest factor associated with lower QoL across nearly all SF-36v2 dimensions when included in regression Model 2, improving the explained variance compared to Model 1.
In the physical functioning model, OI type III/IV diagnosis, higher BMI, and higher pain severity were all associated with lower physical functioning.
Female patients reported significantly higher pain and lower QoL than male patients across multiple SF-36v2 and EQ-5D-5L subscales, including overall VAS QoL.
No significant differences in QoL dimensions (EQ-5D-5L and SF-36v2) were identified between age groups.
The overall sample's subjective QoL (VAS) was significantly lower than age- and gender-adapted general population norm values.
In the hEDS subgroup, no significant correlation was found between Beighton score and any QoL dimension or pain experience.

Despite OI having a higher fracture rate than XLH and hEDS, XLH QoL was comparable to OI type I while hEDS showed worse QoL than all other conditions, indicating that fracture burden does not directly correlate with pain or overall QoL.
Nasal bridge depression was reported in 80% of arthrochalasia EDS patients reviewed.
Downslanting palpebral fissures were found in 80% of kyphoscoliotic EDS patients reviewed.
Deep-set eyes were reported in 34% of classical EDS (cEDS) patients reviewed.
Tooth agenesis was reported in 50% of spondylodysplastic EDS patients reviewed.
Tooth agenesis was reported in 75% of dermatosparactic EDS patients reviewed.
Pulpal calcifications were observed in 11 of 89 classical EDS patients reviewed.
Dental root fusion was observed in 8 of 31 vascular EDS patients reviewed.
Excessive dental root length was observed in 11 of 31 vascular EDS patients reviewed.
Gingival hyperplasia was reported in all reviewed cases of dermatosparactic EDS.
The literature is inconclusive regarding whether absence of labial and/or lingual frenula is a reliable feature of EDS.
Genetic counselors reported a general increase in EDS awareness and referrals to genetics clinics.

Clinics use varied triage tools including decline letters and patient questionnaires, with unique referral eligibility requirements shaped by clinic threshold, scope of practice perceptions, lack of nearby alternative practices, and limited resources.

Genetic counselors reported a discrepancy in care between EDS patients accepted for genetics evaluation and those declined, particularly affecting hypermobile EDS (hEDS) patients, and expressed guilt over declining hEDS patients who lack good diagnostic and management options.

Participants identified benefits of their triage processes and felt triage was meeting their clinic's goals, though goals, composition, and factors affecting EDS genetics triage varied widely across US clinics.

An AI facial-analysis classifier trained on a subgroup of 18 White adult females with vEDS versus age-, sex-, and ethnicity-matched CFD controls achieved excellent discrimination using as few as 13 training images.
When trained on the full set of 30 vEDS facial images against the full ethnically and age-diverse CFD control dataset, the AI classifier achieved very high discriminative performance.

Facial-image classification performance showed no significant difference between vEDS cases with COL3A1 glycine substitution variants and those with nonglycine (splice-site or haploinsufficiency) variants.
The AI classifier effectively distinguished facial images of vEDS patients from those of hEDS patients with high accuracy.
