The AI classifier found no significant difference between hEDS facial images and matched healthy controls, suggesting hEDS patients do not have a distinct facial phenotype like vEDS.
LIME-based heatmap analysis showed the model prioritized the eyes, nose, and lips as the facial regions most predictive of vEDS, consistent with known clinical facial characteristics.
Citing prior literature, the authors note that beta-blockers have been shown to reduce vascular events in patients with vEDS, motivating an ongoing clinical trial.
Patient 1 carried a pathogenic COL3A1 splice-site mutation (IVS44+1G→A), confirming a diagnosis of vascular EDS presenting with pulmonary hemorrhage.

Patient 2 carried two maternally inherited heterozygous COL3A1 proline-substitution variants predicted to destabilize the collagen triple helix, associated with severe, persistent diffuse alveolar hemorrhage.
Patient 3 carried a paternally inherited COL3A1 variant of uncertain significance previously linked to vascular events by two other groups.
Patient 4 carried a maternally inherited COL1A1 glycine-substitution mutation predicted to be harmful, associated with pulmonary vascular wall disruption.
Patient 5 carried a novel, paternally inherited COL1A1 glycine-substitution mutation not previously reported in the EDS Variant Database.
Patient 6 carried a paternally inherited COL1A2 glycine-substitution mutation previously reported in another child with classic EDS features.
Patient 7 and his affected mother carried a TNXB variant (c.211G>T) previously reported in a patient with joint hypermobility, considered likely pathogenic given consistent dermatopathology.

Patient 8 carried a novel COL4A2 mutation affecting the C-terminal collagen structure; the authors hypothesize COL4A2 disrupts vascular endothelium/basement membrane integrity and may be a potential candidate gene for vEDS-like pulmonary hemorrhage, pending further functional confirmation.
Immunohistochemistry showed significantly lower type III collagen (COL3A1) expression in skin samples from patients 1 and 2 compared with control tissue.
Dermatopathological IHC in patient 7 showed markedly reduced collagen/tenascin XB expression in the basement membrane compared with controls.
Immunofluorescence staining showed reduced and unevenly distributed type I collagen in skin fibroblasts of patient 4 compared with uniformly distributed collagen in normal control fibroblasts.
Hemosiderin-laden cells were observed in alveolar lavage/gastric fluid specimens and lung pathology of all eight patients, confirming pulmonary/alveolar hemorrhage.

Chest CT scans revealed abnormalities in all eight patients, most frequently multifocal ground-glass opacities (six patients), with additional pneumothorax, cavities, cysts, nodular opacities, and vascular/lymph node changes.

Among the eight EDS patients with pulmonary hemorrhage, diffuse hemorrhagic manifestations occurred in six, localized hematomas in two, hemoptysis in four, cough in three, wheezing in two, pallor in three, fatigue in four, poor activity tolerance in one, and chest pain in one.
Activity restriction significantly improved pulmonary hemorrhage in patients 1 and 6.
Bronchial artery embolization (BAE) was effective in treating pulmonary hemorrhage in patient 4.

Glucocorticoids were administered to all patients during the acute phase pending definitive diagnosis, but in the non-acute phase hormonal therapy was noted to be less effective for immune-mediated pulmonary hemorrhage.
Vitamin C and E supplementation combined with activity restriction alleviated persistent pulmonary hemorrhage in patient 2 and was recommended as adjunct therapy for all patients.
Children with EDS had a significantly higher prevalence and risk of obstructive sleep apnea compared to a non-EDS control cohort.
Pediatric EDS patients had a significantly higher risk of dysphagia compared to controls.
Pediatric EDS patients had a significantly higher risk of dysphonia compared to controls.
Children with EDS were more likely to undergo adenotonsillectomy compared to controls, reflecting greater surgical management of OSA in this population.
Mutations and/or aberrant expression of the FLNA gene are associated with Ehlers-Danlos syndrome among other brain-related disorders.
FLNA is described as a regulator of neurodevelopment, neuronal migration, and actin organization in the brain, with mutations linked to periventricular heterotopia and impaired cognitive function.

A 46-year-old man with suspected Ehlers-Danlos syndrome presented with a thrombosed 17 mm superior mesenteric artery aneurysm causing postprandial pain and weight loss, and was successfully treated with open aortomesenteric bypass surgery using a great saphenous vein graft.

The patient with suspected Ehlers-Danlos syndrome had a prior history of splenectomy for a ruptured splenic artery aneurysm and cholecystectomy for acute cholelithiasis, suggesting a multi-site vascular aneurysm predisposition.

The authors state that collagenous disorders such as Ehlers-Danlos syndrome and fibrodysplasia are better managed with open surgical strategies using autologous grafts (saphenous vein or arterial substitutes) or prosthesis, which provide more long-lasting results than endovascular repair.

A 65-year-old man without collagenous disease but with atherosclerotic risk factors and multiple comorbidities had a dissecting SMA aneurysm that enlarged from 24 mm to 29 mm over 6 months and was treated with an interposition graft using the superficial femoral artery with a Dacron bypass, with successful patency at 6-month follow-up.
Visceral artery aneurysms are rare (incidence 0.02%) but carry mortality as high as 90% if not promptly treated when ruptured.
The superior mesenteric artery is reported to be the site of aneurysm development in up to 15% of visceral aneurysm cases, encompassing both true and false aneurysms.
Current guidelines indicate interventional treatment for SMA aneurysms exceeding 25 mm in diameter in asymptomatic patients, but recommend repair regardless of size in women of childbearing age.

For infected visceral aneurysms, open surgery with debridement of infected tissue is preferred over endovascular repair because endograft insertion could result in further colonization and infection relapse.
A novel homozygous missense variant in COL1A1 (c.4340T>G; p.(Val1447Gly)) was identified in one family with a distinctive skeletal phenotype resembling osteogenesis imperfecta but without fractures.
A recurrent heterozygous COL1A2 variant (c.1171G>A; p.(Gly391Ser)) was identified in one family with an osteogenesis imperfecta-like phenotype lacking classic EDS features.
A recurrent heterozygous COL1A2 variant (c.1253G>C; p.(Gly418Ala)) was identified in another family presenting an osteogenesis imperfecta-like phenotype.
A novel heterozygous COL1A1 variant (c.1678G>A; p.(Gly560Ser)) was identified in a third family with an osteogenesis imperfecta-like phenotype.
Despite clinical manifestations resembling osteogenesis imperfecta, none of the five patients had documented bone fractures, the cardinal feature of osteogenesis imperfecta.
Patients also lacked the characteristic features of Ehlers-Danlos syndrome despite harboring COL1A1/2 variants, supporting a distinct overlap phenotype rather than classic EDS or OI.

Among 47 individuals from 22 families presenting with non-inflammatory musculoskeletal complaints resembling rheumatic disease, pathogenic or likely pathogenic variants were identified in all cases, establishing ten distinct genetic diagnoses.
Nine patients were diagnosed with Hereditary Multiple Exostoses presenting with non-inflammatory musculoskeletal findings mimicking rheumatic disease.
Twelve patients were diagnosed with Camptodactyly-Arthropathy-Coxa Vara-Pericarditis (CACP) syndrome among those presenting with non-inflammatory musculoskeletal complaints.
Seven patients were diagnosed with Progressive Pseudorheumatoid Dysplasia, a disorder known to closely mimic juvenile arthritis.
Five patients were diagnosed with Trichorhinophalangeal Syndrome types I/II.
Six patients were diagnosed with Spondyloenchondrodysplasia with Immune Dysregulation (SPENCD).
Three patients were diagnosed with Pseudoachondroplasia.
One patient was diagnosed with Primary Hypertrophic Osteoarthropathy type 1.

One patient was diagnosed with Multicentric Osteolysis-Nodulosis-Arthropathy, a genetic condition associated with pathogenic variants typically found in MMP2, which can mimic inflammatory joint disease.
One patient in the cohort was diagnosed with Mucopolysaccharidosis type VI, a lysosomal storage disorder that can present with joint and skeletal findings mimicking rheumatic disease.
The study identified seven novel genetic variants across the cohort, expanding the known mutational spectrum for these rare skeletal/connective-tissue disorders.
Loeys-Dietz syndrome types 1 and 2 arise from loss-of-function mutations in TGFBR1 or TGFBR2 that disrupt receptor-ligand interactions and downstream signal transduction.
Among genes causing LDS, TGFBR2 mutations account for 55-60% of cases, more common than TGFBR1 (20-25%), TGFB2, SMAD3, TGFB3, and SMAD2.
Contrary to the reduced-signaling paradigm, LDS patient aortic tissues show a paradoxical increase in TGFβ signaling activity.
Aortic walls of LDS and MFS patients show increased nuclear accumulation of phosphorylated Smad2 alongside medial degeneration, smooth muscle cell loss, and elastic fiber fragmentation.
A chromosomal breakpoint disrupting only TGFBR2 in a Japanese family with Marfan-like features (no FBN1 mutation) established TGFBR2 as the cause of Marfan syndrome type 2 (MFS2).
Three missense TGFBR2 mutations (L308P, S449F, R537C), all located in the highly conserved STK domain, were identified in Marfan-like patients lacking FBN1 mutations.
In a cohort of 49 patients with Marfan-like symptoms without FBN1 mutations, TGFBR1 or TGFBR2 mutations were found to account for about 5-10% of all Marfan syndrome cases.
Despite loss-of-function TGFBR2 mutations, aortic walls of MFS2-affected individuals show upregulated TGFβ signaling, suggesting compensatory regulatory mechanisms.

Germline TGFBR2 mutations affecting arginine 460 in the cytoplasmic STK domain cause familial thoracic aortic aneurysm and dissection (TAAD) in about 5% of cases, with both ascending and descending aortic disease observed.

In Multiple Self-healing Squamous Epithelioma (MSSE), tumor DNA from patients with constitutional heterozygous TGFBR1 mutations shows somatic loss of heterozygosity retaining the mutant allele, indicating TGFBR1 acts as a tumor suppressor requiring a 'second hit'.

TGFBR1 mutation types differ between diseases: MSSE arises mostly from truncating (nonsense/frameshift) variants in the STK or ligand-binding domain, whereas Marfan-related disorders arise from missense mutations or in-frame deletions/duplications, a divergence proposed to explain why MSSE confers cancer risk while vascular disorders do not.

An aortopathy next-generation sequencing panel in Ehlers-Danlos Syndrome patients identified four novel variants in FBN1, TGFBR1, and TGFBR2, three of which were considered potentially pathogenic, with two located in the STK domain of TGFBR1/TGFBR2 (region linked to LDS).

In a cohort of 199 patients with hereditary arthropathies, NGS identified pathogenic FBN1/SMAD3 variants in 7.5% and likely pathogenic variants (including 13 novel ones in genes such as TGFBR1 and TGFBR2) in 9.6% of patients.

Although vascular Ehlers-Danlos Syndrome is primarily caused by COL3A1 mutations, its phenotypic overlap with LDS (particularly vascular fragility) has prompted research into potential TGFBR2 mutation roles in vEDS-like presentations.
A de novo heterozygous TGFBR2 splicing defect (IVS5-2A>G), causing a 10-amino acid insertion in the STK domain, was found in a patient with Shprintzen-Goldberg syndrome (SGS).
A clinically diagnosed Shprintzen-Goldberg syndrome patient carried a novel TGFBR2 missense mutation substituting lysine for threonine at position 516 in the STK domain.
SGS is also caused by dominantly inherited heterozygous in-frame deletions in exon 1 of the SKI gene, specifically within the R-Smad binding domain that normally suppresses TGFβ signaling.

Specific TGFBR2 mutations (R528C, R528H, R537C, R537P, R460H) exert dominant-negative effects that interfere with wild-type receptor activity, with the degree of Smad/ERK signaling impairment correlating with clinical severity in MFS2 and LDS.
TGFBR1 mutations K232R and R487P are not merely loss-of-function but exert dominant-negative effects on receptor function in LDS.
A splice donor site variant in intron 5 of TGFBR1 (c.973+1G>A), causing in-frame deletion of exon 5 in the STK domain, is anticipated to have a dominant-negative effect in a familial LDS case.

TGFBR1 splice-site variants c.973+1G>A and c.806-2A>C cause LDS and MSSE respectively, activating distinct cryptic splice sites resulting in in-frame versus out-of-frame transcripts, explaining how the same gene produces two clinically distinct diseases.

The identical TGFBR2 variant (p.Arg356Pro) caused classic LDS features in one patient, yet a father carrying the same variant was clinically healthy except for a minor decrease in left ventricular diastolic function, demonstrating incomplete penetrance/variable expressivity.

Two distinct missense substitutions at TGFBR2 residue 537 (R537C causing MFS2, R537P causing LDS) are proposed to have differing biophysical impacts on helix stability, potentially explaining their divergent phenotypes despite affecting the same residue.

Experiments combining wild-type with mutant TGFBR1 or TGFBR2 receptors showed only a slight reduction in TGFβ signaling, with signal loss no greater than 50%, indicating that mutant/WT receptor combinations can still transmit signal.

Preformed receptor complexes containing both TGFBR1 and TGFBR2 (independent of ligand binding) account for about 25% of receptor complexes at the plasma membrane, as quantified by immunofluorescence co-patching assay.

Cells carrying TGFBR2 mutations exhibit pronounced mitochondrial dysfunction, supporting a model linking TGFβ-driven ECM remodeling to mitochondrial impairment in connective tissue disorder pathogenesis.

Specific TGFBR2 missense variants (R528C, R528H, R537C, R537P, R460H) not only lose normal receptor function but also exert dominant-negative effects on the remaining wild-type receptor in MFS2 and LDS, with severity correlating to degree of Smad/ERK impairment.
Cardoso et al. showed that TGFBR1 mutations K232R and R487P are not merely loss-of-function but also exert a dominant-negative effect on receptor activity in LDS.

A TGFBR1 splice donor site variant in intron 5 (c.973+1G>A) causes haploinsufficiency in a familial LDS case and is predicted to have a dominant-negative effect via in-frame deletion of exon 5 within the STK domain.

Ex-vivo minigene splicing assays showed that TGFBR1 c.973+1G>A and c.806-2A>C activate distinct cryptic splice sites producing in-frame versus out-of-frame transcripts respectively, explaining why the same gene causes clinically distinct LDS versus MSSE.

The same TGFBR2 p.Arg356Pro variant that caused classic LDS symptoms in a patient was found in the patient's father who was clinically healthy apart from a minor decrease in left ventricular diastolic function, illustrating variable penetrance.
Homology modeling showed that TGFBR2 R460 substitutions disrupt F-helix–D-helix communication in the STK domain, reducing receptor signaling capacity and contributing to TAAD.

Two distinct missense variants at the same TGFBR2 residue, R537C and R537P, are predicted to have differing biophysical consequences (moderate destabilization vs severe helix disruption), potentially explaining the phenotypic divergence between MFS2 (R537C) and LDS (R537P).

TGFB3 variants p.Arg300Trp and p.Leu401Pro disrupt key ionic and hydrophobic interactions, impairing protein stability and receptor binding, analogous to structure-function effects seen in TGFBR1/TGFBR2 variants.

TGFBR2 variants R528C and R537C exert dominant-negative effects that markedly impair Smad signaling, whereas R460C (linked to TAAD) showed a milder dominant-negative effect with preserved partial Smad phosphorylation, suggesting signaling disruption severity correlates with clinical severity.

Mutant endoglin proteins misfold, are retained in the ER, and form WT/mutant mixed dimers that impede trafficking of wild-type endoglin, producing a compound loss of function that underlies HHT1 dominant-negative mechanisms.

ALK1 variants linked to HHT2 produce misfolded proteins that accumulate in the ER and exert a dominant-negative effect by forming non-functional heterodimers with wild-type ALK1 at the plasma membrane.

Approximately 12%-15% of newly synthesized proteins fail to reach correct conformation and are eliminated via ERAD normally, a proportion that rises substantially for mis/mal-folded mutant proteins such as TGFBR variants.

ECM sensing initiates a wound-healing-like response with localized hypoxia and metabolic shift from mitochondrial oxidative phosphorylation to anaerobic glycolysis; in chronic connective tissue disorders like MFS and LDS this persistent ECM remodeling may sustain mitochondrial suppression contributing to chronic inflammation and fibrosis.
TGFBR2-mutant cells exhibit pronounced mitochondrial dysfunction, supporting a link between TGFβ-driven ECM remodeling and mitochondrial impairment in TGFBR-associated connective tissue disorders.

A dominantly inherited heterozygous in-frame deletion in exon 1 of the SKI gene, affecting the R-Smad binding domain, was identified in Shprintzen-Goldberg syndrome via family-based exome sequencing, causing loss of SKI-mediated inhibition of Smad2/3 signaling.
A de novo heterozygous TGFBR2 splicing defect (IVS5-2A>G) causing a 10-amino acid insertion in the STK domain was identified in a patient with Shprintzen-Goldberg syndrome.
A novel TGFBR2 missense mutation causing a lysine-to-threonine substitution at position 516 in the STK domain was reported in a clinically diagnosed Shprintzen-Goldberg syndrome patient.

A NGS aortopathy panel applied to EDS patients identified four novel variants in FBN1, TGFBR1, and TGFBR2, with two of three potentially pathogenic variants located in the STK domain of TGFBR1/TGFBR2 (linked to LDS-type variants) and the third near SMAD3's MH2 domain.

In a cohort of 199 patients with hereditary arthropathies, NGS gene testing detected pathogenic variants in FBN1 or SMAD3 in 15 patients (7.5%) and at least one likely pathogenic variant in 19 patients (9.6%), including thirteen novel pathogenic/likely pathogenic variants in genes including TGFBR1 and TGFBR2.
Preformed TGFBR1/TGFBR2 receptor complexes (independent of ligand) were quantified to account for 25% of receptor complexes on the plasma membrane using an immunofluorescence co-patching assay.

TGFBR1 mutation spectra differ by disease: MSSE is primarily caused by loss-of-function nonsense/frameshift variants clustered in the STK or extracellular ligand-binding domain, whereas MFS-related TGFBR1 mutations (MFS2, LDS, TAAD) are mostly non-truncating missense mutations or in-frame deletions/duplications hypothesized to enhance TGFβ pathway activation.

Loss of heterozygosity at the TGFBR1 locus with retention of the mutant allele in microdissected MSSE tumor DNA supports TGFBR1 acting as a tumor suppressor gene requiring a somatic 'second hit' for tumorigenesis, since constitutional heterozygous loss-of-function does not itself disrupt TGFβ signaling enough to cause tumors.
A 19-year-old male with EDS who underwent occipitocervical fusion (OCF) developed complete reabsorption of the bone graft and non-union of the fusion construct.
Revision surgery using custom-made, anatomically conforming 3D-printed titanium alloy (Ti-6Al-4V) facet joint spacers at C1-2 achieved solid bony fusion where the original OCF had failed.
The patient's Neck Disability Index (NDI) score improved from 56% before revision surgery to 30% six months after revision surgery.

The literature indicates that complications associated with occipitocervical fusion (OCF) are more common in patients with EDS and other hereditary disorders of connective tissue (HDCTs) compared with the general surgical population, though data on fusion rates and implant failure remain limited.

Chi et al. (2024) compared 533 patients with EDS to 2,634 matched controls undergoing anterior cervical discectomy and fusion (ACDF) and found significantly higher rates of wound complications, surgical site infections, pseudoarthrosis, and implant failure in the EDS group.

Wu et al. found a higher incidence of adjacent segment disease (ASD) in EDS patients undergoing transforaminal lumbar interbody fusion (TLIF) compared to matched non-EDS controls, but no significant difference in pseudoarthrosis rates between groups.
Okamoto et al. reported an implant failure rate of 4.2% in a case series of 142 patients undergoing posterior occipitocervical fusion and cervicothoracic fusion.

The C1-2 level is described as the most susceptible level to nonunion and implant failure in OCF procedures due to its extensive mobility across axial rotation, flexion-extension, and lateral bending, making stability at this level particularly difficult to achieve for successful fusion.

Prior to occipitocervical fusion, the patient had an abnormal clival-axial angle (117.8° in flexion, 150.8° in extension) consistent with atlantoaxial instability, compared to a typical range of 150° in flexion to 180° in extension.
Cutis verticis gyrata predominantly affects postpubescent men, with a male-to-female ratio of 4:1 and an incidence of 1 in 100,000 men versus 0.26 in 100,000 women.
The precise cause of CVG is unknown, but hormonal imbalance and genetic factors have been hypothesized as contributing mechanisms.
A 47-year-old man with CVG and neurosarcoidosis developed communicating panventricular hydrocephalus and underwent uncomplicated placement of a right frontal VP shunt with a Strata II valve.

One month after shunt placement, the patient developed low-grade fevers and swelling at the shunt site with cultures growing Staphylococcus aureus, requiring shunt externalization and antibiotic treatment before reinternalization.

Five months after shunt revision, the proximal catheter had migrated out of the ventricle and was found dislodged and looped around the valve in the subgaleal pocket, attributed to excess scalp mobility in CVG causing catheter traction.

Securing the VP shunt valve and ventricular catheter segment to the skull with titanium plates and screws, rather than relying on the underlying hypermobile soft tissue, resolved the migration complication with no further issues on follow-up.

A prior case report described a patient with CVG undergoing craniotomy for decompression of malignant cerebral edema, noting difficulties achieving hemostasis and preventing CSF leakage due to the altered scalp anatomy.

In a cochlear implant case report, skin rippling from CVG increased the distance between internal and external magnets causing the external processor coil to fall off frequently; this was managed by increasing the strength of the external magnet.

Patients with CVG may have an increased risk of pruritus, dysesthesia, tenderness, and pain, and a higher procedural complication rate including wound infections due to altered scalp morphology and hygiene difficulties.

The authors suggest that techniques minimizing skin incisions and tunneling-related complications, such as the one-step edge-to-edge technique, may offer additional benefit for VP shunt surgery in CVG patients.
Connective tissue disorder (CTD) features, most commonly joint conditions, were identified in 26.7% of patients with spontaneous coronary artery dissection.
In propensity-matched analysis, SCAD patients with CTD features had significantly higher rates of the composite outcome (recurrent MI, stroke, or death) than those without.
Presence of joint conditions independently predicted worse adverse outcomes in SCAD patients on multivariable logistic regression.
Grouped CTD features (broader than joint conditions alone) independently predicted worse adverse outcomes in SCAD patients.
Recurrent myocardial infarction was significantly more frequent among SCAD patients with CTD features compared to those without.
Myofascial Techniques (MTA) produced greater improvements in pain, central sensitization, and sleep quality compared to other interventions reviewed.
Cranial electrotherapy stimulation (CES) was associated with pain alleviation, improved emotional health, and enhanced functional capabilities in fibromyalgia patients.
S-ketamine treatment was associated with pain alleviation, improved emotional health, and enhanced functional capabilities in fibromyalgia patients.
Resistance exercise was associated with pain alleviation, improved emotional health, and enhanced functional capabilities in fibromyalgia patients.
Therapy dog interaction was associated with pain alleviation, improved emotional health, and enhanced functional capabilities in fibromyalgia patients.
The FIBROOut intervention group showed a marked reduction in both mental and general fatigue compared to baseline levels.
Exercise interventions alleviated fatigue in fibromyalgia patients.

Sleep quality improved across all treatment groups, with Myofascial Techniques (MTA) and cranial electrotherapy stimulation (CES) showing the most drastic changes in PSQI scores, decreasing from 15.5 ± 3.7 to 12.2 ± 4.8.
The review notes that genetic factors are implicated in fibromyalgia susceptibility and pathophysiology, though no specific genes are detailed in the abstract.
The review reports that biomarker levels changed following treatment interventions, supporting the usefulness of these biomarkers in tracking fibromyalgia management.
The review highlights that fibromyalgia is associated with multisystemic comorbidities alongside central sensitization and neuroinflammation.
Widespread Pain Index (WPI) scores decreased after two weeks of auricular vagus nerve stimulation and further improved by week four in fibromyalgia patients.
The revised Fibromyalgia Impact Questionnaire (rFIQ) total score significantly decreased after four weeks of AVNT™ treatment.
The rFIQ general health component score significantly decreased after four weeks of AVNT™ treatment.
The rFIQ symptoms component score significantly decreased after four weeks of AVNT™ treatment.
The Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index (PSQI) score significantly improved after four weeks of AVNT™ treatment, indicating better sleep quality.
Serum BDNF levels did not change significantly after two or four weeks of AVNT™ treatment in fibromyalgia patients.
Serum BDNF levels did not change significantly after either two or four weeks of AVNT treatment in fibromyalgia patients.
Substance P was markedly overexpressed in the spinal dorsal horn of fibromyalgia model rats, and acupressure treatment significantly suppressed this overexpression.
Astrocyte activation, marked by elevated GFAP expression and hypertrophic morphology, was observed in the FM model group and was significantly reduced by acupressure treatment.
Microglial activation, evidenced by upregulated OX-42 expression and morphological hypertrophy, occurred in FM model rats and was normalized by acupressure treatment.
Phosphorylated JNK co-localized predominantly with GFAP-positive astrocytes in FM model rats, and acupressure significantly reduced this p-JNK/GFAP co-localization.
Phosphorylated P38 strongly co-localized with OX-42-positive microglia in FM model rats, and this co-localization was significantly suppressed by acupressure treatment.
Spinal TNF-α levels, elevated in FM model rats, were significantly reduced following acupressure treatment.

Spinal IL-1β showed a paradoxical expression pattern that mirrored the anti-inflammatory cytokines TGF-β and IL-10 rather than the expected pro-inflammatory pattern, suggesting a non-canonical secretion mechanism or M2 microglial polarization in the FM model.
Spinal TGF-β, reduced in the FM model, was significantly increased following acupressure treatment as part of a coordinated anti-inflammatory shift.
Spinal IL-10, reduced in FM model rats, was significantly increased by acupressure treatment.

Prostaglandin E2 levels in the lumbar spinal cord did not differ significantly among control, model, and acupressure groups, arguing against involvement of the prostaglandin pathway in spinal central sensitization in this model.
Phosphorylated P38 MAPK was elevated in FM model rats and was significantly reduced by acupressure treatment, without changes in total P38 protein.
Phosphorylated JNK MAPK was elevated in FM model rats and significantly reduced by acupressure treatment, without changes in total JNK protein.
MKK3, an upstream activator of P38 MAPK, was elevated in FM model rats and reduced following acupressure treatment.
MKK6, an upstream activator of P38 MAPK, was elevated in FM model rats and reduced following acupressure treatment.
MKK7, an upstream activator of JNK MAPK, was elevated in FM model rats and significantly reduced following acupressure treatment.
MKK4 expression showed no significant differences among control, model, and acupressure groups, suggesting it is not a major contributor to JNK/P38 activation in this fibromyalgia model.
FM model rats developed reduced mechanical paw withdrawal thresholds (hyperalgesia) after modeling, and this hyperalgesia was significantly improved after acupressure intervention.

Gait analysis showed FM modeling increased resting, propulsion, and braking time and decreased stride time; acupressure significantly reduced resting, propulsion, and braking time, improving motor function, while swing time did not differ between groups.

Total distance traveled in the open field test was reduced in FM model rats, reflecting movement restriction, and was significantly increased after acupressure intervention, while head movement latency and stationary time showed no significant differences.

Histopathological (HE staining) examination of the tibialis anterior muscle showed disorganized, damaged fibers with inflammatory infiltration in the FM model group, which was largely restored to a more orderly, intact structure after acupressure treatment.

FMS patients showed reduced fractional anisotropy in the left corticospinal tract, right cingulate/hippocampus, right fornix/stria terminalis, and superior occipitofrontal fasciculus compared to healthy controls.

FMS patients showed higher fractional anisotropy in the right superior corona radiata, right posterior corona radiata, sagittal stratum, and left medial lemniscus compared to healthy controls, potentially reflecting compensatory neural remodeling.

FMS patients showed reduced amplitude of low-frequency fluctuation (ALFF) in the left corticospinal tract, left medial lemniscus, right posterior corona radiata, right cingulate/hippocampus, and right fornix/stria terminalis compared to controls, with no regions showing increased ALFF.
The degree of ALFF reduction in the right cingulate/hippocampus and left medial lemniscus was positively correlated with anxiety and depression scores in FMS patients.
The degree of ALFF reduction in the right cingulate/hippocampus and left medial lemniscus was positively correlated with pain severity (VAS) in FMS patients.
No statistically significant correlations were found between ALFF values in any white matter regions and neurocognitive performance as measured by MoCA scores.
FMS patients had significantly higher depression, anxiety, sleep disturbance, and pain scores than healthy controls, alongside lower MoCA cognitive scores.
Some studies report altered gut microbiota composition in fibromyalgia patients, but these findings are preliminary and derived from small, heterogeneous cohorts.

Faecal microbiota transplantation studies in animals and limited human trials suggest a possible link between gut microbiota manipulation and pain sensitivity in fibromyalgia, though further validation is needed.

Nutritional interventions including prebiotics, probiotics and specific dietary strategies have shown early promise in modulating gut microbiota and alleviating fibromyalgia symptoms, though definitive clinical recommendations are lacking.

Nutrients such as magnesium, selenium and omega-3 fatty acids, as well as antioxidant compounds, may influence pain and inflammation pathways in fibromyalgia, but definitive clinical recommendations are lacking.
IC/BPS patients with the widespread pain phenotype frequently have co-occurring chronic overlapping pain conditions including fibromyalgia, IBS, chronic fatigue syndrome, and chronic migraine.

The widespread pain phenotype in IC/BPS is proposed to arise from central sensitization, in which afferent CNS signaling amplifies pain perception, with reduced descending inhibition in some patients.

In a prospective survey of urologic chronic pelvic pain patients, most reported pain beyond the pelvis, with over a third reporting widespread pain in three or more non-pelvic regions, and greater widespread pain correlated with worse psychological and QoL measures.
The widespread pain phenotype in IC/BPS patients appears stable over time, with very few patients switching between pelvic-only and widespread pain categories over a year of follow-up.
Higher toll-like receptor (TLR)-4-mediated inflammatory response was associated with greater likelihood of endorsing extra-pelvic pain in IC/BPS patients.
Brain MRI showed increasing gray matter volume with increasing widespreadness of pain in IC/BPS/chronic pelvic pain patients, hypothesized to reflect strengthened synaptic connections.

Patients with widespread pain showed increased functional connectivity involving the sensorimotor and insular cortices, limbic system, and nucleus accumbens, a neuroimaging pattern similar to that seen in fibromyalgia.

In a review of RCT data, amitriptyline improved pain in both high and low widespread pain groups but reached statistical significance only in the high widespread pain group, suggesting systemic (noradrenergic/serotonergic) therapies may better address centralized pain.
Local therapies (pentosan polysulphate plus hydroxyzine) improved symptoms preferentially in the low widespread pain group, consistent with a locally-acting mechanism.
Hunner lesion (HL) IC/BPS represents a small minority of overall IC/BPS patients, with reported prevalence ranging widely but consensus estimates around 5-7%.

In 66 IC/BPS bladder biopsies (27 with Hunner lesions), HL tissue showed greater lymphoplasmacytic infiltration, greater urothelial loss, and clonal expansion of light-chain restricted B-cells not seen in non-HL tissue.

HL patients had higher bladder inflammatory markers but less bladder fibrosis than non-HL patients, with fibrosis-promoting genes more highly expressed in non-HL tissue; both groups showed degraded urothelium.
Among IC/BPS patients, those with Hunner lesions had significantly greater bladder IgE concentrations than non-HL patients, suggesting IgE-mediated inflammation in HL pathogenesis.

Urinary CXCL8 and CXCL10 were significantly increased in HL IC/BPS patients compared to non-HL patients in a 60-patient comparison, and CXCL10 elevation was independently replicated with a proposed diagnostic cutoff.
Bladder nitric oxide production was significantly greater in HL patients compared to non-HL IC/BPS patients.
Urinary macrophage migratory inhibitory factor (MIF) levels were elevated in HL patients compared to non-HL IC/BPS patients and controls in a 198-participant female cohort.
Serum BAFF (B-cell activating factor) was elevated in HL IC/BPS patients compared to non-HL patients with or without glomerulations, supporting a B-cell overactivation role in HL pathogenesis.
HIF1α levels were elevated in HL patients, leading authors to conclude ischemia and inflammation are key to HL phenotype pathogenesis.
MMP9 was specifically upregulated in HL patients compared to controls/non-HL, and serum MMP9 correlated with worse ICSI symptom scores.
Serum 1-linoleoylglycerophosphocholine was lower in HL patients and proposed as a serum biomarker for the HL phenotype.

A meta-analysis found HL patients tend to be older than non-HL IC/BPS patients with no sex differences in distribution, and pain scores were not significantly different between HL and non-HL patients across nine studies.
Anesthetic bladder capacity tends to be smaller in Hunner lesion patients than non-HL IC/BPS patients, despite HL patients rarely showing fibrosis (a typical cause of reduced capacity).
Triamcinolone injection into Hunner lesions improves ICSI and ICPI symptom scores, urinary frequency, and nocturia in IC/BPS patients.

Gene expression in bladder tissue from IC/BPS patients with non-low bladder capacity was more similar to control tissue than to that of low bladder capacity patients, indicating distinct molecular subtypes.

In a cohort of 94 IC/BPS patients, greater bladder capacity positively correlated with more comorbid psychological symptoms such as childhood trauma, depression, and alexithymia, consistent with low-capacity patients being more bladder-centric.
Presence of a Hunner lesion predicted a 1.9 times greater likelihood of also having low bladder capacity, though the two phenotypes are not exclusive and cluster differently at the genomic level.
Female mice exhibited more severe allergic symptoms and a greater drop in body temperature than males following peanut extract and cholera toxin challenge.
Females showed higher levels of interstitial macrophages and neutrophils in leukocyte responses to peanut allergen challenge compared to males.
Males showed increased eosinophil and lymphocyte influx in response to peanut allergen challenge compared to females.
Elevated cytokines IL-4, IL-5, and IL-9 in females correlated with increased IgE and histamine levels, indicating heightened mast cell activation in the female peanut allergy response.
Expression of the circadian gene Rev-erbα was reduced in female intestines after peanut allergen challenge, suggesting a link between the inflammatory allergic response and circadian disruption.
IgE/mast cell-mediated and IgG/neutrophil-mediated pathways both appeared to be involved in the heightened allergic response seen in female mice.
Patients with idiopathic MCAS most commonly had cutaneous involvement (100%), followed by respiratory (90%), cardiovascular (76.2%), and neurologic (40%) symptoms.
Most patients (90.5%) experienced grade V (most severe) anaphylaxis episodes requiring adrenaline at baseline.
Serum tryptase levels were higher during an acute anaphylaxis episode than at baseline in iMCAS patients.
Most iMCAS patients (90.5%) required omalizumab after a median of 3 years due to unresponsiveness to other treatments.
By the end of one year of treatment, patients were maintained on varying omalizumab doses (150 mg in 47.4%, 300 mg in 36.8%, 450 mg in 10.5%, and 600 mg in 5.2%).
Symptom severity as measured by the visual analog scale significantly decreased at both 6 months and 1 year of omalizumab treatment compared with diagnosis and with treatment initiation.
The number of anaphylaxis episodes was significantly higher at diagnosis and at omalizumab initiation compared with 6 months and 1 year after starting omalizumab.
Disease control as measured by the Likert scale was significantly better at 6 months and 1 year of omalizumab treatment compared with both diagnosis and treatment initiation.
Sputum IgE levels did not differ significantly between patients with atopic versus non-atopic asthma.
Serum IgE levels were significantly higher in patients with atopic asthma than in those with non-atopic asthma.
Sputum and serum IgE levels were not significantly correlated with each other.
Sputum IgE levels were significantly higher in patients with uncontrolled asthma compared to controlled and partly controlled asthma groups.
Serum IgE levels did not differ significantly among controlled, partly controlled, and uncontrolled asthma groups.
Higher sputum IgE levels correlated with worse asthma control test scores.
Higher sputum IgE levels correlated with worse asthma control questionnaire scores.
Higher sputum IgE levels correlated with worse asthma quality of life questionnaire scores.
No significant association was found between sputum IgE levels and lung function parameters.
Sputum IgE levels were significantly higher in patients with eosinophilic asthma compared to those with non-eosinophilic asthma, while serum IgE showed only a non-significant trend.
Sputum IgE levels positively correlated with urine EDN levels, a marker of eosinophil degranulation.
Sputum IgE levels positively correlated with serum EDN levels.
A major group of anaphylactic reactions occur via classical type I hypersensitivity, in which IgE mediates activation of mast cells and basophils.
IgG-associated neutrophil activation has emerged as another relevant signaling pathway underlying anaphylactic reactions.
Complement activation is described as one of the relevant signaling pathways contributing to anaphylactic reactions.
Cyclooxygenase metabolism is implicated as a signaling pathway in anaphylactic reactions.
In drug-induced anaphylaxis, the Mas-related G protein-coupled receptor MRGPRX2 directly triggers mast cell degranulation, independent of the classical IgE pathway.
Contact, coagulation, and metabolic systems are also activated during anaphylactic reactions, contributing to altered homeostasis.
Homeostatic proteins including albumin, phospholipids, and apo- and lipoproteins are modulated during anaphylactic reactions, indicating altered homeostasis.
The endothelium is actively involved in the pathophysiology of anaphylactic reactions, being impacted by mediator release and system dysregulation.
Recent evidence points to extracellular vesicle- and microRNA-mediated communication between cellular compartments as a mechanism in anaphylaxis.
Extracellular vesicles are proposed to mediate communication between cellular compartments during anaphylactic reactions.
microRNAs are implicated as mediators of intercellular communication contributing to anaphylaxis pathophysiology.
Hereditary alpha-tryptasemia, a genetic trait, is associated with increased risk of severe anaphylactic reactions.
Serum tryptase was markedly elevated at the time of the allergic/cardiac reaction and fell substantially during convalescence, confirming acute mast cell degranulation.

Administration of iodine-based contrast during coronary angiography triggered an acute hypersensitivity reaction with diffuse coronary vasospasm, hypotension, rash, and ST-segment elevation, consistent with Type II Kounis syndrome.
Continuous low-dose adrenaline infusion rapidly improved the patient's blood pressure during the acute Kounis syndrome episode.
Follow-up coronary angiography after treatment with corticosteroids and antihistamines showed resolution of the diffuse coronary vasospasm.
Latex-specific IgE testing was negative, ruling out latex as the causative allergen in this Kounis syndrome episode.

Kounis syndrome is diagnosed in approximately 1.1% of patients hospitalized for allergic, hypersensitivity, or anaphylactic reactions in the United States, equating to roughly 19.4 cases per 100,000 emergency department visits, occurring more often in adults aged 40–70 and in males.

Non-selective beta-blockers are contraindicated in Kounis syndrome because they can inhibit β2-mediated bronchodilation and reduce responsiveness to epinephrine, potentially worsening hypotension and bronchospasm.
Morphine is contraindicated in Kounis syndrome because it possesses mast cell-activating activity.
Hereditary alpha-tryptasemia (HαT), caused by TPSAB1 copy number gain, has an overall prevalence of about 5.2% (150/2,872) across multiple control cohorts, including a UK birth cohort.
A US cohort study found HαT prevalence of 12.2% (10/82) among patients with systemic mastocytosis, independent of bST levels, atopy, venom allergy, or anaphylaxis history.
A German cohort found HαT prevalence of 17.2% (31/180) in mastocytosis patients overall, and 21.3% (13/61) in an independent indolent systemic mastocytosis (ISM) cohort.
An Italian multicenter cohort found HαT prevalence of 13.3% (59/385) among patients with mastocytosis or monoclonal MCAS (MMAS).
A French multicenter cohort reported HαT prevalence of 13.5% (79/583) in patients with mastocytosis or MMAS.
A Spanish cohort reported HαT prevalence of 17.9% (83/464) among patients with mastocytosis.
The over-representation of HαT was specific to mast cell-related hematological malignancies and was not observed in other myeloid neoplasms.
Across cohorts, patients with HαT-associated mMCD or mastocytosis consistently show higher baseline serum tryptase (bST) levels than HαT-negative patients.

Mastocytosis patients with HαT tend to show features of lower mast cell burden—lower KIT D816V variant allele frequency in blood and bone marrow, lower BM infiltration, and fewer BM mast cell clusters—though this was not observed in the Spanish cohort.
In a US SM cohort, 90% (9/10) of HαT-positive patients had a history of anaphylaxis compared to 43% (31/72) of HαT-negative SM patients.
The German study found hymenoptera venom allergy to be more frequent in HαT-positive mastocytosis patients compared to HαT-negative patients, in both discovery and validation cohorts.

Greiner et al. reported that mast cell activation-related symptoms, including hypotension and anaphylaxis, were more frequent and more severe in HαT-positive mastocytosis patients than HαT-negative patients.
The Spanish cohort reported higher prevalence of headaches and paresthesia, but lower prevalence of syncope, in HαT-positive mastocytosis patients compared to wild-type patients.
Some studies reported a positive dose-response correlation between the number of additional TPSAB1 copies and either the risk of anaphylaxis or the severity of mast cell-related symptoms.
HαT-positive mastocytosis patients are less prone to cutaneous involvement and have a lower prevalence of osteoporosis or osteopenia than HαT-negative patients.
Overall survival and progression-free survival did not differ significantly between HαT-positive and HαT-negative mastocytosis patients in the Italian cohort.
bST levels in HαT follow a gene-dosage effect, with TPSAB1 triplications producing higher levels than duplications, and even higher levels reported with quintuplications.

Elevated bST levels observed in HαT subjects with a normal TPSAB1 copy number but a co-inherited tryptase gene deletion in trans suggest that an enlarged, overactive promoter element—not gene copy number alone—drives tryptase overexpression.

In the German cohort, HαT-positive SM patients were strongly enriched for indolent/smoldering SM (ISM/SSM) rather than advanced SM; among those with TPSAB1 triplications or more, 95% (21/22) had ISM/SSM versus 70% (104/149) in HαT-negative SM patients.
In the French cohort, HαT enrichment was statistically significant in the bone marrow mastocytosis (BMM, 19.7%) and ISM (11.7%) SM variants, but not in other SM variants.

α/β-tryptase heterotetramers (produced when α-tryptase is expressed alongside β-tryptase) can preactivate the mechanosensory receptor EMR2, promoting vibration-elicited urticaria, and can activate PAR2 to cause smooth muscle constriction, epithelial activation, and increased vascular permeability.

Familial pedigree studies of HαT described five clusters of clinical manifestations in affected members versus unaffected relatives, including cutaneous, connective tissue, atopic, gastrointestinal, and neuropsychiatric symptoms such as dysautonomia, POTS, chronic pain, and fibromyalgia.

An unselected cohort study first confirmed a higher prevalence of systemic venom reactions, cutaneous flush/pruritus, inflammatory bowel syndrome, dysautonomia, and retained primary dentition in HαT-positive individuals.

The initial clinical description linking HαT to broad multisystem symptoms in the general population was not confirmed by a more recent study, and the debate over HαT's clinical penetrance remains unresolved.
HαT has recently been linked to cold-induced urticaria and cold-induced anaphylaxis, reigniting debate about the nature and penetrance of HαT symptoms outside of monoclonal mast cell disorders.

In the Spanish cohort, although history of anaphylaxis at SM diagnosis was more common in HαT-positive patients, there was no higher incidence of new anaphylactic events during follow-up in HαT-positive versus HαT-negative SM patients, arguing against HαT as a genuine symptom modifier.
Within the ISM/SSM subgroups, HαT-positive patients had lower KIT D816V allele burden and lower bone marrow mast cell infiltration despite having higher baseline serum tryptase levels.
Recent data suggest that standardization of SM evaluation, including adaptation of the bST threshold, could substantially lower the prevalence of HαT in ISM toward that of the general population.
Sordi et al. found that applying a genotype-adjusted bST threshold would reclassify only 7 of 51 SM patients to MMAS, insufficient to lower HαT prevalence in SM to general-population levels.

α/β-tryptase heterotetramers, produced by individuals expressing α-tryptase, preactivate the mast cell mechanosensory receptor EMR2, promoting vibration-elicited urticaria commonly seen in HαT individuals.

α/β-tryptase heterotetramers can activate protease-activated receptor-2 (PAR2), potentially contributing to mast cell activation manifestations such as smooth muscle constriction, epithelial activation, and increased vascular permeability.

In familial pedigrees, HαT-affected individuals exhibited a broad constellation of symptoms compared to unaffected relatives, grouped into cutaneous, connective tissue, atopic, gastrointestinal, and neuropsychiatric/autonomic categories including joint hypermobility, dysautonomia, POTS, chronic pain, fibromyalgia, and vulvodynia.

An unselected cohort confirmed a higher prevalence of systemic venom reactions, cutaneous flush or pruritus, inflammatory bowel-type symptoms, dysautonomia, and retained primary dentition in HαT-positive individuals.
The original clinical description of HαT-associated symptoms was not confirmed by a more recent study, leaving the true clinical penetrance of HαT in the general population debated.
HαT has recently been linked to cold-induced urticaria and cold-induced anaphylaxis, reigniting debate about the nature and penetrance of HαT-associated symptoms outside mMCD.

In the Spanish SM cohort, although anaphylaxis history at diagnosis was more frequent in HαT-positive patients, there was no higher incidence of new anaphylactic events during follow-up compared to HαT-negative SM patients, arguing against HαT as a genuine symptom modifier.

HαT-positive individuals with non-monoclonal MCAS display a higher frequency of unclustered bone marrow mast cells that are often larger, hypogranulated, and sometimes spindle-shaped, and may be associated with eosinophilia.
HαT-positive individuals with gastrointestinal symptoms exhibit higher mast cell numbers in the intestine, often associated with class-switched B-cells.
HαT prevalence in pure cutaneous mastocytosis (CM) ranged from 9.1% to 23% across studies, with an overall prevalence of 16.2%, higher than in the general population.
HαT was recently found to affect 19.4% (6/31) of children with solitary mastocytoma, a condition where extracutaneous mediator-related symptoms are not the chief complaint.

In advanced SM, where diagnosis is driven by organ impairment rather than MCAS or anaphylaxis, HαT prevalence ranged from 10.6% to 13.2% across cohorts, with an overall prevalence of 11.7%, similar to ISM and higher than the general population.
A low baseline serum IgE (typically <18 IU/mL) correlates with significantly reduced response to omalizumab.
Elevated total serum IgE has been associated with complete response to omalizumab, defined as 90% improvement in symptoms after two doses.
In 158 omalizumab-treated patients, baseline serum IgE cut-offs of 42.5 and 59.5 IU/mL had sensitivity 76.6% and specificity 93% for predicting complete response.
Serum circulating free IgE has not been shown to predict response to omalizumab.
A positive ASST has been associated with a slower response (rather than nonresponse) to omalizumab, ranging from 1 to 3 months.
IgG anti-IgE and IgG anti-FcεRIα autoantibody levels were significantly higher in individuals who did not respond to omalizumab within 4 weeks.
Serological evidence of autoimmunity, including a positive ANA test and presence of IgG anti-TPO antibodies, has been associated with a poorer response to omalizumab.
Coexistence of IgG autoantibodies with IgE autoantibodies predicted late or nonresponse to omalizumab.
A study of 89 patients found that higher baseline blood basophil count (20 cells/µL) predicted response to standard-dose omalizumab.
Individuals with peripheral basopenia (<1700 cells/mL) and lower basophil CD63 activation were more likely to be omalizumab nonresponders.

Basophils with lower IgE receptor-mediated histamine degranulation showed slower omalizumab response, while >10% cellular histamine release was associated with fast, complete response; baseline FcεRI expression was lower in nonresponders and higher in responders after 6 months of omalizumab.
Eosinopenia in CSU is associated with the need for higher doses of omalizumab and with complete nonresponse.
Data on the association between elevated D-dimer and omalizumab treatment response are conflicting, with one study showing elevated D-dimer predicts prompt response while others show no relationship.
An elevated D-dimer prior to omalizumab initiation was associated with a 4.8-fold increase in requirement for updosing to 600 mg.

A positive BHRA, aligned with autoimmune Type IIb CSU, has been identified as a marker of response to ciclosporin, with responders showing higher baseline disease activity, low baseline IgE and normal baseline D-dimer levels.
A normal baseline D-dimer was associated with complete response to ciclosporin in a prospective study of 29 patients with CSU.
Evidence for the impact of sex on omalizumab treatment response is conflicting: one study found males more likely to require longer courses, another found females had higher recurrence rates.
There is no reported association between age and response to omalizumab or ciclosporin.
Patients with a reported comorbid autoimmune condition were more likely to have been switched from omalizumab to ciclosporin due to omalizumab inefficacy.
Evidence on the role of concomitant angioedema and inducible urticaria in predicting omalizumab treatment response is conflicting between single-center and multicentre studies.

Responders to three doses of omalizumab (UAS7 >16 improvement) had significantly higher baseline numbers of Galectin 9+ eosinophils, while Galectin 9+ basophils were numerically but not statistically significantly higher.
Myeloid and mast cell progenitors in CSU patients identified by flow cytometry predicted treatment response to omalizumab, confirmed with transcriptomic data.

Plasma proteomics in 96 CSU patients found protein changes (e.g., MMP-9, thrombospondin) related to angioedema but no significant association between plasma proteins and omalizumab treatment response.
In omalizumab-intolerant/partial-responder patients (n=54) whose trial was halted early, UAS7 improved after 24 weeks of dupilumab but findings were not statistically significant.
In omalizumab-naïve patients (n=138), dupilumab produced a significant improvement in UAS7 scores after 24 weeks, and baseline serum IgE did not predict response.
Remibrutinib showed a mean reduction in UAS7 scores at week 12 of -20±7 versus placebo -13.9±1, with efficacy regardless of prior omalizumab use or baseline IgE stratification.

In vitro, remibrutinib inhibits activation and degranulation of basophils and mast cells exposed to sera of CSU patients, regardless of whether the sera were from omalizumab responders or nonresponders.
Phase 2b trials of benralizumab (anti-IL-5Rα) in CSU were discontinued as it showed no benefit versus placebo at 12 weeks.
A meta-analysis of 67 observational studies found the average omalizumab nonresponse rate was 7%, with a partial response rate of 17.8%.

In a 12-centre international study of 182 patients, strict criteria (positive ASST, positive IgG anti-FcεR1/anti-IgE immunoassay, and positive basophil test) identified fewer than 10% of patients as having Type IIb autoimmune urticaria, who had lower baseline serum IgE, more severe disease (higher UAS7), and higher anti-TPO antibody levels.
High-fat diet feeding for 12 weeks significantly increased body weight in mice compared with normal diet controls.
Electroacupuncture stimulation at LI11 significantly reduced body weight, fat cell area, and eWAT weight in HFD-fed obese mice compared with untreated HFD mice.
High-fat diet feeding increased plasma IL-1β, TNF-α, IL-6, and TGF-β levels and eWAT il-1β and tnfα mRNA expression compared with normal diet controls.
Electroacupuncture reduced plasma IL-1β, TNF-α, IL-6, and TGF-β levels and eWAT il-1β/tnfα mRNA expression compared with HFD-only mice.
Electroacupuncture suppressed sympathetic nerve activity recorded in eWAT (but not scWAT), contrary to the hypothesis that it would activate sympathetic nerves.
HFD feeding increased NPY protein expression in eWAT compared with normal diet, and electroacupuncture inhibited this NPY upregulation.
HFD induced upregulation of NPY2R and NPY5R and downregulation of NPY1R in eWAT, while electroacupuncture reversed this pattern, upregulating NPY1R and downregulating NPY2R and NPY5R.
Immunohistochemical staining confirmed that electroacupuncture increased NPY1R expression in eWAT, but this increase did not occur in sympathetically ablated mice.
HFD suppressed NPY1R expression in F4/80+ macrophages in eWAT compared with normal diet, and electroacupuncture increased NPY1R expression specifically within macrophages.
HFD increased total macrophage numbers and decreased the proportion of M2 macrophages in eWAT; electroacupuncture reduced overall macrophage numbers and increased the M2 macrophage proportion.
Pretreatment with the NPY1R antagonist BIBP3226 blocked electroacupuncture's ability to induce M2 macrophage polarization in eWAT.
NPY1R antagonism with BIBP3226 alone (without ES) increased plasma and eWAT IL-1β and TNF-α expression compared with vehicle saline, indicating NPY1R signaling normally restrains inflammation.
BIBP3226 blocked electroacupuncture's anti-inflammatory effect, so that IL-1β and TNF-α expression remained elevated in plasma and eWAT despite ES treatment.

In vitro, conditioned medium from ES-treated adipose tissue increased NPY1R protein expression and reduced IL-1β and TNF-α expression in RAW 264.7 macrophages compared with conditioned medium from HFD adipose tissue.

The authors propose an overall mechanism in which electroacupuncture suppresses sympathetic activity in eWAT, reducing NPY release and thereby activating NPY1R on macrophages, which drives M1-to-M2 macrophage polarization and reduces chronic inflammation in obese mice.
Gabapentinoid prescribing prevalence in the UK IBD population more than doubled from 2.5% to 5.6% between 2010 and 2019.
Chronic strong opioid prescribing (>90 days) among IBD patients increased from 3.6% to 4.6% between 2010 and 2019.
Chronic weak opioid prescribing (>90 days) remained largely stable, from 3.6% to 3.7% between 2010 and 2019.
Chronic Z-drug prescribing (>28 days) increased modestly from 2.1% to 2.2% between 2010 and 2019.
Chronic benzodiazepine prescribing (>28 days) decreased from 3.3% to 2.8% between 2010 and 2019.
Co-prescribing of two or more pain/sedative medications increased over the decade, with 3.9%-6.3% of patients co-prescribed an opioid with a gabapentinoid or sedative.
Comorbid IBS diagnosed prior to IBD onset was significantly associated with increased likelihood of chronic strong opioid, chronic sedative, and co-prescription of pain/sedative medications.
Comorbid fibromyalgia diagnosed prior to IBD onset was significantly associated with increased likelihood of chronic strong opioid, chronic sedative, and co-prescription of pain/sedative medications.

Individuals with comorbid anxiety or depression were more than twice as likely to receive a chronic strong opioid prescription, and this comorbidity was also associated with chronic sedative and co-prescribing patterns.
Current smokers with IBD were more than twice as likely as non-smokers to receive chronic strong opioid or sedative prescriptions and to have a co-prescription of pain or sedative medications.
Female sex and older age at IBD diagnosis were associated with increased risk of chronic strong opioid, chronic sedative, and co-prescriptions.
Individuals with Crohn's disease were 1.5 times more likely to be prescribed strong opioids long-term compared with those with ulcerative colitis.
Comorbid inflammatory arthropathy was associated with chronic strong opioid prescribing and co-prescribing but not with chronic sedative prescribing.
Compared with the general UK population, individuals with IBD had higher prescribing rates of gabapentinoids (5.4% vs. 3.3%), benzodiazepines (5.8% vs. 3.1%), and Z-drugs (3.7% vs. 2.3%).
UK IBD opioid prescribing has plateaued at approximately 10% annually, notably lower than the 21% opioid use reported among US IBD outpatients.
In 2019, 8.4% of the IBD population received a sedative prescription, over half of which were chronic, and 39% were co-prescribed with an opioid or gabapentinoid.
Sensory neuron-derived CGRP inhibits inflammatory mediator release from TRPM8-immunoreactive CD103+ dendritic cells, thereby alleviating IBS symptoms.

TRPV1 antagonists significantly alleviate visceral pain in patients with constipation-predominant IBS (IBS-C), while the NHE3 inhibitor tenapanor indirectly suppresses TRPV1 activation by restoring epithelial barrier integrity.
Melatonin reduces DRG neuron excitability and TTX-resistant sodium channel current density via MT2 receptors, blocking nociceptive signal transmission relevant to IBS.
Reduced ChAT expression in the colons of diarrhea-predominant IBS (IBS-D) patients diminishes acetylcholine levels, and patchouli alcohol alleviates diarrhea by activating ChAT in IPANs.

Overexpression of the voltage-gated calcium channel alpha2delta1 subunit in IPANs disrupts neuronal homeostasis via increased calcium influx, and pregabalin, targeting this subunit, attenuates pain and corrects AHP abnormalities in IBS.

Sustained upregulation of NMDAR activity in IPANs enhances postsynaptic potentials and neuronal hyperexcitability in post-infectious or inflammatory IBS, validated in colonic biopsies from patients and animal models.

The EphrinB2/EphB2 signaling axis dynamically regulates synaptic connectivity in the myenteric plexus via NR2B pathway activation, and pharmacological blockade of EphB2 reduces pain thresholds and suppresses aberrant neuronal firing in IBS.

High-FODMAP diets exacerbate IBS symptoms by altering gut microbial communities, increasing Gram-negative bacteria and LPS levels, resulting in intestinal inflammation, barrier dysfunction, and visceral hypersensitivity.
Microbial-derived glutamate decarboxylase (GadB) attenuates visceral hypersensitivity by enhancing intestinal GABAergic signaling and inhibiting DRG sensory neurons.

Serine proteases produced by gut microbiota, particularly Faecalibacterium spp., reduce DRG sensory neuron excitability through PAR-4 receptor activation, a mechanism relevant to alleviating pain-related gastrointestinal disorders.
Post-inflammatory increases in SCFAs (primarily butyrate) activate TRPV1-expressing DRG sensory neurons, inducing post-inflammatory visceral pain.

Bacteroides thetaiotaomicron enhances epithelial integrity by downregulating claudin-3, restores L-cell numbers, and balances intestinal neurochemical levels, modulating enteric neurons and colonic activity.
Dysbiosis-induced cysteine proteases specifically activate nociceptive sensory neurons through the PAR-2-Nav1.8+ signaling pathway, leading to immune-independent visceral hypersensitivity.

In IBS, mast cells stimulated by SP and CGRP release histamine and proteases, activating TRPV1+ neurons to establish a self-reinforcing 'neuro-immune positive feedback loop' that perpetuates visceral hypersensitivity and chronic inflammation.

IgE-mediated mast cell activation enhances neuronal hyperexcitability via FcεRI-dependent calcium influx, with downstream STAT6 signaling amplifying Th2 immune responses through IL-4/IL-13 upregulation, potentiating nociceptive transmission in the gut.

Interferon-gamma exerts dual inhibitory effects on sensory neurons, suppressing Nav1.7 sodium channel membrane trafficking via JAK1-STAT1 and blocking IL-17-induced TRPV1 sensitization, showing innate immunity can directly mitigate pain transduction.
A clinical cohort study reveals a 2.3-fold increased IBD incidence in vagotomized patients, whereas vagus nerve stimulation significantly reduces colonic IL-1β levels and promotes mucosal healing.
A randomized controlled trial found that PENFS significantly alleviates abdominal pain in pediatric IBS patients while reducing long-term healthcare costs.

A case-control study of refractory IBS patients with obsessive-compulsive disorder found that DBS alleviated anxiety symptoms, reduced abdominal pain intensity by 62% (VAS score), and normalized defecation frequency.

A systematic review involving 644 patients (including IBD, IBS, and functional dyspepsia) demonstrates that non-invasive VNS significantly improves abdominal pain, diarrhea, and bloating with favorable safety profiles.

Somatostatin agonists such as octreotide inhibit TRPA1 channel mechanosensitivity in DRG and downregulate the TLR4/NF-κB axis in intestinal epithelium, an effect clinically validated in multicenter RCTs for Crohn's disease-associated fibrosis and radiation enteritis.

Cav3.2 drives colonic hypersensitivity in IBD pathogenesis; genetic silencing or pharmacological blockade of spinal dorsal horn Cav3.2 significantly suppresses non-inflammatory colonic hypersensitivity in DSS-induced colitis models.

In IBS, ATP exacerbates visceral hypersensitivity and hypermotility via P2X3-mediated calcium influx in sensory neurons, and selective P2X3 antagonists (e.g., AF-219) attenuate abdominal pain and colonic hyperreactivity by reducing c-Fos expression in spinal dorsal horns.
Rifaximin alleviates visceral hyperalgesia in IBS models through downregulation of TRPV1 in peripheral and central pathways, mediated by microbiota-dependent neuroinflammation suppression.

The classical herbal formula Tongxie Yaofang alleviates visceral hypersensitivity in IBS models by inhibiting the bile acid-TGR5-CGRP axis, with efficacy linked to microbiota-dependent bile acid metabolic remodeling.

Lactiplantibacillus plantarum demonstrates multidimensional therapeutic effects in IBS models by restoring ChAT+ neuronal function, concurrently improving intestinal motility, inflammation, and epithelial barrier integrity.
Bifidobacterium longum alleviates visceral hypersensitivity by activating potassium channels while suppressing HCN channels, thereby reducing excitability of IPANs.

TAAR1, co-localized with calbindin-positive sensory neurons, modulates colonic motility, neuroimmune signaling, and enteroendocrine function, collectively increasing gut microbial alpha-diversity and altering specific bacterial family abundances.
Galectin-9 levels were significantly elevated in nasopharyngeal swabs of COVID-19 patients compared with healthy individuals.
TGF-β levels were significantly elevated in nasopharyngeal swabs of COVID-19 patients versus healthy controls.
L-kynurenine (LKU), a downstream product of IDO1 activity, was highly upregulated in COVID-19 swabs relative to healthy controls.
PD-L1 mRNA levels were significantly increased in nasopharyngeal swabs of COVID-19 patients compared with healthy individuals.
CD3ε mRNA levels were significantly upregulated in COVID-19 swabs, indicating increased infiltration of CD3-positive T lymphocytes.

mRNA levels of HIF-1α and its downstream target VEGF were significantly increased in swabs of COVID-19 patients, indicating heightened HIF-1 transcriptional activity despite normal tissue oxygenation.
2-hydroxyglutarate was undetectable in swabs of healthy individuals but clearly detectable in swabs of COVID-19 patients, supporting a proposed mechanism of HIF-1α stabilization.
Transfection of BEAS-2B bronchial epithelial cells with Wuhan strain Spike protein plasmid induced detectable 2-hydroxyglutarate, whereas wild-type and empty-vector-transfected cells showed none.

LDHA activity using 2-oxoglutarate as substrate was higher in S protein-expressing BEAS-2B cells, and this conversion was significantly reduced by the LDHA inhibitor FX11, confirming LDHA's role in 2-OG conversion.
In S protein-expressing BEAS-2B cells, HIF-1α prolyl hydroxylase activity was attenuated while HIF-1 DNA-binding activity and TGF-β production were highly upregulated compared to controls.

Glycolysis and downstream methylglyoxal production were significantly upregulated in S protein-expressing BEAS-2B cells compared to controls, a byproduct implicated in AGE/RAGE-driven MAPK activation supporting viral protein expression.
Phospho-Smad3 was highly upregulated along with increased galectin-9 and PD-L1 expression in S protein-expressing BEAS-2B cells versus controls.
IDO1 activity and consequent L-kynurenine release were highly increased in S protein-expressing BEAS-2B cells relative to controls.
ChIP with anti-HIF-1α antibody in BEAS-2B cells confirmed direct interaction of HIF-1α with the TGF-β gene promoter region, especially after CoCl2-induced HIF-1 activation.

Co-culture of S protein-expressing BEAS-2B cells with Jurkat T helper cells showed significantly higher released galectin-9, significantly lower IL-2, and increased SHP-2-like phosphatase activity in T cells, consistent with activation of PD-1-type inhibitory signaling.

In tri-culture of LN-18 glioblastoma cells, S protein-expressing BEAS-2B cells, and TALL-104 cytotoxic T cells, granzyme B injection into adherent target cells was completely attenuated while T-cell killing and galectin-9 secretion were highest, indicating S protein-transfected cells enhance cancer cell immune evasion against cytotoxic T cells.
SSc-ILD patients showed a significantly increased type 1 interferon gene signature in both whole blood and skin compared to SSc patients without ILD.
Pathway analysis showed upregulation of inflammatory signaling (IFN-α/γ, heme metabolism, IL-6/JAK/STAT3, cytokine storm) in SSc-ILD blood and skin compared to SSc-no ILD.

In blood, ECM-related pathways (EMT, ECM organization, collagen degradation) were downregulated in SSc-ILD compared to SSc-no ILD, while skin showed loss of keratinization signaling with upregulated collagen/ECM pathways.
Enriched interferon gene modules in SSc-ILD blood positively correlated with increased plasma levels of complement C9 and fibrinogen alpha chain (FGA), both associated with inflammation.
Enriched interferon gene modules negatively correlated with reduced levels of APOH, APOC3, and albumin (ALB) in SSc-ILD.
Plasma proteomics showed elevated FGA, C9 (inflammation-related) and APOB (platelet-activation-related) in SSc-ILD compared to SSc-no ILD.
Clotting factor F12 and APOC3 were found at lower levels in SSc-ILD plasma compared to SSc-no ILD.
Circulating Galectin-3, a lectin implicated in fibrogenesis via macrophage recruitment, was significantly increased in SSc-ILD patients.
Hexosylceramide, a membrane sphingolipid, was increased in SSc-ILD plasma compared to SSc-no ILD.
Lyso-phosphatidylcholine and the polyunsaturated fatty acids arachidonic acid, DHA, and EPA were reduced in SSc-ILD plasma compared to SSc-no ILD.
In the larger retrospective cohort, baseline triglyceride levels were significantly higher in SSc-ILD (n=20) versus SSc-no ILD (n=10) patients.
CRP levels showed no significant difference between SSc-ILD and SSc-no ILD patients, either cross-sectionally or over longitudinal follow-up.
Frequency of CD4/CD8 double positive T cells was significantly reduced in SSc-ILD patients compared to healthy volunteers.
SSc-no ILD patients showed reduced CD8+ naive T cells and increased CD8+ effector T cells compared to healthy volunteers.
CD56-CD16+ NK cells (the most cytotoxic NK subset) were increased in SSc-no ILD patients compared to healthy volunteers, with a similar trend in SSc-ILD patients.
Unswitched memory B cell frequency was significantly reduced in both SSc-ILD and SSc-no ILD groups compared to healthy volunteers.
No significant differences were observed in myeloid cell populations between SSc groups and healthy volunteers.
CCL2 was elevated at baseline in SSc-ILD versus SSc-no ILD plasma, but this difference did not persist through longitudinal follow-up.
CX3CL1 was elevated in SSc-ILD versus SSc-no ILD plasma at baseline, and elevated in pooled SSc patients versus healthy volunteers at both timepoints.
Over an average 5-year follow-up, triglycerides and β-alanine (a carnosine precursor) were significantly higher in SSc-ILD plasma compared to SSc-no ILD.
IGHM (IgM constant region) and JCHAIN (favoring IgM/IgA multimerization) protein levels were decreased over the 5-year follow-up in SSc-ILD progression patients.
ORM1 (acute-phase protein) and HP (haptoglobin) levels were increased over the 5-year follow-up in SSc-ILD progression patients.
Over a 6-month follow-up, serotonin, a vasoactive inflammatory mediator, increased in SSc-ILD plasma.
Over the same 6-month period, two bile acids (GCDCA, GCA) and triglycerides decreased in SSc-ILD plasma, contrasting with the longer-term (5-year) triglyceride increase reported.
After 6 months, cytoskeleton proteins, THBS1 (thrombospondin-1), and CXCL17 were significantly elevated in SSc-ILD plasma.
LTBP1 gene expression, which controls TGF-β1 activation, was significantly upregulated after 6 months in SSc-ILD patients.
Over an average 5-year follow-up in Cohort 2, plasma triglyceride levels were significantly higher in SSc-ILD patients compared to SSc-no ILD patients.
Beta-alanine, a rate-limiting precursor of carnosine, was found at significantly higher levels in SSc-ILD plasma compared to SSc-no ILD after an average 5-year follow-up (Cohort 2).
Levels of the protein IGHM (immunoglobulin mu chain C region, IgM isotype marker) were decreased in the 20 SSc-ILD patients with progression over the 5-year follow-up (Cohort 2).
Levels of the protein JCHAIN, which favors multimerization and secretion of IgM and IgA, were decreased in SSc-ILD patients with progression over the 5-year follow-up (Cohort 2).
ORM1 (orosomucoid, a key acute-phase plasma protein) was increased in SSc-ILD patients with progression over the 5-year follow-up (Cohort 2).
Haptoglobin (HP), which inhibits the oxidative activity of free hemoglobin, was increased in SSc-ILD patients with progression over the 5-year follow-up (Cohort 2).
A significant increase in serotonin, a vasoactive mediator of inflammation, was observed in SSc-ILD patients (Cohort 1) over a 6-month follow-up.
A decrease in the two biliary acids glycochenodeoxycholic acid (GCDCA) and glycocholic acid (GCA), as well as triglycerides, was observed in SSc-ILD patients (Cohort 1) over 6 months of follow-up.
In contrast to the 5-year follow-up trend, triglyceride levels decreased in SSc-ILD patients (Cohort 1) over a shorter 6-month follow-up period.
Several cytoskeleton proteins (TLN1, CFL1, ACTN1, PFN1, VCL, ACTB) were found at significantly higher levels in SSc-ILD patients (Cohort 1) after 6 months of follow-up.
THBS1 (thrombospondin-1), released after platelet activation and involved in cell-to-matrix interactions and latent TGF-β activation, was elevated in SSc-ILD patients after 6 months of follow-up.

CXCL17, released by platelets and involved in ECM synthesis, was found at higher levels in SSc-ILD patients after 6 months of follow-up, consistent with prior reports of elevated CXCL17 in SSc versus healthy volunteers.
Gene expression analysis showed a significant upregulation of LTBP1, which controls TGF-β1 activation and its deposition in the ECM, in SSc-ILD patients after 6 months of follow-up.

No significant correlation was found between the multi-omic measured parameters and autoantibody profiles, comorbidities, overlap syndrome, gender, age, or treatment that could explain why ILD progressed in some SSc patients but not others.
Among ME/CFS patients receiving CBT-F, fatigue treatment outcomes did not differ between those with and without co-occurring insomnia.
Among insomnia disorder patients receiving CBT-I, insomnia treatment outcomes did not differ between those with and without co-occurring severe fatigue.
In ME/CFS patients treated with CBT-F, reductions in fatigue severity were positively correlated with reductions in insomnia severity.
In insomnia disorder patients treated with CBT-I, reductions in insomnia severity were positively correlated with reductions in fatigue severity.
Among ME/CFS patients who were no longer severely fatigued after CBT-F, 31% still reported clinically significant insomnia.
Among insomnia patients no longer meeting criteria for clinical insomnia after CBT-I, 24% remained severely fatigued.
Plasma FGF-21 was significantly elevated in ME and ME+FM patients versus healthy controls, but not in FM alone.
FGF-21 was not significantly elevated in FM patients without ME comorbidity compared to healthy controls.
No significant sex-based differences in circulating FGF-21 were found within any diagnostic group or healthy controls.
SF-36 general health scores were significantly reduced in all patient groups compared to healthy controls.
MFI-20 fatigue and DSQ symptom severity scores were significantly elevated in patients relative to healthy controls.
No significant differences in SF-36, MFI-20, or DSQ scores were observed between FM, ME, and ME+FM groups, indicating comparable fatigue/symptom burden across diagnostic groups.
In FM patients, low FGF-21 levels correlated strongly with greater DSQ-assessed PEM severity, particularly items reflecting acute post-exertion fatigue.
In FM, FGF-21 levels showed no significant correlation with objectively-provoked PEM measured by the DPEMQ after a standardized passive exercise protocol.
FM patients with low FGF-21 had significantly lower BrainCheck mental flexibility scores than normal/high FGF-21 FM patients.
Across the whole FM group, FGF-21 did not significantly correlate with overall BrainCheck cognitive performance.
In ME patients, low FGF-21 correlated with greater DSQ autonomic/endocrine/immune symptom severity.
In ME patients, low FGF-21 correlated with greater PEM severity measured objectively by the DPEMQ following a standardized passive mechanical challenge.
In ME patients, FGF-21 was not significantly associated with the broader, subjective DSQ PEM measure, unlike its correlation with the objective DPEMQ.
In ME, FGF-21 was not significantly correlated with DSQ cognitive scores or SF-36 mental health ratings.
ME patients with low plasma FGF-21 had significantly lower BrainCheck immediate memory recognition scores than normal/high FGF-21 ME patients.
Across the whole ME cohort, higher FGF-21 correlated positively with BrainCheck combined percentile, immediate memory recognition, and delayed memory recognition.
