In ME+FM patients, low FGF-21 was associated with greater cognitive dysfunction (DSQ) and poorer self-perceived mental health (SF-36).
In ME+FM, non-significant trend negative correlations were observed between low FGF-21 and autonomic/endocrine/immune symptoms and PEM severity.
In ME+FM, no significant differences in BrainCheck cognitive domains were observed across FGF-21 strata.
Among healthy controls with similarly low FGF-21 levels, no significant correlations were observed with fatigue or symptom burden, unlike in patient groups.
Participants with FGF-21 in the normal range (51-200 pg/mL) showed no significant associations between FGF-21 and symptom severity across all diagnostic groups.
Among ME patients with high circulating FGF-21, higher FGF-21 correlated with lower MFI-20 mental fatigue scores, suggesting a possible protective/compensatory role.
ME patients with high FGF-21 showed higher BrainCheck immediate memory, delayed memory, and global cognitive performance scores.

The paper cites a 2024 RCT showing metformin did not change circulating FGF-21 levels in type 2 diabetes patients but suppressed FAP activity and upregulated FGFR1c and β-klotho expression, potentially enhancing FGF-21 signaling, and is proposed as a candidate therapy for ME/FM patients with low FGF-21.

Efruxifermin, a long-acting FGF-21 analogue, achieved histologic resolution and fibrosis reduction in phase 2b trials for NASH with moderate fibrosis over 24 weeks, cited as a potential FGF-21-axis therapy.

Pegozafermin (BIO89-100), another FGF-21 analogue, has demonstrated favorable effects on liver fat and fibrosis in phase 2 trials for NASH and hypertriglyceridemia, cited as a potential FGF-21-axis therapy.

SGLT2 inhibitors (dapagliflozin, canagliflozin, empagliflozin) have been shown in rodent and human studies to upregulate hepatic FGF-21 expression and increase plasma FGF-21 concentrations, suggested as a means of augmenting FGF-21 activity in low-FGF-21 ME/FM patients.

A 2025 hepatocyte model study found glucosamine induces dose- and time-dependent increases in FGF-21 mRNA and protein via the Akt/mTOR/p70S6K axis with essential dependence on PGC-1α, though it may impair insulin sensitivity.

Clinical and preclinical studies cited show low-carbohydrate, high-protein diets can reduce plasma FGF-21 levels by improving metabolic efficiency, while protein restriction directly induces FGF-21 expression, suggested as relevant for ME+FM patients with high FGF-21/suspected resistance.

PPARγ agonists such as rosiglitazone have demonstrated efficacy in upregulating β-klotho and restoring FGF-21 responsiveness in metabolically stressed tissues, proposed as a strategy for FGF-21 resistance in ME+FM patients with high FGF-21.

Synthetic FGF-21 mimetics/receptor agonists such as bispecific proteins and monoclonal antibodies (mimAb1, Avimer C3201) directly activate the FGFR1/β-klotho complex, replicating FGF-21 metabolic effects without requiring elevated endogenous hormone, proposed to bypass upstream resistance mechanisms.

Senolytic therapies and anti-inflammatory agents such as IL-1β inhibitors or NF-κB pathway modulators may indirectly restore β-klotho expression and improve FGF-21 receptor sensitivity by reducing chronic inflammation and tissue stress.

Objective BrainCheck cognitive testing in ME+FM patients showed no significant differences across FGF-21 strata in any cognitive domain, and correlations between FGF-21 and cognitive scores remained weak and non-significant in this group.
ME patients scored significantly worse than healthy controls on SF-36, MFI-20, and DSQ questionnaires including PEM, cognitive dysfunction, and sleep disturbance domains.
Baseline plasma proteomic comparison between ME and HC groups showed no proteins meeting multiple-testing-corrected significance, with only a handful of nominal (uncorrected) differences.
Plasma haptoglobin levels significantly decreased from baseline to 90 minutes after a standardized post-exertional stress test in ME patients, identified via label-free proteomics.
In healthy controls, Hp levels remained undetectable and unchanged between baseline and post-stress timepoints, contrasting the ME-specific reduction.
An orthogonal high-sensitivity HPLC assay on non-depleted plasma replicated the post-stress reduction of Hp in ME patients with a medium effect size.
HPLC quantification confirmed no significant change in Hp levels in healthy controls following the stress challenge, supporting disease specificity of the effect.
Lower baseline plasma Hp levels were negatively correlated with greater cognitive dysfunction scores in ME patients.
ME patients with severe fatigue (MFI-20 severe category) had lower baseline plasma Hp levels than those with mild-to-moderate fatigue.
Hp phenotype distribution differed between ME patients and healthy controls in the discovery cohort, with underrepresentation of the protective Hp1-1 phenotype in ME.
Validation cohort (n=89 ME patients) replicated the Hp phenotype distribution pattern seen in the discovery cohort, with underrepresentation of Hp1-1 in ME relative to HC.

ME patients with Hp2-1 or Hp2-2 phenotypes experienced more severe PEM (higher DPEMQ scores) than those with Hp1-1, though the difference did not reach significance in a non-parametric test with small unbalanced groups.
Dizziness severity (a DPEMQ item) significantly differed among Hp phenotypes, with Hp1-1 patients reporting the lowest dizziness and Hp2-1 patients the highest.
ME patients with the Hp1-1 phenotype showed better post-exertional cognitive performance (Stroop, immediate recognition, total BrainCheck score) at T90 compared to Hp2-1 and Hp2-2 carriers.

HPLC structural analysis revealed distinct Hp oligomeric profiles for each phenotype: Hp1-1 a single dimer peak, Hp2-1 five peaks (dimer through hexamer), and Hp2-2 two overlapping peaks (tetramer/pentamer).
In ME patients with the Hp2-1 phenotype, higher-order Hp tetramer and pentamer forms were significantly more abundant than in HC with the same phenotype, with shorter chromatographic retention times.

The percentage of Hp tetramer correlated positively with PEM severity (DSQ) and negatively with cognitive function (BrainCheck), while higher Hp pentamer levels were linked to greater cognitive dysfunction and reduced mental flexibility.
Plasma soluble LRP-1 (sLRP-1) levels were significantly elevated in ME patients compared to healthy controls.
Higher plasma sLRP-1 levels significantly correlated with poorer sleep quality scores in ME patients.
sLRP-1 levels were highest in ME patients with the Hp2-1 phenotype, who also had the most severe PEM symptoms, suggesting phenotype-dependent oxidative stress dysregulation.
Non-invasive cerebral NIRS monitoring showed a significant post-PEM increase in cerebral total hemoglobin in ME patients, a pattern absent in healthy controls.
ApoA1 was significantly upregulated in ME patients from baseline to 90 minutes post-stress.
Fibulin-1 showed opposite post-stress trajectories between groups: downregulated in ME patients but upregulated in healthy controls.
Alpha-2-HS-glycoprotein (FETUA) was upregulated post-stress in ME patients but downregulated in healthy controls, an inverse response between groups.
The majority of the cohort (61%, 25/41 patients) was diagnosed with hypermobile EDS or Hypermobility Spectrum Disorder.
Classical EDS (types 1 and 2) accounted for 22% of the cohort.
Vascular EDS was diagnosed in 7.3% of the cohort.
Musculoskeletal symptoms were the most common complication in the cohort (90.2%), with chronic joint pain the most frequent feature (63.4%).
Feet deformities occurred in 41.5% of patients, most commonly pes planus.
Bone fractures were relatively rare in the cohort, occurring in only 4.9% of patients.
A higher Beighton hypermobility score was significantly associated with the presence of recurrent joint dislocations.
Cutaneous manifestations were observed in up to 68.3% of patients, most frequently skin hyperextensibility and easy bruising.
Atrophic scarring was significantly less frequent in patients with hypermobile EDS compared to other EDS subtypes.
Classical EDS showed the highest cutaneous involvement among subtypes, with 88.9% of patients presenting skin manifestations.
All patients with vascular EDS had skin manifestations, primarily hematomas.
Psychiatric symptoms were reported in 57.1% of GJH/hypermobile EDS patients, 55.6% of classical EDS patients, and 50% of vascular EDS patients.
Older age was significantly associated with the presence of psychiatric disorders overall in this pediatric EDS/HSD cohort.
When stratified by specific psychiatric diagnosis, the age association was not statistically significant for ADHD or for anxiety and depression individually.
Cardiovascular manifestations were observed in 26.8% of patients, most frequently syncope (17.1%).
Structural cardiac abnormalities identified included mitral valve prolapse in three patients and mitral valve insufficiency in two, with no cases of aortic root dilation.
Only one case of postural orthostatic tachycardia syndrome (POTS) was documented in this pediatric EDS/HSD cohort.
Neurological manifestations were reported in 51.2% of patients, with migraine headaches being the most common finding; no Arnold-Chiari malformations were identified.
Digestive disorders were present in 41.5% of patients, with chronic abdominal pain being the most frequent (22%).
Chronic abdominal pain was significantly associated with the presence of migraines in this cohort, suggesting a shared systemic dysautonomic or psychosomatic mechanism.
Ophthalmological manifestations, limited to refractive defects, were present in 43.9% of patients.
Over half of patients (51.2%) had affected first-degree relatives, and relatives' diagnosis preceded the child's diagnosis in 83.3% of cases.
Genetic testing of parents showed maternal inheritance in 13.2% of cases, while nearly 34% of mothers had compatible symptoms without formal genetic study.
Diagnostic yield of clinical exome sequencing was 100% among EDS subtypes with known molecular basis (representing 74% of tested patients).
No clear candidate pathogenic variants were detected in 26% of tested patients, all clinically compatible with hEDS/HSD, consistent with the lack of a known molecular marker for hEDS.

Variants of uncertain significance (VUS) in TNXB, ELN, PIEZO2, and MYH11 were identified in some hEDS/HSD patients, all inherited from a parent, mostly with similar clinical features, but pathogenicity remains unconfirmed.
A UK population-based study found diagnosed prevalence of hEDS and Hypermobility Spectrum Disorder combined to be roughly 1 in 500, far higher than the traditional estimate of 1 in 5000-20,000.

Patients experiencing diagnostic delay for rare diseases report significantly higher emotional distress (frustration, irritability, anxiety, fear, depressive symptoms), and only about a third receive mental health support during the pre-diagnostic period.

Low-dose naltrexone (LDN) is cited as potentially effective for pain reduction, mood stabilization, and energy enhancement at individualized doses in patients with nociplastic pain conditions like hEDS, with proposed effects on microglial activity and mast cell modulation.

A nationwide Swedish study found individuals with EDS have heightened risk for bipolar disorder, ADHD, depression, and attempted suicide, though it is unclear whether this reflects genetic or environmental (illness-burden) contributions.

Eccles and Owens propose that the high co-occurrence of joint hypermobility and autonomic hyperactivity may be relevant to neurodevelopmental profiles, noting overlapping features between hEDS and ADHD such as heightened sensory sensitivity, anxiety, and difficulty with focus and organization.

Casanova et al. (2020) reviewed literature/clinical data concluding individuals with hEDS and HSD exhibit significantly higher rates of neurodevelopmental conditions (ADHD, autism spectrum disorder) and psychiatric issues (anxiety, depression, mood instability).
As a woman, the author cites literature indicating she is more likely to experience medical gaslighting than male patients.
Chronic pain often correlates with higher risk of anxiety and depression, particularly when individuals feel powerless over their condition.
Rare diseases significantly reduce social participation, with unemployment, mobility limitations, and poor access to support systems intensifying social isolation.

Cognitive-behavioural techniques and Acceptance and Commitment Therapy (ACT) show promise in managing chronic symptoms by targeting maladaptive thought patterns, increasing psychological flexibility, and improving functioning in individuals with persistent pain and complex conditions.
Research supports the importance of vocational and educational adjustments in improving quality of life for individuals with chronic conditions.

De Percin et al. describe how families affected by EDS experience a mix of emotions including relief upon diagnosis but also frustration, fear about the future, and tension between family members who understand the condition differently.

hEDS management typically includes symptomatic care, physical therapy to improve joint stability and proprioception, lifestyle modifications to prevent injuries, and management of comorbidities like chronic fatigue, gastrointestinal issues, and autonomic dysfunction to improve quality of life.

The first author was diagnosed with hypermobile EDS (hEDS) in 2014 by a geneticist at UCSF, following a 2011 ankle surgery in which the surgeon noted a shredded tendon, prompting suspicion of an underlying connective tissue disorder.

The author reports coexisting conditions including premenstrual dysphoric disorder (PMDD), ADHD, spatial and auditory processing disorders, dysautonomia, mast cell activation disorder, and possible periodic paralysis, described as secondary to her EDS.
The author calculated that EDS-related out-of-pocket living expenses (alternative therapies, special diet, travel to specialists) amount to approximately $500 per month.
hEDS patients had markedly higher total autonomic symptom burden (SAS) scores than healthy controls.
Almost all hEDS patients had a clinically significant abnormal autonomic symptom score, versus none of the controls.
hEDS patients had substantially higher total sensory/neuropathic symptom scores (NTSS-6) than controls.
Nearly 89% of hEDS patients had a clinically significant sensory symptom score compared to none of the controls.
Pain was more common and more severe over the preceding 7 days in hEDS patients compared to controls.
Supine systolic and mean cerebral blood flow velocity in the middle cerebral artery were lower in hEDS than in controls.
Supine cerebrovascular resistance index was higher in hEDS patients than controls, suggesting baseline cerebrovascular dysregulation.
Orthostatic systolic, mean, and diastolic cerebral blood flow velocities during head-up tilt were all significantly lower in hEDS patients than in controls.
Head-up tilt induced a much greater percentage decline in mean cerebral blood flow velocity in hEDS patients than controls.
Orthostatic cerebrovascular resistance index and cerebrovascular reactivity were higher in hEDS than controls, consistent with abnormal cerebral autoregulation.
Orthostatic end-tidal CO2 was lower in hEDS patients than controls, consistent with a hypocapnic component of cerebral hypoperfusion in some patients.
Autonomic failure (mild in most cases, involving cardiovagal, adrenergic, and sudomotor domains) was detected in the large majority of hEDS patients and none of the controls.
Epidermal nerve fiber density on skin biopsy at both proximal thigh and calf was reduced in hEDS patients compared to controls.
Sweat gland nerve fiber density was reduced in hEDS patients compared to controls, providing new direct structural evidence of sudomotor autonomic fiber degeneration.

SFN, defined by combinations of clinical sensory symptoms with abnormal epidermal or sweat gland nerve fiber density or sudomotor testing, was highly prevalent in hEDS patients, with rates depending on diagnostic criteria used.
A subset of hEDS patients had mixed SFN, with both abnormal epidermal and sweat gland nerve fiber densities alongside symptoms.

During head-up tilt testing, distinct orthostatic syndromes characterized by reduced cerebral blood flow velocity without orthostatic hypotension were identified in hEDS, including POTS, hypocapnic cerebral hypoperfusion, and orthostatic cerebral hypoperfusion syndrome (OCHOS), the latter being newly linked to hEDS in this study.
Orthostatic hypotension was present in a minority of hEDS patients, with neurogenic orthostatic hypotension (a marker of more advanced sympathetic adrenergic failure) present in fewer still.
Orthostatic lightheadedness/dizziness during head-up tilt was much more common in hEDS patients than in controls.

Reduced orthostatic cerebral blood flow velocity (and age), but not autonomic failure, abnormal end-tidal CO2, tachycardic heart rate response, or orthostatic hypotension, significantly predicted the presence of orthostatic lightheadedness/dizziness in logistic regression.
A substantial proportion of hEDS patients had a history of symptoms associated with mast cell activation syndrome and used antihistamine medication.

The authors hypothesize that aberrant mast cell activation near connective tissue surrounding small fibers may release vasoactive and inflammatory mediators contributing to small fiber neuropathy in hEDS.
Depression, headaches, anxiety, irritable bowel syndrome, and mast cell activation symptoms were the most common comorbidities among hEDS patients.
A subset of hEDS patients showed abnormal laboratory inflammatory and autoimmune markers, most commonly high-sensitivity CRP, TNF-alpha, trisulfated heparin disaccharide antibody, and ferritin.

A prior study found that a subgroup of patients with ME/CFS and joint hypermobility syndromes had reduced orthostatic cerebral blood flow measured by Doppler ultrasound of neck arteries, a finding this study's authors extend using transcranial Doppler in a larger hEDS-specific cohort.

Prenatal exome sequencing of amniotic fluid identified a novel de novo heterozygous COL3A1 variant (c.4109A>G, p.Tyr1370Cys), classified as likely pathogenic, causing vascular Ehlers-Danlos syndrome in the fetus.

Early second-trimester ultrasound at 16+2 weeks detected micrognathia (inferior facial angle 42°, below normal) and trigonocephaly, prompting differential diagnosis for genetic syndromes including connective tissue disorders.

At follow-up ultrasound at 19+3 weeks gestation, the fetus showed absence of cardiac activity and generalized hydrops involving the chest, abdomen, and face, followed by induced labor and fetal demise.
Placental histology showed reduced weight, feto-maternal malperfusion, and superficial implantation, which the authors suggest may be linked to the COL3A1 alteration compromising collagen integrity.

Prior literature indicates fetal vEDS is primarily associated with preterm birth, low birth weight, and premature rupture of membranes, likely due to reduced type III collagen affecting amniotic sac integrity.
Hip dislocation and amniotic band syndrome are reported as common anomalies in fetal vEDS, attributed to increased membrane fragility causing amnion rupture.
Postnatal literature describes facial anomalies in vEDS including micrognathia, a thin vermilion border, a narrow nose, and prominent eyes.
Among 2,695 patients evaluated using the 2017 diagnostic criteria, 60.6% were diagnosed with HSD, 18.3% with hEDS, 10.7% with L-HSD or H-HSD, and 10.4% were controls without any of these diagnoses.
Controls seen at the EDS Clinic were significantly older on average than patients diagnosed with hEDS or any type of HSD.
Over 85% of patients in each diagnostic group self-reported as female, with the highest percentage of females among patients diagnosed with HSD.
BMI was lower in controls and hEDS patients compared to patients with HSD or L-HSD/H-HSD.

Patients with historical or localized HSD (L-HSD/H-HSD) self-reported significantly more joint pain, subluxations, sprains, easy bruising, muscle weakness, TMJ dysfunction, and dislocations compared to controls.
L-HSD/H-HSD patients self-reported joint pain and muscle weakness more often than patients diagnosed with hEDS or HSD, suggesting greater musculoskeletal symptom severity in this subgroup.

L-HSD/H-HSD patients self-reported all examined allergy/asthma-related symptoms (allergy/atopy, palpitations, multiple sensitivities, chest discomfort, shortness of breath, sun sensitivity, hives, rash, oral ulcers, wheezing) significantly more often than controls.
L-HSD/H-HSD patients reported multiple sensitivities, shortness of breath, sun sensitivity, and wheezing more often than patients diagnosed with hEDS or HSD.

L-HSD/H-HSD patients self-reported all examined neurological symptoms and comorbidities—including brain fog, headache, light-headedness, numbness/tingling, migraine, autonomic dysfunction, and ASD—significantly more often than controls.

L-HSD/H-HSD patients reported abdominal pain/cramps, heat and cold intolerance, multiple sensitivities, ADD/ADHD, hearing difficulties, and autism spectrum disorder (ASD) more often than patients diagnosed with hEDS or HSD.

Over half of the GI symptoms/comorbidities examined (abdominal pain, diarrhea, constipation, bowel cramps, GERD, IBS, dyspepsia, loss of appetite, frequent loose stools, vomiting, hemorrhoids, rectal prolapse) were self-reported more often in L-HSD/H-HSD patients than controls.
L-HSD/H-HSD patients reported abdominal pain/cramps, constipation, bowel cramps, and GERD more often than patients diagnosed with hEDS or HSD.

Half of the sleep-related symptoms examined (difficulty falling/staying asleep, insomnia, idiopathic hypersomnia, snoring, narcolepsy, circadian rhythm disorders) were self-reported more often in L-HSD/H-HSD patients than controls.
L-HSD/H-HSD patients reported snoring and narcolepsy more often than patients diagnosed with hEDS or HSD.

Over half of psychological symptoms/comorbidities examined (anxiety, depression, depressed mood, nervousness, abuse history, PTSD, ADD/ADHD, ASD) were self-reported more often in L-HSD/H-HSD patients than controls, but other psychological symptoms were not elevated.

L-HSD/H-HSD patients self-reported significantly more of the 100 examined symptoms/comorbidities than controls (62%) or HSD patients (58% relative to controls), while hEDS patients differed from controls for only 20% of symptoms, indicating L-HSD/H-HSD and HSD share a similarly high symptom burden distinct from hEDS.

Twenty of the 100 symptoms/comorbidities examined (including joint pain, muscle weakness, multiple sensitivities, wheezing/shortness of breath, GERD, abdominal pain/cramps, constipation, heat/cold intolerance, hearing difficulties, ADHD, ASD, snoring, and narcolepsy) were significantly higher in L-HSD/H-HSD patients than in those diagnosed with hEDS or HSD, supporting inclusion of L-HSD/H-HSD within the HSD diagnostic category.

Approximately 70% of patients seen at the Mayo Clinic Florida EDS Clinic (including L-HSD/H-HSD) were previously found to also carry a diagnosis of fibromyalgia, and those with comorbid fibromyalgia reported significantly more symptoms/comorbidities than those without, suggesting more severe disease.

A cited study found plasma biomarkers reflecting extracellular matrix (ECM) degradation (collagen I and fibronectin fragments) in both hEDS and HSD patients but not in controls, suggesting mast cell-driven ECM breakdown as a shared mechanism underlying hypermobility and overlapping symptoms.
A cited RNA-sequencing study of skin fibroblasts from 20 hEDS, 20 HSD, and 40 control patients found overlapping gene expression profiles between hEDS and HSD.

hEDS participants reported symptom onset around age 9.3 but were not diagnosed until age 31.4, an average diagnostic delay of 22.1 years; HSD participants had a shorter but still lengthy delay of 17.5 years from a later symptom onset of 12.3 years.
A large majority of participants reported a specific triggering event (puberty, viral/bacterial pathogen, trauma, or pregnancy) preceding or worsening symptom onset, more commonly in hEDS than HSD.
Participants reported a high burden of co-occurring conditions, averaging 24 diagnoses in hEDS and 17 in HSD out of 192 conditions assessed.
Individuals with hEDS spent substantial time and resources managing healthcare, including 5+ hours/week coordinating care, more specialist visits than HSD, and greater travel distances for care.
Chronic pain was reported by nearly all hEDS and HSD participants, with the neck, lower back, and shoulders as the most frequent pain sites, and it was the symptom most often ranked as most severe.
Among pain treatments tried, hEDS participants rated medical marijuana and ketamine as the most effective for chronic pain.
SSRIs and SNRIs, though increasingly used for pain in hEDS, were considered effective by only a small proportion of participants who tried them.

hEDS participants were over twice as likely as HSD participants to experience anesthesia complications including shortened effect, insufficient pain control, intubation complications, and anaphylaxis.
hEDS participants were over 40 times more likely to report tendon rupture than the general population (All of Us dataset).
Migraine was the most frequently reported neurological diagnosis in both groups, significantly more common in hEDS than HSD.
Small-fiber neuropathy, along with tinnitus, herniated disks, spinal stenosis, Chiari malformation, kyphoscoliosis, and tethered cord syndrome, were more common in hEDS than HSD.

Autonomic dysfunction was highly prevalent, reported by 71.4% of hEDS and 40.3% of HSD participants as at least one diagnosed autonomic disorder, with fatigue, dizziness, and brain fog the most common symptoms.
POTS was the most frequently diagnosed autonomic disorder, more common in hEDS than HSD, with an extraordinarily elevated risk in hEDS compared to the general population.
The hEDS group had approximately 1.5 times higher risk of GERD compared to both the HSD group and the general population.
IBS was the most reported GI diagnosis in hEDS and HSD, with the mixed subtype most prevalent.
MCAS and chronic urticaria were dramatically more common in hEDS relative to the general population, with MCAS over 1000-fold and chronic urticaria over 230-fold more common.
Pineal cysts were over 160 times more likely to be reported in hEDS participants than in the general population.
The risk of central adrenal insufficiency was nearly fivefold higher in hEDS relative to the general population.
hEDS participants had almost 14 times higher risk of pernicious anemia compared to the general population.
The risk of DVT was over threefold higher in hEDS compared to HSD participants.
The risk of pelvic organ prolapse was nearly four times higher in hEDS compared to HSD, and endometriosis was also more common in hEDS.

Among those who had been pregnant, the majority in both groups reported pregnancy complications (spontaneous abortion, preterm labor, failure to progress, premature rupture of membranes, stillbirth), with significantly higher prevalence in hEDS.
Recurrent UTIs were over 130 times and voiding dysfunction nearly 880 times more common in hEDS than the general population, and both were also more frequent in hEDS than HSD.

Neurodivergent diagnoses (ADHD, ASD, OCD, learning disorder) were significantly more common in hEDS than in the general population, with about half of hEDS participants reporting at least one neurodiversity-related disorder.

Anxiety, depression, PTSD and most sleep disorders (insomnia, restless legs syndrome) were significantly more prevalent in hEDS than in the general population, while obstructive sleep apnea and substance use disorder were significantly lower and bipolar disorder showed no difference.

Comorbidity co-occurrence analysis revealed strong overlap clusters, with anxiety-depression (43.3%), anxiety-allergies (39.3%), depression-allergies (37.2%), and allergies-migraine (37.0%) showing the highest Jaccard overlap indices among hEDS participants.

About half of survey respondents with a reported HSD diagnosis actually met formal 2017 diagnostic criteria for hEDS, while about a quarter of those reporting hEDS did not meet the criteria, indicating substantial diagnostic discordance between self-reported and criteria-validated classification.

Participants with hEDS had significantly higher Beighton hypermobility scores and higher rates of joint dislocations/subluxations than HSD participants; the most affected joints (shoulders, hips) are notably not part of the Beighton scoring system.

Allergy-related disorders were reported by 89.7% of hEDS and 78.0% of HSD participants, with hEDS showing increased risk of MCAS, chronic urticaria, and general allergies, and more frequent anaphylaxis episodes compared to HSD.

Structural cardiac abnormalities such as mitral valve prolapse and aortic root dilatation were relatively low in prevalence in this dataset despite being part of the 2017 hEDS diagnostic criteria, though mitral valve defects, stroke, and tricuspid valve defects were significantly higher than the general population, and lung disease and atrial fibrillation were significantly lower.
Pelvic organ prolapse was reported at nearly four times the rate in hEDS participants compared to HSD participants.

Endometriosis was reported more commonly in hEDS participants than HSD participants, and hEDS participants also had markedly increased risk of PCOS, vaginismus, and pelvic congestion syndrome compared to the general population.

The majority of pregnant participants in both groups reported pregnancy complications, with a significantly higher prevalence among hEDS participants, including spontaneous abortion, preterm labor, failure to progress, premature rupture of membranes, and stillbirth.
Recurrent urinary tract infections were 1.63 times more common in hEDS participants compared to HSD, and over 130 times more common compared to the general All of Us population.

Voiding dysfunction occurred at nearly twice the rate in hEDS compared to HSD, with a similar increase for overactive bladder syndrome, and voiding dysfunction was nearly 880 times more common in hEDS versus the general population.
The hEDS group had a significantly higher risk of atopic dermatitis compared to the All of Us general population group, though dermatological diagnosis rates were similar between hEDS and HSD.

Skin-related symptoms including soft/velvety skin, abnormally stretchy skin, and unexplained stretch marks were all more prevalent in hEDS compared to HSD, consistent with their inclusion in the 2017 hEDS diagnostic criteria.
89.7% of hEDS and 78.0% of HSD participants reported at least one allergy-related disorder, with allergies present at a higher rate in hEDS than HSD.

Compared to HSD, hEDS participants had increased risk of mast cell activation syndrome, chronic urticaria, and allergies; relative to the general population, chronic urticaria was over 230 times more common and MCAS over 1000 times more common in hEDS.
Anaphylaxis episodes were reported significantly more frequently in hEDS compared to HSD participants.

29.9% of hEDS participants and 22.0% of HSD participants reported at least one autoimmune condition, with psoriasis, rheumatoid arthritis, and systemic lupus erythematosus showing comparable prevalence between groups.

82.1% of hEDS and 72.7% of HSD participants reported at least one ocular disorder, with hEDS showing higher prevalence of astigmatism, myopia, hyperopia, macular degeneration, and keratoconus compared to the All of Us dataset, but similar retinal detachment rates.
All dental disorders assessed in the survey, including TMJ disorder, enamel defects, and early onset periodontitis, were significantly more frequent in the hEDS group than in the All of Us group.

Anxiety, depression, and PTSD were highly prevalent in both groups, and each mental health and sleep-related disorder assessed (except obstructive sleep apnea and substance use disorder, which were lower, and bipolar disorder, which was not significantly different) was reported at significantly higher rates in hEDS compared to All of Us.

49.1% of hEDS and 39.7% of HSD participants reported at least one neurodivergence-related diagnosis, with ADHD, autism spectrum disorder, OCD, and learning disorder present at significantly higher rates in hEDS than in the All of Us general population.

A comorbidity co-occurrence matrix in hEDS revealed the strongest condition-pair overlaps were between anxiety and depression (43.3%), anxiety and allergies (39.3%), depression and allergies (37.2%), and allergies and migraine (37.0%), indicating clustering across psychiatric, immunologic, and neurological domains.

Half of survey respondents with a reported HSD diagnosis actually met the diagnostic criteria for hEDS, while a quarter of those with an hEDS diagnosis did not meet the 2017 criteria, revealing substantial diagnostic discordance between self-reported and criteria-validated classification.

The three most frequently affected joints reported by hEDS participants (shoulders and hips, among others) are not included in the Beighton score, a recognized limitation that may contribute to misclassification or underdiagnosis.

The authors hypothesize that the observed high prevalence of immune dysregulation, autonomic dysfunction, and gastrointestinal dysmotility supports the possibility that neuroimmune or inflammatory pathways contribute to the broader hEDS/HSD phenotype, suggesting overlap with autoimmune or autoinflammatory conditions rather than purely connective tissue pathology.

The association between viral infections as symptom triggers and worsening symptoms is proposed to support a potential link between hEDS, immune dysregulation, and post-viral syndromes such as long COVID and ME/CFS.

The study population was predominantly white, female, and digitally literate, limiting generalizability, and reliance on self-reported data introduces recall and diagnostic-uncertainty biases without clinical verification.
Patients with celiac disease had a significantly higher prevalence of Ehlers-Danlos syndrome diagnosis compared with matched controls (2.7% vs 0.3%).
In univariable logistic regression, celiac disease was associated with a 9.73-fold increased odds of an Ehlers-Danlos syndrome diagnosis.

After adjusting for autoimmune diseases (Sjogren's syndrome, rheumatoid arthritis, systemic lupus erythematosus), celiac disease remained associated with an 8.93-fold increased odds of Ehlers-Danlos syndrome diagnosis.
Among over 400,000 All of Us participants, 721 had an EDS diagnosis, yielding an overall prevalence of approximately 0.18%.

The authors hypothesize that connective tissue dysfunction in EDS may cause intestinal barrier instability ('leaky gut'), allowing luminal antigens to enter the bloodstream and trigger autoimmune activation, potentially predisposing to celiac disease.
Whole-exome and Sanger sequencing identified a heterozygous COL3A1 splicing variant (c.3417+5G>A) predicted to cause exon skipping, confirming the diagnosis of vascular Ehlers-Danlos syndrome (vEDS).

The patient presented with an atypical initial manifestation of vEDS consisting of massive spontaneous hemothorax and a large right chest wall hematoma, without prior visceral or major arterial rupture.
Interleukin-6 was elevated at admission in this vEDS patient presenting with hemothorax.
Selective embolization of dilated intercostal arteries via DSA successfully controlled bleeding and stabilized hemoglobin levels, avoiding surgical thoracotomy.
Beta-blocker therapy (recommended, e.g., propranolol) may reduce arterial wall stress and hemodynamic load in vEDS patients, potentially decreasing vascular events, though evidence remains limited.
Epidemiological literature indicates 25% of vEDS patients manifest prominent symptoms before age 20, over 80% have disease onset before age 40, and median survival is 48 years.

The most common initial manifestations of vEDS reported in the literature are arterial rupture (46%) and gastrointestinal perforation (19%), whereas pneumothorax and hemothorax as initial presentations are relatively rare (12.5% and 3%, respectively).

Some studies report that spontaneous pneumothorax/hemothorax may precede arterial lesions in 17.7% of vEDS patients, supporting consideration of vEDS in young patients with unexplained spontaneous P/HTX.

The patient had a strong family history of premature arterial rupture (maternal uncle died in his 40s from abdominal aortic rupture; maternal grandmother died in her 50s from rupture of a major abdominal artery), which raised suspicion of an underlying hereditary connective tissue disorder.

The patient exhibited multisystem arterial abnormalities (recurrent bilateral pneumothoraces, right subclavian artery aneurysm requiring vascular replacement, carotid artery dissection, and right common iliac artery dissection) that had not previously prompted genetic evaluation for a hereditary connective tissue disorder.

Multiple pulmonary bullae predominantly in the upper lobes were present in this non-smoking patient, suggesting that underlying connective tissue abnormality contributed to subpleural vascular fragility and hemothorax, distinct from typical smoking-related bullous disease.
All three tested pathogenic variants (Y182C, D207H, G217S) caused complete loss of function of recombinant β3GalT6 enzyme expressed and purified from E. coli.
Circular dichroism showed the mutant proteins retained a WT-like α-helical secondary structure, ruling out gross structural misfolding as the cause of loss of function.

Molecular dynamics simulations identified a consistent loss of the K193-D242 salt bridge stabilizing the catalytic domain loop as a common structural mechanism underlying loss of function in all three mutants.

Enzyme activity was barely detectable, at or just above background, in patient fibroblasts (P2, P3, P5) and in B3GALT6-KO cells re-expressing mutant enzymes, confirming near-complete loss of galactosyltransferase activity in a cellular context.

Despite complete loss of enzymatic activity in vitro, B3GALT6-KO cells re-expressing WT or Y182C retained substantial GAG synthesis capacity, indicating residual/compensatory GAG biosynthesis in cellulo.

siRNA knockdown of B3GAT3 (encoding GlcAT-I) in spEDS patient fibroblasts further reduced decorin GAG-substitution, implicating GlcAT-I in the residual GAG synthesis occurring despite β3GalT6 loss of function.

Recombinant GlcAT-I was highly active toward the canonical trisaccharide analogue Gal-Gal-Xyl-OMN and showed lower but significant activity toward the disaccharide Gal-Xyl-OMN, demonstrating it can generate a noncanonical trisaccharide linker bypassing β3GalT6.

Transcriptome profiling of spEDS patient fibroblasts (P2, P3, P5) versus 6 controls identified 11 genes with transcriptome-wide significance, including collagen-crosslinking genes LOXL1, LOXL2, LOX and PLOD1, which showed higher expression in spEDS samples.

Developmental transcription factor genes HOXC9, HOXC10 and TBX5 were among the most strongly up- and downregulated genes in spEDS patient fibroblasts, suggesting perturbation of developmental/morphogenesis pathways.

Gene ontology and pathway analyses of differentially expressed genes in spEDS fibroblasts revealed enrichment of collagen maturation processes (peptidyl-lysine oxidation, collagen fibril organization) and disturbance of the Rho GTPase signaling pathway.

COL12A1 (encoding collagen XII) was identified in the upregulated gene cluster when comparing spEDS transcriptomic data to a curated spEDS gene signature, highlighting a potential transcriptional role of collagen XII in the ECM alteration seen in spEDS.

Comparison of the spEDS transcriptome with 4 other EDS-subtype microarray datasets (B3GALT6-deficient siblings, JHS/EDS-HT, vEDS, cEDS) showed no genes common to all 5 studies and only 11.2% overlap between any two datasets, indicating largely subtype-specific transcriptomic signatures.

SULF1, encoding an enzyme involved in heparan-sulfate GAG chain maturation, was among 12 genes dysregulated in both the current spEDS cohort and a prior B3GALT6-deficient sibling transcriptome, and was also dysregulated in a JHS/EDS-HT cohort, suggesting shared involvement in cell-signaling/growth-factor pathways.

In an ATDC5 3D pseudotissue model, CRISPR-mediated B3galt6 knockout led to reduced abundance of GAG chains on large proteoglycans (primarily aggrecan) and barely detectable glycosylation of endogenous decorin.
Decorin glycosylation was dramatically reduced in spEDS patient fibroblasts compared with controls, with the size of remaining CS/DS chains increased in patients P2 and P5 but not P3.

In B3galt6-KO pseudotissue, collagen XII (a FACIT collagen also acting as a proteoglycan) was present as an unglycosylated long-form band lacking GAG chains, whereas control cells expressed the GAG-substituted long form.
Histological analysis showed that B3galt6-KO ATDC5 pseudotissue had an irregular surface and less coherent matrix compared with control, indicating disrupted ECM integrity upon gene knockout.
Gravity assays showed significantly increased tissue extensibility (~27%) in B3galt6-KO pseudotissue compared with control, indicating disturbed biomechanical behavior of the ECM.

Atomic force microscopy nanoindentation showed B3galt6-KO pseudotissues had significantly higher tissue stiffness (Young's modulus) than control, attributed to loss of proteoglycan-GAGs and disrupted collagen microarchitecture.

Based solely on osteological evidence, the authors excluded Ehlers-Danlos syndrome (along with Marfan syndrome, malignancy, and syphilis) as the primary cause of the chronic sternal erosion attributed to an ascending aortic aneurysm in this 17th-18th century skeleton.

Proteomic analysis of Myh11ΔK/ΔK aortas identified 1730 significantly differentially expressed proteins out of 6499 quantified, comprising 922 downregulated and 808 upregulated proteins compared with wild-type aortas.
Multiple integrin subunits, components of focal adhesion complexes, were downregulated at the protein level in Myh11ΔK/ΔK aortas.

KEGG pathway analysis and fold-change-specific enrichment analysis both showed strong enrichment of extracellular matrix and focal adhesion related pathways among dysregulated proteins in Myh11ΔK/ΔK aortas.

Coagulation-related proteins including platelet factors 2, 4, 5, 10, and 13b and thrombomodulin were downregulated, and coagulation/wound-healing pathways were among the most altered biological processes in Myh11ΔK/ΔK aortas.

Proteins comprising mitochondrial respiratory chain complexes I, II, and III, as well as mitochondrial ribosomal proteins, were upregulated in Myh11ΔK/ΔK aortas, suggesting increased aerobic respiration and translation.

Cross-referencing proteomic and prior transcriptomic FSEA identified 19 pathways commonly attenuated in both datasets, with transmembrane transporter activity, cell projection, and plasma membrane-bound cell projection (which include focal adhesion components integrins, paxillin, and Src) most strongly downregulated at both protein and transcript levels.

Protein-protein interaction network analysis identified a high-scoring MCODE cluster in which Myh11 directly interacts with paxillin, integrin subunit β5, and vinculin, and indirectly with vinculin, integrin subunit α5, Src, VASP, and zyxin.

Using public microarray data of stretch-stimulated zyxin-knockout VSMCs, the authors found 621 genes downregulated relative to wild-type, and 51 of these overlapped with proteins downregulated in Myh11ΔK/ΔK aortas, implicating zyxin as a direct transcriptional regulator of these genes.

Among the 51 zyxin-regulated downregulated genes, Itga5 and syndecan 4 mapped to ECM-receptor interaction and cytoskeleton-in-muscle-cells pathways, and Itga5 and PDGFRβ mapped to the focal adhesion pathway, linking zyxin regulation to ECM/focal adhesion dysregulation.
Tenascin XB, a protein whose haploinsufficiency or pathogenic variants cause Ehlers-Danlos syndrome, was found downregulated in Myh11ΔK/ΔK aortas, suggesting overlapping molecular pathology with EDS.
TGFβ2 and TGFβ receptors 1 and 2, genes mutated in Loeys-Dietz syndrome, were downregulated in Myh11ΔK/ΔK aortas, suggesting shared molecular features with this connective tissue disorder.

The authors propose a mechanistic model in which Myh11 K1256del misfolding reduces recruitment of paxillin and vinculin to focal adhesions and impairs zyxin binding, preventing TRPC3/ET1/ANP/cGMP/PKG-mediated zyxin phosphorylation and nuclear translocation, thereby blocking zyxin-activated transcription of mechanoresponsive genes.

The authors suggest that downregulated coagulation and wound-healing pathways may explain why 75% of Myh11ΔK/ΔK mice died within four days of angiotensin II-induced aortic dissection in the earlier study.

Compared with the control group, pregnant women completing an 8-week prenatal Pilates program showed no significant change in ACL laxity (measured under 134N and 200N anterior forces) across baseline, week 4, and week 8, whereas the control group exhibited significant increases in laxity at both forces.

Beighton scores for generalized joint hypermobility remained stable in the Pilates group over 8 weeks, while the control group showed a small but significant increase, with a significant between-group difference favoring the Pilates group.

Pelvic Girdle Questionnaire (PGQ) scores remained stable within the Pilates group across all time points, whereas the control group experienced significant worsening at weeks 4 and 8, with a large, significant between-group effect favoring Pilates.
Weekly step counts (physical activity) were comparable between groups at 4 weeks but significantly higher in the Pilates group than the control group at 8 weeks.
The prenatal Pilates program had high adherence (91% of scheduled sessions) and no adverse events or exercise-related complications were reported in either group.
The procollagen N-proteinase responsible for maturation of type I procollagen, absent in dermatosparaxis, was identified as ADAMTS2, a 1211-amino-acid zinc metalloproteinase.
All reported patients with the dermatosparaxis type of Ehlers-Danlos syndrome (dEDS) carry biallelic pathogenic variants in ADAMTS2.
Only 16 dEDS patients from 15 independent families have been reported in the literature to date.

Homozygous Adamts2 knockout mice develop craniofacial abnormalities, thin/soft/fragile skin, and decreased fur density with thinner hair follicles compared to wild-type littermates by two months of age, recapitulating dEDS.

Lungs of Adamts2 knockout mice show an emphysema-like appearance with decreased parenchymal density and significantly reduced type I and III procollagen processing, though no gross collagen abnormalities were seen histologically.

Arthrochalasia EDS (aEDS), caused by heterozygous COL1A1 or COL1A2 defects skipping exon 6 (the ADAMTS2 cleavage site), has a milder skin phenotype than dEDS but more pronounced generalized joint hypermobility, congenital hip dislocation, and recurrent dislocations.
Autocatalytic cleavage that partially removes the procollagen N-propeptidase domain increases ADAMTS2 enzymatic activity 3- to 4-fold, indicating a negative regulatory role for this domain.
TGFβ1 induces ADAMTS2 mRNA and protein levels in MG-63 human osteosarcoma (fibroblastic) cells.
Interleukin-1α and interleukin-6 induce ADAMTS2 mRNA and protein levels in MG-63 and Saos-2 cells, likely via JNK-mediated signaling.
Hypoxia-inducible factor-1 (HIF-1) increases ADAMTS2 mRNA and protein levels in human umbilical vein endothelial cells by activating hypoxia response elements in the ADAMTS2 promoter.
Glucocorticoid treatment increases ADAMTS2 mRNA levels in monocyte/macrophage cell lines (via the glucocorticoid receptor) but not in epithelial/fibroblast lines or T/B lymphocytes.

Recombinant ADAMTS2 inhibits proliferation of endothelial cells in vitro, induces morphological changes and anoikis-like apoptosis, reduces vessel density in embryoid bodies, and ADAMTS2-overexpressing tumors implanted in nude mice were smaller and less vascularized than controls, indicating an anti-angiogenic, pro-apoptotic, anti-tumorigenic activity independent of catalytic function.
Adamts2 knockout mice displayed higher levels of neovascularization than wild-type after laser burn-induced choroidal injury, consistent with an anti-angiogenic role for ADAMTS2.

Adamts2−/− and Adamts14−/− mice showed reduced lymphatic vessel diameter and spatial distribution in dorsal ear skin, exacerbated in Adamts2−/−;Adamts14−/− double knockouts, with Adamts2−/− and double KO mice (but not Adamts14−/− alone) developing lymphedema and impaired lymphatic drainage.

ADAMTS2 significantly contributes to N-terminal cleavage and inactivation of Reelin in postnatal cerebral cortex and hippocampus (less so in cerebellum), as shown using Adamts2 knockout mice; reduced Reelin signaling has been linked to neurological diseases including autism, schizophrenia, ataxias, Alzheimer's disease, and traumatic brain injury.

Adamts2−/−;Adamts14−/− double knockout mice develop epidermal lesions from a dysregulated immune system, preceded by T-lymphocyte accumulation in the dermis and keratinocyte apoptosis; blood T lymphocytes were more activated and secreted higher IL-2 and IFNγ than wild-type, with similar cytokine trends seen in single knockouts that do not develop lesions.

Male Adamts2 knockout mice are sterile due to lack of active mature sperm, with seminiferous tubules showing reduced thickness and increased lumen, potentially via impaired cleavage of the DKK3/Wnt signaling substrate.
A genome-wide association study found ADAMTS2 (along with ADAMTS12, ADAMTS13, and ADAMTS17) associated with pediatric stroke.
An ADAMTS2 variant was identified as a risk factor for cerebral aneurysm.

ADAMTS2 and type I procollagen, along with ADAMTS3 and ADAMTS13 (but not ADAMTS14), are up-regulated in endothelial cells and macrophages within injured fibrous caps of culprit plaques in acute myocardial infarction.

ADAMTS2 expression is up-regulated in failing human hearts, aortic banding-induced hypertrophic mouse hearts, and angiotensin II-treated neonatal rat cardiomyocytes, and Adamts2 knockout mice show exacerbated cardiac hypertrophy, dilatation, and dysfunction after aortic banding, while cardiac-specific ADAMTS2 overexpression blunts this phenotype, indicating a protective role via PI3K/AKT signaling.
MYC-driven ADAMTS2 overexpression can reverse elevated TGFβ activity seen in cardiac fibroblasts and endothelial cells during heart failure progression, via PI3K/AKT and MAPK pathways.

A 2012 transcriptome study found increased ADAMTS2 expression strongly associated with schizophrenia in patients' blood, and this expression normalized in two independent studies following antipsychotic treatment targeting D1/D2 dopamine receptors, with D1-CREB/MAPK-Erk signaling implicated in ADAMTS2 activation.
A transcriptome study identified ADAMTS2 as the gene most strongly associated with cognitive decline in an Alzheimer's disease cohort, with its expression related to amyloid and tau accumulation.

Across multiple cancer types, dysregulated ADAMTS2 expression is generally associated with worse outcomes, although mechanistic insight is largely lacking and results require careful interpretation due to potential confounding by desmoplastic reaction and antibody specificity issues.
In contrast to most cancers, elevated ADAMTS2 levels in non-metastasized versus metastasized colorectal cancer tumors were associated with a good prognosis.

In human dEDS patients and Adamts2 knockout mice, the percentage of fully matured type I collagen varies markedly by tissue, from only 20-30% in skin to 80% in tendon and almost 100% in bone, suggesting compensatory processing enzymes exist.
Adamts2-knockout mice show increased choroidal neovascularization following laser-induced injury, supporting an anti-angiogenic role for ADAMTS2 in vivo.
ADAMTS2-overexpressing tumors implanted in nude mice were smaller and less vascularized than control tumors, without ADAMTS2-overexpressing cells accumulating, suggesting an anti-tumorigenic effect.
Recombinant ADAMTS2 and ADAMTS14 can cleave pro-VEGF-C in vitro, activating VEGFR3 signaling important for lymphangiogenesis.
Adamts2−/− and Adamts14−/− mice show reduced lymphatic vessel diameter, impaired lymphatic drainage, and lymphedema, with effects exacerbated in Adamts2−/−;Adamts14−/− double knockouts.
In an adult corneal lymphangiogenesis model, Adamts2/Adamts14 double knockout mice showed drastically reduced lymphangiogenesis, with single knockouts showing intermediate effects.

Human dEDS patients show only mild lymphatic dysfunction (congenital eyelid edema in most, generalized post-partum edema in one), suggesting a limited role for ADAMTS2/14 loss in primary lymphedema in humans.
ADAMTS2 can cleave and inactivate Reelin in vitro, causing loss of Disabled-1 (Dab1) phosphorylation and decreased downstream neuronal signaling.

Using Adamts2 knockout mice, ADAMTS2 was shown to significantly contribute to N-terminal cleavage/inactivation of Reelin in the postnatal cerebral cortex and hippocampus, but much less so in the cerebellum.
Reduced Reelin expression/signaling has been reported in aging and in several neurological conditions including ataxias, Alzheimer's disease, schizophrenia, autism, and traumatic brain injury.

ADAMTS2 and ADAMTS14 have potential cleavage sites in immune-related proteins including immunoglobulins and complement proteins (C3, C4-B, factor B, factor H) identified in mouse skin proteomic studies.

Adamts2/Adamts14 double knockout mice develop epidermal lesions preceded by T-lymphocyte infiltration in the dermis and keratinocyte apoptosis, with more activated T cells secreting higher IL-2 and IFNγ compared to wild-type.
Male Adamts2 knockout mice are sterile due to lack of active mature sperm, with seminiferous tubules showing reduced thickness and increased lumen.

DKK3, a Wnt/TGFβ signaling modulator involved in testis development, is a substrate of ADAMTS2; reduced DKK3 cleavage in Adamts2-/- mice is proposed to inhibit Wnt signaling and contribute to seminiferous tubule abnormalities.
ADAMTS2 was elevated in non-metastasized colorectal cancer tumors compared with metastasized tumors, associated with good prognosis.
Multiple studies found ADAMTS2 overexpression in gastric cancer tissue versus healthy/adjacent tissue, generally associated with worse prognosis.

ADAMTS2 promotes pancreatic stellate cell differentiation into pro-invasive myofibroblasts in vitro, probably via altered TGFβ signaling, and its overexpression via FTO-mediated demethylation is associated with poor prognosis in pancreatic cancer.
ADAMTS2 and Adamts2 were elevated in highly metastatic murine ovarian cancer cell lines and in omental metastases compared to primary sites, correlating with bad prognosis.
ADAMTS2 was overexpressed in clear cell renal cell carcinoma tissue and increased with tumor progression, correlating with worse prognosis in tumors of stage T2 or greater.
ADAMTS2 was overexpressed in papillary thyroid carcinoma tissue versus adjacent non-neoplastic tissue, associated with poor prognosis, though not confirmed in a larger TCGA dataset comparison.

A complex chromosomal rearrangement between chromosomes 5 and 14 involving the ADAMTS2 locus caused upregulated ADAMTS2 expression in a case of T/myeloid mixed phenotype acute leukemia; ADAMTS2 levels normalized following successful acute lymphoblastic leukemia-based treatment.
ADAMTS2 hypermethylation was observed in buccal rinse cells of cancer-free heavy smokers versus cancer-free non-smokers, potentially reflecting an adaptive/protective response.
ADAMTS2 shows differential expression across thyroid adenoma subclasses and follicular thyroid tumors, suggesting potential as a diagnostic marker for thyroid cancer subtypes.
ADAMTS2 was identified as a candidate prognostic gene in breast cancer.

ADAMTS2 was upregulated in insulin-treated chondrosarcoma cells in vitro, suggesting insulin may mediate effects on chondrosarcoma progression and potentially indicating a negative effect of diabetes therapy on chondrosarcoma.
A genome-wide association study found an association between ADAMTS2 (together with ADAMTS12, ADAMTS13, and ADAMTS17) and pediatric stroke.
An ADAMTS2 genetic variant was identified as a risk factor for cerebral aneurysm.
Reduced Reelin expression and signaling has been reported in several neurological conditions, including autism, alongside ataxias, Alzheimer's disease, schizophrenia, and traumatic brain injury.
A 2012 transcriptome study found a strong association between increased ADAMTS2 expression and schizophrenia in blood from affected individuals.

In two independent drug studies, antipsychotic treatment targeting dopamine D1/D2 receptors reverted elevated ADAMTS2 expression to normal levels in peripheral blood mononuclear cells of schizophrenia patients.
A recent transcriptome study identified ADAMTS2 as the gene most associated with cognitive decline in an Alzheimer's disease cohort, with its expression linked to amyloid and tau accumulation.
A genome-wide association study linked ADAMTS2 (along with ADAMTS12, ADAMTS13, and ADAMTS17) to pediatric stroke.
A subsequent study identified an ADAMTS2 variant as a risk factor for cerebral aneurysm.

ADAMTS2 and type I procollagen, together with ADAMTS3 and ADAMTS13 but not ADAMTS14, were upregulated in endothelial cells and macrophages within injured fibrous caps of culprit plaques in acute myocardial infarction.
ADAMTS2 expression was up-regulated in failing human hearts, in aortic banding-induced hypertrophic mouse hearts, and in angiotensin II-treated neonatal rat cardiomyocyte cultures.

Adamts2 knockout mice had no baseline cardiac phenotype but developed exacerbated cardiac hypertrophy, dilatation, dysfunction and more prominent fibrosis than wild-type after aortic banding surgery, indicating a protective role for ADAMTS2 against pressure-overload cardiac damage.
Cardiac-specific transgenic overexpression of ADAMTS2 blunted the cardiac hypertrophy, fibrosis, and dysfunction phenotype seen after aortic banding.

MYC transcriptionally upregulates ADAMTS2, which was shown to reverse high TGFβ activity in cardiac fibroblasts and endothelial cells during heart failure progression, seemingly via PI3K/AKT and MAPK pathways.

A co-expression network analysis of catecholamine-driven cardiac hypertrophy in mice suggested ADAMTS2 modulates expression of heart failure-related genes Nppa and Nppb in response to isoproterenol treatment, confirmed by siRNA knockdown reducing cardiomyocyte hypertrophy.
DKK3, a known ADAMTS2 substrate with a cardioprotective role, was found to be strongly co-expressed with ADAMTS2 in the heart failure gene network.
Across multiple cancer types, dysregulated ADAMTS2 expression was associated with worse patient outcomes, although the underlying mechanism is generally unclear.
Elevated ADAMTS2 levels were found in non-metastasized colorectal cancer tumors compared with metastasized tumors, associated with a good prognosis.
Elevated ADAMTS2 in the cytoplasm of tumor cells and fibroblasts of gastric carcinoma versus noncancerous tissue was associated with a bad prognosis.
ADAMTS2 overexpression in pancreatic cancer, driven by FTO-mediated epigenetic demethylation, was involved in cell migration and invasion and was associated with poor prognosis.
Elevated ADAMTS2 levels were found in omental metastases compared with primary sites of ovarian cancer, associated with bad prognosis.

ADAMTS2 was overexpressed in clear cell renal cell carcinoma tumor tissue compared with paracancerous tissue, with expression increasing alongside tumor progression, and was associated with bad prognosis in another cohort.

Meprin α and/or β, metalloproteinases capable of cleaving N- and C-propeptides of recombinant type I and III procollagen in vitro, are proposed as candidate enzymes that could partially compensate for absent ADAMTS2 activity in a time- and tissue-dependent manner.

In Adamts2-/- mice and human dEDS patients, the percentage of fully matured type I collagen varies markedly by tissue, from only 20-30% in skin to 80% in tendons and nearly 100% in bone, implying tissue-specific compensatory enzymes.
Tamoxifen-induced Cre recombination reduced Col5a1 expression by 48% (0.52-fold) in I-Col5a1-/- tendons compared to WT, confirming effective knockdown.
Acan gene expression was decreased in I-Col5a1+/- tendons compared to WT and I-Col5a1-/-, suggesting a dose-dependent response to partial collagen V knockdown.
Aspn expression was reduced in both I-Col5a1+/- and I-Col5a1-/- tendons compared to WT.
Col1a1 expression was greater in I-Col5a1-/- tendons relative to WT, suggesting compensatory matrix remodeling in the absence of collagen V.
Col11a1 expression was increased in I-Col5a1-/- tendons relative to WT, though this upregulation was not sufficient to rescue the mechanical deficit from Col5a1 knockdown.
Mmp9 expression was increased in I-Col5a1-/- tendons relative to WT, suggesting increased matrix remodeling activity following collagen V knockdown.
Dcn expression was decreased in I-Col5a1-/- tendons compared to WT, suggesting coordinated downregulation of SLRPs with collagen V loss.
Lum and Runx2 expression showed trending but statistically nonsignificant differences between genotypes.
Collagen V knockdown did not produce histological abnormalities, and had no effect on tendon cellularity or cell shape.
Collagen fibril diameter distributions differed significantly between all three genotypes as measured by TEM.
I-Col5a1-/- tendons had a greater proportion of collagen fibrils with diameters between 104-155 nm compared to I-Col5a1+/- tendons.
Tendon cross-sectional area was not affected by Col5a1 genotype.
Tendon gauge length was subtly decreased in I-Col5a1+/- samples compared to WT and I-Col5a1-/-.
Tendon stiffness and modulus were not affected by collagen V knockdown genotype.
Maximum load at failure was decreased in I-Col5a1-/- tendons compared to I-Col5a1+/- tendons.
Maximum stress at failure was decreased in I-Col5a1-/- tendons compared to WT, indicating impaired tendon mechanical integrity after 30 days of collagen V knockdown.
Dynamic modulus and phase shift under cyclic loading were not affected by genotype at any strain or frequency tested.
All tendon samples failed at the tibial insertion (enthesis), suggesting collagen V may have a unique role in regulating enthesis matrix integrity.
Mutations in COL5A1 cause Classic Ehlers-Danlos Syndrome (cEDS) in humans, with an estimated prevalence of 1 in 20,000 people.
Patients with classic EDS experience joint hypermobility and other orthopaedic complications, likely due to connective tissue dysregulation from absent/deficient collagen V.
This study examined only female mice because prior reports indicate a greater incidence of EDS in females than males.
Children with connective tissue disease (CTD) did not have a significantly different rate of proximal junctional kyphosis compared with idiopathic EOS patients after growth-friendly instrumentation.
There was a non-significant trend toward a greater increase in proximal junctional angle from post-implant to 5-year follow-up in CTD patients compared to idiopathic EOS patients.
CTD and idiopathic EOS patients gained similar amounts of thoracic height with growth-friendly instrumentation.
Although overall complication rates did not differ between groups, CTD patients experienced a greater number of complications per patient than idiopathic EOS patients.

Proximal junctional kyphosis is a common complication across the overall early onset scoliosis cohort undergoing growth-friendly instrumentation, occurring in nearly a quarter of patients, though only a small fraction required revision surgery.
No surgical factors or radiographic variables examined were found to be associated with development of proximal junctional kyphosis.
After adjusting for age and gender, aerobic power (estimated VO2max via shuttle run test) was significantly lower in young adults with generalized joint hypermobility compared to controls.
Body mineral percentage/mass was significantly lower in the GJH group compared to controls after adjusting for age and gender.

No significant difference was found between GJH and control groups in fat-free mass percentage, muscle mass percentage, fat mass percentage, body water percentage, protein percentage, or anaerobic power after adjusting for age and gender.

No significant differences were observed between GJH and control groups in demographic/clinical variables including age, weight, height, BMI, total physical activity (IPAQ), smoking status, or gender distribution.
Gender was a significant covariate affecting fat-free mass, muscle mass, fat mass, body water, protein percentage, anaerobic power, and aerobic power across both groups.
Age was a significant covariate for mineral percentage and showed a marginal (non-significant) trend for aerobic power.

There was no statistically significant association between pediatric generalized joint hypermobility and sustaining an injury during intensive interdisciplinary pain treatment, though injury rates were numerically higher in the pGJH group.
Patients with and without pGJH showed similar, statistically significant improvements in health-related disability, pain-catastrophizing, and parent-reported emotional functioning during IIPT.
Treatment gains for both pGJH and non-pGJH patients were maintained and further improved across all outcomes at 1-, 6-, and 12-month follow-up after IIPT completion.
Among 304 patients admitted for chronic pain treatment, 14.8% (n=45) were identified as having pediatric generalized joint hypermobility.

Add-on therapy with LAC and PEA to standard of care produced a significantly greater reduction in FIQR scores over 12 weeks compared to standard of care alone in fibromyalgia patients with clinical signs of small fiber neuropathy.
Patients receiving standard of care alone showed no statistically significant change in FIQR scores from baseline to 12 weeks.
Before matching, fibromyalgia patients with clinical signs suggestive of small fiber neuropathy had higher baseline disease burden (FIQR) than those without such symptoms.

Prior literature cited indicates that loss of peripheral small nerve fibers occurs in approximately 50% of fibromyalgia patients, with small fiber damage associated with more severe symptoms and poorer quality of life.

Small fiber pathology is hypothesized to contribute to neurogenic microvasculopathy, potentially explaining fibromyalgia manifestations such as skeletal muscle perfusion deficits, deep pain, exercise intolerance, and cognitive 'fibro fog'.

It has been hypothesized (Martinez-Lavin et al.) that fibromyalgia may originate from peripheral nerve trauma, with neuropathic changes spreading to the dorsal root ganglia, leading to neuroplastic alterations and altered pain perception.

A previously published randomized controlled trial (Salaffi et al.) found that PEA plus LAC add-on therapy to duloxetine and pregabalin produced superior outcomes in widespread pain and FIQR-measured disease burden in a heterogeneous fibromyalgia cohort.
A large epidemiological study of patients hospitalized with duodenal ulcers found a 70% increased risk of esophageal adenocarcinoma.
Recent large-scale studies show Hp infection is not inversely associated with Barrett's esophagus, and no significant association was found with erosive esophagitis, BE length, or dysplasia degree.
Eradication of Hp improves control of GERD symptoms and promotes healing of esophagitis.

Hp infection induces oncogenic gastrin that promotes Barrett's esophagus cell proliferation via JAK2 and Akt-dependent NF-κB activation, and exerts anti-apoptotic effects via Bcl-2 and survivin upregulation and COX-2 stimulation.
Studies of Barrett's esophagus biofilms show high levels of atypical nitrate-reducing Campylobacter spp. in BE tissues compared to non-BE specimens.
Patients infected with Hp show greater mast cell infiltration than uninfected individuals, with mast cell concentration significantly correlating with inflammation severity.
CagA induces IL-33 production in epithelial cells via ERK and p38 signaling, further activating mast cells, and IL-33 is elevated in Hp-infected patients.
IL-33 is overexpressed during the transition from GERD to esophageal adenocarcinoma and promotes carcinogenesis in EAC cells through the ST2 receptor.
The median number of mast cells identified by tryptase staining is significantly higher in patients with erosive reflux esophagitis than in healthy controls.
The median number of mast cells identified by tryptase staining is significantly higher in patients with Barrett's esophagus than in healthy controls.
The proportion of Th2 effector cells, including mast cells, is higher in Barrett's esophagus than in reflux esophagitis.
Activated mast cells are significantly increased in esophageal adenocarcinoma, and patients with a high-risk score for EAC exhibit increased infiltration of activated mast cells.
The proportion of mast cells is negatively correlated with overall survival in patients with esophageal adenocarcinoma, indicating mast cell infiltration is associated with poor prognosis.

High density of mast cells in esophageal squamous carcinoma is associated with tumor progression and low postoperative survival, potentially via EMT, G2/M checkpoint dysregulation, and TNF-α/NF-κB signaling.

Campylobacter spp.-specific signatures correlate with high levels of active mast cells in metaplastic tissues, contributing to BE progression, and patients progressing through the EAC cascade show higher prevalence and abundance of emerging Campylobacter species compared to controls.
Elevated oxidative DNA lesions such as 8-OHdG have been observed in both gastric and esophageal mucosa of Hp-infected patients.

Loss of p16 expression via genetic deletion or epigenetic silencing is one of the earliest and most frequent molecular events in the BE-EAC sequence, with CDKN2A promoter methylation reported in early metaplastic and dysplastic lesions.
CDKN2A deletion synergizes with KRAS activation to accelerate neoplastic transformation in the esophageal epithelium.
Transformation of murine mast cells via constitutive KIT activation was associated with Cdkn2a/Arf loss, suggesting mast cells can intrinsically influence tumor suppressor pathways.
Probiotics such as Lactobacillus rhamnosus and Bacillus inhibit mast cell degranulation by downregulating FcεRI and histamine H4 receptor expression.
In vitro and in vivo studies show Limosilactobacillus fermentum attenuates mast cell degranulation by significantly reducing release of β-hexosaminidase, a marker of mast cell activation.

Some studies report an inverse association whereby Hp infection may reduce GERD risk and eradication may actually increase that risk, contradicting the eradication-benefit findings discussed elsewhere in the review.
The long non-coding RNA NEAT1 is proposed as a core RNA that sponges microRNAs to deregulate signaling pathways involved in sustained mast cell activation in chronic urticaria.
miR-155 is described as a shared microRNA acting as a bridge between upstream core RNAs and downstream effector molecules in the ceRNA network driving mast cell activation.
STAT3 is proposed as an effector molecule that ultimately drives mast cell activation downstream of the ceRNA/miRNA regulatory tiers in chronic urticaria.
Approximately 30% of chronic urticaria patients show poor response to existing therapies, motivating the search for novel ceRNA-targeted precision therapeutics.
RNA-based therapeutics and exosome delivery technologies targeting the ceRNA regulatory axes are proposed as potential novel strategies for treating refractory chronic urticaria.
The review proposes a novel three-tiered hierarchical model (core RNAs, shared miRNAs, effector molecules) describing how the ceRNA network sustains mast cell activation in chronic urticaria.
Treatment of IgE-sensitized RBL-2H3 mast cells with LP-5264, BL-RAPO, or the BCL-2 combination at 10^7 CFU/mL significantly reduced DNP-BSA-induced IL-4 secretion.
The multi-strain BCL-2 combination produced a greater reduction in IL-4 secretion than either single strain alone, suggesting a synergistic anti-mast cell effect.
Dexamethasone-treated AD mice (G3) showed significant body weight loss over the 4-week treatment period compared to untreated AD mice.
Unlike dexamethasone, BCL-2 treatment at any dose did not cause body weight loss in AD mice, suggesting a favorable safety profile.
AD induction significantly increased spleen weight compared with healthy controls, indicating systemic immune activation.
BCL-2-treated groups showed no significant reduction in spleen weight compared to untreated AD mice, unlike dexamethasone.

Clinical dermatitis severity scores (erythema, edema, excoriation, scaling) at day 28 were highest in untreated AD mice and lowest with dexamethasone, with BCL-2 groups showing intermediate, dose-related improvement.
Peripheral blood neutrophil counts were highest in untreated AD mice and significantly decreased in dexamethasone- and all BCL-2-treated groups.
Peripheral blood eosinophil counts were highest in untreated AD mice and significantly reduced in all treatment groups including BCL-2.

Among AD-induced groups, the low-dose BCL-2 group (G4) showed the highest splenic Th1/Th2 ratio while untreated AD mice showed the lowest, with no significant change in dexamethasone or higher BCL-2 dose groups.
Dexamethasone treatment significantly increased skin IFN-γ expression and decreased IL-17, IL-4, IL-5, IL-6, TNF-α, IL-1β, TARC and eotaxin compared to untreated AD mice.

Low- and mid-dose BCL-2 (G4, G5) significantly decreased skin expression of IL-17, IL-5, IL-6, TNF-α, IL-1β, TARC and eotaxin, and significantly increased IL-12 and IFN-γ, compared to untreated AD mice, while IL-4 reduction was not significant.
The highest BCL-2 dose (G6, 10^8 CFU) also significantly decreased skin expression of IL-17, IL-5, IL-6, TNF-α, IL-1β, TARC and eotaxin compared to untreated AD mice.
The anti-inflammatory cytokine IL-10 was significantly elevated in dexamethasone- and BCL-2 (low/mid dose)-treated AD mice compared to untreated AD mice.

Skin histopathology showed dexamethasone most effectively reduced epidermal hypertrophy, hyperkeratosis, and epidermal inflammation, while among BCL-2 doses, G6 had the lowest hypertrophy/hyperkeratosis scores and G5 the lowest epidermal inflammation; dermal inflammation was lowest with dexamethasone and highest with the high-dose BCL-2 group.
Toluidine blue-stained mast cell infiltration in skin was significantly reduced in dexamethasone- and low/mid-dose BCL-2-treated AD mice compared to untreated AD mice.

In ear tissue, hyperkeratosis scores were significantly lower in all AD-induced treatment groups compared to untreated AD mice, while hypertrophy reduction reached significance only in the mid-dose BCL-2 group, and dermal inflammation was reduced only with dexamethasone and high-dose BCL-2.
Mast cell counts in ear tissue were lowest in the dexamethasone and low-dose BCL-2 groups.
Vincristine administration induced mechanical allodynia in mice, with significantly lower paw withdrawal thresholds versus vehicle controls at days 1, 3, and 7.
BIO101 treatment produced a complete recovery of normal mechanical sensitivity in vincristine-treated mice compared with vehicle-treated vincristine mice.
Co-administration of the MasR antagonist A779 abolished the beneficial effect of BIO101 on vincristine-induced allodynia, restoring tactile hypersensitivity comparable to vehicle-vincristine mice.
Vincristine-treated mice showed significantly lower intraepidermal nerve fiber (IENF) density in footpad skin compared with vehicle controls.
BIO101 treatment partially mitigated the vincristine-induced decrease in IENF density, with no significant difference from vehicle controls.
Co-administration of A779 abolished the protective effect of BIO101 on IENF density loss caused by vincristine.
Vincristine administration significantly decreased DRG neuron density compared to vehicle controls.
Pre-treatment with BIO101 prevented the vincristine-induced decline in DRG neuron density, with no significant difference from vehicle controls.
The density of unmyelinated nerve fibers in the sciatic nerve was significantly lower in vincristine-treated mice compared to vehicle controls.
BIO101 administration from day -1 prevented the vincristine-induced reduction in unmyelinated nerve fiber density, with no significant difference from vehicle controls.

Unlike small (unmyelinated) fibers, myelinated nerve fiber density in the sciatic nerve was not significantly different between vincristine-treated and control mice, indicating large fibers were spared at this stage.
Mice receiving vincristine, BIO101, or their combination showed no significant difference in weight gain compared with controls, suggesting good drug tolerability.
Among SFN patients, fatigue was rated as the most intense and prevalent symptom in the week prior to skin biopsy.
Itch sensation was significantly less severe than all other assessed SFN symptoms.
SFN patients reported significantly higher intensity of all assessed symptoms than healthy controls, and no healthy control reported burning pain.
SFN patients had significantly higher BMI than healthy controls.
Dyslipidemia was the most common comorbidity in SFN patients and was significantly more frequent than in healthy controls, consistent with higher BMI.
Unsupervised k-medoid machine learning identified three distinct phenotypic clusters of SFN patients, validated in an independent cohort.
The 'algesic' cluster was characterized by especially severe numbness, burning pain, fatigue, and muscle cramps, with itch significantly lower than other symptoms.
The 'myalgic' cluster, comprising ~60% of patients, was defined by fatigue significantly more severe than other symptoms, with weakness and myalgias more intense than burning pain.
The 'pauci-symptomatic' cluster showed mild symptoms overall, with burning pain as the highest intensity symptom present in only about half of patients.
Symptom localization patterns differed by cluster: the algesic cluster showed a stocking-glove distribution while myalgic and pauci-symptomatic clusters showed more generalized/proximal involvement.
Sex distribution differed significantly across clusters, with the pauci-symptomatic cluster containing the highest proportion of males.
Symptom duration prior to biopsy was significantly longer in the algesic cluster than in the other two clusters.
BMI was highest in the algesic cluster compared to the other two SFN clusters.
BMI and fatigue intensity were positively correlated in the algesic and pauci-symptomatic clusters but not in the myalgic cluster.
Age/sex-adjusted IENFD loss was greatest in the algesic cluster compared to the other two clusters.
Lower IENFD at the ankle was modestly but significantly associated with higher overall SFN symptom intensity across the cohort.
In the algesic cluster, reduced IENFD at the ankle was significantly linked to more severe burning pain.
