Use of neuropathic pain medications differed significantly across clusters, with the highest use in the algesic cluster and lowest in the pauci-symptomatic cluster; gabapentin was most commonly prescribed.
Within each cluster, fatigue intensity did not significantly differ between patients on neuropathic pain medications and those who were not.
Comorbidities including dyslipidemia, fibromyalgia, and depression/anxiety did not significantly differ between the three SFN clusters.
Despite symptomatic overlap with fibromyalgia, only 9% of patients in the myalgic cluster had a chart diagnosis of fibromyalgia, a proportion similar across all clusters.

Dysautonomia symptoms were most commonly reported by patients in the algesic cluster, followed by the myalgic and then pauci-symptomatic clusters, with bladder/bowel incontinence least frequent across all clusters.
The authors suggest that blocking axon degeneration, e.g., with SARM1 inhibitors, may be a promising therapeutic avenue for SFN patients with intense neuropathic pain in the algesic cluster.
Skin biopsy for IENFD assessment provides strong diagnostic confirmation of SFN, with reported sensitivity of 94.3% and specificity of 91.9% in this clinical context.

Reported prevalence of diabetic peripheral neuropathy (DPN) in children/adolescents with type 1 diabetes varies widely across studies, from 3% to 62%, largely due to differences in age ranges, definitions, and diagnostic tests used.

In the Pittsburgh Epidemiology of Diabetes Complications Study, diagnosed diabetic neuropathy prevalence increased sharply with age, from 3% in patients under 18 to 18% at 18-29 years and 58% in those over 30.
The EURODIAB IDDM Complications Study reported diabetic neuropathy in 19% of patients aged 15-29 years, one of the largest European T1D cohorts studied.

The Danish Study Group found subclinical neuropathy, diagnosed by vibration detection threshold, in 62% of patients aged 12-27 years, with age-stratified prevalence of 5% (10-15 years) and 46.8% (15-20 years).
Nelson et al. identified neuropathy in 57% of pediatric T1D patients using nerve conduction study (NCS), a gold-standard method, at a mean age of 13.7 years.
The SEARCH for Diabetes in Youth study found 7% of adolescent T1D patients had evidence of neuropathy as diagnosed by the Michigan Neuropathy Screening Instrument (MNSI).
Moser et al. reported a 10.6% prevalence of DPN in patients aged 8-21 years using combined MNSI and NCS (in positive/high-risk cases).
Compared with the 10-g monofilament test, the Ipswich Touch Test showed 76% sensitivity and 90% specificity and can be performed at home without equipment.
Compared to the biothesiometer, the tip-therm thermal perception device showed high specificity (100%) and sensitivity (97.3%) for diagnosing diabetic neuropathy.
IENF density, assessed via skin biopsy, is the gold standard for diagnosing small fiber neuropathy; a decrease may be evident at the earliest disease stage and correlates with SFN severity.
The Neuropad sudomotor color-change test showed sensitivity of 70-83% when validated against the Neuropathy Disability Score, NCS, and VDT.

Sudoscan, which measures electrochemical skin conductance via reverse iontophoresis to assess small C-fiber sudomotor function, showed sensitivity of 70-87.5% in validation studies for screening DPN using foot ESC results.

A meta-analysis of over 3,000 participants found reduced corneal nerve fiber parameters (density, branch density, length, inferior whorl length) via corneal confocal microscopy in DPN patients versus healthy controls, with a lesser but significant reduction in diabetics without overt DPN, suggesting utility for detecting subclinical disease.

Corneal nerve fiber loss detectable by corneal confocal microscopy has also been observed in patients with impaired glucose tolerance and in children with type 1 diabetes, indicating early small-fiber involvement.

A Slovak study found a strong association between the CYBA gene polymorphism rs4673 (encoding the p22phox NADPH oxidase subunit) and diabetic peripheral neuropathy in children and adolescents with T1D.
Polymorphic markers Ala(-9)Val in SOD2 and Arg213Gly in SOD3, genes encoding antioxidant superoxide dismutase isoforms, were associated with higher risk of diabetic peripheral neuropathy.
The distribution of a VEGF gene promoter polymorphism (-7C/T) differed significantly between T1D patients with and without neuropathy, implicating VEGF in DPN pathogenesis.

Tall stature was associated with higher prevalence of diabetic peripheral neuropathy, in contrast to nephropathy/retinopathy which occur more often with short stature; hypothesized mechanisms include longer nerve length and increased hydrostatic pressure while standing.

A cross-sectional study demonstrated increasing subclinical motor nerve impairment, reduced sensory nerve conduction velocity, and reduced sensory nerve action potential amplitude during and after puberty, attributed to pubertal hormonal changes and poor metabolic control/self-care.
Studies of multi-ethnic groups found a greater prevalence of DPN in Caucasian patients compared to other ethnic groups.

In SEARCH, patients with DPN had significantly longer diabetes duration than those without, while HbA1c values were similar between groups, indicating that diabetes duration is a crucial factor for DPN independent of metabolic control.
In EURODIAB, higher levels of total cholesterol, LDL cholesterol, and triglycerides were significantly associated with the cumulative incidence of diabetic neuropathy.

SEARCH found increased triglycerides and LDL-c and lower HDL-c to be risk factors for DPN in youth with T1D, with lower HDL-c suggested as a crucial pathogenic factor via impaired anti-inflammatory, antioxidant, and vasodilatory effects.
Hypertension, and specifically increased diastolic blood pressure (per EURODIAB), was associated with prevalence of neuropathy and impaired nerve conduction in young people with T1D.

ACE inhibitor therapy may improve peripheral neuropathy even in normotensive diabetic patients, potentially by blocking the renin-angiotensin system and reducing hyperglycemia-induced oxidative stress and endothelial/vascular damage.

Obesity is an emerging risk factor for neuropathy independent of hyperglycemia; central adiposity (rather than general obesity) is associated with insulin resistance and inflammation in adolescents regardless of BMI, potentially via pro-inflammatory cytokines (TNF-alpha, IL-6), CRP elevation, and free fatty acid-mediated neural damage.
Oberhauser et al. found that high glycemic variability was an unexpectedly strong predictor of slowed nerve conduction velocity in children and adolescents with T1D.
Among individuals with the GLA I198T variant, males had higher Lyso-GL3 levels than females.
Males with the I198T variant had lower alpha-galactosidase A enzymatic activity than females with the same variant, consistent with X-linked inheritance.
A mild cardiac phenotype on imaging was observed in three of four females over age 60 with the I198T variant, suggesting a potential later-onset cardiac risk.
The predominant early presenting features in the I198T cohort were numbness and tingling suggestive of small fiber neuropathy, and angiokeratomas.
None of the males in the I198T cohort showed evidence of end-organ damage.
The A143T cohort exhibited no signs of end-organ damage except for one female who presented with concentric left ventricular hypertrophy at a young age.
Gastrointestinal symptoms were a common early presenting feature among individuals with the GLA A143T genotype.
Recurrent headaches were another common presenting symptom among individuals with the A143T genotype.
The authors propose reclassifying I198T and A143T as 'Variants of Varying Clinical Consequence (VVCC)' given their uncertain pathogenicity and heterogeneous clinical presentations.
The right pallidum was significantly smaller in MS patients with neuropathic pain compared to MS patients without pain, as detected by SynthSeg segmentation.

Diffusion tensor imaging showed significant white-matter microstructural changes in the external capsule, internal capsule, posterior thalamic radiation, and superior longitudinal fasciculus associated with neuropathic pain.
Quantitative analysis of spinal cord lesions showed no significant differences between MS patients with pain, MS patients without pain, and SFN patients.
Genetically predicted bipolar disorder significantly increased the risk of pruritus in bidirectional MR analysis.
Genetically predicted bipolar disorder significantly increased the risk of small fiber neuropathy, identified as a novel causal comorbidity link.
Genetically predicted bipolar disorder significantly increased the risk of attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (hyperkinetic disorders).
Genetically predicted bipolar disorder significantly increased the risk of anorexia nervosa.
Genetically predicted bipolar disorder significantly increased the risk of autism spectrum disorder (ASD).
Genetically predicted bipolar disorder showed no significant causal association with bodily pain.
Genetically predicted bipolar disorder showed no significant causal association with tinnitus.
Genetically predicted bipolar disorder showed no significant causal association with general motor disorders.
Genetically predicted bipolar disorder showed no significant causal association with olfactory dysfunction.
The MR estimate for bipolar disorder's effect on multiple sclerosis risk was nominally positive but statistically uninterpretable due to an extremely wide confidence interval.
Genetically predicted bipolar disorder was weakly associated with a slightly reduced risk of substance use disorders, though the effect was marginal.
Genetic liability to pruritus significantly increased the risk of bipolar disorder in the reverse-direction MR, supported by weighted median analysis.
Genetic liability to psoriasis was strongly associated with increased risk of bipolar disorder, with a very large but imprecise odds ratio, supported by weighted median analysis.
Genetic liability to motor disorders was associated with a decreased risk of bipolar disorder, though this did not reach significance in the weighted median method.
Genetic liability to bodily pain showed no significant causal association with bipolar disorder risk, with an extremely wide and uninterpretable confidence interval.
Genetic liability to tinnitus showed no significant causal association with bipolar disorder risk.
Genetic liability to autism spectrum disorder showed no significant causal association with bipolar disorder risk in the reverse direction.
Genetic liability to multiple sclerosis showed no significant causal association with bipolar disorder risk, with an extremely wide, uninformative confidence interval.
Genetic liability to olfactory dysfunction showed a borderline, methodologically inconsistent positive association with bipolar disorder risk that did not reach significance overall.

An EEG study in fibromyalgia patients found that the hypnotic state was characterised by increased theta, beta, and slow-gamma power in specific parietal, occipital, frontal, and temporal regions, suggesting a possible electrophysiological marker of hypnosis.
A randomised controlled trial by Aravena et al. found that hypnosis significantly decreased pain intensity and fatigue in fibromyalgia patients, along with reduced depressive symptoms.

IBS symptoms have been reported to improve with hypnotherapy across multiple studies, suggesting a rationale for incorporating hypnosis into routine IBS management for both efficacy and cost-effectiveness reasons.

In children with functional chronic recurrent abdominal pain of unknown aetiology, a single session of hypnosis led to full symptom resolution in 14 of 17 patients, with no residual side effects during follow-up.
Migraine pain has been shown to improve with hypnosis and acupuncture, with effects reported as comparable to current standard treatment.
Children with connective tissue disease and thrombocytopenia (CTD-TP) had a significantly older age of onset than those with primary immune thrombocytopenia (pITP).
Leukocyte count was significantly lower in the CTD-TP group compared with the pITP group.
Eosinophil count was significantly lower in the CTD-TP group compared with the pITP group.
Lymphocyte count was significantly lower in the CTD-TP group compared with the pITP group.
Complement C4 level was significantly lower in the CTD-TP group compared with the pITP group.
C-reactive protein was significantly higher in the CTD-TP group compared with the pITP group.
Serum IgE was significantly higher in the CTD-TP group compared with the pITP group.
Serum IgM was significantly higher in the CTD-TP group compared with the pITP group.
Logistic regression identified age, IgE, IgM, total B cells, and complement C4 as predictive factors for distinguishing pITP from CTD-TP.
A combined model of age, IgE, IgM, total B cells, and complement C4 showed good discriminative validity for distinguishing pITP from CTD-TP, with an AUC of 0.944.
In the pITP group, serum IgG level was negatively correlated with platelet count.
In the CTD-TP group, NK cell levels were positively correlated with platelet count.
Phosphorylated alpha-synuclein at Ser129 (pS129-α-Syn) is significantly increased in the colonic myenteric plexus of rats with opioid-induced constipation compared to controls.

Inhibiting pS129-α-Syn reversed colonic dysmotility in OIC rats and increased expression of synaptic vesicle proteins (Synapsin-1, Synaptotagmin-1, VAMP-2, Syntaxin-1) and enteric neurotransmitter synthases (nNOS, ATPB).
Opioids downregulate GSK3β phosphorylation at Ser9 via activation of μ-opioid receptors (MOR), increasing GSK3β kinase activity and driving pS129-α-Syn overexpression.

Model mice with chronic restraint plus glacial acetic acid enema showed increased PVN CRF/c-fos co-labelling, indicating heightened CRFergic neuronal activity, which was reduced by electroacupuncture.
Serum CRF concentration was increased in model mice compared with controls and was reduced after electroacupuncture treatment.
Colonic CRF-R1 protein expression was significantly higher in model mice than controls and was reduced by electroacupuncture.
Co-localization of CRF-R1 with mast cell marker CD117 in the colon was increased in model mice and reduced after EA, indicating CRF-R1 expression on colonic mast cells.
Colonic mast cell degranulation rate (toluidine blue staining) was increased in model mice compared to controls and reduced by electroacupuncture.
Colonic expression of MCT, PAR2, and TRPV1 (downstream mast cell activation pathway) was increased in model mice and reduced by electroacupuncture.
Intestinal mucosal TRPV1 expression by immunofluorescence was increased in model mice compared with controls and decreased after EA.
Chronic restraint combined with glacial acetic acid enema induced visceral hypersensitivity in mice, indicated by decreased saline volume required to elicit abdominal withdrawal reflex.
Model mice exhibited anxiety-like behavior in the open-field test, with significantly decreased distance and time spent in the center compared to controls.
Electroacupuncture at Baihui (GV20) alone significantly improved negative emotion-like behavior in model mice but did not significantly reduce visceral hypersensitivity.
Electroacupuncture at Tianshu (ST25) combined with Dachangshu (BL25) significantly reduced visceral hypersensitivity but did not significantly improve negative emotion behavior.
The combination of GV20, ST25, and BL25 electroacupuncture produced the best overall improvement in both negative emotion and visceral hypersensitivity compared to single acupoint groups.
Chemogenetic activation of PVN CRFergic neurons (hM3Dq+CNO) increased visceral hypersensitivity, and this was reversed by electroacupuncture.
Chemogenetic activation of PVN CRFergic neurons increased anxiety-like behavior (reduced distance/time in center), which was reversed by electroacupuncture.
Chemogenetic inhibition of PVN CRFergic neurons (hM4Di+CNO) alleviated visceral hypersensitivity in model mice compared with model+hM4Di+saline.
Chemogenetic inhibition of PVN CRFergic neurons reversed the anxiety-like behavior seen in model mice, increasing distance and time spent in center.
Chemogenetic inhibition of PVN CRFergic neurons reduced colonic mast cell degranulation and CRF-R1, MCT, and TRPV1 protein expression compared with model+hM4Di+saline mice.
Model mice developed diarrhoea, shown by increased fecal moisture content and diarrhoea index compared with controls.

Colonic mucosa in model mice showed histopathological damage including disorganized cell arrangement and impaired crypt structure, along with reduced/disorganized colonic villi and organelles by electron microscopy.
Colonic biopsies stained with CD117 immunohistochemistry revealed increased mast cell infiltration consistent with mastocytic enterocolitis in a patient with chronic diarrhoea.
Treatment with cromolyn sodium prior to meals was ineffective at improving the patient's chronic diarrhoea symptoms.
Combined H1 and H2 antihistamines along with prebiotic supplementation provided significant clinical improvement in the patient's diarrhoea symptoms.
The authors suggest that in patients with refractory diarrhoea-predominant IBS, colonic biopsies with immunohistochemical mast cell staining should be considered as part of workup.
Three distinct likely pathogenic SAMD9L variants were identified in 9 of 14 (64.3%) Kazakh SSc-ILD patients, all of whom also had pronounced autoimmune features.
Two distinct IRAK1 variants were found in 4 of 14 (28.6%) SSc-ILD patients, who tended to have more severe clinical features consistent with diffuse cutaneous and lung involvement.
A pathogenic CD40 variant was identified in 3 of 14 (21.4%) Kazakh SSc-ILD patients, distinct from the previously reported rs4810485 polymorphism.
A pathogenic SMAD3 variant was found in 2 of 14 (14.3%) patients, both with vascular manifestations including Raynaud's syndrome, and was absent in controls.
IL6R variants were detected in 3 of 14 (21.4%) SSc-ILD patients and absent in controls, suggesting possible involvement of IL6R pathway alterations in disease immunopathogenesis.

A likely pathogenic REL variant, encoding c-Rel (NF-κB family transcription factor), was identified in one SSc-ILD patient, supporting a potential role of REL dysregulation in immune-mediated disease.
A LY96 (MD-2) variant was detected in the cohort; carriers showed elevated ESR-based inflammatory profiles despite IL-6 levels remaining within the normal range.

A heterozygous likely pathogenic ITGA2B variant was found in one patient who showed significant platelet activation alongside fibrosis markers, though the contribution to ILD/vascular severity was unclear.
One AIRE variant was found in the study group, in an individual with mixed autoimmune features including autoimmune thyroiditis, consistent with AIRE's role in immune tolerance.

A novel likely pathogenic TREX1 variant was identified in one SSc-ILD patient; TREX1 dysfunction is linked to dsDNA accumulation and interferon-mediated inflammation relevant to connective tissue disease pathogenesis.
Antinuclear antibody titers were positive (>1:160) in 12 of 14 SSc-ILD patients while all 18 healthy controls were negative for ANA.

Four of 14 (28.6%) SSc-ILD patients had elevated serum IL-6 (>10.0 pg/mL), associated with skin and joint involvement, and in some cases pulmonary arterial hypertension and esophagitis; all 18 controls had normal IL-6.
Raynaud's phenomenon was observed in 12 of 14 (86%) SSc-ILD patients in the Kazakh cohort.
Frequent gastrointestinal tract lesions were present in 10 of 14 (71.4%) SSc-ILD patients.
Secondary Sjögren's syndrome was diagnosed in 5 of 14 (36%) SSc-ILD patients in the Kazakh cohort.

A Kazakh male patient with elevated anti-Scl-70 antibodies had a rapidly progressive course of SSc-ILD with pulmonary arterial hypertension, Raynaud's syndrome, skin injury, esophagitis, arthritis, and secondary Sjögren's syndrome with anti-SS-A/60 and SS-A/52 antibodies.
Literature review indicates STAT4 polymorphism rs7574865 is significantly involved in susceptibility to SSc and associated ILD manifestations, based on studies including a Russian population.
The IRF5 rs2004640 T allele was significantly associated with pulmonary fibrosis in SSc patients.
The STAT4 rs7574865 T allele was significantly associated with pulmonary fibrosis in SSc patients in the cited genetic categorization study.
The CTGF G-945C C allele was significantly associated with pulmonary fibrosis in SSc patients, showing the strongest effect size among the four SNPs analyzed.
The IRAK1 rs1059702 T allele was significantly associated with pulmonary fibrosis in SSc patients.
MMP7 was identified in the literature as a consistently upregulated gene potentially involved in SSc-ILD fibrosis via G-protein coupled receptor signaling.
Baseline serum CXCL10 levels above 78.5 pg/mL are associated with a 2.74-fold increased risk of developing ILD in SSc patients.
Elevated baseline serum CCL18 is associated with a significant decline in lung function (FVC decrease >10%), with a 2.9-fold increased risk (HR = 2.90, p = 0.014).
Presence of anti-Scl-70 antibodies was associated with a six-fold increased risk of developing ILD in SSc patients.
SSc-ILD patients with anti-U1-snRNP antibodies had worse baseline lung function than those without, with lower mean FVC (82.0% vs. 86.0%, p<0.001) and lower DLCO (57.0% vs. 60.5%, p=0.003).
SSc occurs far more frequently among relatives of SSc patients (1.6%) than in the general population (0.026%), supporting a genetic predisposition to the disease.
A large U.S. population study found that individuals of African ancestry had a higher adjusted prevalence ratio of SSc-ILD compared to individuals of European ancestry.

Choctaw Native Americans have the highest reported prevalence of SSc among ethnic groups studied, at 66 cases per 100,000 population, and European-descent SSc patients have lower ILD frequency, slower lung function decline, and better survival than African, Japanese, or Choctaw patients.

Tenascin-C, an endogenous TLR4 activator, is elevated in SSc tissues and promotes collagen production via TLR4 signaling, while tenascin-C-deficient mice show reduced fibrosis, suggesting it as a therapeutic target.
A composite biomarker index combining surfactant protein D (SP-D), cancer antigen 15-3 (CA15-3), and ICAM-1 was proposed to effectively identify SSc-ILD.

In a study of SSc patients from Paris and Oslo, SP-D was identified as a potential diagnostic biomarker for SSc-associated ILD, KL-6 as a marker of pulmonary fibrosis severity, and CCL18 as a predictor of ILD progression.

SSc-ILD patients with anti-U1-snRNP antibodies had significantly worse baseline lung function (lower FVC and DLCO) and higher prevalence of limited cutaneous SSc, joint synovitis and myositis than those without, though 3-year FVC decline and mortality trajectories were comparable.

In newly diagnosed SSc patients, CXCL10 levels decline over time while CCL2 levels remain stable, reflecting a shift from a Th1-driven inflammatory phase to a Th2-dominant fibrotic phase; CXCL10 is particularly associated with severe organ involvement including lungs and kidneys.
Baseline CXCL10 levels greater than 78.5 pg/mL are associated with a 2.74-fold increased risk of developing ILD in SSc patients.
Elevated baseline serum CCL18 in SSc-ILD patients is associated with a significant decline in FVC (>10%), with a 2.9-fold increased risk of this decline.

TGF-β, IL-4, IL-8, CCL2, and CCL4 were found to have a strong correlation with lung involvement in SSc, while IL-6 and IL-7 showed weaker correlation, with IL-7 predicting 20-30% decline in DLCO and IL-6 predicting mortality in a subset of patients.

Serum IL-6 levels may predict early disease progression in patients with mild ILD and could help tailor treatment approaches, and IL-6 gene knockout in an SSc animal model significantly reduced lung inflammation and collagen deposition.

ET-1 levels are increased in bronchoalveolar lavage and serum of SSc-ILD patients, and histological studies show overexpression of ET-1 in the lungs, contributing to vasoconstriction, myofibroblast differentiation, and ECM deposition.

TGF-β induces expression of CUX1 isoforms in SSc lung fibroblasts, which act as transcriptional activators that increase COL1 and pro-fibrotic cytokines (CTGF, Wnt1, ET-1, β-catenin) and stimulate fibroblast-to-myofibroblast transition by binding the COL1A2 enhancer.

Higher serum levels of CTGF have been identified in SSc-ILD patients and correlate with the degree of skin sclerosis and severity of pulmonary fibrosis, with CTGF polymorphisms also associated with lung involvement.
Serum levels and tissue expression of MMP-12 were elevated in SSc-ILD patients, correlated with severity of lung restriction and with severity of skin and peripheral vascular damage.

The p53 signaling pathway is the most prominent molecular signature in SSc-ILD, associated with senescent, apoptosis-resistant myofibroblasts, impaired gas exchange, and involving regulatory genes EEF2, EEF2K, PHKG2, VCAM1, PRKACB, ITGA4, CDK1, CDK2, FN1, and HDAC1.
In the Kazakh SSc-ILD subgroup (n=14), Raynaud's phenomenon was observed in 12 patients (86%), and gastrointestinal tract lesions were present in 10 patients (71.4%).
Among the 14 Kazakh SSc-ILD patients, five (36%) were diagnosed with secondary Sjögren's syndrome, four had both pulmonary arterial hypertension and ILD, and two (14.3%) had cardiovascular disorders.
In the Kazakh cohort, ANA was positive (titer >1:160) in 12 of 14 SSc-ILD patients with a mean antibody titer of 1200 ± 1446, whereas all control group members had negative ANA (<1:80).

In the Kazakh cohort, 4 of 14 SSc-ILD patients (28.6%) had elevated serum IL-6 (>10.0 pg/mL), all with skin and joint involvement, two of four with PAH, and three of four with esophagitis; all control participants had normal IL-6.

A prior meta-analysis found a significant association between the CD40 rs4810485 polymorphism and susceptibility to rheumatoid arthritis and systemic lupus erythematosus in European populations, distinct from the CD40 variant identified in this study's Kazakh cohort.

Previous genome-wide association studies in Japanese and Chinese populations linked AIRE polymorphisms to increased risk of rheumatoid arthritis, and given AIRE's central role in immune tolerance, even heterozygous variants may contribute to widespread autoimmune dysregulation.

Variants in miR-146a may influence disease susceptibility by affecting regulation of IRAK1, IRAK2, and TRAF6, key components of TNF and NF-κB signaling pathways, thereby modulating inflammatory responses in SSc.

In the Kazakh cohort, one male patient with elevated anti-Scl-70 antibodies had a rapidly progressive course of SSc-ILD with pulmonary arterial hypertension, Raynaud's syndrome, skin injury, esophagitis, arthritis, and secondary Sjögren's syndrome with anti-SS-A/60 and SS-A/52 antibodies.
CryoEM resolved the ternary complex structure of ALK2-ActRIIB bound to BMP6 at 3.2 Å resolution, showing two ALK2 and two ActRIIB ectodomains bound to dimeric BMP6.
The ALK3-ActRIIB:BMP6 complex was solved by cryoEM to 3.3 Å resolution, showing the canonical BMP receptor assembly.
SPR showed that heterodimeric ALK2-ActRIIB-Fc and ALK3-ActRIIB-Fc traps bind glycosylated BMP6 with picomolar affinity, comparable to a bivalent ActRIIB2-Fc and higher than a monovalent ActRIIB1-Fc.

ActRIIB binds the knuckle of BMP6 through a conserved hydrophobic triad (Tyr60, Trp78, Phe101) engaging the BMP6 IAP motif (Ile22, Ala23, Pro24), and this interface is unaffected by the identity of the tethered type I receptor.

ALK2 buries substantially less surface area on BMP6 than ALK3 and engages a distinct region of the ligand, with a 27-degree shift in overall type I receptor positioning within the concave ligand cleft.
Enzymatic deglycosylation of BMP6 (dgBMP6) reduces its binding affinity for ALK2 by 3.5-fold, whereas ALK3 binding is essentially unaffected by loss of glycosylation.

In cell-based signaling assays with ALK3 blocked, only glycosylated and EndoH-treated BMP6 activated SMAD1/5/8 signaling through ALK2, while fully deglycosylated BMP6 failed to signal, and this was confirmed in ALK2-/- and ALK3-/- mouse embryonic stem cells.

The cryoEM structure shows no direct contact between BMP6's carbohydrate chain and ALK2, but the primary carbohydrate moiety forms a hydrophobic interaction with His452 and a hydrogen bond with Lys482 within the same BMP6 monomer, stabilizing the prehelix loop for ALK2 binding.

Mutating ALK3 Asp69 to glycine (mimicking ALK2) or swapping the ALK3 β1β2 loop for the ALK2 equivalent significantly reduces binding to deglycosylated BMP6 but not to BMP2, demonstrating that the Asp69-Arg413 salt bridge is ALK3's alternative mechanism to stabilize the BMP6 prehelix loop independent of glycosylation.

Mutating ALK2 residue Tyr74 to alanine, valine, or glutamate ablates ActA-induced signaling in ALK2.R206H reporter cells while leaving BMP6-induced signaling largely intact, identifying Tyr74 as a key fingertip-interface residue specific for Activin A engagement.

Loss of the Activin A fingertip residue Asp406 significantly reduces ActA's ability to assemble ALK2/type II receptor complexes, consistent with a modeled hydrogen bond between ActA Asp406 and ALK2 Tyr74.

Mutating the conserved knob-in-hole residue Met79 to alanine did not ablate ALK2 signaling in response to either BMP6 or ActA, indicating ALK2 relies more on interactions outside the conserved anchor interface.
The FOP-causing ALK2 R206H variant was used as a signaling-competent background to demonstrate that both BMP6 and Activin A activate SMAD1/5/8 luciferase reporter signaling.

Overexpression of the Drosophila ALK2 homolog Saxophone has no effect on Activin homologs Dawdle or dActB, indicating that the activin-binding capability of ALK2 is an evolutionarily more recent acquisition than its conserved BMP-binding/nonsignaling-complex function.

Transcutaneous vagal nerve stimulation is reported across randomized trials to relieve abdominal pain, improve GI symptoms, and accelerate GI motility in patients with functional dyspepsia, gastroparesis, constipation, irritable bowel syndrome, and inflammatory bowel disease by enhancing parasympathetic/vagal activity.
Multiple studies reviewed reported irritable bowel syndrome, fibromyalgia, and chronic pelvic pain as common somatic comorbidities in patients with psychogenic non-epileptic seizures (PNES).

Overlapping somatic complaints such as fibromyalgia and IBS in PNES patients were proposed by reviewed literature to reflect central sensitization mechanisms that reinforce the functional symptom pattern.
Patients with fibromyalgia or chronic widespread pain frequently had a reported history of PNES, and vice versa, suggesting a bidirectional clinical association.

In general/mixed FND presentations, functional somatic syndromes such as non-cardiac chest pain and irritable bowel syndrome frequently co-occur, supporting shared mechanisms of central sensitization and altered interoception.

Fatigue, chronic pain, and migraine were among the most commonly reported physical comorbidities in functional movement disorder (FMD), contributing to a high overall comorbidity burden that can obscure primary motor diagnoses.
Migraine was reported as a comorbid condition in patients with Persistent Postural-Perceptual Dizziness (PPPD), further complicating the clinical picture.
Orthostatic intolerance was reported as a comorbid autonomic condition in patients with Persistent Postural-Perceptual Dizziness (PPPD), underscoring the need for a transdiagnostic approach.

Comorbid somatic conditions including sleep disturbance, fibromyalgia, and migraine are commonly reported in Functional Cognitive Disorder (FCD) and reinforce illness convictions, complicating distinction from early neurodegenerative disease.

Somatic and pain-related comorbidities (chronic pain, fibromyalgia, fatigue syndromes, gastrointestinal disturbances, functional sensory symptoms) were discussed in 11 of 54 PNES-focused studies, with many PNES patients meeting criteria for central sensitivity syndromes.

A review by Carle-Toulemonde et al. proposed that interoceptive distortion and heightened autonomic responsivity serve as common mechanistic threads linking functional somatic syndromes (e.g., fibromyalgia, IBS-type GI disturbance) with functional neurological disorders.
Macrophage (CD68+) accumulation in periaortic tissue, especially PVAT, at the aortic root tended to be greater in MFS patients than in non-MFS controls.
Fbn1C1041G/+ mice showed more F4/80+ macrophage accumulation in periaortic tissue compared with Fbn1+/+ wild-type mice.
mRNA expression of macrophage marker genes and inflammatory cytokines Il1a, Il1b, and Serpine1 (Pai1) were significantly upregulated in perivascular tissue of Fbn1C1041G/+ mice.
Protein expression of IL-1β and MCP-1 was significantly upregulated in the perivascular tissue of Fbn1C1041G/+ mice compared with wild-type.
High-fat diet feeding increased aortic root diameter in Fbn1C1041G/+ mice compared with normal chow, coinciding with increased PVAT inflammation.
Low-dose pitavastatin suppressed HFD-induced macrophage accumulation, inflammatory cytokine/MMP expression in perivascular tissue, and aortic root expansion in Fbn1C1041G/+ mice.
The dose of pitavastatin used did not alter metabolic profiles (serum cholesterol, blood sugar, blood pressure) in HFD-fed Fbn1C1041G/+ mice.
Fbn1C1041G/+ mice showed elastic fiber fragmentation, fibrosis, and proteoglycan accumulation compared with wild-type, more pronounced with HFD feeding.
Phosphorylated ERK1/2 and SMAD2 expression and MMP activity in the aortic media increased in Fbn1C1041G/+ mice, were enhanced by HFD, and were attenuated by pitavastatin.
AA-FAI was significantly higher in patients with Marfan syndrome than in patients without hereditary connective tissue disorders.
The area of ct-PVAT (perivascular fat tissue) was smaller in patients with Marfan syndrome than in those without HCTDs.
AA-FAI was significantly higher and ct-PVAT area smaller in Loeys-Dietz syndrome patients compared with those without HCTDs.
In non-HCTD patients, aortic diameter alone was not significantly associated with AA-FAI, but ASI (diameter adjusted for body surface area) was significantly correlated with AA-FAI.

AA-FAI remained significantly higher in MFS patients than non-HCTDs patients even when comparing only those with advanced aortic enlargement (≥50 mm) or the highest ASI tertile, suggesting a distinct MFS-specific inflammatory mechanism.
A positive correlation was found between the speed of aortic diameter expansion (by ultrasound over the 2 years before surgery) and AA-FAI.
ROC analysis showed AA-FAI predicted MFS with AUC 0.73 (95% CI 0.63-0.83), with an optimal cutoff of –55.3 HU (sensitivity 0.61, specificity 0.81).
No statistical association was found between age, BMI, or total cholesterol level and AA-FAI in patients without HCTDs with normal aortic diameter.
AA-FAI was not correlated with hypertension, dyslipidemia, or chronic kidney disease.
AA-FAI was lower in patients using statins than in non-statin users, though ct-PVAT area was unaffected by statin use.
MFS patients still showed higher AA-FAI than non-HCTDs patients even after excluding statin users from the analysis, indicating the MFS-associated elevation is not explained by statin use.
The machine-learning-based image recognition program correctly identified the ascending aorta and calculated AA-FAI in 94.4% of cases.
A 3-month low-protein diet in mice reduced endothelium-dependent relaxation of aortas in response to acetylcholine compared with normoprotein diet.
Extracellular vesicles isolated from post-COVID-19 patients at 1 and 6 months after hospital discharge restored endothelium-dependent relaxation in aortas from protein-restricted mice.

The EV-induced restoration of relaxation was abolished by catalase (which degrades hydrogen peroxide) but not by L-NAME or indomethacin, indicating an H2O2-dependent rather than nitric oxide- or cyclooxygenase-dependent mechanism.
Aortas from low-protein-fed mice incubated with post-COVID EVs showed reduced catalase expression.
Aortas from low-protein-fed mice incubated with post-COVID EVs exhibited increased 4-hydroxynonenal (4-HNE) protein adducts, indicating increased oxidative/lipid peroxidation stress.
In vitro amino acid restriction of endothelial cells increased cell death and reduced nitric oxide and hydrogen peroxide levels compared to control conditions.

In vitro incubation with post-COVID-19 EVs for 24 hours increased hydrogen peroxide (H2O2) levels specifically in amino acid-restricted endothelial cells, with no such effect under normal amino acid conditions.
Post-COVID-19 EVs had no significant effect on acetylcholine-induced endothelium-dependent relaxation in aortas from mice fed a normal-protein (normoprotein) diet.
Post-COVID-19 EVs had no significant effect on endothelial cell parameters (death, nitric oxide, H2O2) in vitro under normal (control) amino acid conditions.
At the selected 0.9 probability threshold, the re-engineered long COVID computable phenotype (LCM 2.0) achieved a true positive rate of 0.843 and a false positive rate of 0.149 in the validation set.
Applying the model to the full COVID-enriched RECOVER cohort, 17.9% of patients scored above the 0.9 threshold, an estimate of long COVID prevalence before correction for false positives.

Using a historical control experiment (patients' own pre-pandemic 2018-19 EHR data), 7.5% of patients scored above the 0.9 threshold despite COVID-19 not yet existing, indicating an estimated false positive rate of the model.

After subtracting the estimated false positive rate from the raw prevalence, the corrected estimated prevalence of long COVID in the RECOVER cohort was 10.4%, corresponding to approximately 1,051,045 patients.

Nearly all top 20 model features (predominantly pulmonary, cardiac, and neurological diagnoses) increased the predicted probability of long COVID when present, except patient age (non-linear relationship) and essential hypertension, which decreased the predicted score.

Requiring two or more U09.9 codes or long COVID clinic visits (versus one) still yielded over 30,000 patients for the training set, supporting use of the more stringent, less error-prone labeling criterion.

43% of patients with at least two U09.9 codes received their first such code earlier than the standard 12-week post-acute-COVID window (median 26 days from acute infection), leading the authors to reject a 12-week data-censoring blackout period as it would invalidate nearly half of clinician-diagnosed long COVID cases.

The re-engineered LCM 2.0 model performed similarly to the original LCM 1.0 model while eliminating dependence on an acute COVID-19 index date and properly accounting for reinfections via time-window censoring.
A chart review of 50 patients from a single site was performed to further assess model accuracy, but the authors note its limitations mean results cannot be considered true performance metrics.

Long COVID shares many overlapping symptoms with myalgic encephalomyelitis/chronic fatigue syndrome, other post-viral syndromes, dysautonomia, and various respiratory illnesses, complicating differentiation of true long COVID cases in EHR-based phenotyping.
The review proposes that age-related decline in immune function (immunosenescence) drives chronic inflammation that contributes to the onset and persistence of fatigue in ME/CFS.
Chronic inflammation driven by aging immune cells is proposed to impair mitochondrial ATP production and promote muscle catabolism in ME/CFS.
The review describes HPA-axis suppression as amplifying immune dysregulation and energy imbalance in ME/CFS.
β2-adrenergic dysfunction is described as amplifying immune dysregulation and energy imbalance alongside HPA-axis suppression in ME/CFS.
The review suggests that cytokines and immune exhaustion markers may serve as clinically relevant biomarkers reflecting immunosenescence-driven pathology in ME/CFS.
Estimated prevalence rates are 2-6% for fibromyalgia, 0.5-1% for ME/CFS, 6-10% for long COVID, and 25-35% for Gulf War veterans with GWI, with all conditions predominantly affecting women.
In Gulf War veterans, autonomic dysfunction affecting cholinergic pathways manifests as dizziness, POTS, and gastrointestinal dysfunction.
Dysautonomia is a common feature of ME/CFS, particularly with regard to orthostatic intolerance, gastrointestinal problems and body thermoregulation.
Long COVID patients show dysautonomia-related symptoms including orthostatic intolerance, breathlessness, and palpitations resulting from virus-induced disruption of the autonomic nervous system.
Imaging studies in ME/CFS patients have found reduced gray matter density in brain regions associated with pain processing and cognitive function.
More than 50% of long COVID patients report cognitive slowing as a significant symptom.
Elevated markers of myeloid inflammation and complement activation have been identified in blood samples from long COVID patients.
Gulf War veterans with GWI show mitochondrial DNA damage and impaired mitochondrial bioenergetic function, assessed via muscle biopsy and 31P-NMR spectroscopy.
GWI illness severity was shown to be related to mitochondrial haplogroups in veterans studied by muscle biopsy and 31P-NMR spectroscopy.
In fibromyalgia, impaired oxidative phosphorylation and reduced mitochondrial ATP production have been reported, with the degree of mitochondrial dysfunction correlating with FM symptom severity.
Muscle biopsies in ME/CFS have confirmed mitochondrial degeneration, deletions in mitochondrial DNA, and reduced mitochondrial activity.
Mitochondrial dysfunction in ME/CFS results in impaired ATP production and reduced bioenergetic reserve capacity that correlates with illness severity and may explain post-exertional malaise.
Research has identified mitochondrial dysfunction in the blood immune cells of long COVID patients, potentially linking to post-exertional malaise via compromised ATP production.
Szögi et al. documented structural and metabolic abnormalities in mitochondria from long COVID patients.
Fibromyalgia patient blood samples show increased lipid peroxidation and decreased antioxidants including CoQ10, superoxide dismutase, and catalase.
Increased levels of oxidative stress biomarkers and reduced antioxidant levels have been reported in long COVID patients.
Elevated plasma levels of pro-inflammatory cytokines (interferon-gamma, IL-2, IL-6, TNF-alpha) and C-reactive protein have been found in Gulf War veterans.
Gulf War veterans with GWI show elevated plasma levels of T- and B-cells and reduced levels of NK cells.
NK cells and CD8+ T cells in ME/CFS may exhibit signs of exhaustion, potentially limiting the ability to effectively fight persistent infection.
Transfer of antibodies from the blood of fibromyalgia patients into mice was found to induce fibromyalgia-like symptoms, suggesting an autoimmune component to FM.
HPA axis dysregulation with hypocortisolism and altered cortisol rhythms is particularly evident in ME/CFS, linked to fatigue, PEM, autonomic dysfunction and sleep disturbance.
In a mouse model of GWI, andrographolide restored gut microbiome balance, improved gut barrier function, and reduced neuroinflammation.
In ME/CFS, gut microbiome shifts show increased Alistipes and decreased Faecalibacterium.
Serum from GWI patients has been reported to increase apoptosis in cultured neuroblastoma cells, suggesting a mechanistic link to neurocognitive and mood dysfunction in veterans.
Supplementation with CoQ10 in Gulf War Illness veterans improved physical function, self-reported health, fatigue, pain, and muscle strength.
Castro-Marrero et al. reported that combined supplementation with CoQ10 and NADH improved fatigue in ME/CFS patients.
Fibromyalgia patients have depleted tissue CoQ10 levels, typically 40-50% of normal levels.

A randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial of 300 mg/day CoQ10 for 40 days significantly reduced chronic pain and fatigue in fibromyalgia patients with improved mitochondrial energy production.

In a prospective observational study, long COVID patients supplemented with 200 mg CoQ10 plus 200 mg alpha-lipoic acid daily for 2 months had substantially reduced fatigue severity compared to placebo.

A randomized controlled trial of 500 mg/day CoQ10 for 6 weeks in 121 long COVID patients reported no significant benefit on illness symptoms, contrasting with a prior observational study showing benefit.

In older adults with low selenium levels, CoQ10 plus selenium supplementation resulted in less telomere shortening compared to placebo, and longer telomeres correlated with reduced cardiovascular mortality.
Mesenchymal stem cell therapy has been reported to improve sleep quality, energy levels, pain, and cognitive function in ME/CFS patients.
Mokhemer et al. reported symptomatic improvement in a rat model of fibromyalgia following stem cell therapy.
Tsilibary et al. showed, using a cell culture system, that stem cell therapy could protect cells against toxic factors present in serum from Gulf War Illness veterans.

Selenium administration reduced increased apoptosis markers and decreased cell viability observed in animal models of fibromyalgia, and reduced hyperalgesia and oxidative stress by modulating TRPM2 and TRPV1 channels.
Elevated levels of anti-annexin antibodies, associated with apoptosis, have been reported in some fibromyalgia patients, particularly those with Sjögren's syndrome.
Magnesium hexacyanoferrate nanocatalysts, acting as ferroptosis inhibitors, alleviated fibromyalgia symptoms in mouse models by reducing oxidative stress and mitochondrial dysfunction.
ME/CFS patients have an increased rate of apoptosis in neutrophils compared to healthy individuals, potentially impairing immune response to pathogens.

Cezar et al. found CD4+ T cells from participants who later developed long COVID were more apoptotic in culture at month 1 than those from participants who remained symptom-free, suggesting acute-phase T cell death may pave the way for long COVID.
A low baseline level of the ferroptosis marker SLC7A11 may indicate increased risk for long COVID and associated cardiovascular and neurological dysfunction.
Rajeevan et al. found that the association between ME/CFS and shorter telomeres was largely moderated by females under 45 years old, suggesting premature immunosenescence in this subgroup.
Fibromyalgia is associated with telomere shortening, with the degree of shortening correlating with pain frequency/severity, and effects being more pronounced when accompanied by anxiety/depression.
Acute SARS-CoV-2 infection can accelerate telomere shortening in blood cells independent of chronological age, and shorter leukocyte telomeres are linked to worse COVID-19 prognosis.
Goebel et al. found that transfer of antibodies from the blood of fibromyalgia patients into mice could induce fibromyalgia-like symptoms, suggesting an autoimmune component to FM.

Tsilibary et al. investigated the anthrax vaccine given to Gulf War veterans in inducing apoptosis in cultured neural cells, and found that IgG isotype anti-protective antigen protein antibodies could neutralize the adverse effects of GWI serum on neural cultures, including reducing apoptosis.
Serum from Gulf War Illness patients increased apoptosis in cultured neuroblastoma cells, suggesting apoptosis may contribute to neurocognitive and mood dysfunction in some veterans.
In a mouse model of GWI, andrographolide restored gut microbiome balance, improved gut barrier function, and reduced neuroinflammation, potentially alleviating GWI symptoms.
In ME/CFS, specific bacterial groups such as Alistipes may be increased while Faecalibacterium is decreased, reflecting gut microbiome imbalance.

Chen et al. identified damage to mitochondrial DNA in Gulf War veterans, and Koslik et al. and Golomb et al. reported impaired mitochondrial bioenergetic function, with GWI severity related to mitochondrial haplogroups.
In fibromyalgia, impaired oxidative phosphorylation and reduced mitochondrial ATP production have been reported, with the degree of mitochondrial dysfunction correlating with FM symptom severity.

Mitochondrial dysfunction in ME/CFS results in impaired ATP production and reduced mitochondrial bioenergetic reserve capacity correlating with illness severity, which could explain post-exertional malaise; muscle biopsies confirmed mitochondrial degeneration and mtDNA deletions.
In long COVID, structural and metabolic abnormalities in mitochondria have been documented in blood immune cells, with post-exertional malaise linked to compromised ATP production.
Elevated plasma levels of interferon-gamma, IL-2, IL-6, TNF-alpha, and C-reactive protein have been found in Gulf War veterans, along with elevated T- and B-cells and reduced NK cells.
In ME/CFS, NK cells and CD8+ T cells may exhibit signs of exhaustion, potentially limiting their ability to effectively fight persistent infection.
In Gulf War veterans, suppression of ACTH and cortisol has been linked to environmental exposures (chemical warfare agents, pesticides), possibly contributing to long-term GWI symptoms.

Low cortisol levels and altered cortisol rhythms (hypocortisolism) are particularly evident in ME/CFS, associated with a dysregulated stress response that can lead to fatigue, PEM, autonomic dysfunction, and sleep disturbances.
More than 50% of long COVID patients experience cognitive slowing, possibly resulting from neuroinflammation or virus-induced vascular damage affecting cerebral blood flow.
Elevated markers of myeloid inflammation and complement activation have been identified in blood samples from long COVID patients.
Imaging studies in ME/CFS patients have found reduced gray matter density in brain regions associated with pain processing and cognitive function.
A meta-analysis of nine studies found the pooled prevalence of ME/CFS among endometriosis patients to be 17%, with very high between-study heterogeneity.
Pooled analysis of five comparative studies showed individuals with endometriosis had nearly three times higher odds of ME/CFS diagnosis compared to controls, with no observed heterogeneity.
A meta-analysis of four studies estimated the pooled prevalence of endometriosis among ME/CFS patients at 13%, with extreme heterogeneity across studies.
Two large-scale studies (27,556 ME/CFS cases, 108,172 controls) pooled to show ME/CFS patients had 2.52-fold higher odds of endometriosis, with minimal heterogeneity.
Individual comparative studies showed consistent elevated odds of ME/CFS in endometriosis patients, ranging from OR 2.48 (Tietjen et al.) to OR 3.11 (Shafrir et al.).
Fall et al.'s retrospective cohort using clinically validated diagnoses reported a statistically significant OR of 2.27 for the endometriosis-ME/CFS association.
Surrey et al.'s large cross-sectional study using self-reported diagnostic information found an OR of 2.52 for association between ME/CFS and endometriosis.
The discussion cites prior literature that elevated IL-17, driving a Th17 response important in endometriosis lesion formation, also correlates with symptom severity and fatigue intensity in ME/CFS.

Discussion of prior literature notes dysregulation of the IL-1β/IL-1RA axis, with endometriosis showing increased peritoneal IL-1β and ME/CFS patients showing elevated systemic IL-1RA, suggesting ineffective anti-inflammatory compensation.

The paper cites literature indicating TNF-α and IL-6, mediators of sickness behavior, are consistently elevated in both endometriosis and ME/CFS, correlating with cognitive dysfunction and post-exertional malaise in ME/CFS.

The discussion contrasts HPA axis dysfunction patterns: endometriosis shows blunted diurnal cortisol variation with elevated evening/reduced morning cortisol, while ME/CFS shows a flattened profile with low 24-hour urinary free cortisol and attenuated cortisol awakening response.

The authors propose that central sensitization, driven by persistent nociceptive signaling in endometriosis, may perpetuate widespread pain and post-exertional malaise central to ME/CFS, reflecting overlapping neuroimmune mechanisms.
Trim-and-fill analysis of the ME/CFS-in-endometriosis prevalence funnel plot identified four potentially missing studies, suggesting modest publication bias favoring higher prevalence estimates.
JBI risk-of-bias assessment found cohort studies uniformly high risk (Fall, Smorgick, Signorile, Surrey), while cross-sectional and case-control studies generally had better risk-of-bias profiles.
PCS individuals with ME/CFS symptoms performed significantly worse on the six-minute walk test than those without ME/CFS symptoms.
PCS individuals with ME/CFS symptoms performed significantly worse on the 1-minute sit-to-stand test than those without ME/CFS symptoms.
PCS individuals with ME/CFS symptoms reported significantly more shortness of breath during activity, chest pain, dizziness, and fatigue than those without ME/CFS symptoms.
Increased severity of each individual PCS symptom (SOB, chest pain, dizziness, fatigue) was independently associated with a lower daily step count on the same day.
After adjusting for all symptoms simultaneously and ME/CFS status, only dizziness remained significantly associated with lower same-day step count.
Greater dizziness was significantly associated with a lower step count on the following day, independent of ME/CFS symptoms.
Walking at least 5,000 steps/day was associated with lower fatigue severity the following day, independent of same-day fatigue, age, sex, and ME/CFS status.
Walking at least 5,000 steps/day was associated with lower chest pain the following day, independent of same-day chest pain, age, sex, and ME/CFS status.
Dizziness was a highly prevalent symptom, reported by 78% of the PCS study participants.
The urinary-to-plasma ratio of soluble SMPDL3B was significantly lower in ME patients than in healthy controls.
Estimated renal clearance was significantly lower in ME patients than in healthy controls.
Plasma creatinine levels were similar between ME patients and healthy controls, indicating preserved gross renal function.
In ME patients, plasma soluble SMPDL3B levels were inversely correlated with renal clearance, a relationship absent in controls.

ME patients had significantly lower plasma 1,5-anhydrosorbitol, consistent with impaired renal tubular reabsorption, and this metabolite was inversely correlated with plasma SMPDL3B in ME but not in controls.
In multiple linear regression, the urinary-to-plasma SMPDL3B ratio independently predicted renal clearance in ME, alongside plasma creatinine, 1,5-anhydrosorbitol, and age as significant covariates.
Female ME patients showed a markedly lower urinary-to-plasma SMPDL3B ratio than male ME patients, a disparity not seen in controls.
Renal clearance was significantly lower in female ME patients than male ME patients, with no such difference in healthy controls.
Female ME patients reported higher overall symptom severity than male ME patients, with no such sex difference in controls.
Both female and male ME patients reported significantly more severe autonomic, endocrine, and immune-related symptoms than their sex-matched healthy controls.
Plasma citrate showed a sex-dependent reversal in its correlation with plasma SMPDL3B: a non-significant negative trend in females but a significant positive correlation in males.
Hippurate and threonine were positively correlated with plasma SMPDL3B in the overall ME cohort and remained significant in females but not males.
Urinary SMPDL3B correlations with citrate also showed a sex-dependent reversal, positive in females and negative in males.
Hippurate and threonine were positively correlated with urinary SMPDL3B in the overall ME cohort; hippurate remained significant in females but neither metabolite was significant in males.
Plasma succinic acid was significantly lower in ME patients than controls, potentially reflecting mitochondrial/TCA cycle dysfunction.
Plasma benzoic acid, a gut-derived renally excreted metabolite, was significantly reduced in ME patients.
Plasma phenyllactic acid, an inhibitor of succinate dehydrogenase, was significantly reduced in ME patients, possibly reflecting microbial metabolite accumulation during organ dysfunction.
Plasma L-tryptophan was significantly reduced in ME patients, indicating dysregulated amino acid/kynurenine pathway metabolism.
Plasma L-glutamine was significantly reduced in ME patients, potentially impairing nitrogen balance and energy metabolism.
Plasma L-kynurenine was significantly reduced in ME patients, supporting dysregulation of the kynurenine pathway linked to cognitive/neuro symptoms.
Plasma citrate was slightly elevated in ME patients relative to controls, possibly indicating altered organic acid handling or citric acid cycle activity.

Stratifying ME patients into low, intermediate, and high plasma SMPDL3B endophenotypes revealed a gradient in urine-to-plasma SMPDL3B ratio, with the high group showing the most impaired renal elimination.
Kidney clearance and plasma 1,5-anhydrosorbitol were lowest in the high SMPDL3B endophenotype group, indicating compromised tubular function.

Six membrane sphingolipids showed strong positive correlations with SMPDL3B in the low-SMPDL3B endophenotype group but strong negative correlations in the high-SMPDL3B group, with no significant associations in the intermediate group, suggesting a non-linear modulatory effect of SMPDL3B on membrane lipid metabolism.
PE 38:5 was lowest in the intermediate SMPDL3B endophenotype group, while PC 40:4 and CE 20:3 were highest in the low SMPDL3B group.
Comorbidities frequently reported in ME (allergy, depression, fibromyalgia, anxiety) were not associated with significant differences in renal clearance within the ME cohort.
At the phylum level, Bacteroidetes was more abundant in CFS patients compared to healthy controls.
At the phylum level, Firmicutes was less abundant in CFS patients compared to healthy controls.
At the class level, Bacteroidia abundance was higher in CFS patients than in healthy controls.
At the class level, Clostridia, Negativicutes, and Actinobacteria abundance were all lower in CFS patients compared to healthy controls.
At the order level, Bacteroidales was more abundant in CFS patients than in healthy controls.
At the order level, Selenomonadales was less abundant in CFS patients than in healthy controls.
At the family level, Bacteroidaceae abundance was higher in CFS patients than in healthy controls.
At the family level, Lachnospiraceae and Veillonellaceae abundances were lower in CFS patients than in healthy controls, consistent with reduced butyrate-producing taxa.
At the genus level, Bacteroides, Alistipes, and Ruminococcaceae abundances were higher in CFS patients than in healthy controls.
Gut microbial alpha-diversity (Shannon's H) and evenness (Shannon's E) did not differ significantly between CFS patients and healthy controls.
Gut microbial richness, measured as the number of observed OTUs, was significantly lower in CFS patients compared to healthy controls.
Overall gut microbial community structure (beta-diversity) significantly differed between CFS patients and healthy controls by both dbRDA and PERMANOVA.

A sparse PLS-DA model perfectly discriminated CFS from healthy controls (AUC=1), with Oscillibacter (ASV191), Ruminococcus_2 (ASV44), and Roseburia (ASV75) as the top discriminating ASVs, all more abundant in healthy controls than in CFS.
Gut microbial community composition significantly interacted with cognitive function, as measured by Trail Making Test Part B and the TMT B-A difference score, in both CFS and healthy controls.

The pattern of genus-level correlation with TMT B cognitive score differed between groups: in CFS, 8 genera correlated with TMT B and all were negative (higher abundance associated with better cognition), whereas in HCs, 29 genera correlated with TMT B, with a mix of 9 negative and 20 positive correlations.
Ruminococcaceae UCG-014 abundance was negatively correlated with TMT B score (i.e., associated with better executive function) in both CFS and healthy control groups.

Ruminococcaceae_UCG-010 correlation with TMT B score was in opposite directions between groups: positively correlated (worse cognition) in healthy controls, but negatively correlated (better cognition) in CFS patients.

Six genera (Christensenellaceae_R-7_group, Faecalibacterium, Prevotella_9, Roseburia, Ruminiclostridium_6, Terrisporobacter) were negatively correlated with TMT B score specifically in CFS patients (higher abundance linked to better executive function), a relationship not observed as strongly in healthy controls.

The gut microbial co-occurrence network in CFS patients had significantly lower node degree and eigenvector centrality compared to the network built from healthy controls, indicating altered network topology and connectivity in CFS.
A strong positive co-occurrence association between Dorea (ASV20) and Bacteroides (ASV2) was observed in CFS patients but was absent in healthy controls.

Among nine machine learning classifiers tested to distinguish CFS from healthy controls using gut microbial ASV data, Neural Network (multilayer perceptron, AUC up to 0.94) and SVM performed best, while XGBoost, Random Forest, and AdaBoost failed to reach an acceptable AUC (all below 0.7).

SHAP-based feature importance identified ASV 3979, ASV 5362, and ASV 272 as the top three amplicon sequence variants best discriminating CFS patients from healthy controls in the top-performing machine learning model.
Children with transfusion-dependent thalassemia (TDT) had significantly higher total Fibro-Fatigue (CFS) scale scores than healthy controls.
TDT children had significantly higher depressive symptom scores (CDI) than healthy controls.
TDT children had significantly higher anxiety symptom scores (SCAS) than healthy controls.
Serum CRP was significantly higher in TDT patients than controls (16.13 vs 4.00 mg/l).
Serum copper was significantly higher in TDT patients than controls.
Serum IL-6 was significantly higher in TDT patients than controls.
Serum IL-10 was significantly higher in TDT patients than controls.
Serum NSE was significantly higher in TDT patients than controls.
Serum GFAP was significantly higher in TDT patients than controls, surviving FDR correction.
Serum NFL was significantly higher in TDT patients than controls.
Serum magnesium, calcium, and zinc levels were significantly decreased in TDT patients compared with controls.
Serum nestin and albumin levels did not significantly differ between TDT patients and healthy controls.
Composite z-score indices of IRS activation (Comp_IRS) and neuronal injury (PC_neuronal, derived from GFAP, NSE, and nestin) were both significantly elevated in TDT patients compared to controls.
The Fibro-Fatigue (CFS) score was positively correlated with CRP, copper, IL-6, IL-10, GFAP, and NFL, and inversely correlated with magnesium, calcium, and zinc.
The CDI depression score was positively correlated with CRP, IL-10, NSE, GFAP, and NFL, and inversely correlated with magnesium, calcium, and zinc.
The SCAS anxiety score was positively correlated with CRP, copper, IL-10, and NFL, and inversely correlated with calcium and zinc.

Lower erythron status (Comp_erythron, based on hemoglobin and hematocrit) was significantly associated with higher CRP, copper, IL-6, IL-10, NSE, GFAP, and NFL, and with lower magnesium, calcium, and zinc.
Iron overload composite (Comp_IO, based on iron and ferritin) was positively correlated with CRP, copper, IL-6, IL-10, NSE, GFAP, and NFL, and inversely correlated with magnesium and calcium.
An integrated severity index of affective and CFS symptoms (Comp_severity) was significantly correlated with IRS activation, iron overload, and inversely with erythron status.
Multiple regression showed that CRP, copper, and NFL (positive) and calcium and magnesium (negative) together predicted 42.9% of the variance in the Fibro-Fatigue (CFS) score.
Multiple regression showed CRP, IL-10, and NFL (positive) and calcium (negative) predicted 31.8% of the variance in the CDI depression score.
Multiple regression showed NFL, CRP, and copper (positive) and zinc (negative) predicted 23.2% of the variance in the SCAS anxiety score.
IL-10 predicted 9.5% of the variance in serum NSE levels in TDT patients.
IL-6 and IL-10 jointly predicted 12.67% of the variance in serum GFAP levels.
Copper (positively) and hemoglobin (inversely) predicted 16.5% of the variance in serum NFL levels.
IL-6 (positively) and calcium (inversely) predicted 10.6% of the variance in serum nestin levels.
IL-6, IL-10, and ferritin together predicted 24.2% of the variance in the PC_neuronal (composite neuronal injury) score.
Ferritin (positively) and PCV% (inversely) predicted 27.1% of the variance in the Comp_IRS composite immune activation score.
IL-10 significantly predicted 9.5% of the variance in neuron-specific enolase levels in TDT patients.
IL-6 and IL-10 together explained 12.67% of the variance in serum GFAP levels in TDT patients.
Serum copper (positively) and hemoglobin (inversely) together explained 16.5% of the variance in neurofilament light chain levels.
IL-6 (positively) and calcium (inversely) together explained 10.6% of the variance in nestin levels.
IL-6, IL-10, and ferritin together explained 24.2% of the variance in the PC_neuronal composite score of neuronal injury.
Ferritin (positively) and PCV% (inversely) together explained 27.1% of the variance in the Comp_IRS immune activation composite score.

The composite severity index of affective and CFS symptoms (Comp_severity) was significantly positively correlated with immune-inflammatory activation (Comp_IRS) and iron overload (Comp_IO), and inversely correlated with erythron status (Comp_erythron).

The Comp_erythron index (based on hemoglobin and hematocrit) was significantly and inversely correlated with NSE, GFAP, and NFL, and with CRP, copper, IL-6, and IL-10, while positively correlated with magnesium, calcium, and zinc.

The Comp_IO composite (iron and ferritin, reflecting iron overload) was significantly correlated with NSE, GFAP, NFL, and nestin, as well as CRP, copper, IL-6, and IL-10, and inversely with magnesium and calcium.

The authors propose that IRS activation, neurotoxicity, and neuronal/astroglial injury pathways may represent drug targets, and neuroprotective agents may have therapeutic potential in TDT, pending validation in longitudinal studies.
A high proportion of JHS/hEDS patients tested ANA positive, with 131 of 210 patients (62.4%) showing a positive ANA test.

Most clinical manifestations of JHS/hEDS (arthralgias, patellofemoral pain, myofascial pain, fatigue, skin laxity, easy bruising, POTS, GI symptoms, urticaria, livedo reticularis, sicca, ocular disease, Raynaud's, thyroid disease) did not differ significantly between ANA+ and ANA- patients.
Joint dislocations were more common in the ANA-negative subgroup compared to the ANA-positive without SAID subgroup, the only clinical manifestation reaching statistical significance.
Patients with definitive systemic autoimmune disease (SAID) tended to have higher ANA titers than ANA-positive patients without SAID.
ANA-positive patients with definitive SAID were more likely to react to dsDNA, Smith, U1-RNP, Smith/RNP, SS-A, and SS-B autoantigens than ANA-positive patients without SAID.
The specific autoantigen target remained unidentified in 79.81% of ANA-positive patients without SAID compared to only 35.00% of ANA-positive patients with SAID.
The majority of ANA-positive patients, regardless of SAID status, showed a speckled ANA staining pattern (coarse and fine).
Beighton score and age at presentation were similar across different ANA titer subgroups, with no difference in clinical manifestations between subgroups.

Common comorbid features in JHS/hEDS patients included patellofemoral pain, dysautonomia (including POTS), gastrointestinal symptoms (GERD, IBS), and cutaneous manifestations (skin laxity, easy bruising, urticaria, livedo reticularis).

Of 131 ANA-positive JHS/hEDS patients, 20 (15.3%) met criteria for a definitive systemic autoimmune disease (SLE, MCTD, Sjögren's syndrome, pauci-articular JIA, sarcoidosis, polymyositis, primary biliary cirrhosis, HLA-B27+ spondylarthritis), while 111 remained ANA+ without SAID.
In a cited study, 43% of MALS patients lacked GI symptoms, and those with GI symptoms had a higher incidence of joint hypermobility and orthostatic intolerance (dizziness, syncope, POTS).
MALS is reported to predominantly affect young females aged 30-50 years, with a female-to-male ratio of 4:1.
EDS has been linked to other vascular compression syndromes including nutcracker syndrome, SMA syndrome, and May-Thurner syndrome.
A J-shaped 'hook-sign' configuration of post-stenotic dilation of the celiac artery is an imaging feature supporting MALS diagnosis.
Doppler ultrasound criteria supportive of MALS include celiac artery peak systolic velocity >200 cm/s and deflection angle >50 degrees.
The patient met 2017 international diagnostic criteria for hEDS with a Beighton score of 4 (one point below adult threshold) plus two positive responses on the five-part historical questionnaire.

A HIDA scan revealed gallbladder dyskinesia (ejection fraction 27%), leading to cholecystectomy, but the patient's abdominal pain persisted postoperatively, indicating the gallbladder was not the primary cause.
PPI and H2 blocker therapy trials were ineffective at relieving the patient's abdominal pain.
A trial of rifaximin for suspected small intestinal bacterial overgrowth failed to provide symptom relief.
Duplex ultrasound showed elevated SMA velocities suggestive of stenosis, but subsequent CT angiogram ruled out SMA syndrome, illustrating imaging discordance in this patient.

A vascular surgeon identified a low-riding median arcuate ligament abutting the celiac artery producing a 'hook sign', establishing the diagnosis of MALS after nearly 18 months of inconclusive evaluations.
A diagnostic celiac plexus block produced temporary symptom relief, supporting the MALS diagnosis.

Robotic-assisted median arcuate ligament release with bilateral celiac ganglionectomy revealed intraoperative fibrosis and chronic inflammation confirming chronic celiac artery compression, and resulted in initial symptom improvement.
The patient exhibited anatomical vascular variants including a hepatic artery originating from the SMA and a celiac artery dividing only into splenic and left gastric branches.
After initial post-surgical improvement, the patient developed recurrence of epigastric pain to preoperative severity along with 10-pound unintentional weight loss by July 2024.
Computed tomography in September 2024 showed possible scar tissue formation and postoperative inflammation at the surgical site, consistent with post-surgical fibrosis contributing to recurrence.
Image-guided cryoablation of the local splanchnic nerves was performed in May 2025 to target persistent pain after failed initial surgical relief.
An epigastric bruit, often more pronounced on inspiration, may be heard in up to 83% of MALS patients.
Unlike other EDS subtypes, hEDS currently lacks a known genetic marker and remains a purely clinical diagnosis.
A cited study found that patients with hEDS exhibited a higher incidence of MALS and other vascular compression syndromes, consistent with the presentation in this case.
Elective surgical management of MALS and other vascular disorders is associated with good outcomes, per cited literature, though long-term follow-up is recommended given recurrence risk.
Other case reports have documented symptom recurrence after surgical decompression for MALS, with fibrosis and residual autonomic dysfunction suggested as contributing mechanisms.

The patient reported significant psychosocial burden, including physical and emotional exhaustion and depressive episodes, resulting from years of chronic pain, delayed diagnosis, and repeated medical interventions.

The patient's small intestinal myenteric plexus showed an interganglionic distance of approximately 800 μm, far exceeding the established normal range of 380-570 μm seen in control specimens without dysmotility, indicating a structural ENS abnormality.

Standard immunostaining for c-Kit (interstitial cells of Cajal) and S100 (ganglionic marker) within the myenteric plexus showed no significant abnormality in the resected tissue, despite the patient's severe dysmotility.
The patient had a history of an FBN1 gene mutation in the context of hypermobile Ehlers-Danlos syndrome.
Nuclear medicine gastric emptying study demonstrated delayed gastric emptying, with 38% of ingested activity remaining in the stomach at 4 hours.

Anorectal manometry showed delayed balloon expulsion, decreased anal resting and squeeze pressures, poor intrarectal pressure augmentation with push, and paradoxical contractions during simulated defecation, consistent with a rectal evacuation disorder.
Magnetic resonance defecography demonstrated anal dyssynergia with an anorectal junction position of 3.3 cm below the pubococcygeal line, compared with a normal range of 2-3 cm.
An abnormal Sitz Marker study was consistent with slow transit constipation, showing 6 markers remaining in the left side of the colon after 5 days.

The patient trialed numerous pharmacologic agents (hyoscyamine, nortriptyline, ondansetron, scopolamine patch, compazine, metoclopramide, cyproheptadine, dronabinol, pyridostigmine, linaclotide, plecanatide, erythromycin, baclofen, mirtazapine, pregabalin), which were either ineffective or not tolerated due to side effects.
A trial of 10 sessions of pelvic floor physical therapy with biofeedback did not produce significant improvement in the patient's bowel movements.
Gastrointestinal dysmotility manifestations (abdominal pain, nausea, constipation, heartburn, IBS) are commonly reported in EDS patients and occur more frequently in women, per cited literature.

A prior study by Malagelada et al found that abnormal intestinal manometry was associated with abnormal histopathologic findings in 73% of full-thickness biopsies, but there was no clear correlation between specific manometric patterns and histopathologic findings.
Genetic testing confirmed the patient had vascular Ehlers-Danlos syndrome due to a pathogenic variant in COL3A1.

In a patient with vEDS and post-stroke spasticity, a routine passive hamstring stretching session at standard rehabilitation intensity caused sudden intramuscular hemorrhage with large hematomas in the biceps femoris and semitendinosus muscles.

The patient's left lower limb muscle tone fluctuated and was frequently observed to increase for unknown reasons in the days preceding the muscle injury, despite this not being reflected in formal MAS scores.
Spasticity causes muscle fiber degeneration with a shift from fast-twitch (Type II) to slow-twitch (Type I) fibers, improving endurance but reducing overall muscle power.
Spasticity is associated with increased extracellular matrix (ECM)/collagen deposition within muscle, contributing to stiffness and impaired flexibility.

Prolonged spasticity can lead to fatty infiltration and fibrosis of muscle, replacing muscle fibers with fat and connective tissue and causing significant decline in muscle function, more pronounced in underutilized or chronically spastic muscles.
Persistent spasticity and inactivity cause muscle atrophy, decreasing muscle mass and strength-related fibers, contributing to functional limitations.

In spastic muscle with concurrent vEDS, the quantitatively increased extracellular matrix is proposed to also have structural abnormalities at the type I collagen fibril level due to the qualitative defect in type III collagen, rendering it more prone to rupture, as supported by studies in homozygous Col3a1 knockout mice showing irregular, disorganized type I collagen fibrils.

Vascular fragility inherent in vEDS predisposes to arterial dissection, rupture, and bleeding tendencies, which combined with compromised microcirculation from sustained spastic muscle contraction increases susceptibility to micro-hemorrhage or hematoma formation in muscle.

Antiplatelet medication (clopidogrel, given for secondary stroke prevention before vEDS was diagnosed) likely contributed to increased bleeding tendency, resulting in severe intramuscular hemorrhage, and was discontinued due to progressive anemia after the muscle injury.

Discontinuation of clopidogrel, compression bandaging, and hemostatic agents (carbazochrome sodium sulfonate and tranexamic acid) led to resolution of the intramuscular hematoma within five days, with the patient resuming and progressively increasing walking exercises.

Review of six previously reported cases plus the present case found that muscle injury with spasticity commonly occurred in individuals with long-standing spasticity (three from spinal cord injury, three from cerebral injury, one from spastic paraparesis) during stretching-type activities such as transfers or passive stretching exercises, suggesting these injuries are likely underreported.
About 10.2% of competitive swimmers (29 of 285) reported a history of lumbar spine injury, including spondylolysis, lumbar strain, disc pathology, and facet joint pain.
Higher pool training volume was independently associated with more than double the odds of lumbar spine injury after adjustment.
Swimmers with hypermobility had over four times greater odds of lumbar spine injury compared to non-hypermobile swimmers.
Greater use of kickboards during training was associated with reduced odds of lumbar spine injury, suggesting a protective effect.
Injured swimmers were older and competed at a higher competitive level compared to uninjured swimmers, based on unadjusted group comparisons.
GJH, assessed via the 5PQ, was a significant predictor of self-reported long COVID in the full sample after adjusting for sex, age, infection count and vaccine doses.
The novel 'extreme hypermobility' measure (top 10th percentile within age/sex group) was a stronger predictor of long COVID than GJH in the full sample.
Among respondents with mild or no initial COVID-19 symptoms, GJH significantly predicted subsequent development of long COVID.

Among respondents with mild or no initial COVID-19 symptoms, extreme hypermobility significantly predicted subsequent development of long COVID, suggesting a pathway independent of initial infection severity.

Among respondents with severe initial COVID-19 symptoms, neither GJH nor extreme hypermobility significantly predicted long COVID, suggesting severe infection may swamp any connective-tissue-related risk.
GJH significantly predicted having severe initial symptoms during at least one COVID-19 infection.
Extreme hypermobility significantly predicted having severe initial symptoms during at least one COVID-19 infection, indicating a second (severity-mediated) pathway to long COVID.
Having severe initial symptoms from any COVID-19 infection was an independent, strong predictor of subsequently developing long COVID.
