Mediation analysis showed extreme hypermobility was both directly associated with long COVID and indirectly associated via the mediator of severe initial symptoms during at least one COVID-19 infection.

Using a sensitivity-analysis alternative definition of extreme hypermobility (answering 'yes' to ≥6 of 9 hypermobility questions, not stratified by age/sex), the association with long COVID in the full sample remained significant but was somewhat weaker than the primary measure.

In the subgroup with mild or no initial COVID-19 symptoms, the alternative (non-age/sex-stratified) extreme hypermobility definition was not significantly associated with long COVID, unlike the primary definition.
Respondents with long COVID were more likely than those without to report a parent, child or sibling also having long COVID, suggesting possible familial predisposition.
Respondents with long COVID were more likely to report two or more COVID-19 infections than those without long COVID.
In unadjusted group comparisons, the long COVID and non-long COVID groups differed significantly in the prevalence of extreme hypermobility, but not in the crude prevalence of GJH.

Among respondents with extreme hypermobility, the median reported degree of hypermobility was largely unchanged relative to pre-infection, but a significant share reported becoming more or less hypermobile since contracting COVID-19.

In an external cited cohort (JH-Crown Consortium database), patients with one of three connective tissue disorders had a substantially higher rate of developing PASC/long COVID than the overall cohort.

In a cited case-control study of ME/CFS patients, those with joint hypermobility showed a greater reduction in cerebral blood flow under orthostatic stress compared with those without joint hypermobility.

A cited study of women with venous-origin chronic pelvic pain (56% with EDS or hypermobility spectrum disorder) found substantial symptomatic improvement after surgical treatment of vascular compression, across symptoms overlapping with ME/CFS and long COVID.

The authors hypothesize, drawing on prior literature, that the interaction of connective tissue and mast cells may render people with EDS/HSD particularly vulnerable to mast cell activation disorders, which can in turn contribute to POTS, long COVID and ME/CFS.
In a 61-year-old woman with hypermobile Ehlers-Danlos syndrome, REMS-based BMD and TBS assessment identified osteoporosis with values comparable to those obtained by DXA and TBS.
Cited literature indicates that patients with Ehlers-Danlos syndrome tend to have reduced bone mineral density and increased fragility fracture risk.
Vertebral fractures are highly prevalent in adults with EDS even when DXA-measured BMD is normal, indicating DXA underdetects skeletal fragility in this population.
The presence and severity of vertebral fractures in EDS were significantly associated with back pain.
EDS patients show a cortical bone size deficit compared with controls, possibly related to reduced muscle cross-sectional area.
In 41 adults with osteogenesis imperfecta, BMD measured by both DXA and REMS at all skeletal sites was significantly lower than in healthy controls.
DXA-measured lumbar spine BMD did not differ significantly between OI type I and OI type III/IV subgroups.
REMS-measured lumbar spine BMD and TBS were significantly lower in OI type III/IV compared to OI type I, a distinction DXA failed to detect.
TBS correlated strongly with REMS-measured lumbar spine BMD but only marginally with DXA-measured lumbar spine BMD in OI patients.
In OI, bone microarchitecture shows reduced trabecular thickness and volumetric bone mass along with decreased cortical thickness and increased intracortical porosity.
Vitamin D-dependent rickets type 1A is caused by harmful mutations in the CYP27B1 gene, resulting in impaired vitamin D activation.
In a young woman with VDDR1A, REMS detected a decline in lumbar spine BMD Z-score from the first trimester of pregnancy to breastfeeding, while cortical bone density remained stable.
McCune-Albright syndrome is caused by somatic gain-of-function mutations of the GNAS gene.

In a McCune-Albright syndrome case with polyostotic fibrous dysplasia, DXA showed markedly elevated (artifactually high) T-scores at the femurs, while REMS showed much lower, more plausible T-scores, indicating better characterization of bone structure by REMS in the presence of fibrous dysplasia.
In 33 patients with acromegaly, BMD values at all skeletal sites measured by REMS did not differ significantly from those measured by DXA, and both correlated similarly with IGF-I levels.

REMS can be performed at the bedside or in a wheelchair without ionizing radiation, offering a feasible alternative to DXA for patients with Rett syndrome who have mobility and positioning limitations.
A prospective study of 1,989 patients found that the REMS-derived Fragility Score better predicts fracture risk in both men and women than BMD T-scores from DXA or REMS.
In patients with type 2 diabetes mellitus, lower lumbar spine BMD measured by REMS was significantly associated with a history of major fragility fractures, whereas DXA-measured BMD was not.
Over a 5-year follow-up, REMS showed higher sensitivity than DXA in identifying women prone to fragility fractures.
Fibromyalgia was one of the most frequently hashtagged conditions in chronic illness Instagram posts, appearing in 56 of 279 posts, and was noted as susceptible to self-diagnosis.
Mast cell activation syndrome was hashtagged in a small subset of posts and was listed among conditions with susceptibility to self-diagnosis.
ME/CFS was among the frequently hashtagged 'functional disorders' in chronic illness Instagram posts, appearing in 27 of 279 posts.
IBS was hashtagged in a small number of chronic illness posts, categorized as a functional disorder.
Headache was hashtagged in 14 of 279 posts and classified by the authors as a 'functional disorder'; the text uses 'headache' generically rather than specifying migraine diagnosis.

The authors speculate that web-based chronic illness communities may drive pursuit of 'popularized' diagnoses such as POTS or fibromyalgia, potentially prolonging diagnostic odysseys as users seek validation.
Longer Instagram captions were associated with significantly higher odds of a post overperforming (higher engagement), even after multivariate adjustment.

Posts containing health care content (medical equipment photo, medical location photo, or a health care experience caption) had significantly higher odds of overperforming, even after multivariate adjustment.
Photos depicting invasive medical equipment (e.g., IVs, PICC lines, feeding tubes) were strongly associated with higher odds of a post overperforming, the largest effect size in the model.
The vast majority of chronic illness Instagram posts referenced specific medical conditions via hashtags, spanning 107 distinct conditions.
A minority of analyzed posts depicted medical equipment in photos, with invasive devices (IVs, feeding tubes) rarer than noninvasive equipment (mobility aids).
Lateral pterygoid muscle (LPM) length measured on CBCT was significantly greater in male than in female TMD patients for the right, left, and total joints.
LPM length differed significantly according to TMJ movement type, being highest in hypermobile joints compared to normal or hypomobile joints across right, left, and total joints.
In patients with unilateral TMJ hypomobility, resting LPM length was significantly shorter on the hypomobile side compared with the contralateral side, suggesting muscle spasm.
There was no significant difference between males and females in the distribution of TMJ movement types (normal, hypomobile, hypermobile) for right, left, or all joints.
Among the 498 TMJs evaluated, hypermobility was the most common movement type in both sexes and for right, left, and all joints combined.
The CBCT-based LPM length measurement method showed excellent inter-observer and intra-observer reproducibility.
Adolescents with Down syndrome showed higher joint flexibility on the Beighton hypermobility test compared with typically developing peers.
Adolescents with Down syndrome had significantly lower lower-extremity strength (30-second Sit-to-Stand) and overall physical performance compared with typically developing peers.
Physical performance levels measured via timed up-and-go and Six-Minute Walking Test were lower in adolescents with Down syndrome than in typically developing peers.
Quality of life scores were lower in adolescents with Down syndrome than typically developing peers across all domains except emotional functioning.

In adolescents with Down syndrome, BMI was positively correlated with the PedsQL-A quality-of-life score and negatively correlated with the Physical Activity Questionnaire for Adolescents (PAQ-A) score.
The majority (83.33%) of adolescents with Down syndrome were classified as obese or overweight.

At 6 weeks postoperatively, 94% of patients showed confirmed osseous healing and were able to return to full weightbearing following an early weightbearing protocol after modified Lapidus arthrodesis.
Six percent of patients had delayed osseous healing at 6 weeks but demonstrated healing by 3-months follow-up.
Postoperative hallux valgus (HV) angle showed a significant mean reduction of 12 degrees following surgery.
Postoperative intermetatarsal angle (IMA) showed a significant mean reduction of 5 degrees following surgery.
Ten percent of patients experienced postoperative complications, including hardware irritation, sesamoiditis, hypertrophic scar, and joint stiffness.
Eight percent of patients required further surgery, mostly for hardware removal due to irritation.
Manchester-Oxford Foot Questionnaire (MOXFQ) scores significantly improved across all domains (total, walking/standing, pain, social interaction) postoperatively, with large effect sizes.
The walking/standing domain of the MOXFQ improved significantly postoperatively with a large effect size.
The pain domain of the MOXFQ improved significantly postoperatively with a large effect size.
The social interaction domain of the MOXFQ improved significantly postoperatively with a large effect size.
Patient satisfaction after surgery was high as measured by the PSQ-10 questionnaire.
Five patients (5%) were lost to follow-up by the 6-month time point.

At the distal (calf) skin biopsy site, the axonal loss degree, a normalized index of intraepidermal nerve fiber loss, was significantly greater in patients with small fiber neuropathy than in those with fibromyalgia-associated small fiber pathology, indicating a milder degree of nerve fiber loss in fibromyalgia.

Quantitative sensory testing showed lower (more abnormal) normalized cold and warm detection thresholds in patients with small fiber neuropathy compared with those with fibromyalgia-associated small fiber pathology.

A non-length-dependent pattern of IENFD reduction (leg/thigh ratio > 0.48) was more common among SFP-FMG patients (71%) than among SFN patients (46%), consistent with prior reports of differing spatial distribution of fiber loss between the two conditions.

Subgroup analysis by SFN etiology showed the ALD difference versus SFP-FMG was maintained across diabetic, autoimmune, genetic, and idiopathic subgroups, but not in the infectious-disease-associated SFN subgroup, likely due to small subgroup size (n=12).

ROC curve analysis of distal ALD showed good discriminative ability between SFN and SFP-FMG, with an optimal threshold of 37.6% ALD yielding high specificity but modest sensitivity for identifying SFN.

In the subgroup of patients with a non-length-dependent IENFD reduction pattern, proximal-site ALD was also significantly higher (greater fiber loss) in SFN than in SFP-FMG, mirroring the distal-site findings.

The authors interpret the milder and clinically non-correlating IENFD reduction in fibromyalgia as evidence that centrally mediated (rather than peripheral small fiber) mechanisms more likely drive pain in fibromyalgia syndrome.

Prior studies cited in the discussion found that abnormal IENFD in fibromyalgia does not correlate with clinically evident sensory disturbances or QST variables, suggesting a limited contribution of peripheral small fiber damage to fibromyalgia symptoms.
Fibromyalgia patients showed markedly higher resting intramuscular pressure in the trapezius muscle compared with patients with other rheumatic diseases.
Myofascial trigger points strongly correlate with the anatomical topography of fibromyalgia tender points.
Fibromyalgia patients show significantly higher muscle damping, indicating increased resting muscle tension, and commonly display palpable myofascial taut bands.

Electron microscopy biopsy studies found segmental muscle fiber necrosis, lipid and glycogen deposition, and subsarcolemmal mitochondrial accumulation in all sampled fibromyalgia muscle biopsies, suggestive of sustained contraction and ischemia.
Peripheral fibroblasts isolated from fibromyalgia patients express significantly higher levels of TGF-β compared with controls.

Fibromyalgia patients were found to have significantly lower amounts of intramuscular collagen and collagen crosslinking abnormalities that may predispose to muscle micro-injury and lower pain thresholds.
Microdialysis studies in fibromyalgia revealed higher interstitial concentrations of lactate, glutamate, and pyruvate.
Peripheral and muscle blood flow is reduced in fibromyalgia patients, suggesting cardiovascular functional disruption.
Fibromyalgia patients show an altered DNA hypomethylation pattern in genes involved in stress response, free radical clearance, and DNA repair, consistent with a role for oxidative stress.
Complete resolution of fibromyalgia symptoms was documented after parathyroidectomy in a case report.
Complete resolution of fibromyalgia after laparoscopic Roux-en-Y surgery and significant changes in fibromyalgia disease trajectory after laparoscopic cholecystectomy have been reported.
Human neuroma samples showed myofibroblasts embedded in a dense glycosaminoglycan matrix and associated with collagen, whereas control peripheral nerve samples lacked myofibroblasts entirely.

Cortical neuronal cultures grown on substrates with 100-fold higher stiffness showed roughly twice the presynaptic density and enhanced action potential/miniature synaptic current frequency compared with softer substrates.

In a case series of 37 plantar fasciitis patients treated with corticosteroid injection into the calcaneal origin of the fascia, plantar fascia rupture occurred in all cases, and while heel pain often improved, new problems such as metatarsal pain, foot weakness, swelling, and metatarsal fracture emerged in some patients.

A follow-up study of corticosteroid-associated plantar fascia rupture found new problems (lateral plantar nerve dysfunction, arch/midfoot strain, hammertoe, stress fracture) with mixed long-term outcomes.
Steroid injection was shown to decrease fibromatosis and myofibroblast content in adhesive capsulitis.
Mechanical stress was shown to increase levels of tau, amyloid beta, and alpha-synuclein proteins in the brains of wild-type mice.
In-vivo evidence indicates that proprioceptor-induced microglial activation could be crucial for initiating and maintaining abnormal pain in chronic fatigue syndrome.
Early evidence suggests tensegrity-principle-based manual therapy aimed at relieving myofascial tension may improve persistent postmastectomy pain.
Trigger point injection has been suggested as a useful treatment for persistent postmastectomy pain.
MRI investigations demonstrated a link between residual pain after total hip arthroplasty and soft tissue/fascial damage from the surgical procedure.
A comprehensive literature review found no convincing evidence that central sensitization can persist as an autonomous pain generator after the initiating injury has healed.
Mice with intermittent cold stress (ICS)-induced fibromyalgia showed a significantly lower mechanical pain withdrawal threshold than normal mice, indicating mechanical hyperalgesia.
2 Hz electroacupuncture (EA) at ST36 significantly reduced mechanical hyperalgesia in fibromyalgia mice compared with untreated FM mice.
Intracerebroventricular (i.c.v.) injection of PD-L1 protein produced an analgesic effect on mechanical hyperalgesia in fibromyalgia mice.
Fibromyalgia mice showed significant thermal hyperalgesia (shorter paw withdrawal latency) on the Hargreaves test compared with normal mice.
2 Hz EA treatment increased thermal withdrawal latency, alleviating thermal hyperalgesia in fibromyalgia mice.
i.c.v. PD-L1 injection increased thermal withdrawal latency, indicating an analgesic effect on thermal hyperalgesia in fibromyalgia mice.
Microglial marker Iba1 and astrocytic marker GFAP were significantly increased in the L3-L5 dorsal root ganglia (DRG) of fibromyalgia mice; EA reduced this activation but PD-L1 injection did not.
HMGB1 and S100B levels were increased in the DRG of fibromyalgia mice, and this was mitigated by EA but not by PD-L1 injection.
PD-1 receptor expression was decreased in the DRG of fibromyalgia mice; EA increased PD-1 expression again, but PD-L1 injection did not.
TLR4, MyD88, TRAF6, and phosphorylated NFκB were all increased in the DRG of fibromyalgia mice, and each was reduced by EA administration but not by PD-L1 injection.

Microglia (Iba1) and astrocyte (GFAP) markers were increased in the spinal cord, thalamus, somatosensory cortex, and cerebellar lobules 5-7 of fibromyalgia mice, and both EA and PD-L1 injection reduced these elevations in all these central regions.
HMGB1 and S100B were increased in the spinal cord, thalamus, somatosensory cortex, and cerebellum (CB5-7) of fibromyalgia mice, and both EA and PD-L1 injection reduced these levels.
PD-1 expression was reduced in the spinal cord, thalamus, and cerebellum (CB5-7) of fibromyalgia mice, and both EA and PD-L1 injection restored PD-1 levels in these regions.

In contrast to other regions, PD-1 was reported as increased in the somatosensory cortex (SSC) of fibromyalgia mice, and this was reduced by both EA and PD-L1 administration; note this contradicts the paper's own figure legend statement that PD-1 was lower in SSC, an internal inconsistency in the text.

TLR4, MyD88, TRAF6 and phosphorylated NFκB were increased across the spinal cord, thalamus, somatosensory cortex, and cerebellum (CB5-7) of fibromyalgia mice, and both EA treatment and PD-L1 injection reduced these levels in all these central regions.

The authors conclude that PD-L1 injection failed to reverse peripheral (DRG) neuroinflammatory and TLR4-pathway changes despite reducing pain behavior, whereas EA reversed both peripheral and central changes, indicating differing peripheral vs central mechanisms of the two treatments.

Reserpine administration significantly increased markers of oxidative stress, neuroinflammation, and behavioral changes including mechanical allodynia, hyperalgesia, anxiety, and depression-like behavior in a murine model of fibromyalgia.
Daily oral Boswellia (BS) extract at 100 mg/kg effectively restored the oxidative stress, neuroinflammatory, and behavioral pathology induced by reserpine.
BS supplementation decreased GFAP expression, indicating prevention of astrocyte activation.
BS supplementation decreased Iba-1 expression, indicating prevention of microglia activation.
Boswellia (BS) extract treatment increased nuclear translocation of Nrf2 and upregulated its downstream antioxidant targets HO-1 and NQO1 in the reserpine-induced fibromyalgia mouse model.
BS treatment limited lipid peroxidation and reactive oxygen species (ROS) production induced by reserpine in the fibromyalgia mouse model.
BS oral supplementation significantly reduced reserpine-induced anxiety- and depression-like (emotional deficit) behaviors in the fibromyalgia mouse model.
BS treatment reduced mechanical allodynia and hyperalgesia (mechanical sensitivity) previously induced by reserpine in the fibromyalgia mouse model.
Adults with fibromyalgia consumed a significantly higher percentage of total energy intake from ultra-processed foods compared to healthy controls.
Patients with fibromyalgia had significantly higher Dietary Inflammatory Index scores than healthy controls, indicating a more pro-inflammatory diet.
Patients with fibromyalgia had a significantly higher BMI compared to healthy controls.
Fat mass percentage was significantly higher in fibromyalgia patients compared to healthy controls.
Muscle mass percentage was significantly lower in fibromyalgia patients compared to healthy controls.
Fibromyalgia patients reported markedly greater pain intensity on the Visual Analog Scale compared to healthy controls.
Fibromyalgia patients reported significantly greater fatigue on the Fatigue Severity Scale compared to healthy controls.
Fibromyalgia patients showed significant impairments in Fibromyalgia Impact Questionnaire scores compared to controls, reflecting greater disease burden.
Nutritional analysis showed lower intakes of magnesium, vitamin C, and polyphenols in fibromyalgia patients compared to controls.
Adults with FMS reported higher consumption of saturated fats and refined carbohydrates compared to healthy controls.
Two of the included studies found reduced alpha diversity of gut microbiota in patients with fibromyalgia compared with controls.

At the phylum level, one study reported both increased Firmicutes and Bacteroidetes and decreased Firmicutes, Bacteroidetes, and Actinobacteria in fibromyalgia patients, indicating inconsistent phylum-level shifts.
At the genus level, the abundance of Bacteroides was reduced in fibromyalgia patients across studies.
Genera Bifidobacterium, Eubacterium, and Clostridium were reduced in fibromyalgia patients, with Bifidobacterium and Eubacterium noted as participants in host neurotransmitter metabolism.
Genera Dorea, Roseburia, Alistipes, Subdoligranulum, and Papillibacter were increased in fibromyalgia patients relative to controls.
One large observational study reported a causal relationship between alteration of five genera (Coprococcus2, Eggerthella, Lactobacillus, FamillyXIIIUCG001, and Olsenella) and fibromyalgia.
At the family level, Ruminococcaceae was decreased in chronic widespread pain patients.
Firmicutes and Lachnospiraceae families were reported as both increased and decreased in chronic widespread pain patients within the same study.

Bifidobacteriaceae and Bacteroidales families were absent from the core microbiota of fibromyalgia patients, alongside decreases in other families, while Rikenellaceae and Lachnospiraceae were increased.
Rikenellaceae and Lachnospiraceae families showed increased abundance in fibromyalgia patients.
At the class level, Actinobacteria was decreased in fibromyalgia patients compared with controls.

At the species level, multiple taxa including I. butyriciproducens, F. plautii, B. desmolans, E. tayi, E. massiliensis, Parabacteroides merdae, Akkermansia muciniphila, and Clostridium scindens were increased in fibromyalgia patients.
F. prausnitzii, B. uniformis, Haemophilus, P. copri, and Blautia faecis were decreased in fibromyalgia patients relative to controls.

In chronic widespread pain patients, increased odontolyticus and decreased excrementihominis, obeum, formicigenerans, splanchnicus, ureilytica, inulinivorans, and Coprococcus comes were reported, with massiliensis identified as the common altered species between CWP and FM.
F. prausnitzii decreased in fibromyalgia patients, corroborated by evidence of altered circulating short-chain fatty acids (SCFA).
Bacteroides spp. abundance was positively correlated with total symptom score on the Fibromyalgia Impact Questionnaire (FIQ) in FM patients.

A high-potency multi-strain probiotic (1x10^10 CFU) was associated with significant improvements in self-reported pain, sleep quality, overall quality of life, depression, and anxiety in fibromyalgia patients.
Two RCTs found no statistically significant differences between probiotic/prebiotic intervention and control groups on VAS or FIQ scores in fibromyalgia patients.

The single RCT investigating FMT in fibromyalgia patients found improvements in widespread pain intensity, anxiety, depression, and sleep at 6 and 12 months, along with changes in certain neurotransmitters.

A one-month prospective cohort study of a synbiotic intervention (probiotic plus prebiotic strains) decreased stress, anxiety, and depression and improved quality of life, with dysregulation of inflammatory and stress responses observed particularly in those without prior chronic fatigue syndrome diagnosis.

Fibromyalgia patients exhibited higher abundance of Clostridium scindens and B. desmolans, species implicated in steroid hormone metabolism via 20alpha-hydroxysteroid dehydrogenase activity that converts cortisol to androgens.

A higher relative abundance of Parabacteroides merdae and Akkermansia muciniphila was found in fibromyalgia patients; these species were previously identified as mediators of the antiseizure effects of a ketogenic diet.
Species with a putative pro-inflammatory role, including P. copri, Bacteroides uniformis, and Haemophilus parainfluenzae, were depleted in fibromyalgia patients.

Roman et al. reported that a probiotic containing Lactobacillus acidophilus or Lactobacillus rhamnosus GG did not significantly improve depressive or anxiety symptoms compared to placebo in fibromyalgia patients.
A preclinical study found that probiotics L. reuteri LR06 or Bifidobacterium BL5b had no significant antinociception effects in chronic pain rats.

In an animal study of chronic widespread pain, Lactobacillus rhamnosus GG (10 billion CFU/150 mL) attenuated muscle mechanical hyperalgesia in early-life stress-induced widespread muscle pain in adult rats.
Sex-dependent microbial signatures were identified with elevated Ruminococcus and Pseudomonas in females with fibromyalgia, potentially relating to female predominance in FM prevalence and severity.

Decreased F. prausnitzii, a prominent butyrate producer, may reduce butyrate-mediated HDAC inhibition and regulatory T-cell differentiation, plausibly contributing to a pro-inflammatory state hypothesized in FM/CWP.
Across three SRs and two SRMAs (52 studies, 1,914 participants), tDCS produced improvements in fibromyalgia-related symptoms including pain, fatigue, pain catastrophizing, and QoL.
One SRMA found a statistically significant reduction in fibromyalgia pain with tDCS compared to sham (SMD −0.35).
Another SRMA showed the analgesic effect of tDCS on fibromyalgia pain was maintained over a 4-week treatment period (SMD 1.22).
A SRMA identified significant analgesic efficacy specifically when tDCS stimulation was applied over the primary motor cortex (M1) in fibromyalgia patients (SMD −0.59).

In fibromyalgia patients, the most effective tDCS protocol was 5–10 sessions at 1.5–2 mA over the left M1 for 20 minutes per day; reported adverse events were mostly mild (skin redness, tingling, itching, sleepiness, headache, mood change, visual perceptual changes, fatigue).

Overall GRADE certainty of evidence for tDCS effects on fibromyalgia (and other conditions) was rated very low in this umbrella review, in contrast to low certainty reported by a prior umbrella review (Kang et al.).
One SR and three SRMAs (25 studies, 1,147 participants) found tDCS reduced headache intensity, severity, and frequency in migraine patients.
In migraine patients, one meta-analysis observed sustained analgesic effects over a 4-week period, and another reported significant reduction in pain intensity and decreased analgesic use with tDCS.
Fibromyalgia was among the etiologies of neuropathic pain examined in SRs/SRMAs of tDCS for neuropathic pain, which overall reported positive effects on pain severity (SMD −0.38).
IL-9 enhances mast cell proliferation, survival and activation, increasing production of cytokines including IL-1β, IL-5, IL-6 and IL-13.

IL-9 responsiveness requires both IL-9Rα and the common gamma chain, and inflammatory conditions can upregulate these subunits to broaden IL-9 responsiveness in non-lymphoid cells including mast cells and epithelium.

IL-9 receptor engagement primarily activates JAK/STAT signaling (JAK1, JAK3, STAT1, STAT3, STAT5), with additional contributions from MAPK and PI3K/IRS pathways, and is negatively regulated by SOCS, PIAS and SH-PTP2.
Autocrine IL-9 signaling upregulates the lactate transporter MCT1 (SLC16A1), driving aerobic glycolysis and effector function in Th9 cells.
Atopic dermatitis lesional skin shows elevated IL-9/IL-9R expression, Th9 cell frequency correlates with disease severity, and IL-9 neutralization ameliorates disease.
IL-9 is a genetic risk factor for asthma and contributes to airway hyperresponsiveness, eosinophilia, and mast cell hyperplasia.
IL-9 deficiency or neutralization protects mice from experimental colitis, while IL-9 directly impairs intestinal epithelial growth, wound healing and tight junction protein expression.
IL-9 protects against intestinal nematode infections by enhancing antibody responses, mast cell function and basophilia.
mTOR-driven IL-9 production is associated with mast cell hyperplasia and pathology in experimental food allergy models.
Rictor deficiency (mTORC2 loss) impairs Th9 polarization and allergic airway inflammation, indicating both mTORC1 and mTORC2 contribute to Th9 differentiation.

Rheumatoid arthritis and psoriatic arthritis patients show elevated IL-9 in synovial fluid/tissue with high IL-9R expression on infiltrating T cells, yet IL-9-deficient mice develop worse antigen-induced arthritis with impaired Treg function.

Systemic lupus erythematosus patients show elevated circulating IL-9 and Th9 cells, and IL-9 neutralization (especially combined with IL-17 blockade) reduces autoantibody production and renal pathology in lupus-prone mice.

In multiple sclerosis models, IL-9 and Th9 cells contribute to pathology, but IL-9R deficiency has been reported to either exacerbate or suppress experimental autoimmune encephalomyelitis depending on the study.
Among CD4 T cell subsets, Th9 cells exhibit the highest glycolytic activity, with mTOR required for optimal IL-9 production.
The synthetic PPAR-γ agonist rosiglitazone suppresses IL-9 production in human Th9 cells, with enhanced suppression when combined with the glycolysis inhibitor 2-deoxy-D-glucose.

Inhibiting ACC1 or culturing Th9 cells under fatty acid-free conditions substantially increases IL-9 production, an effect reversed by exogenous oleic or palmitic acid, indicating de novo fatty acid synthesis suppresses Th9 differentiation.
Pre-treating Th9 cells with an ACC1 inhibitor in vitro enhanced their anti-tumor activity following adoptive transfer into tumor-bearing mice.
The IL-9 neutralizing antibody Medi-528 did not show clinical benefit in an asthma clinical trial, highlighting challenges in translating IL-9-targeted therapy.
High IL-9 expression correlates with improved patient survival in gastric cancer, and recombinant IL-9 augments the efficacy of anti-PD-1 immunotherapy.
Kounis syndrome occurs in about 1.1–3.4% of patients who experience an allergic, hypersensitive, anaphylactic, or anaphylactoid insult.
Type I Kounis syndrome (MINOCA-type MI caused by histamine, chymase, or arachidonic acid products) affects 76.6% of patients with normal or nearly normal coronary arteries.
Type II Kounis syndrome, involving acute myocardial infarction with platelet activation on quiescent preexisting coronary disease, affects 22.3% of patients.

Type III Kounis syndrome, comprising stent thrombosis (IIIa) and/or stent restenosis (IIIb), affects 5.1% of patients and is caused by stent polymers, metals, eluted medications, dual antiplatelets, and environmental exposure.
Patients with nonallergic acute coronary syndromes show blood histamine concentrations more than twice as high as healthy individuals.

In the acute stage of nonallergic myocardial infarction, arachidonic acid metabolites like thromboxane and leukotrienes are substantially more prevalent in systemic arterial circulation compared to normal controls.
Patients with nonallergic acute coronary syndromes have higher levels of interleukin-6, produced from inflammatory coronary plaques and areas of myocardial necrosis.
Mast cell degranulation is found at a 200:1 higher degree at coronary plaque erosion or rupture sites compared to adjacent or farther regions in nonallergic post-mortem myocardial infarction cases.
IgE levels may be elevated in both stable and unstable angina and acute myocardial infarction, correlating with severity of infarction and plaque destabilization.
In a cohort of 270 initially healthy hyperlipidemic men, IgE, IgA, and IgG levels were noticeably higher prior to myocardial infarction compared to matched healthy control subjects.
Patients with multi-vessel coronary disease have substantially higher total serum IgE than patients with single-vessel disease, independent of conventional risk factors.
Tryptase is found almost exclusively in mast cells, with human basophils containing only trace amounts (0.04 pg per basophil).

The current diagnostic standard for mast cell activation/anaphylaxis is a rise in serum tryptase of more than 20% + 2 ng/mL above baseline, measured within about 4 hours of symptom onset (the '20+2 rule').
Tryptase has a short circulating half-life of roughly 90 minutes, similar to other inflammatory mediators.

Asymptomatic controls, including those positive for hereditary alpha tryptasemia (HαT), typically have basal tryptase levels between 1 and 15 ng/mL, a reference range meant to prevent overinterpretation.

COVID-19 patients exhibit cytokine storm with abnormally high IL-6, TNF-alpha, and CRP, mediators linked to coronary vasospasm, plaque destabilization, and thrombus formation implicated in Kounis syndrome pathophysiology.

Mast cell-derived cytokines can increase blood-brain barrier permeability, a proposed mechanism for SARS-CoV-2-associated 'COVID-19 brain fog,' either by directly activating mast cells or via cytokine entry through a compromised barrier.
VAERS received reports of 175 severe allergic reactions, including 21 anaphylaxis cases, among 1,893,360 people who received their first dose of the Pfizer-BioNTech COVID-19 vaccine.

Autopsy data indicate approximately half of deaths following COVID-19 mRNA-lipid nanoparticle vaccine administration are cardiovascular events, with most occurring the same day or day after vaccination, and a cytokine storm-related death rate distinct from conventional vaccine allergic reactions.
Combined use of sodium cromoglycate (mast cell membrane stabilizer) and dexamethasone (anti-inflammatory) has been shown to prevent late thrombotic events.
Omalizumab, a humanized anti-IgE monoclonal antibody, has been effectively used to treat recurrent Kounis syndrome by lowering circulating IgE and preventing IgE receptor cross-linking.

MRGPRX2 is a mast cell receptor mediating IgE-independent degranulation, activated by insect venoms and small-molecule antibiotics, and implicated in a number of mast cell-mediated disorders including cases of Kounis syndrome with normal tryptase or undetected specific IgE.

Transmembrane SCF embedded in lipid nanodiscs or proteoliposomes can prevent mast cell activation, offering a therapeutic/preventive strategy without the toxicity associated with drugs targeting SCF directly.
Mast cells originate from bone marrow mononuclear precursors expressing KIT receptors for SCF, a cytokine essential for mast cell development, growth, adhesion, proliferation, survival, and homing.
Patients with chronic mast cell-mediated angioedema (MC-AE) had a significantly higher BMI than those with chronic spontaneous urticaria (CSU).
Obesity (BMI ≥30) was significantly more prevalent among MC-AE patients than CSU patients at baseline.
Hypertension was significantly more prevalent in MC-AE than CSU at baseline diagnosis.
Ischemic heart disease and myocardial infarction were more prevalent among MC-AE patients than CSU patients at baseline.
Myocardial infarction was more than twice as prevalent in MC-AE patients compared to CSU patients at baseline.
MACE occurred more frequently in MC-AE patients than CSU patients at baseline.
Microalbuminuria was slightly more prevalent in MC-AE at baseline, approaching but not reaching statistical significance.
Type 2 diabetes mellitus was significantly more frequent in MC-AE than CSU patients at baseline.
Food allergy and systemic anaphylaxis did not significantly differ between MC-AE and CSU at either baseline or 10-year follow-up.
Atopic dermatitis was consistently less prevalent in MC-AE than CSU at both baseline and 10-year follow-up.
Contact dermatitis was consistently less prevalent in MC-AE than CSU at both baseline and 10-year follow-up.
Dermatophytosis was consistently less prevalent in MC-AE than CSU at both baseline and 10-year follow-up.
Pityriasis rosea was consistently less prevalent in MC-AE than CSU at both baseline and 10-year follow-up.
Bacterial pneumonia was more common in MC-AE than CSU at baseline, though the authors note this baseline infectious association was modest and transient.
Tonsillitis, viral infections, and viral warts were consistently more prevalent in CSU than MC-AE at both baseline and 10-year follow-up.
Herpes zoster was consistently more prevalent in CSU than MC-AE at both baseline and 10-year follow-up.
Systemic corticosteroid prescriptions were slightly less common in MC-AE than CSU.
Sustained H1-antihistamine use was modestly lower in MC-AE than CSU.
Hypertension remained significantly more prevalent in MC-AE than CSU after 10 years of follow-up.
Ischemic heart disease, myocardial infarction, PCI, congestive heart failure, and MACE were all significantly more prevalent in MC-AE than CSU after 10 years of follow-up.
Chronic kidney disease and microalbuminuria were significantly more prevalent in MC-AE than CSU after 10 years, in contrast to the non-significant baseline finding.
Type 2 diabetes and dyslipidemia complications were significantly more prevalent in MC-AE than CSU after 10 years of follow-up.
Statin use was independently associated with reduced adjusted odds of being classified as MC-AE versus CSU.
Insulin use showed a substantially elevated but statistically non-significant association with MC-AE odds in the adjusted model.

In a stepwise-selected multivariable logistic regression model, hypertension, type 2 diabetes, myocardial infarction, chronic kidney disease, and obesity were the strongest independent predictors of MC-AE classification versus CSU.

In the stepwise-selected multivariable model, atopic dermatitis, contact dermatitis, dermatophytosis, and herpes zoster were significant negative independent predictors of MC-AE (i.e., independently associated with CSU).
After 10 years of follow-up, ischemic heart disease remained more prevalent among MC-AE patients than CSU patients.
Myocardial infarction prevalence remained significantly higher in MC-AE than CSU after 10 years of follow-up.
PCI rates were higher among MC-AE patients than CSU patients at 10-year follow-up.
Congestive heart failure prevalence was significantly higher in MC-AE than CSU at 10-year follow-up.
MACE prevalence was significantly higher in MC-AE than CSU at 10-year follow-up.
Chronic kidney disease was significantly more prevalent in MC-AE patients than CSU patients after 10 years.
Microalbuminuria was significantly more prevalent in MC-AE than CSU after 10 years of follow-up.
Type 2 diabetes mellitus remained significantly more prevalent in MC-AE than CSU at 10-year follow-up.
Dyslipidemia complications were more common in MC-AE than CSU at 10-year follow-up, at borderline significance.
Thyroid diseases were comparable between MC-AE and CSU patients at 10-year follow-up.
Food allergy prevalence did not significantly differ between MC-AE and CSU at 10-year follow-up.
Systemic anaphylaxis rates did not significantly differ between MC-AE and CSU at 10-year follow-up.
Atopic dermatitis remained significantly more common in CSU than MC-AE at 10-year follow-up.
Contact dermatitis remained significantly more common in CSU than MC-AE at 10-year follow-up.
Dermatophytosis remained significantly more common in CSU than MC-AE at 10-year follow-up.
Pityriasis rosea remained significantly more common in CSU than MC-AE at 10-year follow-up.
Tonsillitis continued to be more prevalent in CSU than MC-AE patients at 10-year follow-up.
Viral infections continued to be more prevalent in CSU than MC-AE patients at 10-year follow-up.
Viral warts continued to be more prevalent in CSU than MC-AE patients at 10-year follow-up.
Herpes zoster continued to be more prevalent in CSU than MC-AE patients at 10-year follow-up.
Statin use was independently associated with significantly reduced odds of being classified in the MC-AE group in the comorbidity-adjusted multivariable model.
Insulin use was associated with a substantially elevated but statistically non-significant odds of MC-AE in the adjusted model.

No statistically significant associations were found between MC-AE odds and use of systemic corticosteroids, ACE inhibitors, angiotensin receptor blockers, beta-blockers, calcium channel blockers, or metformin in the adjusted model.
Hypertension was identified as one of the strongest independent predictors of MC-AE diagnosis in the stepwise-selected logistic regression model.
Type 2 diabetes mellitus was an independent predictor of MC-AE diagnosis in the stepwise-selected regression model.
Myocardial infarction was an independent predictor of MC-AE diagnosis in the stepwise-selected regression model, with the largest effect size among cardiometabolic predictors.
Asthma prevalence did not differ significantly between MC-AE and CSU patients, unlike other mast cell-associated comorbidities.
At baseline, psoriasis was infrequent and not significantly associated with either MC-AE or CSU.
After 10 years of follow-up, psoriasis remained unassociated with either MC-AE or CSU, possibly reflecting its predominant Th17/IL-23-driven biology.
The authors hypothesize that mast cells may be involved in vitiligo induction and progression, potentially explaining vitiligo's emergence as an independent predictor of MC-AE.
Dyslipidemia prevalence at baseline did not differ significantly between MC-AE and CSU patients.
Autoimmune thyroid disorders did not differ significantly between MC-AE and CSU patients at baseline.
Graves' disease showed a non-significant trend toward higher prevalence in MC-AE compared with CSU at baseline.
Thyroid diseases remained comparable between MC-AE and CSU groups after 10 years of follow-up.
After 10 years, dyslipidemia complications were more prevalent in MC-AE than CSU patients, at borderline significance.
The higher prevalence of obesity in MC-AE compared with CSU was largely driven by patients in the 30-59 year middle-aged bracket.

Gut microbiome dysbiosis is increasingly linked to hereditary angioedema and is proposed as a causal contributor to chronic spontaneous urticaria, suggesting the microbiome as a potential driver worth exploring in MC-AE.

The authors propose that MC-AE and CSU may arise from distinct mast cell activation pathways, with CSU driven by autoreactive IgG/IgE and MC-AE potentially involving MRGPRX2 stimulation or complement-derived anaphylatoxins (C3a, C5a).

Convergent evidence from prior CSU studies shows elevated chemokines (CXCL8/IL-8, CXCL9/10, CCL2, CCL5, CCL11, CCL17, CCL26, CCL27) and adhesion molecules (P-selectin, ICAM-1, VCAM-1) that decrease with effective therapy, indicating mast cell-driven endothelial activation.

Statins are proposed to reduce MC-AE risk via anti-inflammatory, endothelial-stabilizing, and mast cell-modulating effects, including inhibition of FcεRI expression and reduced mast cell degranulation and cytokine release.

Despite their known role in inducing bradykinin-mediated angioedema, ACE inhibitor use showed no association with chronic mast cell-mediated angioedema, supporting mechanistic heterogeneity among angioedema syndromes.
In a prior study by the same group, low IgE characterized MC-AE while higher IgE characterized CSU, suggesting two distinct types of immune dysregulation.
Pooled RCT data show remibrutinib significantly reduced Urticaria Activity Score over 7 days (UAS7) at week 12 compared with placebo.
Remibrutinib was associated with significant improvement in itch severity score compared with placebo.
Remibrutinib was associated with significant improvement in hives severity score compared with placebo.
Remibrutinib increased the likelihood of achieving complete response (UAS7=0) compared with placebo.
Remibrutinib increased the likelihood of achieving controlled disease (UAS7 ≤ 6) compared with placebo.
Remibrutinib increased the likelihood of achieving minimal quality-of-life impact (DLQI ≤ 1) compared with placebo.
In the REMIX-1 and REMIX-2 trials, remibrutinib showed significantly better disease control (UAS7 ≤ 6) as early as week 2.
Remibrutinib was associated with increased risk of nasopharyngitis compared with placebo.
Remibrutinib was associated with increased risk of upper respiratory tract infection compared with placebo.
Remibrutinib was associated with a markedly increased risk of petechiae compared with placebo.
Single-arm studies (BISCUIT at 24 weeks and Jain 2024 at 52 weeks) suggested that remibrutinib's efficacy and tolerability were sustained over longer-term follow-up.
Using the Fatigue Assessment Scale, about half of Japanese sarcoidosis patients reported fatigue and a smaller subset reported extreme fatigue at baseline.
Using the Small Fiber Neuropathy Screening List, over 40% of patients showed probable/highly probable SFN symptoms and a smaller subset met SFN threshold at baseline.
FAS and SFNSL scores did not significantly differ between male and female patients.
FAS and SFNSL scores were strongly correlated with each other at baseline, suggesting fatigue and SFN symptoms co-occur in sarcoidosis.

Higher FAS (fatigue) scores were strongly associated with worse physical function, vitality, and mental health domains of SF-36 quality of life, and significantly correlated with all eight SF-36 domains.
Higher SFNSL (SFN symptom) scores were strongly associated with worse bodily pain and vitality domains of SF-36 and significantly correlated with all eight SF-36 domains.
Neither FAS nor SFNSL scores correlated with sarcoidosis clinical/laboratory parameters including ACE and soluble IL-2 receptor levels or corticosteroid use.
Over a 1-year follow-up, FAS and SFNSL scores did not significantly change in the overall cohort.
In the longitudinal subcohort, FAS and SFNSL scores remained strongly correlated at both baseline and 1-year follow-up.
Within-subject changes in fatigue (FAS) score over 1 year showed moderate correlation with changes in physical functioning and physical component summary of SF-36.
Within-subject changes in SFN symptom (SFNSL) score over 1 year showed moderate correlation with changes in general health domain of SF-36.
Changes in FAS or SFNSL scores over 1 year did not correlate with changes in ACE or sIL2R levels.
Oral or inhaled corticosteroid treatment during the 1-year follow-up was not associated with significant changes in FAS or SFNSL scores compared with untreated patients.
In a single patient, adjunctive acupuncture alongside corticosteroid therapy was associated with a marked reduction in SFNSL score over 1 year, while the FAS score remained unchanged.
Adolescents with a comorbid diagnosis of Juvenile Idiopathic Arthritis were more likely to have a positive skin biopsy for small-fiber neuropathy than those without JIA.
Adolescents with positive skin biopsies for small-fiber neuropathy had higher median serum ACE levels than those with negative biopsies.
Adolescents with positive skin biopsies for small-fiber neuropathy had higher median free T4 levels than those with negative biopsies.
No specific clinical symptoms were found to predict a positive skin biopsy result for small-fiber neuropathy in this adolescent chronic pain cohort.
Anti-MX1 IgG autoantibody levels measured by indirect ELISA were significantly higher in Definite SFN patients compared to healthy controls.
Within SFN patients, those with an autoimmune etiology had preferentially elevated anti-MX1 autoantibody levels compared to both healthy controls and patients with secondary (non-autoimmune) SFN.
Anti-MX1 autoantibody levels did not differ between healthy controls and SFN patients with non-autoimmune (secondary) causes.

IgG from SFN patient sera (idiopathic and autoimmune) bound to teased rat sciatic nerve fibers and colocalized with peripherin, indicating targeting of unmyelinated nerve fibers, whereas healthy control sera showed no such binding.

Immunocytochemistry on HEK293 cells transfected with MX1-dsRED showed specific binding of SFN patient IgG (e.g., SFN050, SFN088) to MX1-expressing cells but not to wild-type HEK293 cells, confirming specific patient anti-MX1 reactivity.
Flow cytometry identified five SFN patients with anti-MX1 antibody binding ≥3 SD above the mean of 20 healthy controls, shown by a right shift in MX1/WT fluorescence ratio.
Patient sera classified as ICC-Positive for anti-MX1 showed significantly higher flow cytometry MFI change and percent positive cell population compared to ICC-Negative sera.
Anti-MX1 autoantibodies detected in SFN patient sera were exclusively of the IgG1 subclass, with no binding to IgG2, IgG3, or IgG4 on dot blot.
Both TRPC6 and MX1 proteins were localized to the cell surface in surface biotinylation assays, but co-immunoprecipitation showed no direct physical interaction between MX1 and HA-tagged TRPC6.
Co-transfection of MX1 with TRPC6 in HEK293 cells did not significantly alter TRPC6 current density in response to carbachol compared to TRPC6 alone.

Dorsal root ganglion (DRG) neurons overexpressing MX1 via lentiviral transduction showed significant depolarization of resting membrane potential compared to control neurons, indicating a shift toward increased excitability.
DRG neurons overexpressing MX1 showed increased action potential firing frequency compared to control neurons, indicating heightened neuronal responsiveness.

Addition of anti-MX1 antibody to MX1-overexpressing DRG neurons did not significantly change resting membrane potential or action potential firing frequency, suggesting direct antibody binding may not be the sole driver of the electrophysiological phenotype.

In the 59-patient Definite SFN cohort, the most common symptoms were paresthesia (59.3%), pain (44.1%), burning sensation (20.3%), temperature changes (13.6%), hyperalgesia (10.2%), and reduced sensation (8.5%), with autonomic symptoms reported by 66.1% (mostly gastrointestinal, 44.1%).

Among 59 Definite SFN patients, autoimmune/rheumatological causes accounted for 49.2% of etiologies and 42.4% had positive autoimmune blood tests (anti-ENA, ANCA, low C3/C4, high ESR, or ANA titers), while diabetes mellitus accounted for 6.7% and idiopathic classification for 57.6%.
Treatment induced neuropathy of diabetes is an acute, severely painful small fiber neuropathy that develops in association with a rapid drop in glycated hemoglobin levels.

Diabetic radiculoplexus neuropathies (lumbosacral, cervical, thoracic forms) present with pain and weight loss followed by weakness and sensory loss in a single anatomical region, driven by a monophasic inflammatory microvasculitis that does not appear to respond to immunomodulatory therapy.
Diabetic monophasic cranial mononeuropathies are caused by non-inflammatory microvascular ischemia and present acutely with subsequent slow improvement.
Patients with diabetes have an increased risk of compressive neuropathies, particularly involving the median, ulnar, and peroneal nerves.

Several lines of evidence suggest an increased prevalence of chronic inflammatory demyelinating polyneuropathy (CIDP) among patients with diabetes, though definitive CIDP diagnosis is often complicated by coexisting diabetic neuropathy.
Genetic loss of Pcsk9 elevates CD36 in Schwann cells, indicating PCSK9 normally restrains CD36-mediated fatty-acid transport.
Pcsk9 loss increases fatty-acid influx into Schwann cells, promoting lipid droplet expansion and acylcarnitine accumulation.
In the CNS, locally expressed PCSK9 modulates LDLR-family receptor abundance, neuronal survival signaling, and neuroinflammatory tone.
Circulating (peripheral blood) PCSK9 has limited access to CNS parenchyma because of the blood-brain barrier, distinguishing systemic PCSK9 inhibition effects from local CNS PCSK9 biology.
PCSK9 inhibitors used clinically have shown cardiovascular benefit without major neurocognitive adverse signals, but their effects on small-fiber nerve outcomes have not been systematically studied.
DNBS-induced colitis caused loss of nitrergic (nNOS+) myenteric neurons in the distal colon that persisted into the post-inflammatory resolution phase.

Colonic motor complexes (CMCs) recorded ex vivo showed persistent abnormalities after colitis resolution, with oral CMCs longer in duration and less frequent, and aboral CMCs increased in amplitude and duration with decreased propagation velocity.

Following colitis, myenteric neurons in the proximal colon showed larger amplitude Ca2+ responses to descending, ascending, and circumferential focal tract stimulation, indicating persistent circuit-specific hyperexcitability.

A 19% increase in the number of neurons responding to circumferential tract stimulation was observed in the distal colon after colitis, indicating recruitment of additional excitable neurons in IPAN-dominated circuits.

Effects of colitis on myenteric neural circuit hyperexcitability were sexually dimorphic, with distal colon descending-pathway potentiation more prominent in males and ascending/circumferential potentiation more evident in females.

Enteric glial Ca2+ responses to neuron activity (descending, ascending, circumferential pathways) were globally increased after colitis, most prominently in the distal colon and most markedly for circumferential (IPAN-dominated) pathway stimulation.

Glial responsiveness changes after colitis differed by sex and colonic region, with distal descending-pathway glial recruitment increased in both sexes, ascending-pathway glial recruitment more prominent in males, and circumferential-pathway recruitment more prominent in females.

Direct chemogenetic (CNO) stimulation of glia, bypassing neuronal input, produced amplified glial Ca2+ responses in post-inflamed mice (78% larger proximal, 87% larger distal) demonstrating cell-autonomous glial hyperexcitability after colitis.

Chemogenetic glial stimulation elicited exaggerated excitatory neuronal Ca2+ responses (37% larger proximal, 22% larger distal) in post-colitis tissue without changes in the overall proportion of responding neurons, showing hyperactive glia exert abnormal excitatory drive onto neurons.
Chemogenetic stimulation of glia with CNO caused profound tissue motor (displacement) responses in distal colon samples from post-colitis mice that were not observed in healthy controls.

Chemogenetic glial stimulation with CNO enhanced CMC contraction size and further exacerbated excitatory CMC activity in the distal colon (but not proximal) of post-inflamed colons, though it could not restore the colitis-induced reduction in CMC frequency.

Restoring nitrergic tone with the NO donor PAPA NONOate (proximal colon) or the cGMP analog 8-Br-cGMP (distal colon) suppressed abnormally large glial Ca2+ responses to CNO and dampened downstream neuronal responses in post-inflamed samples, without effect in healthy tissue (except 8-Br-cGMP in healthy proximal colon).

Glial connexin-43 hemichannel permeability, measured by ethidium bromide dye uptake, was increased by 43% in myenteric ganglia following colitis resolution, and was partially reduced by the Cx43 hemichannel blocker 43Gap26.

EP3 and EP4 PGE2 receptor antagonists (L-798,106 and L-161,982) reduced glial and neuronal Ca2+ hyperresponses to circumferential pathway stimulation and to glial CNO stimulation specifically in post-inflamed, but not healthy, colon, implicating PGE2 signaling in glial hyperexcitability.

Direct focal tract stimulation of ascending pathways (aFTS) produced no change in evoked motor responses post-colitis, in contrast to more heterogeneous but generally greater motor responses evoked by descending and especially circumferential tract stimulation.

A multi-ancestry GWAS meta-analysis of over 2.5 million individuals identified 26 independent genome-wide-significant risk loci for fibromyalgia, a hundred-fold increase in sample size over prior studies.
An inframe glutamic acid deletion variant in the Huntingtin gene (HTT), part of the HD-associated A1 haplotype, showed the strongest association with fibromyalgia risk, increasing odds by about 9%.

The top Huntington's disease-associated variant was not in strong LD with the fibromyalgia lead variant and showed no association with fibromyalgia, and the fibromyalgia variant's weak association with HD risk disappeared after conditioning on the HD variant.
An intronic RABGAP1L variant near the Huntington's disease drug target GPR52 was associated with reduced fibromyalgia risk.
An intergenic variant near CELF4, a gene that negatively regulates nociceptor excitability and reduces pain sensitivity, was associated with fibromyalgia risk.
A variant near STK31 and further upstream of the neuropeptide NPY, which has pro- and anti-nociceptive effects, was associated with fibromyalgia risk.
An intronic ARHGAP15 variant, also near the kynurenine pathway gene KYNU, was associated with fibromyalgia risk, implicating the kynurenine pathway in pain processing.
An intronic variant in DRD2, encoding the dopamine D2 receptor and previously linked to sleep duration and psychiatric traits, was associated with fibromyalgia risk.
The second-most significant genome-wide association was with a variant upstream of CAMKV, a brain-expressed pseudokinase critical for dendritic spine maintenance and synaptic plasticity.
Variants in MAML3 (Notch pathway coactivator) and near MDGA2 (synaptic organization gene linked to autism spectrum disorder haploinsufficiency) were associated with fibromyalgia risk.
An intronic DCC variant, the sole coding gene within 1 megabase of the locus, was associated with fibromyalgia; DCC guides axon pathfinding and regulates myelin/axon domain organization.

A variant near SRD5A2 (testosterone-to-DHT converting enzyme) and SPAST (hereditary spastic paraplegia gene) was associated with fibromyalgia risk, potentially implicating androgen involvement in pain.
A variant near BCL11A, a transcription factor whose haploinsufficiency causes intellectual disability and autism, was associated with fibromyalgia risk.
An intronic BPTF variant, a NURF chromatin remodeling complex subunit whose haploinsufficiency causes a neurodevelopmental disorder, was associated with fibromyalgia risk.
An intronic PPP2R2B variant, also near the neuropathic-pain-related orphan receptor GPR151, was associated with fibromyalgia risk.

An intronic NPC1 variant in strong LD with missense variants in NPC1 and RMC1 was associated with fibromyalgia risk; NPC1 loss causes Niemann-Pick disease type C1 with neuroinflammation and neuroaxonal dystrophy.

Despite female cases outnumbering males by ~7-fold, the inter-sex genetic correlation was statistically indistinguishable from 1, and lead variant odds ratios did not differ significantly between sexes, suggesting a shared genetic architecture.
Fibromyalgia heritability was strongly and exclusively enriched in brain tissues and neuronal cell types, with no enrichment observed in immune or other non-neural tissues.
Fibromyalgia showed strong genetic correlations with widespread/syndromic pain conditions including cervicobrachial syndrome, myalgia, soft tissue disorders, joint pain, and low back pain.
Fibromyalgia showed a substantial genetic correlation with migraine.
Fibromyalgia showed a strong genetic correlation with hypermobility syndrome, as well as with trochanteric bursitis.

Fibromyalgia showed genetic correlations with mental/behavioral disorders, most notably post-traumatic stress disorder, along with dissociative disorders, somatoform disorder, depression, generalized anxiety disorder, and insomnia.
Fibromyalgia showed a strong genetic correlation with the clinical symptom code for malaise and fatigue.
Fibromyalgia showed strong genetic correlations with irritable bowel syndrome and functional dyspepsia, supporting shared genetic etiology between fibromyalgia and GI functional disorders.
Fibromyalgia showed a significant genetic correlation with polycystic ovarian syndrome.

Fibromyalgia showed relatively modest but significant genetic correlations with autoimmune disorders including psoriatic arthropathies, Sjögren's syndrome, rheumatoid arthritis, psoriasis, and autoimmune hypothyroidism.
Fibromyalgia is more genetically correlated with the less-understood T2-low asthma subtype than with T2-high asthma, and shows no correlation with eosinophil levels.
SNP-based heritability of fibromyalgia was estimated at 10.4% on the observed scale using stratified LD score regression in the European-only meta-analysis.

A polygenic risk score derived from the multi-ancestry leave-UK Biobank-out meta-analysis predicted fibromyalgia with an AUC of 0.59 in Europeans, with reduced accuracy in South Asian (0.55) and African (0.55) ancestry groups.
European-ancestry individuals in the highest fibromyalgia PRS quintile had 1.5-fold higher odds of fibromyalgia compared to the middle quintile.

European-ancestry individuals in the lowest fibromyalgia PRS quintile had reduced odds of fibromyalgia (OR 0.63) compared to the middle quintile, and disease prevalence rose from ~1.0% in the lowest to ~2.4% in the highest quintile.

An earlier family-based study found first-degree relatives of fibromyalgia patients were 8.5 times more likely to have fibromyalgia themselves than first-degree relatives of rheumatoid arthritis patients, indicating substantial familial/genetic contribution.

Prior fibromyalgia genetic studies — a linkage study of 116 families, a GWAS/CNV analysis of 313 cases vs 220 controls, and a GWAS of a quantitative fibromyalgia score in 26,749 individuals — all failed to identify any genome-wide significant loci.

Fibromyalgia heritability was significantly enriched exclusively in brain tissues: all five GTEx tissues reaching Bonferroni significance were brain regions (cortex, caudate, frontal cortex, putamen, and anterior cingulate cortex).

Among 119 single-cell types tested (PanSci mouse atlas), the strongest cell-type heritability enrichment was in dentate gyrus neurons, a hippocampal region involved in contextualizing sensory experience including pain.

Enteric neurons and pulmonary neuroendocrine cells (a sensory cell type with neuron-like properties) also showed significant fibromyalgia heritability enrichment, while no immune cell type or non-neural tissue showed enrichment.
Fibromyalgia showed very strong genetic correlations with musculoskeletal/widespread pain conditions, including cervicobrachial syndrome, myalgia, and soft tissue disorders.
Fibromyalgia showed substantial genetic correlations with joint pain, low back pain, and migraine.
Fibromyalgia showed strong genetic correlation with hypermobility syndrome and trochanteric bursitis.
Fibromyalgia showed a strong genetic correlation with post-traumatic stress disorder, the strongest correlation observed among mental/behavioral disorders.
Fibromyalgia showed strong genetic correlations with dissociative disorders, somatoform disorder, and depression, and more modest correlations with generalized anxiety disorder and insomnia.
Fibromyalgia showed a strong genetic correlation with the core clinical symptom trait of malaise and fatigue.
Fibromyalgia showed a strong genetic correlation with irritable bowel syndrome and functional dyspepsia among digestive disorders.
Fibromyalgia was genetically correlated with polycystic ovarian syndrome and chronic laryngitis, illustrating overlap with genitourinary and respiratory conditions.

Fibromyalgia showed relatively modest genetic correlations with autoimmune disorders including psoriatic arthropathies, Sjögren's syndrome, rheumatoid arthritis, psoriasis, and autoimmune hypothyroidism, weaker than correlations with pain and psychiatric traits.

Fibromyalgia's genetic correlation with asthma was stronger for the less-understood T2-low asthma subtype than for T2-high asthma, consistent with a lack of genetic correlation with eosinophil levels.

Fibromyalgia was more genetically correlated with seronegative rheumatoid arthritis than with seropositive RA, consistent with prior clinical observations, suggesting fibromyalgia genetics align with the more heterogeneous, less well-characterized subtype.

No genome-wide significant signal was found in the MHC region and no heritability enrichment was observed in immune cell types, arguing against fibromyalgia being primarily an autoimmune disorder despite weak correlations with some autoimmune diseases.

Cross-referencing the 26 fibromyalgia lead variants (and proxies) with the GWAS Catalog found the most frequent shared associations were with educational attainment, body mass index, type 2 diabetes, pain intensity, and insomnia.

A phenome-wide association study of the 26 lead variants across 330 disease endpoints (MVP-FinnGen-UKBB) found the most common associations were with dorsalgia (back pain) and gastroesophageal reflux disease.

Analysis of 124 FinnGen drug-prescription GWAS found that fibromyalgia's lead variants were most frequently associated with prescription of analgesics and anti-inflammatory/rheumatic drugs, likely reflecting NSAID prescribing for pain.

Certain fibromyalgia risk loci overlapped (with different lead variants) with previously reported long COVID risk loci (BPTF) and ME/CFS risk loci (OLFM4, RABGAP1L/GPR52), suggesting possible shared genetic factors or diagnostic overlap between these poorly characterized conditions.

Despite the several-fold higher prevalence of fibromyalgia in females, sex-stratified analyses found no evidence of sex differences in genetic architecture, suggesting the prevalence gap arises from non-genetic or gene-environment interaction factors rather than sex-specific risk variants.

A 13-year-old female with Loeys-Dietz syndrome carried a de novo pathogenic missense variant in TGFBR2 (c.1582C>T, p.Arg528Cys) and presented with a vitreoretinopathy phenotype resembling familial exudative vitreoretinopathy (FEVR), including vitreous hemorrhage, neovascularization, and peripheral avascular retina.

This case represents the second reported instance of a missense variant at amino acid residue 528 (Arg528) of TGFBR2 resulting in a FEVR-like phenotype in a patient with Loeys-Dietz syndrome, supporting a genotype-phenotype correlation.
In silico protein structure prediction and machine learning analyses suggest that the p.Arg528Cys variant disrupts the protein kinase domain of TGFBR2.
The authors hypothesize that the TGFBR2 p.Arg528Cys variant influences the Wnt/beta-catenin pathway, leading to abnormal retinal vasculogenesis.
Intravitreal anti-VEGF treatment in the right eye led to visual improvement in a patient with LDS-associated FEVR-like vitreoretinopathy.
Laser photocoagulation of the peripheral retina in both eyes was performed to mitigate future vision-threatening complications from the avascular retina.
Colonic tryptase mRNA was significantly upregulated in post-inflammatory IBS-D model mice compared to normal controls.
Treatment with Changji'an Formula (CJAF) significantly downregulated colonic tryptase mRNA expression in IBS-D mice.
Colonic NGF mRNA was significantly upregulated in IBS-D model mice compared to normal controls.
CJAF treatment dose-dependently downregulated colonic NGF mRNA expression in IBS-D mice.
Colonic TrkA mRNA was significantly upregulated in IBS-D model mice compared to normal controls.
CJAF treatment significantly downregulated colonic TrkA mRNA expression in IBS-D mice.
Colonic GAP43 mRNA was significantly upregulated in IBS-D model mice compared to normal controls.
High and moderate doses of CJAF significantly downregulated colonic GAP43 mRNA, but the low dose had no significant effect.
Colonic NSE mRNA was significantly upregulated in IBS-D model mice compared to normal controls.
CJAF treatment significantly downregulated colonic NSE mRNA expression in IBS-D mice.
Tryptase protein expression, assessed by immunohistochemistry and western blot, was significantly increased in colonic tissue of IBS-D model mice.
CJAF downregulated colonic tryptase protein expression dose-dependently in IBS-D mice.
NGF protein expression in colonic tissue was significantly higher in IBS-D model mice than normal controls.
NGF protein expression was decreased by different doses of CJAF in IBS-D mice colonic tissue.

Total TrkA protein expression in colonic tissue did not differ significantly between IBS-D model mice and normal controls, and was unchanged by CJAF treatment, contrasting with prior literature reporting increased colonic TrkA in IBS.
Phosphorylated TrkA (p-TrkA) protein was significantly higher in colonic tissue of IBS-D model mice than in normal controls.
CJAF treatment decreased phosphorylated TrkA protein expression at different doses in IBS-D mice colonic tissue.
GAP43 protein was significantly upregulated (with submucosal/muscle-layer distribution) in colonic tissue of IBS-D model mice.
GAP43 protein expression was downregulated dose-dependently by CJAF in IBS-D mice.
NSE protein was significantly upregulated in colonic tissue of IBS-D model mice, consistent with increased enteric neuronal marker density.
CJAF at high, medium and low doses downregulated NSE protein expression in IBS-D mice colonic tissue.
Spleen and thymus coefficients (organ-to-body-weight indices reflecting immune activation) were significantly increased in IBS-D model mice compared to normal controls.
CJAF treatment dose-dependently downregulated spleen and thymus coefficients in IBS-D mice, suggesting attenuated immune activation.
IBS-D model mice showed reduced total moving distance and average speed in the open field test compared to normal controls, indicating a depression-like/anxiety-like behavioral state.
CJAF treatment significantly improved total moving distance and average speed in the open field test in IBS-D mice.
IBS-D model mice showed significantly lower sucrose water preference than normal controls, indicating depression-like anhedonia.

UPLC-Q-Orbitrap HRMS analysis identified 36 main chemical components of CJAF spanning 7 chemical classes: 16 flavonoids, 7 triterpenoids, 4 alkaloids, 3 sesquiterpenoids, 2 monoterpene glycosides, 2 organic acids, 1 phenylpropanoid and 1 tannin.
Unlike prior literature reporting increased colonic TrkA in IBS, total TrkA protein expression did not differ between IBS-D model mice and normal controls in this study.
CJAF treatment did not change total TrkA protein expression in colonic tissue of IBS-D mice.
Phosphorylated TrkA (p-TrkA) protein expression in colonic tissue was significantly higher in IBS-D model mice than in normal controls.
CJAF treatment at all doses significantly decreased phosphorylated TrkA protein expression in colonic tissue of IBS-D mice.

GAP43 protein expression, detected by immunohistochemistry and western blot, was significantly upregulated in colonic tissue of IBS-D model mice compared with normal controls, localized mainly to the submucosa and intestinal muscle layer.
CJAF treatment dose-dependently downregulated GAP43 protein expression in colonic tissue of IBS-D mice.
Neuron-specific enolase (NSE) protein expression was significantly upregulated in colonic tissue of IBS-D model mice compared with normal controls.
High, medium, and low doses of CJAF all significantly downregulated NSE protein expression in colonic tissue of IBS-D mice.
Paeoniflorin, a monoterpene glycoside from Paeonia lactiflora detected in CJAF, has been reported in the literature to inhibit mast cell degranulation.

Berberine, an isoquinoline alkaloid from Coptis chinensis in CJAF, has been reported to significantly alleviate chronic water-avoidance-stress-induced visceral hypersensitivity and colonic mast cell activation in rat models.
Rutin, found in Punica granatum and Bupleurum chinense within CJAF, has been reported to alleviate inflammatory pain by inhibiting P2X7 receptor activity in mast cells.
Only 16% of proteins associated with chronic pain overlapped with those associated with acute pain, indicating largely distinct molecular signatures.
In widespread chronic pain, the ten most significantly upregulated plasma proteins compared to controls were CDCP1, IL18R1, GAST, GDF15, ASGR1, CCL7, VSIG2, CHGA, TNFRSF10A, and MRC1.
In widespread chronic pain, the ten most significantly downregulated plasma proteins compared to controls were CA14, APOF, PON3, SELENOP, EGFR, ITGAV, SCT, CELA2A, IGFBP3, and PPY.
256 of 2920 plasma proteins (8.7%) were significantly associated with widespread chronic pain in the proteome-wide association study.

Reactome pathway enrichment of widespread chronic pain-associated proteins highlighted interleukin-10 signaling, TNF binding to physiological receptors, TNFR2 non-canonical NF-κB signaling, and cytokine signaling in the immune system.

A clinical risk model based on six biopsychosocial factors (sleep difficulties, neuroticism, powerlessness, mental health issues, life stressors, obesity) achieved an AUC of 0.791 for predicting widespread chronic pain.
A simple proteomic score (top 10 proteins, S-ProtS) predicted widespread chronic pain with an AUC of 0.723, comparable to the clinical model.
A comprehensive proteomic score (C-ProtS) achieved an AUC of 0.801 for widespread chronic pain, and combining C-ProtS with the clinical model achieved the highest discrimination (AUC 0.880).
The combined proteomic-clinical model for widespread chronic pain showed good calibration between predicted and observed risk (calibration slope 0.860).
Both the comprehensive and simple proteomic scores showed good predictive discrimination for fibromyalgia, with AUCs of 0.75 and 0.70 respectively.

Proteomic scores were significantly associated with nociplastic pain and fibromyalgia but showed no significant association with nociceptive or neuropathic pain, indicating specificity for nociplastic mechanisms.
Proteomic scores showed a strong prospective association with the number of pain sites at both 2019 and 2022 follow-up, with higher scores predicting increased pain spread.

Machine learning (SHAP) analysis identified 15 key proteins contributing most to prediction of widespread chronic pain, including CA14, KIR2DS4, PDCD1, CHI3L1, CNDP1, IL18R1, CRH, GAST, HPGDS, ITGAV, SELENOP, ASAH2, LYPD8, GZMB, and PROCR.
CA14 emerged as the single most impactful protein for predicting widespread chronic pain, based on the highest SHAP value in the machine learning model.
Mendelian randomization identified 18 circulating proteins with significant causal associations with widespread/chronic pain, with 9 consistently validated across both replication cohorts.

Four proteins (PTN, TNF, CA14, LEG1) showed discordant effect directions between observational epidemiological association and Mendelian randomization estimates, suggesting complex state-dependent versus lifelong genetic effects.
CA14, DDR1, and MLN showed strong colocalization evidence (PP.H4 > 0.5) with pain phenotypes, suggesting shared causal genetic variants.

Nine of the 18 causal proteins (BPIFB2, CA14, COL9A1, CTSO, IFI30, LGALS3, PTN, SFTPD, TNF) were significantly associated with nociplastic pain or fibromyalgia, distinguishing this mechanism from nociceptive/neuropathic pain up to nine years in advance.

CA14 is targeted by sulthiame, an approved antiepileptic drug used for obstructive sleep apnea and seizure disorders, and the authors suggest CA14 agonists rather than inhibitors may be more therapeutically relevant given observed non-linear associations.
DPEP1, a renal dipeptidase involved in inflammatory responses and causally linked to widespread chronic pain, is inhibited by cilastatin, a drug co-administered with beta-lactam antibiotics.
LGALS3 (galectin-3), a regulator of immune signaling and fibrosis causally linked to widespread chronic pain, is targeted by several investigational agents (belapectin, davanat, olitigaltin).

TNF, causally linked to widespread chronic pain, is targeted by multiple approved biologics (adalimumab, infliximab, etanercept) used in immune-mediated diseases, suggesting drug-repurposing potential for pain.
Leptin (LEP), a metabolic/energy-regulation hormone, was strongly associated with chronic pain, implicating metabolic dysregulation in chronic pain mechanisms.
Fibromyalgia affects 10-48% of patients with rheumatic diseases compared to approximately 2-6% of the general population, likely reflecting shared immune dysregulation and inflammatory mechanisms.

Carbonic anhydrase 14 and leptin were the primary proteins consistently associated with chronic pain, particularly nociplastic pain/fibromyalgia, and with pain onset, spreading, and recovery in longitudinal analyses.
Both leptin and gastrin showed positive correlations with new-onset pain and pain spread, and were also linked to pain recovery outcomes, suggesting roles in pain development and propagation.
Antibodies against the dUTPase enzymes encoded by early genes of EBV, HHV-6, and VZV were elevated in serum from ME/CFS patients compared with controls.
EBV dUTPase protein was detected in postmortem brain tissue from ME/CFS cases but not in non-ME/CFS control tissue.
In a small ME/CFS cohort, 20% had elevated IgG against EBV, HHV-6, and HSV1/2, but this did not differ significantly from age- and gender-matched controls.
All Dubbo Infection Outcome Study ME/CFS patients were HHV-6 IgG seropositive and 50% HCMV seropositive, but rates did not differ significantly from controls.
A larger study found active co-infections with HHV-6, HHV-7, or parvovirus B19 in over a quarter of ME/CFS patients while none of the controls showed active co-infection.
Active infection with HHV-6A/B, HHV-7, or parvovirus B19V was found in approximately 45% of a larger ME/CFS cohort compared with only 8.7% of healthy controls.
Latent infection/co-infection with HHV-6A/B, HHV-7, and parvovirus B19V was actually less common in ME/CFS patients than in healthy controls in this cohort.
Metagenomic analysis of saliva found similar rates of multi-herpesvirus coinfection in ME/CFS cases and controls.
A significant percentage of ME/CFS patients simultaneously produced IgG against multiple herpesvirus dUTPases compared with controls.
Follow-up longitudinal study found significant herpesvirus reactivation (by dUTPase IgG) in half of female ME/CFS cases compared to 6% of controls.
Levels of anti-dUTPase antibodies directly correlated with severity of fatigue and pain in ME/CFS patients.

Long-term (6 month) antiviral therapy with valaciclovir or valganciclovir improved clinical symptoms and reduced serum antibody titers in ME/CFS patients infected with EBV or EBV/HCMV/HHV-6 combinations in double-blind placebo-controlled trials.
Adolescents who develop heterophile antibody-positive EBV infectious mononucleosis have a 12-23% probability of developing severe ME/CFS.
