Among infectious mononucleosis patients, active co-infection with EBV and HHV-6 was found in nearly 40% of serum samples.
RNA-seq and metagenomic studies of feces, blood, and saliva have not identified significant virome differences between ME/CFS patients and healthy controls.
Peptide microarray and suspension multiplex immunoassay studies found EBV-specific IgG response in ME/CFS patients did not differ significantly from healthy controls.
Multiple studies consistently reported no increase in EBV and/or HHV-6 viral load among ME/CFS patients compared with controls.
ME/CFS patients showed an impaired EBV-specific T cell response and diminished IFN-γ production.
Post-infectious ME/CFS and ME/CFS patients show CD8+ T cell dysfunction, potentially resulting in T cell exhaustion.
Gulf War Illness patients showed a statistically significant increase in antibodies against multiple herpesviruses compared to controls.
Gulf War Illness patients had significantly higher HHV-6 dUTPase antibody levels than controls.
Longitudinal veteran cohorts with chronic multisystem illness/GWI showed markedly increased prevalence of dUTPase IgG and IgM antibodies compared to matched healthy controls.
More than 40% of patients diagnosed with Post-acute Sequelae of COVID-19 (PASC) could also meet the clinical criteria for ME/CFS.
EBV reactivation was identified as one of four biological factors associated with development of PASC in a longitudinal multi-omics study.
A strong association was found between EBV reactivation and fatigue in patients with PASC.
EBV lytic replication induced ACE2 expression and enhanced SARS-CoV-2 entry into epithelial cells, suggesting EBV reactivation may contribute to COVID-19 and PASC.
ME/CFS patients showed significantly reduced observed fungal ASV richness compared to healthy controls, though Shannon diversity did not differ.
PCoA showed statistically significant but weak overall separation in gut fungal community structure between ME/CFS patients and controls using Bray-Curtis and Jaccard distances.
ME/CFS patients showed significantly greater intra-group (within-patient) variability in fungal community structure than healthy controls, comparable in magnitude to the between-group difference.
ME/CFS patients showed a relative increase in the fungal phylum Basidiomycota compared to healthy controls.
The genus Aspergillus was markedly enriched in the gut mycobiome of ME/CFS patients relative to healthy controls, rising from 2.62% to 13.84% mean relative abundance.
Candida relative abundance trended lower in ME/CFS patients but random forest analysis showed no significant discriminatory difference between ME/CFS and healthy controls in any age subgroup.

In the elderly cohort, ME/CFS patients showed significantly higher Shannon diversity and observed ASV richness of gut fungi compared to age-matched healthy controls, an inverse pattern from young and middle-aged cohorts.
Age-stratified PCoA revealed substantially enhanced separation between ME/CFS patients and controls within each age cohort compared to the unstratified analysis.

Beta dispersion analysis showed greater within-group fungal community variability in young and middle-aged ME/CFS patients than controls, but lower within-group dispersion in elderly ME/CFS patients than elderly controls.

A random forest classifier using the top 50 discriminatory fungal genera (unstratified, all samples) achieved moderate diagnostic accuracy for ME/CFS (AUC=0.786), while ASV-level classification achieved AUC=0.807.
Age-stratified random forest classification substantially improved diagnostic accuracy over the unstratified model, achieving near-perfect discrimination in young and elderly cohorts.
In the overall ME/CFS cohort, Wickerhamomyces abundance correlated positively with consequences-of-fatigue and overall fatigue scores.
In the young ME/CFS cohort, the taxon Fungi_gen_incertae_sedis correlated positively with mental, physical, consequences-of, and overall fatigue scores.
In the elderly ME/CFS cohort, Psathyrellaceae_gen_incertae_sedis and Poaceae_gen_incertae_sedis abundances correlated positively with multiple fatigue dimensions.

A paradoxical pattern emerged wherein fungal genera positively correlated with fatigue scores were generally less abundant in ME/CFS patients (except Wickerhamomyces), while those negatively correlated with fatigue were more abundant, in young and middle-aged cohorts, with the pattern reversed in elderly ME/CFS.
Debaryomyces and Symmetrospora were markedly elevated in young ME/CFS patients relative to age-matched healthy controls and served as top random-forest discriminatory genera.
Penicillium (along with Aspergillus and Verticillium) was significantly enriched in the middle-aged ME/CFS cohort compared to age-matched controls.
Chaetomium was more abundant in elderly healthy controls than in age-matched ME/CFS patients, suggesting its depletion may reflect impaired microbial regulation in elderly ME/CFS.

A prior smaller study (17 ME/CFS vs 17 controls, ~100 reads/sample) found no significant differences in eukaryotic/fungal diversity or composition between ME/CFS and controls, contrasting with the current study's findings of significant alterations.

Several discriminatory fungal taxa (Endocarpon, Verticillium, Preussia, Chaetomium) are predominantly environmental fungi, and the authors caution that their presence in gut samples may reflect dietary intake, environmental contamination, or sequencing artifacts rather than true gut colonization.
IgG antibodies against EBV dUTPase were significantly elevated in ME/CFS patients compared to healthy controls.
IgG antibodies against HHV-6 dUTPase were significantly elevated in ME/CFS patients compared to healthy controls.
IgG antibodies against VZV dUTPase were significantly elevated in ME/CFS patients compared to healthy controls.
A majority of ME/CFS patients (72.5%) simultaneously co-expressed antibodies to multiple herpesvirus and HERV-K dUTPases, compared to only 31% of healthy controls.
Chi-square analysis showed strong associations between EBV, HHV-6, and VZV dUTPase antibody seropositivity and ME/CFS disease status.
EBV dUTPase IgG antibody levels showed a significant positive Spearman correlation with fatigue severity in ME/CFS patients.
HHV-6 dUTPase IgG antibody levels showed a significant positive Spearman correlation with fatigue severity in ME/CFS patients.
Heightened dUTPase IgG antibody levels clustered specifically with ME/CFS patients experiencing moderate and severe fatigue, suggesting utility for stratifying patients by severity.
HHV-6 dUTPase IgG antibody levels were positively correlated with fatigue severity in ME/CFS patients.
Heightened dUTPase IgG antibody levels clustered specifically among ME/CFS patients with moderate and severe fatigue, suggesting utility for stratifying patients by symptom severity.
None of the 54 ME/CFS symptoms assessed showed significant differences in prevalence or severity across the three six-monthly time points over the 12-month study.

Although only 9.4% of participants had a formal fibromyalgia diagnosis, 90.6% met the Widespread Pain Index pain criteria consistent with the ACR fibromyalgia case definition, suggesting substantial underdiagnosis of comorbid fibromyalgia.
The most common comorbid entities among pwME/CFS were probable fibromyalgia (93.8%), food intolerance (62.5%) and chemical sensitivity (50.0%).
Over one-third of participants reported comorbid asthma, IBS, orthostatic intolerance and medication sensitivity.
Employment status remained largely unchanged over 12 months, with 59.4% of participants unemployed due to illness at all time points.
Over half of unemployed participants were not receiving the Disability Support Pension at any time point, highlighting a gap in income support access.
All SF-36v2 quality-of-life domain scores were significantly impaired compared with Australian population norms at every time point.
SF-36v2 quality-of-life domain scores did not differ significantly across the three time points over 12 months.
Participants scored poorly and consistently on overall health status scales (AKPS median 60%, Dr Bell's CFIDS Disability Scale median 30%) with no significant change over 12 months.
Life Activities, Mobility and Participation were the most impaired WHODAS 2.0 domains, with no significant change in any WHODAS 2.0 domain across the three time points.
The Physical domain of the Modified Fatigue Impact Scale was the most impacted domain (~80% of maximum fatigue impact), with no significant change across time points.
Post-exertional malaise was near-universal (100% at T0, 93.8% at T1) and remained the highest-severity symptom throughout, though one participant no longer reported it at T2.
The cohort had a median illness duration exceeding one decade (12.5 years) at baseline, supporting the chronic/permanent nature of ME/CFS.

Eleven symptoms, six of which were neurocognitive, had a prevalence exceeding 80% at all time points, including slowed thought, impaired concentration, cognitive overload, difficulty making decisions, impaired reading/comprehension, short-term memory loss, myalgia, unrefreshed sleep, sensitivity to sensations, muscle weakness and general malaise.

The most burdensome symptoms — experienced by >80% of the cohort with median severity of severe — were post-exertional malaise, cognitive overload, impaired reading/comprehension, unrefreshed sleep and general malaise.
The total number of symptoms reported per participant (median 30-34) did not change significantly over the 12-month study.
Almost all participants reported ongoing restriction of occupational, educational, social and recreational life activities due to ME/CFS, with no significant change over 12 months.
Over three-quarters of participants received informal care from family or friends at least once during the study, with over half receiving it consistently at all time points.
CYP with ME/CFS who participated in the online education program reported overall satisfaction, valuing knowledge acquisition/reinforcement and connection with other affected CYP.
Parents of CYP with ME/CFS reported that the online education program met their expectations and needs regarding content and format, based on interviews and an online questionnaire.
The online format of the education program was perceived very positively by both CYP and parents.

A pathogenic frameshift variant in ENO3 (β-enolase) was found in one participant, reducing enolase activity and causally linked to Glycogen Storage Disease XIII-like exertion-induced fatigue, weakness, pain and cramps.
A shared pathogenic ACADM missense variant in a mother-son pair impairs medium-chain fatty acid β-oxidation and was associated with exertion-induced fatigue, cognitive dysfunction, and weakness.
RNA-seq in the ACADM-variant carrier showed increased PGM1 (glycolytic compensation), reduced ACADVL, and elevated NR3C1 expression, changes not observed in the co-affected relative.

A pathogenic HADHA variant affecting mitochondrial trifunctional protein was identified in one participant, linked to long-chain fatty acid β-oxidation deficiency causing fatigue, PEM, weakness, pain and nausea.

A pathogenic MMACHC frameshift variant (p.Arg91LysfsTer14), causal for cobalamin C disease, was identified in a participant with fatigue, cognitive/psychiatric symptoms, incoordination, pain, GI issues and weakness, though no second variant was found.
A previously reported likely pathogenic ELOVL4 variant, causal for dominant SCA34 (spinocerebellar ataxia with very long-chain fatty acid elongation defect), was also found in the MMACHC carrier.

Four unrelated participants carried known pathogenic KCNJ18 variants causing dominant thyrotoxic periodic paralysis, associated with muscle fatigue, cramping, PEM, episodic weakness and exertion intolerance.
Siblings carried a likely pathogenic SLC12A3 frameshift variant linked to Gitelman syndrome, presenting with muscle weakness, cramps, pain, fatigue, hypovolemia, polyuria and exercise intolerance.

HPO-based phenotype-avatar enrichment analysis identified Gitelman syndrome as the 4th most enriched OMIM match for the two SLC12A3-carrying siblings, statistically concordant with their genetic finding.

A pathogenic splice SPTA1 variant, confirmed by RNA-seq to cause intron retention and truncation, was carried by a mother-daughter trio and an unrelated participant, causing hereditary elliptocytosis/hemolytic anemia-type symptoms including fatigue, PEM, dyspnea and pain.

A participant carried a VUS in SLC4A1 adjacent to known pathogenic spherocytosis/ovalocytosis alleles, with RNA-seq showing elevated SLC4A1 expression and dysregulation of erythrocyte membrane genes (SPTA1, SPTB, EPB42, GYPA), suggesting a compensatory red-cell fragility response.
A pathogenic MYH7 variant affecting cardiac myosin heavy chain was found in one participant, consistent with a myopathy causing exercise intolerance, fatigue, dyspnea, dysautonomia and neck pain.

A rare CHRFAM7A splice VUS shared by two siblings and one unrelated participant clustered with overlapping symptoms (fatigue, pain, cognitive issues, bowel irritability, restless legs, paresthesia, sensory/mood/autonomic issues), suggestive of α7 acetylcholine receptor dysfunction if deleterious.
Definitive, ACMG-classified pathogenic molecular findings mapping to biologically plausible ME/CFS-relevant genes were identified in 8 of 25 probands (32%) and 12 of 31 affected individuals (39%).

Enumeration of HPO-based ME/CFS diagnostic 'avatars' meeting Carruthers criteria yielded 110,160 distinct symptom combinations, and enrichment analysis found statistically significant overlap between this avatar space and 135 OMIM-defined Mendelian disorders after multiple-testing correction.

Immune cell-type deconvolution of whole-blood RNA-seq using CIBERSORTx identified 22 immune subsets (dominated by neutrophils, monocytes, lymphocytes) with no significant differences between affected status or molecular category groups after multiple-testing correction, indicating that leukocyte composition did not confound transcriptomic comparisons.

Upregulation of DEFA1, a neutrophil-derived antimicrobial peptide, was observed in some participants (including the two ACADM carriers), consistent with prior reports of innate immune activation in post-infectious syndromes.

Expression changes in ZNF683, LRRN3, PIK3R3, CD248, and POLR3G suggested possible involvement of cytokine-driven T-cell regulatory networks, partially overlapping with a previously reported ME/CFS immunoregulatory dysfunction network.

Principal component analysis of RNA-seq data showed no distinct global transcriptional clustering by affected status, sex, or molecular category, indicating biological grouping did not dominate variance after batch correction.

A pathogenic COL6A3 variant, previously reported in dominant Bethlem myopathy/Ullrich congenital muscular dystrophy, co-occurred with SLC12A3 variation in one participant and may explain her greater pain, fatigue, and musculoskeletal involvement relative to her sibling.

A pathogenic GMPPB variant affecting α-dystroglycan glycosylation was found in the participant with the greatest pain/symptom burden among the SPTA1 group, consistent with a milder later-onset dystroglycanopathy causing exercise intolerance, cramps, myalgia, fatigue and progressive weakness.

The study proposes molecular subtyping of ME/CFS by primary physiological system affected (energy/metabolism ENE, muscle structure STR, red blood cell RBC, solute/ion transport SOL), with RBC and ENE groups trending toward higher pain/symptom severity and SOL cases more often reporting sudden onset.
In a case report, an adolescent with persistent post-COVID symptoms had elevated IL-6, IL-1, and TNFα seven months after mild COVID-19, indicating a sustained pro-inflammatory state.
The same adolescent case showed an increased effector T-cell to regulatory T-cell ratio months after COVID-19, suggesting impaired peripheral immune tolerance.
CD27+ memory B lymphocytes were reduced in the adolescent Long COVID case, alongside high anti-SARS-CoV-2 IgA and IgG levels.

Seven months after mild COVID-19, the adolescent patient showed marked exertional tachycardia (up to 155 bpm) and easy fatigability on a 6-minute walk test, consistent with autonomic/dysautonomic involvement.

Borrelia (Lyme disease agent) modulates PI3K/Akt/mTOR immunometabolic programs in human immune cells ex vivo, with Borrelia-induced cytokine production dependent on glycolysis/HIF-1α, though direct human evidence of mTOR dysregulation in Lyme disease patients is lacking.
EBV latent membrane protein LMP1 activates both mTORC1 and mTORC2, and inhibiting mTORC2 reduces EBV production, implicating mTOR in EBV latency/persistence.

SARS-CoV-2-infected airway/ALI cultures and human autopsy lungs show increased mTORC1 activity and metabolic rewiring, though direct in vivo evidence that this drives post-acute inflammation remains limited.
mTORC1 is required for Th1/Th17 differentiation while mTORC2 supports Th2, and broad mTOR loss favors FoxP3+ regulatory T-cell induction, positioning mTOR as a central switch in CD4+ T-cell fate.
In macrophages, mTORC1 activity promotes M1-like pro-inflammatory programs and restrains M2 polarization, while mTORC2 supports type-2/M2 programs, in a context- and timing-dependent manner.

In preclinical models, excessive brain-endothelial mTOR activity is associated with blood-brain barrier leakage, whereas mTOR inhibition preserves tight-junction integrity (claudin-5, occludin) and reduces permeability.

TSPO-PET imaging has demonstrated microglial neuroinflammation in basal ganglia circuits in PANDAS, supporting a hypothesized role for dysregulated microglial mTOR in sustaining basal-ganglia inflammation.

Persistent inflammatory signaling in Long COVID is proposed to drive mTORC1 hyperactivation in endothelial cells, possibly impairing tight junction integrity and sustaining blood-brain barrier leakiness after acute infection resolves.

Aberrant mTOR signaling in microglia and neurons is proposed to underlie persistent Long COVID symptoms including cognitive dysfunction, fatigue, dysautonomia, and mood disturbances, including in children.

Studies in ME/CFS have consistently shown altered immunometabolism and elevated pro-inflammatory cytokines, particularly IL-6 and TNF-α, suggesting possible involvement of mTOR-regulated pathways in monocytes and T cells.
ME/CFS is accompanied by immune exhaustion and impaired memory T-cell generation, contributing to a persistent inflammatory state.

Functional and structural neuroimaging in ME/CFS shows brainstem and cortical abnormalities including reduced cerebral blood flow, altered brainstem connectivity, and altered glial activity, correlating with post-exertional malaise, sleep disruption, and brain fog.
mTOR contributes to mitochondrial health via regulation of mitophagy and turnover, and mitochondrial dysfunction has been implicated in fatigue syndromes such as ME/CFS.

A pre-print study reported that low-dose rapamycin (6 mg/week) was linked with strong recovery in about 70% of patients (across PANDAS, Long COVID, and ME/CFS), with an ongoing clinical trial testing once-weekly oral rapamycin.

Randomized, placebo-controlled everolimus trials in tuberous sclerosis complex and PTEN hamartoma tumor syndrome did not improve prespecified neurocognitive/behavioral composites over 6 months, indicating mTOR modulation without proving mTOR hyperactivity as a primary driver of neuropsychiatric symptoms.

Rapamycin pretreatment before ketamine in depression failed to blunt the acute antidepressant response and may have prolonged its benefit, indicating pathway modulation without establishing mTOR hyperactivity as a primary causal driver of the antidepressant effect.
Total lymphocyte count was significantly reduced in ME/CFS patients compared to healthy controls.
CD8+ cytotoxic T cell counts were significantly reduced in ME/CFS patients compared to healthy controls.
NK cell (CD16+CD56+) counts were significantly reduced in ME/CFS patients compared to healthy controls.
Total lymphocyte count was significantly reduced in Long COVID patients compared to healthy controls.
CD8+ T cell counts were significantly reduced in Long COVID patients compared to healthy controls.
NK cell counts were significantly reduced in Long COVID patients compared to healthy controls.
No significant differences were detected between ME/CFS and Long COVID groups for total lymphocyte, CD8+ T cell, or NK cell counts.
Serum TNF concentration was significantly elevated in ME/CFS patients compared to healthy controls.
Serum IL-10 concentration was significantly elevated in ME/CFS patients compared to healthy controls.
Serum IL-6 concentration was significantly elevated in ME/CFS patients compared to healthy controls.
Serum IL-4 concentration was significantly elevated in ME/CFS patients compared to healthy controls.
Serum IL-2 concentration was significantly elevated in ME/CFS patients compared to healthy controls.
Serum IL-17A concentration showed no statistically significant difference between ME/CFS patients and healthy controls.
Serum IFN-γ concentration was significantly lower in ME/CFS patients compared to Long COVID patients.

Long COVID patients showed significant elevation of all measured serum cytokines compared to healthy controls, similar to the pattern in ME/CFS, with no significant differences between the two patient groups.

The composite Th1/Th2 + Treg z-score ratio was significantly higher in Long COVID patients compared to healthy controls, and was also elevated in ME/CFS patients, with no significant difference between the two patient groups.
HAM-A anxiety scores were significantly higher in both ME/CFS and Long COVID patients than in healthy controls, with median scores exceeding the mild-anxiety cut-off.
HAMD depression scores were significantly higher in both ME/CFS and Long COVID patients than in healthy controls, with median scores above the mild-depression cut-off.

FibroFatigue scores indicating fatigue and fibromyalgia-like symptom burden were significantly higher in both ME/CFS and Long COVID patients compared to healthy controls, with no significant difference between the two patient groups.

In the ME/CFS group, positive correlations were observed between CD8+ T cell numbers and IL-6, between IL-10 and IL-4, between IL-10 and IL-6, between IL-6 and TNF, and between IL-2 and IFN-γ serum concentrations.
In the ME/CFS group, negative correlations were found between total lymphocyte count and IFN-γ, between CD19+ B cell numbers and Th1 MFI, and between CD19+ numbers and Th1/Th2 + Treg MFI.
In ME/CFS patients, lymphocyte subsets negatively correlated with FibroFatigue scores and, partially, with HAMA/HAMD scores.

In the Long COVID group, positive correlations were found between CD56+ NK cell numbers and IL-2, IL-10 and HAMD, IL-6 and HAMD, total lymphocyte count and HAMA, total lymphocyte count and HAMD, CD19+ numbers and HAMA, IL-6 and IL-10, IL-4 and IL-10, and IL-6 and IL-4.

In the Long COVID group, negative correlations were detected between CD8+ T cell numbers and IL-6, and between IL-2 and HAMA anxiety scores, suggesting higher CD8+ T cell and lower IL-6/IL-2 levels may be protective against severe neuropsychological symptoms.

The CD4+/CD8+ T cell ratio was increased in both ME/CFS and Long COVID groups compared to healthy controls and negatively correlated with the composite qSUM z-score, suggesting it could serve as a marker of disease severity.

The two-stage remote recruitment strategy achieved the target of 100 RCT participants within the scheduled 5-month period, with 139 stage 1 survey responses (38.0% response rate) yielding 100 eligible stage 2 participants (67.0% recruitment rate).
Overall attrition at 3 months in the RCT was 21.0%, with substantially higher dropout in the intervention group (30.6%) than in the wait-list control group (11.8%).
At 3 months, mean CFQ-11 fatigue scores decreased more in the intervention group (change of -4.6, from 27.1 to 22.5) than in the wait-list control group (change of -2.9, from 25.9 to 23.0).

When the wait-list control group subsequently used the intervention after 12 weeks, they experienced a similar reduction in CFQ-11 fatigue scores (mean falling from 26.4 to 19.0 between 3 and 6 months).
No serious adverse reaction events were reported by any participants during the 12-week use of the self-help intervention.

Based on feasibility data (SD estimate of 5.5), the authors calculate that a fully powered efficacy trial would require 230 participants per group (460 total) to detect a two-point reduction in CFQ-11 scores with 90% power, assuming 30% attrition.

The authors suggest spontaneous remission is higher in long COVID than in ME/CFS, noting that three participants (5.9%) in the wait-list arm returned their intervention packs after 3 months rather than using them.

The self-help intervention is based on an osteopathic manual therapy approach hypothesized to improve spinal biomechanics, reduce dysautonomia, and enhance blood flow and lymphatic drainage of muscles and the central nervous system.

The authors hypothesize that many individuals with long COVID will progress to 'long' long COVID after 12-18 months and be diagnosed with ME/CFS, drawing an analogy to the progression from glandular fever/EBV infection to ME.
By 6 months, follow-up response rates converged between arms (61.2% intervention vs 56.9% wait-list), reversing the trend seen at 3 months where wait-list retention was higher.
More than a third of healthcare professionals met MFI-20 criteria for chronic fatigue.
Chronic fatigue syndrome (ME/CFS), defined by the CFS Severity Scale as idiopathic chronic fatigue, was found in 11.2% of healthcare professionals, far exceeding general population estimates.
General fatigue met threshold criteria in two-thirds of participants.
Mental fatigue, encompassing cognitive difficulties, was present in 67.3% of participants despite the lowest mean subscale score.
Physical fatigue was the predominant fatigue dimension among healthcare professionals.
Women showed significantly higher rates of general fatigue, reduced motivation, and total fatigue than men.
Younger workers (≤40 years) had higher rates of general fatigue and reduced activity compared to older workers.
Married participants reported higher physical fatigue rates than unmarried participants.
In bivariate analysis, vitamin D-deficient participants paradoxically had a lower rate of total fatigue than those with insufficient/normal vitamin D levels.
After multivariable adjustment, vitamin D status showed no independent association with chronic fatigue.
Poor physical health-related quality of life was strongly associated with higher rates of total fatigue.
Poor mental health-related quality of life was strongly associated with higher rates of total fatigue.
Moderate-to-severe depression was associated with elevated rates of all fatigue dimensions in bivariate analysis.
Obesity was associated with higher prevalence of total fatigue in bivariate analysis.
Good physical health-related quality of life (PCS-12≥50) was independently protective against chronic fatigue, reducing risk by about 92%.
Good mental health-related quality of life (MCS-12≥50) was independently protective against chronic fatigue, reducing risk by about 90%.
Moderate-to-severe depression independently increased chronic fatigue risk nearly sixfold in multivariable analysis.
Obesity independently increased chronic fatigue risk 2.5-fold in multivariable analysis.

At baseline, MVPA-inactive long COVID patients reported significantly worse physical function, fatigue, pain interference, social roles, and dyspnea scores than MVPA-active patients, with differences exceeding the meaningful change threshold.

Longitudinal mixed-effects modeling showed that being MVPA-active (versus inactive) was associated with worsening PROMIS-29 social roles participation scores over time, an effect exceeding the clinically meaningful change threshold.
MVPA-active status was associated with a modest decline in raw PROMIS-29 physical function scores over time, but this effect was not significant when using T-scores.

MVPA-active patients showed less improvement in sleep-quality-related symptom severity (difficulty falling asleep, staying asleep, or waking on time) over 6 months compared with MVPA-inactive patients.
Growth mixture modeling of daily resting heart rate showed a slight decreasing trend over the study period.
Average daily step counts of long COVID patients remained stable over the study period without a clear trend.

Growth mixture modeling identified two distinct clusters of patients based on daily moderate-to-vigorous physical activity, a small high-activity cluster and a larger low-activity cluster, with stable activity levels over time in both.
Male sex and less severe baseline fatigue were significant predictors of being classified as MVPA-active among long COVID patients.
Post-exertional malaise was highly prevalent among long COVID/ME-CFS patients in this cohort, occurring at similar rates regardless of MVPA activity level.
Differences in Fitbit-measured activity between MVPA-active and MVPA-inactive groups were not explained by employment status.
Patients who met valid Fitbit wear criteria differed demographically from those who did not, being younger and less likely to be Hispanic, Spanish-speaking, or married.
Among 92 screened CFS patients, the two predominant TCM syndrome patterns were Qi-blood deficiency (58.7%) and liver depression-spleen deficiency (29.3%).
Patients with CFS Qi-blood deficiency syndrome showed 223 differentially expressed proteins compared with healthy controls, with more upregulated than downregulated proteins.
Patients with CFS liver depression-spleen deficiency syndrome showed 351 differentially expressed proteins compared with healthy controls, the largest proteomic change among group comparisons.
Direct comparison between the two CFS TCM subtypes identified 188 differentially expressed proteins, indicating distinct proteomic profiles between subtypes.
The liver depression-spleen deficiency group showed the most pronounced histone/protein phosphorylation changes, with 406 differentially phosphorylated sites versus healthy controls.
The Qi-blood deficiency group showed 242 differentially phosphorylated sites versus healthy controls, with a predominance of upregulated phosphorylation events.
Direct comparison between the two CFS subtypes showed 201 differentially phosphorylated sites, with more downregulated than upregulated sites.

"Intracellular signal transduction" (GO:0035556) was the most enriched biological process among differentially expressed proteins in Qi-blood deficiency CFS patients versus healthy controls, involving genes such as MAST3, PRKAR1A, and MARK2.
"Actin filament bundle" (GO:0032432) was the top enriched cellular component in Qi-blood deficiency CFS patients versus controls, comprising FLNA, LCP1, and RFLNB.
"SH3 domain binding" (GO:0017124) was the top enriched molecular function in Qi-blood deficiency CFS patients versus controls, mediated by PTPN12, HCLS1, and LYN among others.
"Intracellular signal transduction" (GO:0035556) was also the top enriched biological process in liver depression-spleen deficiency CFS patients versus controls, involving AKAP11, MAP4K1, and PAK2.
"Cortical cytoskeleton" (GO:0030863) was the top enriched cellular component in liver depression-spleen deficiency CFS patients versus controls, involving CAPZB, FLNA, and ACTB.
"Profilin binding" (GO:0005522) was the top enriched molecular function in liver depression-spleen deficiency CFS patients versus controls, mediated by VASP, EVL, CTTN, HTT, and WIPF1.
"Presynaptic modulation of chemical synaptic transmission" (GO:0099171) was the top enriched biological process distinguishing the two CFS TCM subtypes, involving GIT1, PRKCB, and ADRA2A.
"Cytoskeleton" (GO:0005856) was the top enriched cellular component distinguishing the two CFS TCM subtypes, containing ACTB, CTTN, CAPZB and additional genes.

"Diacylglycerol-dependent serine/threonine kinase activity" (GO:0004697), reflecting PKC family activity, was the top enriched molecular function distinguishing the two CFS TCM subtypes, mediated by PRKCB, PRKCA, PRKCD, PKN1, and PKN3.

KEGG analysis identified the Notch signaling pathway as the most significantly enriched pathway in Qi-blood deficiency CFS patients versus healthy controls, involving NUMB, HDAC1, SNW1, ADAM17, and HDAC2.

KEGG analysis identified the Spinocerebellar ataxia pathway as the most enriched pathway in liver depression-spleen deficiency CFS patients versus healthy controls, involving SP1, VDAC3, TRAF2, PSMD11, ITPR1, PSMA3, PUM2, PRKCB, NOP56, VDAC2, and PRKCA.

KEGG analysis identified the serotonergic synapse pathway as the top-enriched pathway differentiating the two CFS TCM subtypes, involving BRAF, ITPR1, PRKCB, PLA2G4A, and PRKCA, consistent with the central fatigue hypothesis implicating serotonin.
Machine learning analysis of the CFS-associated protein/GO/KEGG dataset identified 397 critical features and established 25 quantitative rules for functional characterization of CFS.
MAST3 phosphorylation was increased in CFS patients and is linked to NF-κB pathway activation and enhanced inflammatory signaling.
ARFGEF2's downstream effector ARF1 deficiency is linked to NLRP3 inflammasome activation, proposed to contribute to chronic low-grade inflammation in CFS.
AKAP11, identified in the liver depression-spleen deficiency subtype, interacts with GSK3β, a regulator of oxidative stress and inflammatory (Nrf2/NF-κB) pathways.
MAP4K1 loss-of-function causes aberrant T cell overactivation and elevated pro-inflammatory cytokines (IL-12, TNF-α, IL-6), proposed as relevant to liver depression-spleen deficiency CFS.
GIT1 dysfunction may disrupt dendritic spine formation and neuronal communication, with GIT1-knockout mice showing impaired learning and reduced adaptability, relevant to CFS cognitive symptoms.

PRKCB-encoded PKCβ is required for B cell development, activation, and antibody production; deficiency impairs NF-κB activation and proliferation, implicating PRKCB dysregulation in CFS-related immune dysfunction.

ADRA2A, identified as differentially expressed between CFS subtypes, transmits sympathetic signals suppressing GLP-1 release and modulates cognition and pain, potentially linking to CFS metabolic and pain symptoms.
RFLNB (encoding filamin B) was among the top actin-filament-bundle genes in Qi-blood deficiency CFS; FLNB impairment is proposed to increase energy expenditure needed for cytoskeletal remodeling.

FLNA is essential for T cell receptor signaling and immune synapse stabilization; its impairment is proposed as a direct mechanism for T cell dysfunction in CFS, plus effects on vascular and blood-brain barrier integrity.

LCP1 facilitates cytoskeletal remodeling and immune cell activation; its dysfunction is proposed to prevent effective T cell immune synapse formation in CFS, impairing viral clearance or immune memory.

CAPZB modulates immune synapse formation via actin dynamics; its knockdown disrupts actin architecture at the immune synapse and impairs complete T cell activation, implicated in liver depression-spleen deficiency CFS.

MPP1 (p55) maintains erythrocyte membrane-cytoskeleton attachment; mutations cause spherocyte formation and hemolytic anemia, proposed as a mechanism for chronic tissue hypoxia contributing to fatigue.
FRMD4B, shared between both CFS subtypes, knockdown reduces axonal elongation and impairs learning/memory, proposed as a molecular basis for CFS concentration and memory deficits.

ADD1 (adducin 1), shared between both CFS subtypes, destabilizes erythrocyte membrane skeleton when deficient and modulates synaptic plasticity via glutamate receptors, linking to chronic hypoxia and cognitive impairment.
PTPN12 (PTP-PEST) is a negative regulator of cell migration; its dysfunction is proposed to impair immune cell migration and adhesion, contributing to delayed immune responses in CFS.

HCLS1, an actin-binding protein predominantly expressed in hematopoietic cells, drives actin cytoskeleton reorganization upon immune receptor activation and is implicated in immune cell activation defects in CFS.

VASP regulates actin dynamics in T cell polarization and dendritic spine stability; its dysfunction is proposed to impair dendritic spine maturation and immune cell migration, contributing to cognitive fatigue and chemotactic deficiency in CFS.
EVL, functionally similar to VASP, is required for activated T cell trafficking, and its dysregulation is proposed to contribute to CFS immune migration deficits.
PKN3 maintains endothelial morphology and cell junctions and regulates angiogenesis; its dysregulation is proposed as a common node between CFS subtypes contributing to endothelial dysfunction.
PKN1 knockout mice show halved peripheral blood lymphocyte counts indicating impaired lymphocyte migration, suggesting PKN1 dysregulation as a novel immune deficiency mechanism in CFS.

Machine learning analysis of the CFS proteomic/phosphoproteomic dataset identified 397 critical features and derived 25 quantitative classification rules, described as validated against prior research.
Graded exercise therapy (GET) produced a clinically meaningful reduction in fatigue compared with waitlist at end of treatment, with moderate certainty evidence.
Qigong significantly reduced fatigue versus waitlist at end of treatment, but low-certainty evidence and CI overlap with the MID limit confidence in clinical relevance.
Running showed the largest point-estimate reduction in fatigue versus waitlist, but based on a single trial with very low certainty evidence.
Strength/resistance training did not significantly reduce fatigue compared with waitlist, with very low certainty evidence.
Yoga did not significantly reduce fatigue compared with waitlist, with very low certainty evidence based on a single trial.
At end of follow-up, GET's effect on fatigue versus waitlist was no longer statistically robust, with a wide confidence interval crossing the null.
Qigong's effect on fatigue at follow-up was not statistically robust, with very low certainty evidence.
GET produced the largest improvement in depressive symptoms versus waitlist at end of treatment, with low certainty evidence.
Qigong showed a statistically significant but very low-certainty reduction in depressive symptoms, with MID overlap limiting clinical interpretation.
Strength/resistance training did not significantly reduce depressive symptoms versus waitlist, with very low certainty evidence.
GET's improvement in depression at end of follow-up was of low certainty and the CI overlapped the MID.
GET showed a statistically significant but MID-uncertain reduction in anxiety versus waitlist at end of treatment.
GET's effect on anxiety at end of follow-up was larger and appeared clinically meaningful, exceeding the MID with a low-certainty rating.
GET produced a statistically significant improvement in physical function versus waitlist at end of treatment, but the effect remained below the clinically meaningful threshold.
Qigong did not significantly or clinically meaningfully improve physical function versus waitlist at end of treatment.
At follow-up, GET showed only minimal, non-significant benefit on physical function, still below the MID threshold.
Graded exercise therapy improved sleep quality compared with waitlist at end of treatment, though the effect fell below the minimally important difference threshold.
Qigong improved sleep quality compared with waitlist at end of treatment but the effect did not reach the minimally important difference.
At end of follow-up, GET showed a modest but likely non-clinically-meaningful improvement in sleep quality versus waitlist.
At end of follow-up, Qigong showed no significant sustained effect on sleep quality versus waitlist.
Subgroup analysis found no evidence that diagnostic criteria used to define CFS modified treatment effects, though this analysis had low credibility.

Sensitivity analyses using standardized mean differences without scale conversion were directionally consistent with the primary harmonized mean-difference analysis, confirming robustness of the GET-fatigue effect.

Safety concerns about GET have been raised, including inadequately controlled study designs, reliance on subjective fatigue measures in unblinded trials, neglect of objective outcomes, insufficient reporting of adverse events, and some patients experiencing symptom exacerbation.
Preliminary evidence suggests exercise therapy may benefit CFS partly through modulation of inflammatory cytokines including IL-6, IL-8, and TNF-α.
Exercise therapy may strengthen functional connectivity of the left frontoparietal network and default mode network and promote functional plasticity of brain networks in CFS patients.
Cognitive behavioral therapy-induced improvements in CFS are often not accompanied by increases in physical activity, suggesting behavioral adaptation rather than true functional recovery.
Chronic fatigue syndrome affects an estimated 0.89% of the global population and is associated with substantial economic burden and impaired quality of life and productivity.
IBS symptom severity was higher in IBS patients with psychiatric and/or somatic comorbidities compared with IBS patients without comorbidities.
As the number of comorbidities in IBS patients increased, fibromyalgia symptom severity increased linearly, showing the strongest linear trend among the measures tested.
Depressive symptom severity increased linearly with increasing number of comorbidities in IBS patients, the strongest linear trend observed.
Anxiety symptom severity increased linearly with increasing number of comorbidities in IBS patients.
General fatigue severity increased linearly with increasing number of comorbidities in IBS patients.
As the number of MINI-diagnosed psychiatric diagnoses increased, anxiety and depressive symptom severity increased linearly among IBS patients.
A history of trauma in IBS patients was associated with more severe overall symptoms (except IBS symptoms themselves), with the strongest association seen for anxiety severity.

Overlap between anxiety, depression, fibromyalgia, and chronic fatigue syndrome was common among IBS patients, with fibromyalgia+CFS and combinations of all four comorbidities among the most frequent groupings.
Diagnosed CFS has previously been reported to occur in 14% of IBS patients, per cited prior literature summarized in this paper's introduction.
The proportion of diagnosed anxiety, depression, fibromyalgia and CFS did not differ significantly among IBS subtypes (IBS-C, IBS-D, IBS-M, IBS-U).
IBS-SSS scores varied significantly by IBS subtype, with IBS-C and IBS-M showing the most severe symptoms, followed by IBS-D, and IBS-U the mildest.
Depression, generalized anxiety disorder, and panic disorder were the most common psychiatric diagnoses, each more frequent among disease controls than IBS patients.
Among IBS patients, 52% had no psychiatric diagnoses, 25% had one, 15% had two, and 8% had three or more, with GAD plus depression being the most common combination (25%).
No differences in rates of appendectomy or cholecystectomy were seen between IBS, disease controls, or healthy controls.
Inability to work was almost exclusively reported by IBS patients and disease controls, indicating substantial functional/occupational impact of these conditions and their comorbidities.
A previous COVID-19 infection was more commonly reported among healthy controls than among IBS patients or disease controls.
Stroke volume index (SV/FFM) was significantly lower in CFS patients than in healthy controls.
HF RRI, a marker of cardiac vagal tone, was significantly lower in CFS patients than in healthy controls.
Mean beat-to-beat HR difference did not differ significantly between CFS patients and healthy controls.
Breathing frequency did not differ significantly between CFS patients and healthy controls.
Mean beat-to-beat dBP difference did not differ significantly between CFS patients and healthy controls, though its distributional pattern still contributed to classification.

A sequential Transformer-then-XGBoost ensemble classifier using six autonomic/hemodynamic features plus Transformer error achieved subject-level MCC 0.79, accuracy 0.89, and ROC AUC 1.0 in distinguishing CFS from healthy controls.
XGBoost alone (using six physiological features) achieved subject-level AUC 0.99, accuracy 0.91, MCC 0.83, outperforming the standalone Transformer model.
The standalone Transformer model performed poorly at subject level, with AUC 0.77 and accuracy only 0.46, underperforming both XGBoost alone and the combined ensemble.
At subject level, the ensemble correctly classified all 12 healthy controls (100% specificity) but only 14 of 23 CFS patients (61% sensitivity), with 9 false negatives.
CFS patients had a significantly higher percentage of adipose tissue than healthy controls.
CFS patients had significantly higher visceral fat levels than healthy controls.
Post-exertional malaise was present in 84% of the CFS cohort.
Brain fog (cognitive impairment) was reported by 92% of the CFS cohort.
SHAP analysis identified the Transformer's prediction error as the single most important feature, with higher error values linked to a greater probability of CFS classification.

Permutation and ablation diagnostics showed the Transformer error feature was highly informative (permutation dropped accuracy from 99.55% to 61.05%; ablation improved accuracy by 4.21%) and correlated with true labels (point-biserial r=0.605), indicating meaningful signal rather than data leakage.

Higher-magnitude beat-to-beat heart rate decelerations were observed more frequently in CFS patients than controls, indicating pronounced but dysregulated parasympathetic (vagal) bursts, whereas controls showed more accelerations.
Increased frequency of beat-to-beat rises in diastolic blood pressure in CFS patients was interpreted as reflecting heightened sympathetic vasoconstrictor activity and/or baroreflex dysfunction.
Reduced beat-to-beat stroke volume variability in CFS was hypothesized to reflect impaired preload/hypovolemia limiting the Frank-Starling mechanism and causing hemodynamic inefficiency.
Reduced SV/FFM in CFS is consistent with previously reported reductions in stroke volume, end-diastolic volume, cardiac output, stroke index, and cardiac index in this population.
The authors propose that the constellation of increased dBP fluctuation with diminished HR and SV responses may indicate a disrupted baroreceptor reflex in CFS patients.
Saffron extract supplementation significantly lowered total CRQ fatigue-related scores compared with placebo over the 8-week trial.
The mastery subscale of the CRQ improved significantly with saffron supplementation relative to placebo.
The CRQ fatigue subscale improved significantly in the saffron group compared with placebo.
The CRQ emotional function subscale improved significantly with saffron supplementation.
The dyspnea subscale of the CRQ did not differ significantly between saffron and placebo groups.
Saffron extract significantly reduced chronic fatigue status as measured by the Manchester COPD Fatigue Scale (MCFS) over the study period.
Total quality-of-life score (SGRQ) improved significantly with saffron extract, along with activity and impact subscales.
The SGRQ symptoms subscale did not improve significantly with saffron extract compared with placebo.
Baseline dyspnea severity (mMRC scale) did not differ significantly between the saffron and placebo groups, indicating comparable groups at baseline.
No adverse events or side effects were reported in either the saffron or placebo groups over the 2-month trial.
In a cited prior trial (Ghobadi et al.), crocin supplementation decreased inflammatory markers including NF-κB and total oxidant status while increasing total antioxidant capacity in COPD patients.
In the cited Ghobadi et al. trial, biochemical modulation by crocin was accompanied by improved 6-minute walking distance and pulmonary function tests in COPD patients.
In a cited pre-post study (Ashtiani et al.) of 30 multiple sclerosis patients, saffron syrup significantly reduced fatigue severity and was well tolerated.
In a cited RCT (Mirzaei et al.) of 75 breast cancer patients, Jollab significantly reduced cancer-related fatigue on VAFS and FSS, with improvements in physical and cognitive fatigue subscales.
In the cited Mirzaei et al. trial, the affective fatigue subscale showed no significant change in either the Jollab or placebo group.
Crocin is reported to modulate dopaminergic, noradrenergic, and serotonergic neurotransmitter pathways, potentially contributing to improved mood and reduced fatigue-related mental symptoms.

Neuroprotective effects observed in animal models are proposed to support saffron's role in alleviating cognitive and physical fatigue via enhanced neurological function and reduced neuroinflammation.
Lumbar trunk rotation, as measured by scoliometer, was significantly lower in the hypermobile AIS group compared to the non-hypermobile AIS group.

No significant differences were found between hypermobile and non-hypermobile AIS groups in Cobb angle (scoliosis degree), lower extremity length discrepancy, pes planus status, static/dynamic balance, or fall risk.

Cobb angle was significantly positively correlated with pes planus status in AIS patients.
Hypermobility status was found to be associated with gender in the AIS study population.
Better dynamic balance (Functional Reach Test) was associated with a lower risk of falling (Morse Fall Scale) among AIS patients.
In this cross-sectional study of 425 hEDS patients, 46.4% were classified as overweight or obese.
hEDS patients consumed high protein and high fat diets that were overall low in total calories.
hEDS patients had low intake of Vitamin B according to dietary assessment.
hEDS patients had low intake of Vitamin D according to dietary assessment.
Only 24.7% of hEDS patients achieved recommended fibre intake requirements.

The 'vegetarian/health conscious' dietary pattern (n=120) had the highest fibre intake among the four dietary patterns identified.

The 'refined/highly processed' dietary pattern subgroup had the highest BMI among the four dietary pattern clusters in hEDS patients.
The 'refined/highly processed' dietary pattern subgroup showed a higher presence of dyspepsia symptoms compared to other dietary pattern groups.
Patients in the 'refined/highly processed' dietary pattern subgroup were least likely to have received a dietetic consultation compared to other subgroups.

Whole-genome sequencing identified a heterozygous missense variant in COL5A1 predicted to substitute a glycine for glutamate within a Gly-X-Y repeat motif, disrupting collagen triple helix formation and confirming classical EDS.
The dog's skin extensibility index was 26%, well above the 14.5% diagnostic threshold used to support an EDS diagnosis.
Transmission electron microscopy of skin biopsies showed marked variation in collagen fibril diameter, abnormal serrated fibril outlines, and irregular interfibrillar spaces, consistent with EDS.

Staged bilateral extracapsular stabilization surgery, performed 8 weeks apart, resulted in uneventful recoveries and long-term stifle joint stability with no lameness at 5-year follow-up.
Pre-anesthetic bloodwork revealed lymphocytosis, mild eosinophilia, and basophilia in the EDS-affected dog.
EDS has been identified as a risk factor for cranial/anterior cruciate ligament rupture in human medicine, but this risk had not previously been documented in veterinary patients.
In human EDS patients, lower bone mineral density and reduced trabecular bone score have been reported, along with an increased prevalence of vertebral fractures.

The dog had bilateral premature closure of the proximal tibial growth plate (tibial plateau deformity), a condition previously associated with increased predisposition to cranial cruciate ligament rupture.

Prior veterinary studies comparing extracapsular repair (ERC) to tibial plateau leveling osteotomy (TPLO) found that TPLO, but not ERC, patients achieve normal limb function compared to normal dogs, making TPLO the generally preferred recommendation.

The dog fulfilled major clinical criteria for classical EDS (skin hyperextensibility, atrophic scarring, joint hypermobility) and two minor criteria (skin fragility, cruciate ligament rupture as a complication of joint hypermobility), matching human diagnostic criteria.

Segregation analysis via Sanger sequencing in additional family members supported the BGN variant as the most likely causal candidate for the disease phenotype.
Western blot of aortic wall tissue from affected patient II.2 showed reduced levels of phosphorylated SMAD2/3 compared to a control aortic sample.

Expression of the Wnt target gene AXIN2 was lower in the patient's aortic wall sample compared to control.
BGN expression levels were similar between the patient's and control aortic wall samples, despite the presence of the pathogenic missense variant.
In MG-63 cells, TGF-β-stimulated p-SMAD2/3 response was attenuated when cells were transfected with mutant BGN compared to wild-type BGN.

Co-transfection of the TOPFlash Wnt reporter with the mutant BGN vector into HEK-293T cells showed significantly reduced luciferase reporter activity compared to the wild-type BGN vector, indicating diminished canonical Wnt pathway activity.
No significant differences were observed in fibroblast proliferation rates or cell survival after serum deprivation when comparing patient-derived and control fibroblast explants.
BGN expression was similar between patient and control skin fibroblasts (ΔCt 2.4 ± 0.1 vs. 1.8 ± 0.8), not statistically significant.
Confocal immunofluorescence of cultured skin fibroblasts revealed no consistent differences in p-SMAD2/3 or β-catenin abundance between patients and controls, including in sex-stratified analyses.
Expression of LGR5, a TGF-β target gene, was slightly higher in fibroblasts grown from patients' skin than in controls.

DXA scan of the index patient revealed low bone mineral density with T-scores of −1.0 at the lumbar spine and −2.3 at the femoral neck.

Additional heterozygous variants in COL1A2, IPO8, and YY1AP1 were identified in the index patient but considered less likely to explain the clinical phenotype compared to the BGN variant.

Structural modeling indicated that the Leu95Pro substitution occurs in a beta sheet forming a hydrophobic pocket that interacts with TGF-β, and free energy calculations (SAAFEC-SEQ, ELASPIC) predicted destabilization of this beta sheet.

A novel de novo heterozygous splice-site variant (c.1977+1G>C) in COL3A1, predicted to disrupt the donor splice site of intron 28, was classified as probably pathogenic (ACMG PVS1, PM2) and considered causal for this patient's vascular Ehlers-Danlos syndrome.
The patient had a history of recurrent muscle/tendon ruptures including biceps, pectoralis major, and penile ruptures (three episodes), a minor diagnostic criterion for VEDS.

The patient exhibited acrogeric facial features (beaked nose, thin upper lip, prominent eyes, sunken cheeks) and thin, translucent skin with visible veins, both classic minor diagnostic criteria for VEDS.

The patient presented with right carotid artery dissection and thrombus in the M1 segment of the right middle cerebral artery, causing an acute ischemic stroke with NIHSS score of 20, a major vascular complication consistent with vascular EDS.
Laboratory testing at presentation showed slightly elevated triglycerides and C-reactive protein levels.
The patient reported a family history of idiopathic death of his father following a bronchoscopy, though the COL3A1 variant identified in the patient was determined to be de novo.
Up to 50% of vascular EDS patients may carry de novo COL3A1 mutations rather than inherited variants.
Vascular Ehlers-Danlos syndrome accounts for 4-5% of all Ehlers-Danlos syndrome cases and is associated with high rates of fatal cardiovascular and gastrointestinal complications.
Mean survival for vascular EDS patients is 51 years, varying with variant type, with patients carrying a null allele exhibiting longer life expectancy than those with glycine substitution variants.
Most pathogenic COL3A1 variants result in substitution of glycine residues within the Gly-X-Y repeat of the triple helical domain of type III procollagen, disrupting normal collagen structure.
Pharmacotherapeutic management of VEDS aims to maintain low-normal blood pressure using diuretics, β-blockers, and angiotensin pathway blockers to minimize risk of arterial dissection or rupture.
Following the acute ischemic stroke secondary to carotid dissection, the patient was started on statin and aspirin (adiro) therapy.

A novel, previously unreported COL3A1 splice-site variant (c.1977+1G>C) was identified in heterozygosity in the patient, predicted to disrupt the intron 28 donor splice site and cause aberrant, non-functional mRNA splicing.
The patient exhibited acrogeric facial features (pointed nose, thin upper lip, prominent eyes, sunken cheeks) and thin, translucent skin with visible veins, consistent with vascular EDS phenotype.
The patient had a personal history of muscle fragility with multiple ruptures involving the biceps, pectoralis major, and penis (three separate occasions).
The patient developed a right carotid artery dissection with thrombus in the middle cerebral artery, causing an acute ischemic stroke with NIHSS score of 20.
The patient's father died of an idiopathic cause following a bronchoscopy, suggesting possible undiagnosed familial vascular fragility.
Laboratory testing showed slightly elevated triglyceride levels in the patient at the time of acute presentation.
Laboratory testing showed slightly elevated C-reactive protein (CRP) in the patient at the time of acute presentation.
The variant was classified as likely pathogenic per updated ACMG criteria, meeting PVS1 and PM2 evidence categories.
No pathogenic or likely pathogenic variants were found in the 81 genes recommended by ACMG v3.2 for secondary findings reporting in this patient's targeted exome.

Vascular EDS accounts for approximately 4-5% of all EDS cases and carries a high rate of fatal cardiovascular and gastrointestinal complications such as cerebrovascular hemorrhage or intestinal rupture.
Approximately 50% of vascular EDS patients carry de novo mutations, meaning absence of family history does not exclude the diagnosis.
Mean survival in vascular EDS is approximately 51 years and depends on the nature of the pathogenic variant, being longer in patients with null variants.

The most common clinical manifestations of vascular EDS reported in the literature include spontaneous pneumothorax (12%) and superficial venous insufficiency (37%), among other vascular and connective tissue complications.

General medical management of vascular EDS aims to keep blood pressure normal-to-low using diuretics, beta-blockers, angiotensin pathway blockers, and other antihypertensives to reduce risk of arterial dissection/rupture.
Following favorable clinical evolution within 24 hours, the patient was discharged home on statin and aspirin (adiro) therapy.
In patients with this connective tissue phenotype, Marfan syndrome should be ruled out using the Systemic Marfan Score or FBN1 analysis before considering atypical collagenopathies.

More than 1,500 COL3A1 variants have been identified as pathogenic in the literature, with most consisting of single amino acid substitutions of glycine residues in the Gly-X-Y repeats of the type III procollagen triple-helical domain.
Fibroblasts from the haploinsufficiency (HI) OI group appeared rounder in shape compared with the more elongated morphology of control fibroblasts.
Fibroblasts from the dominant-negative (DN) OI and EDS groups displayed narrower, more elongated shapes than controls.
Overall collagen deposition, visualized by SHG, appeared reduced in fibroblasts from the HI OI and DN OI groups compared with controls.
Total collagen content per z-stack (SHG pixel count) was significantly reduced in HI OI (4.0±1.7×10^7) and DN OI (7±5×10^7) groups compared with control (10±7×10^7) and EDS (20±5×10^7) groups.
Total fibroblast count per z-stack was lowest in controls (7800±1800 cells) relative to HI OI (11,000±1800), DN OI (11,080±750), and EDS (12,600±800) groups.
Control fibroblasts secreted significantly more collagen per cell (12,900±6800 pixels/cell) than HI OI (3700±1700) and DN OI (6100±4300) fibroblasts.
Neonatal control fibroblasts secreted more collagen per cell than adult control fibroblasts.
Collagen fibers in the EDS group were significantly thinner (0.78±0.18 µm) than in controls (0.94±0.31 µm).
Collagen fiber diameter in HI OI (0.89±0.25 µm) and DN OI (0.84±0.20 µm) groups did not differ significantly from controls.
Adult control cultures formed thicker collagen fibers than neonatal control cultures.
HI OI fibroblasts showed a larger average cell area (1250±430 µm²) and rounder shape (width-to-length ratio 0.15±0.04) than control, DN OI, and EDS fibroblasts.
Fibroblasts from DN OI and EDS groups exhibited significantly narrower shapes compared with controls.
A negative correlation (r=-0.8) was found between average fibroblast cell area and average SHG (collagen) pixel count across the four groups, indicating larger fibroblasts secreted less collagen.

The counterclockwise depth-dependent rotational shift of fibroblast and collagen orientation occurred more gradually in neonatal control samples than in patient-derived (disease) fibroblasts.

After a single sclerotherapy injection, success rate was significantly higher in functional rectal prolapse (78%) than in organic rectal prolapse (21%).

In a mixed EDS/JHS clinic sample, psychological distress was increased relative to norms but did not exceed pathological cutoffs.

73% of an hEDS sample reported anxiety on the Hospital Anxiety and Depression Scale.
74.8% of an EDS sample reported clinical levels of anxiety.

Patients with Loeys-Dietz syndrome (LDS) showed higher clinical levels of anxiety than patients with vascular EDS (vEDS) in molecularly verified cohorts.

A heterozygous, de novo pathogenic variant in the NSD1 gene (c.5990A>G, p.Tyr1997Cys) was identified in a newborn with joint hyperlaxity and other features of Sotos syndrome, consistent with autosomal dominant inheritance.

A novel hemizygous FLNA splice-region variant causing an in-frame two-amino-acid deletion was identified in a proband and his monozygotic twin brothers with cardiac valvular dysplasia.

Robotic-assisted endoscopic debridement combined with percutaneous pars screw fixation of bilateral L5 pars fractures resulted in complete resolution of low back pain and lumbar radiculopathy and full return to competitive downhill skiing within 3 months postoperatively.

Preoperative ATFL signal-to-noise ratio (low vs high) was not correlated with postoperative patient-reported outcomes (FAOS, VAS, Karlsson, Tegner) after modified Broström repair in adolescents with chronic lateral ankle instability.

Secondary outcomes—time to return to sport, recurrent sprain rate, incision numbness, and subjective satisfaction—were comparable between low- and high-SNR groups.
Both SNR groups showed significant improvement in all patient-reported outcomes following modified Broström repair compared with preoperative status.
Trapezius muscle thickness measured by B-mode ultrasound was significantly greater in fibromyalgia patients than in healthy controls.
