A significant positive correlation was found between trapezius elastography stiffness scores and VAS pain intensity in fibromyalgia patients.
No significant correlation was found between ultrasound measurements (muscle thickness, skin thickness) and VAS pain scale in fibromyalgia patients.

Fibromyalgia patients had significantly higher hemoglobin levels than healthy controls, though values remained within normal reference ranges, possibly reflecting hemoconcentration from autonomic dysregulation.
Fibromyalgia patients had significantly higher creatinine levels than healthy controls, though within normal range, possibly reflecting subtle alterations in muscle metabolism or renal efficiency.
The mean VAS pain score in fibromyalgia patients was above 7, indicating severe pain burden in this cohort.
Meta-analysis of beta-endorphin levels in blood and cerebrospinal fluid showed no significant differences between patients with fibromyalgia or chronic low back pain and pain-free controls.
Some studies suggest reduced mu-opioid receptor (MOR) binding in the brain of patients with fibromyalgia, as shown by emerging PET findings, indicating central receptor-level dysregulation.
Decreased mu-opioid receptor expression on immune cells was observed in some studies of patients with fibromyalgia compared to pain-free controls.
Patients with comorbid fibromyalgia and chronic migraine (FM-CM) reported the highest levels of traumatization compared to chronic migraine patients and healthy controls.
Traumatic experiences were significantly associated with central sensitization symptoms across the nociplastic pain spectrum (migraine, fibromyalgia, comorbid FM-CM), independent of diagnostic group.
Traumatic experiences indirectly reduced quality of physical and mental health among nociplastic pain patients via their effect on central sensitization, in a moderated mediation model.

The patient had persistently elevated serum tryptase levels across three samples (17.8 ng/mL and 19.2 ng/mL), above the upper limit of normal but not reaching the mastocytosis diagnostic threshold of >20 ng/mL.
The oncogenic KIT p.D816V mutation, found in >80% of mastocytosis patients, was negative by ASO-qPCR in this patient, and the bone marrow karyotype was normal.

Targeted myeloid NGS identified a pathogenic ZRSR2 variant (p.S447_R448del) at 7.4% variant allele frequency, which was ultimately attributed to clonal hematopoiesis of indeterminate potential (CHIP) rather than to mastocytosis or MDS.

Bone marrow morphology showed moderate trilinear dysplasia (micromegakaryocytes, hypolobated megakaryocytes, granulocytic hypogranulation, erythroid nuclear bridging) affecting >10% of megakaryocytic, granulocytic, and erythroid lineages, despite normal cellularity and blast count.

Bone marrow mast cells showed partial CD25 expression on spindle-shaped CD117-positive mast cells (satisfying one minor mastocytosis criterion), but spindle-shaped cells were <25% of total mast cells, so another minor criterion was not met.
FISH testing for PDGFRA, PDGFRB, and FGFR1 rearrangements and PCM1::JAK2 fusion was negative, excluding these myeloid neoplasm drivers.
Serum tryptase elevation is not specific to mastocytosis and can also be found in up to 25% of myelodysplastic syndrome patients, complicating the differential diagnosis in this case.
ZRSR2 mutations in MDS patients have previously been reported to be associated with male sex and an indolent clinical phenotype, a description this patient closely reflected.

ZRSR2 loss of function, typical of MDS and other myeloid neoplasms, has been shown to impair inflammation and immune response pathways such as Toll-like receptor signaling, offering a possible mechanistic explanation for this patient's dysregulated anaphylactic reaction to a bee sting.

Hereditary alpha-tryptasemia (HαT), a condition associated with elevated tryptase due to TPSAB1 copy number gain, was considered as a differential but ruled out given the absence of family history and suggestive symptoms, so TPSAB1 genetic testing was not performed.

An HA dermal filler injection is reported to have triggered mast cell activation syndrome (MCAS) with refractory vasoplegia that fully resolved within 24 hours after hyaluronidase-mediated dissolution of the filler.
Standard escalating MCAS therapies—IV corticosteroids, antihistamines, and fludrocortisone—failed to control the patient's refractory hypotension prior to hyaluronidase administration.
Postural orthostatic tachycardia syndrome was investigated as a differential diagnosis for the patient's hemodynamic instability but was ruled out by tilt table testing.

The authors hypothesize that HA filler-induced MCAS may occur through IgE-independent direct activation of mast cells and basophils, citing prior reports of anti-hyaluronic acid IgG and IgE antibodies against Restylane/Hylaform fillers.
The patient had been maintained on omalizumab for 2 years prior to this episode with good clinical control of her established MCAS.
Gain-of-function mutations in NLRP3 cause the cryopyrin-associated periodic syndrome (CAPS) spectrum, of which FCAS is the mildest phenotype.

NLRP3 inflammasome activation recruits ASC and activates Caspase-1 and Gasdermin D, leading to pyroptosis and secretion of IL-1β and IL-18, with elevated CRP and SAA, normal IgE, and negative CSTT in FCAS.
Several adult-onset FCAS cases have been linked to low-level somatic NLRP3 mosaicism, requiring high-depth NGS for detection.
FCAS2 is caused by NLRP12 mutations clustered in exon 3, where NLRP12 normally negatively regulates NF-κB signaling and reduces IL-1β, IL-6, and IL-8 production.

In approximately 66% of FCAS2 cases, rashes occur within several hours after cold exposure, accompanied by elevated CRP and ESR, with slight male predominance and about half showing a positive family history.
IL-1 antagonists such as anakinra and canakinumab have shown marked clinical efficacy in FCAS2, whereas TNF-α inhibitors yield inconsistent results.

Pathogenic gain-of-function NLRC4 variants trigger inflammasome activation independent of infection, causing excessive IL-1β and IL-18 secretion and a phenotype ranging from mild rash/arthralgia (FCAS4) to macrophage activation syndrome or infantile enterocolitis.
Elevated IL-18 levels may serve as a biomarker for NLRC4-associated cold autoinflammatory disease.
PLAID patients with PLCG2 cSH2 domain deletions show early-onset cold-induced rash with decreased serum IgM and IgA, reduced class-switched memory B cells, and diminished circulating NK cells.

Mutant PLCG2 causes temperature-dependent calcium flux abnormalities in B cells (hyporesponsive at ambient temperature, spontaneously activated at ~20°C) and induces spontaneous mast-cell degranulation at sub-physiologic temperatures, unlike wild-type cells.

FACAS is caused by a heterozygous F12 p.W268R mutation that enhances FXII autocatalytic cleavage and spontaneous activation, causing sustained contact-system activation with decreased prekallikrein, increased HMWK cleavage, and elevated bradykinin.

Bradykinin stimulates monocytes via the B2 receptor to release IL-1β, which promotes FXII expression and activation, forming an amplifying loop of vascular permeability and inflammation, and BK also induces mast-cell degranulation with heparin/polyphosphate release enhancing FXII activation.
FACAS responds poorly to second-generation antihistamines but shows marked improvement with bradykinin B2 receptor antagonists (icatibant) or IL-1 inhibitors.
Cold-induced urticaria (FP-ACU) may be associated with dysregulation of the cold-sensing ion channel TRPM8.

The genetic susceptibility underlying FP-ACU is proposed as polygenic, with candidate immune-regulatory and cytokine-signaling loci including IFN-γ, IL-6, IL-17RA, IL-10, TGF-β, TNF, PTPN22, IL-1, IL-2, and HLA class I/II alleles.

In FACU, skin biopsies show dermal mast-cell infiltration and degranulation after cold challenge, supporting a mast-cell-mediated mechanism, with symptoms occurring within five minutes of exposure and a negative CSTT.
Omalizumab is effective in approximately half of antihistamine-refractory cold urticaria patients, supporting a role for IgE in disease pathogenesis.
The anti-KIT antibody barzolvolimab has shown potential efficacy in antihistamine-resistant acquired cold urticaria, though larger studies are needed.
More than half of CSU patients have concurrent IgE and IgG autoantibodies against at least one autoantigen (IgE receptor, tissue factor, or thyroglobulin), with 25% showing anti-FcεRI IgE.
Blood CD4+ T cell proliferation in response to FcεRI on mast cells was found in 27% of CSU patients versus 0% of controls.
IFN-γ responses to FcεRI were detected in 53% of CSU subjects and appeared earlier than anti-FcεRI autoantibodies.
Progenitor mast cells (Lin-CD117+CD34+FcεRI+) are increased in the peripheral blood of CSU patients.
Plasma IL-17 and IL-33 are significantly higher in CSU patients than healthy individuals, and higher still in severe versus moderate/mild disease.
Serum IL-4, IL-31, and IL-17 showed the strongest correlation with CSU disease severity in a later study.
Th17-related cytokines IL-17 and IL-21 are significantly increased and positively correlate with CSU disease severity.
Treg-related cytokines TGF-β and IL-35 are significantly decreased and negatively associated with CSU severity.
Upregulation of coagulation factors, D-dimers, and MMP9 has been reported as biomarkers of CSU disease severity.
Co-stimulation of vascular endothelial cells with LPS, TNF-α, IL-33, VEGF, and histamine significantly increased tissue factor expression.
Increased serum levels of the alarmin triad IL-25, IL-33, and TSLP significantly correlate with UAS7 scores and are suggested as prognostic biomarkers in CSU.
Serum miR-125a-5p and CCL17 are upregulated in CSU and correlate with treatment response, suggesting utility as biomarkers.
Serum MRGPRX2 and CCL2 (chemokine C-C motif ligand 2) are increased in CSU patients and correlate with disease activity.
Cutaneous biopsies from urticaria patients show upregulated IL-6 and CXCL8 gene expression, associated with mast cell STAT3 activation and inflammatory cell recruitment.
Significant increases in IL-33+, IL-25+, and TSLP+ cells were found in the dermis of lesional CSU skin, localized to endothelial cells and tryptase+ mast cells, supporting Th2 involvement.

In the authors' own study, CCR5 expression on CD4+ T cells and its ligand CCL3 on mast cells were significantly increased in severe CSU skin compared to healthy skin, with CCR5+ T cells found in close proximity to CCL3+ mast cells.
A prior study by the authors' group found increased CD4+ T cells and mast cells expressing elevated IL-17 in both lesional and non-lesional CSU skin, in close proximity to each other.
Direct proximity measurements show T cells and mast cells are markedly closer together in CSU lesional skin (0.465-0.853 µm) than in normal skin (2.267-13.067 µm).
Cyclosporine A was, for over a decade, the only beneficial therapy for CSU prior to the approval of omalizumab.
Dupilumab (anti-IL-4/IL-13 antibody) has proven efficient in recent clinical studies for CSU, supporting the role of Th2 cells in CSU pathogenesis.

Btk inhibitors such as Remibrutinib are highly effective in CSU by regulating T-cell activity/repertoire, inhibiting ITK, and downregulating inflammatory activities of B cells, basophils, and mast cells, including IgE-mediated FcεR-dependent mechanisms.
The authors' own report describes a beneficial response to anti-IL-17 (Secukinumab) in severe CSU patients, supporting a role for IL-17 in CSU pathogenesis and T/mast cell proximity.
Abrocitinib and tofacitinib (JAK inhibitors) were reported beneficial in omalizumab-refractory cases of CSU.

Large multinational surveillance studies (JESPA in Japan, NAP6 in UK, GERAP in France) report a consistent perioperative anaphylaxis incidence of approximately 1 in 5000 to 10,000 general anesthesia cases.
JESPA identified neuromuscular blocking agents, antibiotics, and sugammadex as the major causative agents of perioperative anaphylaxis in Japan.
The frequency of sugammadex-induced anaphylaxis is reported to be higher in Japan than in other countries, likely reflecting its extensive clinical use.
JESPA identified neuromuscular blocking agents, antibiotics, and sugammadex as the major causative drug classes for perioperative anaphylaxis in Japan.
Sugammadex-induced anaphylaxis occurs at a higher frequency in Japan compared to other countries, likely due to its extensive clinical use.
Perioperative anaphylaxis arises from both immunologic and non-immunologic pathways that converge on mast cell activation and mediator release.
The clinical presentation of perioperative anaphylaxis, primarily hypotension and bronchospasm, is often masked by anesthesia, complicating recognition.
Diagnosis of perioperative anaphylaxis includes measuring tryptase using the EAACI consensus formula (1.2 × baseline + 2 ng/mL) to confirm mast cell mediator release.
Identification of the causative drug in perioperative anaphylaxis relies on skin testing, basophil activation tests, or drug provocation tests.

The authors propose future priorities including expanding access to tryptase testing, strengthening multidisciplinary collaboration, and promoting anesthesiologist-led allergy investigations to improve diagnostic precision and patient safety.
XQLT treatment significantly reduced nasal rubbing and sneezing frequencies in OVA-induced allergic rhinitis mice.
XQLT decreased serum IL-4 levels in OVA-induced allergic rhinitis mice.
XQLT decreased serum ovalbumin-specific IgE (OVA-sIgE) levels in AR mice.

Transcriptomic profiling of nasal mucosa showed XQLT modulated differentially expressed genes linked to immune response, inflammatory signaling, olfactory transduction, and pain sensory perception pathways.
XQLT suppressed LPS-induced nitric oxide (NO) production in macrophages.
XQLT downregulated expression of the pro-inflammatory mediators IL-6, IL-1β, CCL2, iNOS, and COX-2 in LPS-stimulated macrophages.
XQLT inhibited NF-κB nuclear translocation in LPS-stimulated macrophages, indicating suppression of this inflammatory signaling pathway.
XQLT reduced TRPV1 expression in the nasal mucosa of OVA-induced allergic rhinitis mice, as shown by immunohistochemistry.
XQLT treatment downregulated expression of IL-6, IL-1β, CCL2, iNOS, and COX-2 in LPS-stimulated RAW264.7 macrophages and bone marrow-derived macrophages.
XQLT inhibited NF-κB nuclear translocation in LPS-stimulated macrophages.
XQLT reduced TRPV1 expression in the nasal mucosa of OVA-induced AR mice, as shown by immunohistochemistry.
XQLT inhibited TRPV1-mediated calcium influx in HEK293 cells overexpressing TRPV1, assessed by calcium imaging.
XQLT reduced TRPV1 expression in the nasal mucosa of AR mice as shown by immunohistochemistry.
XQLT inhibited TRPV1-mediated calcium influx in HEK293 cells overexpressing TRPV1.
Molecular docking analysis identified Zingiberis Rhizoma (Ganjiang) as the key herb within XQLT responsible for TRPV1 inhibition.
Transcriptomic profiling of nasal mucosa revealed XQLT modulated differentially expressed genes related to olfactory transduction and sensory perception of pain pathways.
XQLT ameliorated lung histopathological remodeling in AR mice without observable toxicity.
Peripheral sensorimotor neuropathy and dysautonomia are common in hemodialysis patients and may contribute to chronic kidney disease-associated pruritus (CKD-aP).
Serum tryptase levels, a mast cell mediator, significantly correlated with itch severity in CKD-associated pruritus patients.
The increased number and cutaneous spread of mast cells in patients with CKD-associated pruritus remains debated across studies.
The role of histamine in the pathogenesis of CKD-associated pruritus is controversial across cited studies.
Serum serotonin levels were reported higher in patients with CKD-associated pruritus compared with controls.
Ondansetron, a 5-HT3-receptor inhibitor, significantly reduced pruritus severity in CKD-associated pruritus.
Mast-cell stabilizers such as cromolyn sodium, zinc sulfate, and ketotifen, which prevent histamine release, produced reasonable antipruritic effects in CKD-associated pruritus.
Topical cromolyn sodium 4% cream applied twice daily for 4 weeks decreased pruritus intensity compared with placebo.
Patients with CKD-associated pruritus had elevated serum levels of interleukin-31, a cytokine that acts on peripheral nerve receptors as a mediator of itch.

A randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial of nemolizumab (anti-IL-31 receptor monoclonal antibody) in hemodialysis patients with CKD-associated pruritus did not show a statistically significant reduction in pruritus severity scores.

PAR2 expression is upregulated in epidermal keratinocytes of CKD patients, likely driven directly or indirectly by protein-bound uremic toxins, and positively correlates with itch severity via a histamine-independent pruritic pathway.

Mas-related G protein-coupled receptors (MRGPRs), located on sensory neurons and mast cells, are non-histamine itch receptors activated by proteases, antimicrobial peptides, and substance P; MRGPRX4-targeting drug EP547 is in clinical development for uremic and cholestatic pruritus.
Increased expression of IL-4 and/or IL-13 in uremic patients is proposed as a mechanism of CKD-associated pruritus, and dupilumab (anti-IL-4/IL-13 receptor antibody) has shown potential benefit.
In a double-blind RCT of hemodialysis patients with CKD-associated pruritus, montelukast (a leukotriene receptor blocker) taken for 30 days reduced pruritus intensity compared with placebo.
Among 31 patients with dry eye disease, 38.7% had abnormal Small-Fiber Symptom Survey scores, indicating a high prevalence of small fiber neuropathy symptoms in this population.
SFN symptom severity (SSS score) was positively correlated with dry eye disease symptom severity as measured by OSDI.
SFN symptom severity (SSS score) was positively correlated with ocular pain severity as measured by OPAS.
SFN symptom severity (SSS score) was negatively correlated with corneal fluorescein staining (CFS), a clinical sign of ocular surface damage.
SFN symptom severity (SSS score) did not correlate with tear breakup time, tear production, or corneal sensitivity.
Despite standard dry eye disease treatments and stable clinical signs over 6 to 12 months of follow-up, most patients with severe SFN symptoms reported worsening dry eye symptoms.
Small-Fiber Symptom Survey scores showed no significant correlation with corneal sensitivity measurements in patients with dry eye disease.

Despite receiving standard dry eye treatments and having clinically stable ocular signs, most patients with severe small fiber neuropathy symptoms reported worsening dry eye symptoms at 6-12 month follow-up.
Skin biopsy showing reduced intraepidermal nerve fiber density (IENFD) at the distal leg is a key diagnostic feature of Small-Fiber Neuropathy.
IENFD from skin biopsy has high intra- and interlaboratory reliability and reproducibility as a pathological parameter.
In HIV infection and diabetes, small-fiber neuropathy has been regarded as an initial phase of neuropathy that can progress to large-fiber polyneuropathy.
In long COVID presenting with painful and/or dysautonomic symptomatology, skin biopsy has been used to explore the role of Small-Fiber Neuropathy.
Morphological alterations of small nerve fibers such as branching and swelling represent early neuropathic changes preceding measurable IENFD reduction, as shown in painful diabetic neuropathy.

Quantitative counting of cutaneous autonomic nerve fibers innervating blood vessels, sweat glands, and arrector pili muscles is technically complex, leading to reliance on qualitative/semi-quantitative expert scoring.
Skin biopsy can reveal non-length-dependent neuropathic processes such as ganglionopathy, where IENFD reduction occurs at proximal sites (thigh) as well as distal leg.
In Guillain-Barré syndrome (AIDP), skin biopsy demonstrated small-fiber impairment that correlated with disability grade.
In the Acute Motor Axonal Neuropathy (AMAN) variant of AIDP, skin biopsy showed normal dermal and epidermal innervation, while motor-point biopsies revealed intramuscular nerve fiber alterations.
An exploratory 2022 study found IENFD similarly reduced in typical and variant forms of CIDP, with moderate correlation to disability scales.

In Fabry disease, neuropathic pain arises from both dorsal root ganglion involvement and small-fiber neuropathy, and skin biopsy can detect Gb3 deposits in blood vessels, arrector pili muscles, and sweat glands.

Amyloidosis is characterized by prominent peripheral nervous system involvement, especially of the autonomic component, and skin biopsy can disclose small-fiber pathology as well as amyloid deposits via Congo red staining and electron microscopy.

Analysis of cutaneous autonomic innervation distinguished Multiple System Atrophy (MSA) from Pure Autonomic Failure (PAF) with comparable disease duration: MSA patients showed preserved autonomic innervation, whereas PAF patients showed impaired dermal annex innervation and depleted adrenergic fibers near arteriovenous anastomoses.
In PAF, DLB, and PD, cutaneous p-syn load was proportional to the severity of autonomic symptoms, with DLB showing an intermediate degree of autonomic involvement.

In hereditary sensory and autonomic neuropathy type 1 (HSAN1), skin biopsy demonstrated complete loss of small nerve fibers at the distal leg site, supporting its use as a repeatable disease biomarker.
Guillain-Barré syndrome (AIDP) characteristically affects autonomic small nerve fibers, which can lead to life-threatening complications such as arrhythmias and blood pressure dysregulation.
In the arms, both N1 and P1 latencies of pain-related evoked potentials were significantly longer in ATTRv-PN patients than in healthy controls.
In the legs, P1 latency was significantly longer in ATTRv-PN patients compared to healthy controls.
In the legs, P1 latency was also significantly longer in presymptomatic TTR mutation carriers compared to healthy controls, suggesting subclinical small fiber involvement prior to symptom onset.
Peak-to-peak amplitude of pain-related evoked potentials was reduced in ATTRv-PN patients compared to healthy controls.
Peak-to-peak amplitude of pain-related evoked potentials was also reduced in presymptomatic TTR mutation carriers compared to healthy controls.
Small fiber neuropathy, as diagnosed by skin biopsy, was present in the large majority of patients with type 1 diabetes, especially those with painful diabetic neuropathy.

Multiple quantitative sensory testing parameters (Cold Detection Threshold, Warm Detection Threshold, Cold Pain Threshold, Heat Pain Threshold, Thermal Sensory Limen, Mechanical Detection Threshold, Mechanical Pain Threshold, and Vibration Detection Threshold) were associated with skin-biopsy-confirmed diagnosis of small fiber neuropathy.
A predictive model combining z-scores of CDT, WDT, CPT, HPT, TSL and MPT showed good diagnostic accuracy for identifying small fiber neuropathy relative to skin biopsy.
After chronic and acute stress modeling, IBS model rats showed significantly lower visceral pain thresholds than control rats, confirming successful model establishment.
Both Biao-Ben (BB) and conventional (CG) acupoint combinations significantly increased visceral pain thresholds compared with untreated IBS rats, indicating improved visceral hypersensitivity.
IBS model rats showed a significant difference in HRV high-frequency power compared to healthy controls, consistent with autonomic imbalance (parasympathetic reduction).
The Biao-Ben acupoint combination significantly altered multiple HRV parameters (SDNN, RMSSD, RR Mean, TP, VLF, LF, HF, LF/HF) compared to untreated IBS rats, indicating restored autonomic balance.
The conventional acupoint combination (CG) significantly improved TP, VLF, and HF values compared to untreated IBS rats, but affected fewer HRV parameters than the Biao-Ben combination.
No significant differences were found between the BB and CG groups across all measured HRV parameters, suggesting similar overall efficacy on HRV between the two acupoint protocols.
IBS model rats had significantly increased ANP levels in both serum and cardiac tissue compared to control rats.
IBS model rats had significantly increased BNP levels in both serum and cardiac tissue compared to control rats.
The Biao-Ben acupoint combination significantly reduced serum ANP and BNP levels compared to untreated IBS rats, while the conventional protocol only significantly reduced BNP.

In cardiac tissue, the BB group showed non-significant reductions in ANP and BNP versus the IBS group, whereas the CG group showed non-significant increases; the difference between BB and CG cardiac tissue levels was statistically significant.
Cardiac metabolomics identified 249 differential metabolites (103 down-regulated, 146 up-regulated) between IBS model rats and healthy controls.
Cardiac metabolomics identified 122 differential metabolites (88 down-regulated, 34 up-regulated) between the Biao-Ben treated group and untreated IBS rats.
Cardiac metabolomics identified 160 differential metabolites (94 down-regulated, 66 up-regulated) between the conventional acupoint group and untreated IBS rats.

Cardiac metabolomics identified 119 differential metabolites (40 down-regulated, 79 up-regulated) between the Biao-Ben and conventional acupoint groups, indicating distinct metabolic effects of the two protocols.

KEGG pathway enrichment of cardiac metabolomics found 4 significantly altered pathways in IBS vs control rats: steroid hormone biosynthesis, African trypanosomiasis, starch and sucrose metabolism, and the 5-hydroxytryptamine (serotonin) metabolic pathway.

KEGG pathway enrichment showed 7 significantly altered pathways with Biao-Ben treatment vs untreated IBS: purine metabolism, olfactory transduction, phototransduction, cGMP-PKG signaling, African trypanosomiasis, FoxO signaling, and morphine addiction pathway.

KEGG pathway enrichment showed 5 significantly altered pathways with conventional acupoint treatment vs untreated IBS: arachidonic acid metabolism, bile secretion, 5-hydroxytryptamine metabolism, inflammatory mediator regulation of TRP channels, and linoleic acid metabolism.

KEGG pathway comparison between Biao-Ben and conventional groups showed 6 significantly differing pathways: arachidonic acid metabolism, African trypanosomiasis, renin secretion, inflammatory mediator regulation of TRP channels, FoxO signaling, and platelet activation.
In the IBS model, cardiac ADP concentration increased while ATP and AMP remained stable, indicating a high metabolic flux, energy-stressed cardiac state likely linked to sympathetic overactivation.
The Biao-Ben acupoint combination reduced cardiac ADP and AMP levels relative to untreated IBS rats, suggesting improved cardiac energy metabolism and reduced unnecessary cardiac energy load.

Cardiac kynurenine and kynurenic acid levels were significantly increased in the IBS model group compared with controls, while tryptophan and serotonin were unchanged, indicating specific activation of IDO1-driven kynurenine pathway metabolism in the heart.
The Biao-Ben acupoint combination was reported to decrease cardiac kynurenine pathway metabolites (KYN and KYNA), consistent with reduced systemic inflammation and IDO1 activity.
Patients with ME/CFS/FM showed significantly higher OPRM1 promoter methylation than healthy controls at two of three CpG sites and in mean methylation.
Age was weakly but significantly positively associated with OPRM1 promoter methylation across participants.
When the composite symptom factor was included in the model, the between-group difference in OPRM1 methylation remained stable, with patients showing higher methylation than controls.
The composite symptom factor (derived from PCA of clinical questionnaires) was not significantly associated with OPRM1 promoter methylation.
ME/CFS/FM patients showed significantly greater cold pain sensitivity than healthy controls.
ME/CFS/FM patients showed significantly greater heat pain sensitivity than healthy controls.
ME/CFS/FM patients showed significantly greater pressure pain sensitivity than healthy controls.
OPRM1 promoter methylation was not associated with thermal or mechanical pain thresholds.

Patients showed a significantly larger conditioned pain modulation (CPM) response to cold stimuli than healthy controls, a counterintuitive result relative to expected reduced descending pain inhibition in chronic pain conditions.
No significant between-group difference was found in conditioned pain modulation to heat stimuli.
When both CPM outcomes were added as covariates to the model, the between-group difference in OPRM1 methylation was no longer significant.
Global DNA methylation (5mC) and hydroxymethylation (5hmC) levels did not differ between ME/CFS/FM patients and healthy controls.
OPRM1 promoter methylation was strongly positively correlated with BDNF promoter I (3/4 amplicons) and exon III (2/2 amplicons) methylation at both study timepoints.
OPRM1 promoter methylation showed weak-to-moderate negative correlations with two of three S-COMT promoter amplicons and with COMT exon IV methylation, but only at the first timepoint.
Approximately 70% of ME/CFS patients also meet fibromyalgia diagnostic criteria, and this comorbidity is associated with greater symptom burden and disability than ME/CFS alone.

A previously cited PET study found that fibromyalgia patients exhibit decreased mu-opioid receptor availability in the nucleus accumbens and amygdala, associated with reduced pain-evoked brain activity.
Prior literature cited in this paper reports that fibromyalgia patients have paradoxically elevated levels of endogenous opioids in cerebrospinal fluid.
Prior literature cited notes that individuals with a history of heroin use on methadone maintenance, and prior opioid users, show increased OPRM1 promoter methylation in peripheral leukocytes.

In prior work from the same cohort, ME/CFS/FM patients showed higher methylation on the MB-COMT promoter and lower methylation on the BDNF exon IX coding region compared to healthy controls, with BDNF hypomethylation accompanied by higher serum BDNF concentrations.

In a tilt-table study of 429 ME/CFS patients, 90% had an abnormal cerebral blood flow reduction on extracranial Doppler, with a mean 26% reduction versus 7% in healthy controls, including patients with normal heart rate/blood pressure responses.
A sitting test was found to be an adequate alternative to tilt-table testing for diagnosing orthostatic intolerance in severely ill ME/CFS patients too unwell for standard tilt-table testing.
The illustrative case patient (Paula) had a 45% reduction in cerebral blood flow on tilt table testing, indicating very severe POTS.

Hornig et al. found distinct pro- and anti-inflammatory cytokine activation and disrupted intercytokine regulatory networks early in ME/CFS that were not present in longer-duration illness, with cytokine alterations correlating more with illness duration than severity.

Tomas et al. found that severely affected ME/CFS patients have both mitochondrial and glycolytic energy production impairments, whereas moderately affected patients show only mitochondrial impairment, potentially explaining differences in disease severity.
Charlton et al. reported that ME/CFS and long COVID patients have lower aerobic exercise capacity and mitochondrial respiration than healthy individuals, not explained by deconditioning.

Xiong et al. used AI-based multi-omics (metabolome, immune profile, microbiome) to distinguish ME/CFS from depression and fibromyalgia, finding microbial dysbiosis predominantly in short-duration illness and metabolic/clinical aberrations with resolved dysbiosis in long-duration illness.
A UK Biobank study found that levels of 511 blood-based biomarkers differed significantly between ME/CFS cases and controls, arguing against a purely psychosomatic interpretation of the disease.

Using invasive CPET, Jothi et al. found impaired skeletal muscle oxygen diffusion in both ME/CFS and long COVID patients compared to healthy controls, though the study was limited by small sample size.

A large iCPET study of 160 ME/CFS patients versus healthy controls identified two forms of peripheral neurovascular dysregulation contributing to exertional intolerance: depressed cardiac output from impaired venous return and impaired peripheral oxygen extraction.

Squires et al. found in a large iCPET study that ME/CFS and long COVID share reduced aerobic capacity at peak exercise driven by preload insufficiency and impaired systemic oxygen extraction, compatible with peripheral left-to-right shunting and/or limb skeletal muscle dysfunction.
A 2-day CPET study comparing mild, moderate, and severe ME/CFS patients found that the deterioration in peak workload from day 1 to day 2 was largest in the severe group.
A large study found that up to 85% of patients diagnosed with the Oxford criteria for ME/CFS are, in fact, healthy people, supporting the criteria's abandonment.

Jason et al. found high rates of healthy controls meeting ME/CFS diagnostic criteria without severity thresholds (Fukuda 33.7%, CCC 20.7%, ME-ICC 14.6%), which dropped dramatically when minimum symptom severity/frequency thresholds were added.

A study of 100 ME/CFS patients found 68% had vitamin D deficiency, 22% had insufficient levels, and only 10% had sufficient levels, likely underestimating deficiency since homebound/bedbound patients were excluded.

A large Dutch study testing whether ME/CFS patients with unhealthy lifestyles are more functionally impaired found instead that ME/CFS patients had a healthier lifestyle than the general Dutch population, refuting the hypothesis.

The PACE trial (using Oxford criteria) found that 46% of ME/CFS patients had a comorbid anxiety and/or depression diagnosis (14% anxiety alone, 14% depression alone, 18% both), with 54% having no mental health disorder.

A hand grip strength study by Neu et al. found significantly greater force decrease and fatigability during phasic trials in ME/CFS patients compared to healthy controls, despite the authors labeling ME/CFS a psychosomatic condition.
A study of 2138 ME/CFS participants found 25.7% were severely affected and 4.2% were bedridden, implying large numbers of homebound and bedbound patients nationally.

A small study comparing 20 severe ME/CFS patients to healthy controls found a physical functioning score of 13 versus 99 in controls (0-100 scale), while emotional well-being was comparatively less impacted, contradicting frequent misdiagnosis as depression.

A small non-randomized, uncontrolled study found an immediate improvement in muscle strength and orthostatic function after a 30 mg dose of the acetylcholinesterase inhibitor pyridostigmine, though causality could not be established.

A small study found that ME/CFS patients taking low-dose naltrexone (3.0-5.0 mg/day) had restored TRPM3-like ionic currents in natural killer cells compared to untreated state, supporting a potential immune-modulating mechanism for LDN.

Ruan et al. reported that low-dose rapamycin (6 mg/week) led to recovery in fatigue, PEM, and orthostatic intolerance in 74.3% of ME/CFS patients after 30 days, but the study had a high dropout rate and no control group.

A reanalysis of four IVIG trials found that treatment was either not effective at all or highly effective, particularly in severely affected ME/CFS patients, with predictors of response linked to abnormal cell-mediated immunity indicators.

In a NIH study of 17 ME/CFS patients, patients switched to anaerobic metabolism earlier than healthy controls, indicating less efficient oxidative respiration and supporting a physical rather than psychosomatic basis for the disease.

Exposing healthy human muscle cells to serum from ME/CFS patients caused muscle weakness and severe muscular/mitochondrial deterioration, with short exposure increasing glycolysis and reducing contractile strength, and prolonged exposure causing muscle fragility.

In a study of 1104 ME/CFS patients, severe cases had a much higher rate of family history of ME/CFS (37.9%) than mild cases (17.1%), with a strong association specifically to maternal (not paternal) ME/CFS, consistent with a maternally-inherited mitochondrial DNA contribution.
A Swiss survey found that 39.3% of ME/CFS respondents had experienced suicidal thoughts, most commonly attributed to being told their disease was psychosomatic, exhaustion, and feeling misunderstood.

Hornig et al. found distinct plasma immune/cytokine signatures in early-stage ME/CFS compared with healthy controls, with activation of both pro- and anti-inflammatory cytokines and disrupted intercytokine regulatory networks that were not present in patients with longer illness duration.

Tomas et al. found that severely affected ME/CFS patients have both mitochondrial and glycolytic impairments, whereas moderately affected patients show only mitochondrial impairment, potentially explaining differences in severity.

Charlton et al. found that ME/CFS and long COVID patients exhibit lower aerobic exercise capacity and mitochondrial respiration than healthy individuals, which could not be explained by deconditioning.

Xiong et al.'s multi-omics AI analysis of metabolome, immune profile, and microbiome distinguished ME/CFS from depression and fibromyalgia, showing significant microbial dysbiosis in short-duration illness versus resolved dysbiosis but metabolic/clinical aberrations in long-duration illness.
Invasive CPET by Jothi et al. found impaired skeletal muscle oxygen diffusion in ME/CFS and long COVID patients compared to healthy controls, though the study was limited by small sample size.

Joseph et al. used invasive CPET in 160 ME/CFS patients versus healthy controls and identified two forms of peripheral neurovascular dysregulation contributing to exertional intolerance: depressed cardiac output from impaired venous return, and impaired peripheral oxygen extraction.

Squires et al.'s large iCPET study comparing ME/CFS, long COVID, and controls found both patient groups share symptomatic, reduced aerobic capacity at peak exercise driven by preload insufficiency and impaired systemic oxygen extraction.

In 429 ME/CFS patients undergoing tilt table testing, 86% reported orthostatic intolerance symptoms and 90% showed abnormal cerebral blood flow reduction, with a mean CBF reduction of 26% versus 7% in healthy controls, present even in patients with normal heart rate/blood pressure responses.

A study of 100 severely ill ME/CFS patients compared to healthy controls suggested that a sitting test is an adequate alternative to tilt table testing for diagnosing orthostatic intolerance in patients too ill for standard testing.
A UK Biobank study by Beentjes et al. of 1455 ME/CFS cases and 131,303 controls found that levels of 511 blood-based biomarkers differed significantly between people with and without ME/CFS.

A study of 100 ME/CFS patients found 68% had vitamin D deficiency, 22% insufficient levels, and only 10% sufficient levels, likely underestimating deficiency since homebound/bedbound patients were excluded.

A large Dutch study (n=247) found ME/CFS patients had a healthier lifestyle than the general Dutch population (fewer overweight, fewer smokers, more alcohol abstainers), refuting the hypothesis that unhealthy lifestyle drives greater functional impairment.
The PACE trial (n=641), using Oxford criteria, found 14% of ME/CFS patients had comorbid anxiety, 14% had comorbid depression, and 18% had both, with 54% having no mental health disorder.

Neu et al.'s hand grip strength testing found a significant difference in force decrease and fatigability during phasic trials between ME/CFS patients and healthy controls, contradicting their own framing of CFS as a psychosomatic condition.

A small non-randomized study without a control group (n=20) using handgrip strength testing showed an immediate effect on muscle strength and orthostatic function after administering 30 mg of the acetylcholinesterase inhibitor pyridostigmine, though causality cannot be established from the design.

Case series by Bolton et al. described three ME/CFS patients on low-dose naltrexone (4-12 mg) with varying benefit from partial symptom reduction to life-changing improvement, with initial fatigue/headache side effects reported.

A small study of nine ME/CFS patients and nine healthy controls found that low-dose naltrexone (3.0-5.0 mg/day) restored TRPM3-like ionic currents in NK cells, supporting its potential as a treatment.

Ruan et al. reported that low-dose rapamycin (6 mg/week) led to recovery in fatigue, PEM, and orthostatic intolerance in 74.3% of patients at 30 days, with high dropout undermining tolerability conclusions.

A reanalysis by Brownlie et al. of four prior IVIG trials found the treatment was either not effective at all or highly effective, especially in severely affected patients, with several adolescent cases achieving complete recovery over two years.
A retrospective matched case-control study of 10 long COVID patients treated with IgG confirmed a benefit similar to that seen in severely affected ME/CFS patients.
A survey by de Becker et al. (n=2703) found 93% of ME/CFS patients had attention deficits, 85% memory disturbances, 75% difficulty finding words, and 71% speech difficulties.

A British ME Association survey (n=450) found 88% of respondents with ME/CFS suffer from brain fog or cognitive difficulties; a separate survey (n=785) found cognitive dysfunction varies in 61% and is constant in 38%, being very disabling in 16% of all respondents.

Constant et al. found objective impairment in attention and memory in ME/CFS, but unlike major depressive disorder where cognitive impairment strongly correlates with depression and fatigue, ME/CFS showed only weak correlation with depression and none with fatigue.
Freitag et al. reported that autoantibodies against G-protein-coupled receptors correlate with symptom severity, autonomic dysfunction, and disability in ME/CFS.

Mughal et al. exposed 3D in vitro skeletal muscle tissue from healthy people to serum from ME/CFS patients: short exposure (48h) increased glycolysis and reduced contractile strength, while prolonged exposure (96-144h) caused severe muscular and mitochondrial deterioration, fragility, and weakness.

A NIH study by Walitt et al. (n=17 ME/CFS vs healthy controls) concluded post-infectious ME/CFS is defined by altered effort preference leading to activity avoidance and deconditioning, but the authors argue this single-day CPET design cannot distinguish true pathophysiology from deconditioning and mischaracterizes PEM as mere discomfort avoidance.

Pheby et al.'s study of 1104 patients found 37.9% of severe ME/CFS cases reported a family history of ME/CFS versus 17.1% of mild cases, with a strong association specifically to maternal (but not paternal) history, consistent with a mitochondrial DNA-linked mechanism.

A Swiss survey found 39.3% of ME/CFS respondents had suicidal thoughts at some stage, driven primarily by being told the disease was psychosomatic (89.5%), being at the end of one's strength (80.7%), and not feeling understood (80.7%).
Only about 5% of ME/CFS patients recover spontaneously overall, and among the very or extremely severely ill, spontaneous recovery occurs in only 0.2% of cases.
Daily step count was not significantly associated with average daily heart rate or percentage of time spent in tachycardia, before or after adjusting for age, sex, and ME/CFS symptoms.
Higher physical activity intensity levels measured by accelerometer counts per minute were associated with increased average heart rate.

Participants spent a significantly lower percentage of time in tachycardia during moderate-to-vigorous physical activity than during sedentary periods, even after adjusting for age, sex, and ME/CFS symptoms.
Individuals with PCC who had ME/CFS symptoms covered 27% less distance on the 6-minute walk test than those without ME/CFS symptoms.
Individuals with PCC who had ME/CFS symptoms completed 19% fewer repetitions on the 1-minute sit-to-stand test than those without ME/CFS symptoms.
Individuals with ME/CFS symptoms reported greater difficulties in the EuroQoL-5D-5L domains of mobility, self-care, usual activities, and pain/discomfort than those without ME/CFS symptoms.
The PCC cohort demonstrated low overall physical activity, averaging 3,503 ± 1,445 steps per day, classifying them as sedentary.
The majority of participants (81.3%) self-reported themselves as physically inactive.

The authors propose that elevated resting heart rate/tachycardia in PCC may stem from autonomic dysfunction involving downregulation of the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system, hyperadrenergic activity, and direct viral infection of the brainstem.
The overall PCC cohort performed below age- and sex-predicted normative values on both the 6-minute walk test and 1-minute sit-to-stand test.
Pacing was used far more frequently by ME/CFS participants than by those with depression, with the largest effect size in the intervention-use MANOVA.
ME/CFS participants rated pacing as substantially more helpful than participants with depression, showing the largest effect in the helpfulness MANOVA.
Dietary supplement use was significantly higher among ME/CFS participants than those with depression.
Psychotherapy use and perceived helpfulness were significantly higher among participants with depression than ME/CFS.
Antidepressant use and perceived helpfulness were markedly higher in the depression group than the ME/CFS group.
Opioid antagonists (including low-dose naltrexone) were used and perceived as helpful far more often by ME/CFS participants than by those with depression.
Sleep medication use did not significantly differ between ME/CFS and depression groups, unlike most other medications.
Exercise therapy was rated helpful much more often by depression participants than by ME/CFS participants, contrasting with graded exercise therapy's contraindicated status in ME/CFS.
Coenzyme Q10 supplement use and perceived helpfulness were markedly higher in ME/CFS participants than depression participants, showing the largest DS-helpfulness group effect.
NADH supplement use and perceived helpfulness were markedly higher among ME/CFS participants compared to those with depression.
Quercetin use and helpfulness were substantially higher in ME/CFS than depression participants, showing the second-largest DS-helpfulness effect size.
Despite being the most commonly used supplement in both groups, perceived helpfulness of vitamin D did not significantly differ between ME/CFS and depression after covariate adjustment.

Self-initiated (non-medically-recommended) dietary supplement use was associated with higher perceived helpfulness ratings for several supplements, including magnesium, arginine, omega-3, ashwagandha, and vitamin E.
Younger age was significantly associated with higher perceived helpfulness ratings and use of several supplements (e.g., melatonin, iron, glutathione, quercetin, greens powder, vitamin D).

Among supplements specifically marketed for fatigue reduction, ginseng/rhodiola multi-ingredient formulations and Q10-based products showed the highest (though still low) use and helpfulness, both greater in ME/CFS than depression.

Open-text responses showed ME/CFS participants frequently mentioned low-dose naltrexone, aripiprazole, and pyridostigmine as used medications, while depression participants mentioned various antidepressants (sertraline, duloxetine, mirtazapine).
Cortisone use and perceived helpfulness were higher among ME/CFS participants than those with depression.

Despite widespread intervention use, perceived helpfulness ratings for most interventions remained generally modest in both ME/CFS and depression groups, indicating persistent therapeutic uncertainty.
Duration of fatigue symptoms was longer on average in the ME/CFS group than in the depression group.
The ME/CFS sample had a higher proportion of women than the depression sample, consistent with known sex differences in ME/CFS prevalence.
Babesia species DNA was detected in blood or enrichment blood cultures from 12 of 50 individuals with chronic fatigue and neurological symptoms.
Bartonella species DNA was detected in blood or enrichment blood cultures from 13 of 50 individuals with chronic fatigue and neurological symptoms.
Two of 50 participants tested positive for both Babesia and Bartonella species DNA, indicating co-infection.

Myoblasts cultured with ME patient sera did not show a significantly different oxygen consumption rate at maximal respiratory capacity compared to those cultured with healthy control sera, failing to replicate the Fluge et al. 2016 finding.
ECAR at maximal respiratory capacity did not differ significantly between myoblasts treated with ME sera versus healthy control sera.
ME serum exposure did not affect OCR under basal (amino acids), basal plus glucose, or proton leak conditions.
ME serum exposure did not affect ECAR under basal (amino acids), basal plus glucose, or proton leak conditions.
Stratifying ME cases by disease severity showed no severity-dependent effect on myoblast maximal respiratory capacity.
BMI did not correlate significantly with myoblast OCR at maximal respiratory capacity, and adding BMI to the primary model did not change the null result.
Age did not correlate with myoblast OCR at maximal respiratory capacity.
Sample storage/collection batch had no significant effect on OCR at maximal respiratory capacity despite greater dispersion of values in batch 2.
Sample batch had no significant effect on ECAR at maximal respiratory capacity.
Average myoblast cell counts did not differ significantly between wells treated with ME sera versus healthy control sera across all plates.
BMI was slightly but statistically significantly higher in the ME cohort compared to healthy controls.
A prior DecodeME genome-wide association study identified FBXL4, a gene involved in mitophagy and mitochondrial DNA depletion, as a candidate gene associated with ME.

A cited cell-free RNA plasma profiling study identified 743 unique features differing between ME cases and controls, related to platelets, plasmacytoid dendritic cells, monocytes, T cells, and dysregulated mitochondrial RNA expression.
Technical plate-to-plate variation explained 42% of total variance in OCR measurements while well position explained only 4%, with technical repeatability between replicates estimated at 0.56.
16.5% of the entire post-COVID referral cohort met 2015 CDC ME/CFS criteria, representing about 21% of those presenting with fatigue.
Fatigue Severity Scale scores were high across the cohort, with 67% scoring >4.5 and 29% scoring >6, and scores increased incrementally with additional ME/CFS criteria met.
About a third of the cohort (32%) had MOCA scores indicating mild cognitive impairment or worse, but scores did not differ significantly across the No Fatigue, Fatigue, and ME/CFS categories.
Depression scores (PHQ-9) were elevated in the cohort overall, averaging 11.5 with 30% scoring in the moderate-or-higher range.
Anxiety scores (GAD-7) were high overall (41% >10, 29% >12) but did not differ significantly across fatigue categories.
Physical functioning (ECOG) was restricted in a third of patients (33% >2), with the degree of impairment correlating incrementally with meeting more ME/CFS criteria, though no patient was bed-bound.
Memory disturbance was the only minor ME/CFS criterion that showed a stepwise change across the No Fatigue, Fatigue, and ME/CFS categories, being reported least often in the ME/CFS group.
New-onset migraine, though uncommon overall (3%), was absent in patients without fatigue and enriched in the fatigue/ME-CFS groups.
Worsened headache was present in 36% of the cohort and overrepresented in those with ME/CFS and Fatigue compared to No Fatigue.
A pre-existing history of sleep apnea/sleep disordered breathing was initially associated with fatigue, but this association was no longer significant after adjusting for covariates.
A history of Type 2 diabetes (13% of cohort) was overrepresented in the Fatigue categories compared to No Fatigue.
Pre-existing psychiatric history was a significant predisposing factor for meeting ME/CFS criteria.
A history of Generalized Anxiety Disorder (GAD) was significantly associated with meeting ME/CFS criteria.
A history of Major Depressive Disorder (MDD) was significantly associated with meeting ME/CFS criteria.
A history of depression alone (as opposed to anxiety/psychiatric management broadly) was not clearly enriched in post-COVID fatigue relative to anxiety, per the discussion summary.
Brain fog was reported by 51.9% of the entire cohort, including 27% of those without fatigue as a primary complaint, and was not associated with any demographic feature.
Brain fog was reported more often in patients with headache (43% vs 29%) and with rash (12% vs 2%), and was associated with higher FSS and PHQ-9 scores.
In patients who completed home sleep testing, apnea-hypopnea index (AHI) severity categories (5-15, 15-30, >30) did not differ significantly among No Fatigue, Fatigue, and ME/CFS groups.

Among symptoms reported by more than 20% of the cohort, dyspnea, myalgia, new psychiatric issues, and GI distress differed between those with and without fatigue as a primary complaint, while dyspnea itself was not specifically linked to fatigue status.

The authors interpret post-COVID chronic brain dysfunction as consistent with an inflammatory mechanism triggered by acute illness, with persistence documented in plasma samples of long COVID patients in prior literature.

Peripheral blood mononuclear cells from patients with chronic fatigue syndrome and documented humidifier disinfectant exposure (HD-CFS) showed significantly more mitochondrial abnormalities than controls.
Intratracheal administration of PHMG-p, a major humidifier disinfectant component, caused mitochondrial abnormalities in mice, mirroring findings in HD-CFS patient PBMCs.
PHMG-p exposure decreased expression of oxidative phosphorylation (OXPHOS) complex proteins in mice.
PHMG-p exposure downregulated expression of genes related to mitochondrial membrane potential in mice.
PHMG-p exposed mice exhibited glymphatic dysfunction on neurological assessment.
PHMG-p exposed mice showed blood-brain barrier (BBB) disruption on neurological assessment.
PHMG-p exposed mice showed reduced oxidative phosphorylation complex expression specifically in the hypothalamus.
PHMG-p exposed mice exhibited glymphatic system dysfunction in the brain.
PHMG-p exposure caused disruption of blood-brain barrier integrity in mice.
The authors propose PHMG-p, a major component of humidifier disinfectants, as a candidate environmental trigger contributing to CFS pathogenesis via mitochondrial and neurological dysfunction.
A meta-analysis found that 45.2% of COVID-19 patients had CFS-like symptoms at 4 weeks post-infection.
In a cohort of 140 COVID-19 patients, 43% met ME/CFS criteria, and this was more common among females with obesity and poor functional status.
Netherlands population survey of 94,516 participants found CFS prevalence of 1.3%, fibromyalgia 3.0%, and IBS 9.7%.
In a Norwegian cohort of 427 CFS patients and controls, SNPs in the TPPP gene region were associated with CFS but did not reach genome-wide significance.
Epstein-Barr virus infection is described as an important environmental trigger associated with development of CFS.
In a study of 166 CFS patients, 55 reported childhood trauma (mostly emotional neglect/abuse), and personality disorders in patients were significantly linked to childhood emotional trauma.
Retrospective analysis of 300 CFS patients found mannose-binding lectin (MBL) deficiency in 15% versus 6% of historical controls.
Metabolomic analysis of ME/CFS plasma across two cohorts found consistently reduced lipid fatty-acid sub-pathway metabolites (e.g., acylcholine), steroids, and dipeptides.
Sphingolipid levels were increased in ME/CFS patients in metabolomic plasma studies.

MRI of 25 CFS patients versus 25 controls showed increased T1-weighted signal intensity in ventrolateral thalamus, internal capsule, and prefrontal white matter with increasing CFS severity, plus T2 changes in right middle temporal white matter.

In 36 women with ME/CFS, resting-state fMRI showed reduced intrinsic connectivity within the left frontoparietal network and reduced connectivity between anterior cingulate-sensorimotor and posterior cingulate-salience networks.

Arterial spin labeling connectivity study found ME/CFS patients had comparable prefrontal/ACC/precuneus/angular gyrus connectivity to controls, but left parahippocampal gyrus connectivity correlated with overall clinical fatigue.
A GWAS chip analysis using >906,600 SNPs identified 442 candidate SNPs associated with ME/CFS, including missense variants and SNP clusters in the T-cell receptor locus.

23andMe-based analysis of 383 ME/CFS participants found SNPs related to immune, hormone, metabolic, and extracellular matrix pathways, with 517 SNPs among the top 10% most deleterious substitutions by CADD score.

Methylation analysis of PBMC DNA from 10 ME/CFS patients vs 10 matched controls found 76 differentially methylated fragments and 394 differentially methylated cytosines across 17 regulatory regions related to metabolism and immune activity.
A larger GWAS across Norwegian, Danish and UK Biobank ME/CFS cohorts (n=427, 460, 2105 respectively) found no genome-wide-significant risk loci, and the TPPP association was not replicated.

A UK Biobank ME/CFS analysis found 199 SNPs mapped to 14 genes across 15 clusters significantly associated with 91% of ME/CFS cases, implicating stress/infection susceptibility, mitochondrial dysfunction, sleep disorders, and autoimmune development, replicated in post-viral fatigue and fibromyalgia cohorts.
A Mendelian randomization study found the gut genera Paraprevotella and Ruminococcaceae_UCG_014 were positively associated with ME/CFS risk, suggesting a causal role for gut microbiota.
Utah Population Database analysis found significant genetic correlations for ME/CFS and related chronic diseases across first-, second-, and third-degree relatives.

In a study of 48 ME/CFS patients, no reproducible differences in NK cell number, cytotoxicity, or cytokine production were found versus controls, though one patient carried the PRF1 p.A91V variant with low perforin expression.

In 300 CFS patients, 25% had reduced levels of at least one antibody class/subclass (most commonly IgG3/IgG4 deficiency), while another 25% had increased immunoglobulin levels, especially IgM and IgG2 excess.
A meta-analysis of 42 studies found tumor necrosis factor, IL-2, IL-4, TGF-β, and CRP levels significantly elevated in CFS patients, though results were inconsistent across studies.

In 21 CFS patients versus 20 controls, dexamethasone inhibition of LPS-induced IL-6/TNF-α was more pronounced (increased glucocorticoid sensitivity), though cortisol response to the Trier Social Stress Test did not differ significantly between groups.

Adolescents with CFS had significantly higher plasma norepinephrine, epinephrine, and FT4, and lower urinary cortisol/creatinine ratio than healthy controls, with stronger multi-system network interconnection.

Metabolomic analysis of 200 ME/CFS patients versus 102 healthy individuals found reduced TCA-cycle-fueling amino acids (especially in women) and significantly increased 3-methylhistidine with increased protein catabolism in men.

PBMC analysis showed increased mRNA expression of PDH-inhibitory kinases 1, 2, and 4, sirtuin 4, and PPARδ, supporting impaired pyruvate dehydrogenase function consistent with insufficient ATP production and excess lactate during exercise.

Plasma metabolomics found 74 differentially accumulated metabolites in ME/CFS (35 significant after adjustment), involving taurine, glycerophosphate, primary bile acid, and purine/pyrimidine metabolism.
A retrospective analysis of 300 CFS patients found 25% had reduced serum levels of IgG3/IgG4 subclasses, while another 25% had increased IgM and IgG2 levels.
A meta-analysis of 42 studies found tumor necrosis factor, IL-2, IL-4, TGF-β, and CRP levels significantly elevated in CFS patients, though results were inconsistent across studies.

In a study of 21 CFS patients vs 20 healthy controls, CFS patients showed increased glucocorticoid sensitivity in vitro, with more pronounced dexamethasone inhibition of LPS-induced IL-6/TNF-α, but no significant cortisol difference after the Trier Social Stress Test.

Adolescents with CFS showed significantly higher plasma norepinephrine, epinephrine, and FT4, and lower urinary cortisol/creatinine ratio versus healthy controls, with stronger interconnection among immune, neuroendocrine, and metabolic indicators.

In 200 ME/CFS patients vs 102 healthy individuals, amino acids fueling the TCA cycle were reduced (especially in women), while 3-methylhistidine was significantly increased in men along with increased protein catabolism.

Analysis of PBMCs from ME/CFS patients showed increased mRNA expression of PDH-inhibitory kinases 1, 2, 4, sirtuin 4, and PPARδ, supporting impaired pyruvate dehydrogenase function consistent with insufficient ATP production and excess lactate during exercise.

Plasma metabolomics in ME/CFS patients found 74 differentially accumulated metabolites (35 significant after adjustment), involving taurine, glycerophosphate, primary bile acid, and purine/pyrimidine metabolism pathways, implicating lipid metabolism disorders in disease mechanism.

In CFS rat models, TCA cycle, alanine/aspartate/glutamate metabolism, and steroid hormone biosynthesis were significantly affected before and after exercise, with sphingolipid metabolism changed post-exercise, indicating exercise-linked metabolic abnormality.
In a study of 310 CFS patients treated with acupuncture combined with psychotherapy, the clinical survival rate was 88.7% and effective rate was 97.7%.
In an RCT, CFS patients receiving acupuncture aimed at modulating inflammatory pathways showed greater symptom improvement than controls, suggesting inflammatory regulation as a mechanism of action.
Acupuncture at specific acupoints is reported to regulate the autonomic nervous system and improve heart rate variability, alleviating fatigue symptoms via sympathetic/parasympathetic balance.

A multi-center RCT of 150 CFS patients found that the body acupuncture group's fatigue severity scale (FSS) score was significantly lower than controls after 5 weeks, with significant improvement also in Stress Reaction Inventory and Beck Depression Inventory scores.
A network meta-analysis of 51 RCTs found the total effective rate of acupuncture and moxibustion was higher than other treatment methods, with better performance on the FS-14 fatigue scale.
An RCT comparing moxibustion and acupuncture found the moxibustion group's total effective rate was 88.9% versus 72.2% for acupuncture, with greater improvement in the fatigue assessment index (FAI).

A systematic review/meta-analysis of 16 studies with 1346 total patients found acupuncture superior to sham acupuncture and traditional Chinese medicine in overall effective rate and significantly reduced fatigue severity.

In 40 chronic fatigue rats, combined Pishu-point acupuncture plus ginsenoside Rg3 significantly outperformed acupuncture alone, ginsenoside alone, or blank control in improving weight and correcting immune imbalance.
In a study of 72 CFS patients, electroacupuncture produced greater reductions in fatigue and more significant improvements in cerebral cortical function than routine needling.

In 60 CFS patients with spleen-kidney Yang deficiency, acupoint catgut embedding combined with ginger-partitioned moxibustion significantly improved clinical signs/symptoms and regulated T lymphocyte subset and NK cell activity.
In 60 CFS patients, combining Chaihu Longgu Muli Decoction with acupuncture at back-shu points produced better improvement in fatigue and anxiety scales than TCM decoction alone.

Acupuncture treatment is generally safe but can cause local pain, bleeding, infection, or (with moxibustion) skin burns/allergy; a related study of acupuncture for dry eye reported five patients with mild adverse events.

Cited systematic reviews and network meta-analyses generally rated the certainty of evidence for acupuncture/moxibustion in CFS as low to very low, due to unclear randomization/allocation concealment, insufficient protocol/outcome reporting, and potential publication bias.
Loneliness was the most robust and consistent predictor of poorer physical, mental, and social wellbeing outcomes among individuals with hEDS.
Perceived support from friends predicted some wellbeing indicators in individuals with hEDS.
Perceived family support had minimal predictive value for wellbeing outcomes in individuals with hEDS.
Dog guardianship had minimal predictive value for physical, mental, and social wellbeing outcomes in individuals with hEDS.

58.6% of EDS/G-HSD patients reported a lifetime diagnosis of at least one mental health disorder, substantially higher than the roughly one-third lifetime prevalence reported in the general German population.
60.2% of participants met the PHQ-9 cut-off (≥10) for probable moderate-to-severe depression, with a mean score of 11.0, exceeding general German population point-prevalence estimates of 8.1-11.6%.
45.4% of participants scored above the DASS anxiety threshold, substantially higher than the 15.3% anxiety prevalence reported in the German DEGS1 general-population study.
28.9% of participants scored above the DASS depression threshold, with a mean score of 6.7.
41.1% of participants reached the DASS stress threshold, with a mean score of 8.4.

Depression was the most commonly self-reported lifetime mental health diagnosis, affecting 30.3% of participants, though this is notably lower than the 60.2% probable depression rate found by screening, suggesting underdiagnosis.
PTSD was the second most common self-reported lifetime mental health diagnosis, affecting 21.2% of the EDS/G-HSD cohort, higher than most previously reported rates.
13.1% of participants reported a lifetime clinician diagnosis of an anxiety disorder, far lower than the 45.4% identified by DASS screening, suggesting substantial underdiagnosis.

Eating disorders (bulimia nervosa or binge eating disorder) were identified in 5.2% of respondents by PHQ-D screening, and 8.1% reported a lifetime eating disorder diagnosis, both markedly higher than the 0.9% 12-month prevalence in the general German population.
Alcohol abuse prevalence in the cohort (2.1%) was comparable to that of the general German population.

68.7% of participants had received psychotherapy during their lifetime, with a mean duration of 5.8 years and 41.4% attending more than 50 sessions; cognitive behavioral therapy was the most common modality (53.5%).
All respondents rated psychotherapy as at least 'slightly helpful', with over 40% rating it 'helpful' or 'very helpful'.
30.2% of patients reported lifetime use of antidepressant medication (21.9% currently), with tricyclic antidepressants (17.7%) most commonly used, likely for their additional pain-modulating effect.
Among the 59 participants with a PHQ-9 score ≥10 (probable depression), only 35.6% reported currently receiving antidepressant treatment, indicating pharmacological undertreatment of depression.

No statistically significant differences in PHQ-9, DASS, or PHQ-D scores, or in self-reported mental health disorders and treatments, were found between the monogenetic EDS (cEDS/clEDS) subgroup and the hEDS/G-HSD subgroup.
85.7% of participants graded their mental health burden attributable to EDS/G-HSD as moderate (39.8%) or severe (45.9%).
Patients in this cohort experienced a mean diagnostic delay of 23 years, considerably longer than the 10.4 years reported in an international Ehlers-Danlos Society survey.

A prior clinical study cited by the authors found that patients with panic disorder and agoraphobia were 16 times more likely to have joint hypermobility syndrome than control patients with other mental or somatic illnesses.

A vision pose-tracking based system for calculating the Beighton score achieved 91.9% sensitivity and 92.3% negative predictive value for clinician-diagnosed generalized joint hypermobility while screening out 32.0% of referred individuals on the held-out test set.
On the training set, the vision-based Beighton system achieved a recall of 89.1% at a screen-out rate consistent with the test set, indicating the method generalizes across data splits.
The best-performing spine hypermobility detection algorithm achieved a recall of 85.0% and precision of 83.6% (F1=0.843) on the training set.
The best-performing thumb hypermobility detection algorithm achieved a recall of 97.0% and precision of 94.0% (F1=0.960) on the training set.

Empirically-derived video-based angle thresholds (rather than standard 10°/90° goniometric criteria) best distinguished hypermobile from non-hypermobile joints: >3° for knee hyperextension, >15° for elbow hyperextension, and >77.5° for fifth finger hyperextension.

The vision-based screening system substantially outperformed random participant removal, ranking above the 99.9th percentile for recall, precision, and specificity across 100,000 simulated random screen-out trials.

Varying the vision-based Beighton cut-off score changes the sensitivity/screen-out trade-off: a threshold of 3 yielded 97.3% recall but only 13.1% screen-out, while a threshold of 5 yielded 75.7% recall but 54.9% screen-out.

The current system has low specificity (42.4% on the test set), meaning about 58% of individuals who screen positive would not meet clinical criteria for GJH on formal assessment, reflecting a deliberate design trade-off prioritizing sensitivity for a triage tool.

Thumb hypermobility assessment from video frequently failed due to occlusion of the thumb by the participant's other hand or incorrect hand positioning/framing, requiring imputation of missing values.

Video-based joint angle measurements correlate only moderately to strongly (not perfectly/calibrated) with goniometric measurements from clinician physical exams, per the authors' prior work cited in this study.

A 25-year-old woman with hypermobile Ehlers-Danlos Syndrome and slipping rib syndrome experienced complete pain resolution and was able to taper off opioids after bilateral T7-T10 intercostal nerve radiofrequency ablation.

Slipping rib syndrome, a condition caused by hypermobility of costal cartilage leading to chronic thoracic wall pain, occurred as a comorbidity in a patient with hypermobile Ehlers-Danlos Syndrome who developed recurrent rib fractures.
Following the temporary benefit of RFA, the patient underwent bilateral rib fixation surgery and remained pain-free postoperatively.
The recurrently reported synonymous variant c.1095C>T in PLOD1 creates a new active splice site causing abnormal mRNA splicing and loss of gene function.
A novel frameshift variant, c.1262delC, in PLOD1 is predicted to cause a premature stop codon and loss of gene function, and was found in compound heterozygosity with c.1095C>T.

Real-time qPCR showed that PLOD1 mRNA expression in the patient's peripheral blood was significantly decreased compared to both parents and a healthy control, consistent with loss of function via nonsense-mediated decay.
A 15-year-old boy with kEDS-PLOD1 developed a superior mesenteric artery pseudoaneurysm from vessel rupture, related to collagen crosslinking damage characteristic of the disease.

Emergency hybrid surgery (laparotomy hemostasis with endovascular stent graft placement) temporarily stabilized the patient's superior mesenteric artery bleeding, but the patient died 10 days later from an abdominal aortic rupture.

LH1 (lysyl hydroxylase 1) enzymatic activity in fibroblasts is lower in kEDS-PLOD1 patients compared with healthy individuals, and animal studies show collagen fiber degeneration and smooth muscle abnormalities leading to aortic dissection.

kEDS-PLOD1 patients are reported to have increased risk of complications such as spontaneous aneurysm or rupture of medium-to-large arteries with increasing age, as well as non-vascular complications including recurrent pneumonia, heart failure, chronic respiratory failure, glaucoma, and retinal detachment.
hEDS prevalence is estimated at 1 in 500 to 1 in 5000 individuals, a much more frequent rate than previously believed due to increased awareness and improved diagnostics.
About 70% of diagnosed hEDS cases occur among women.

hEDS is a genetic hereditary connective tissue disorder associated with systemic complications including joint hypermobility, skin hyperextensibility, musculoskeletal pain, dislocations, scoliosis, vascular/cardiovascular anomalies, gastrointestinal and autoimmune conditions, respiratory issues, and autonomic dysfunction.
Common hEDS symptoms include chronic pain and fatigue, orthostatic intolerance (e.g., POTS), poor sleep quality, depression, anxiety, and headaches.
Chronic musculoskeletal pain, high risk of dislocations/injury, and POTS often lead to kinesiophobia (activity avoidance) in hEDS, resulting in deconditioning and worsened disability.

Nearly all study participants reported chronic musculoskeletal pain (hands, wrists, shoulders, knees, ankles, lower back/pelvic floor), poor proprioception, kinesiophobia, digestive issues, and depression.
Individual participants had additional comorbidities: Tricia had Atrial Fibrillation; Lara had Raynaud's Disease and dysautonomia; Janessa had eosinophilic esophagitis.
One participant (Emilia) had POTS with dizziness and instability that required her to perform the movement program mainly on the floor rather than standing.
Participation in the EDS-HEART performative/embodied movement program improved body awareness, balance, proprioception, sensations of fluidity, and excitement about physical activity.
The gentle, controlled EDS-HEART movement sequences helped participants more easily and quickly return to regular exercise after stopping due to sickness.
The holistic, embodied, performative program is reported as the first to show it can eliminate/decrease kinesiophobia (fear of movement) and its negative health consequences in people with hEDS.
Participants reported the program was safe and pleasant, with no injuries or symptom aggravation occurring during sessions, unlike typical exercise experiences for people with hEDS.
Incorporating breathing techniques into the movement program raised participants' awareness of habitual breath-holding during exercise and produced sensations of fluidity.
Exercising within a supportive community of other hEDS patients reduced social comparison and kinesiophobia, and increased feelings of belonging and motivation.
One previously less-active participant (Lara) increased her exercise levels as a result of the performative and holistic elements of the EDS-HEART program.

Program attendance varied across the seven weekly sessions: one participant attended all seven, two missed only the final session, one missed two sessions, and two others attended only two or three sessions due to medical/family reasons.
The performative/imaginative elements of the program provided a mental 'reprieve' from pain and pain-related anxiety during sessions.
The patient presented with a 10-year history of progressive, painless loosening and wrinkling of the skin of the face, neck, and upper back with no systemic symptoms.
Skin biopsy histopathology showed marked reduction and fragmentation of elastic fibers within the dermis, producing a loose, redundant connective tissue appearance.
Verhoeff-Van Gieson (VVG) special staining showed near-complete absence of elastic fibers in the sampled dermis, confirming the diagnosis of cutis laxa.

Despite clinical elastic fiber loss, some acquired cutis laxa cases paradoxically show increased elastin gene expression at the molecular level, but these fibers fail to assemble properly into functional elastic fibers.

Ehlers-Danlos syndrome was excluded as a differential diagnosis because EDS is characterized by hyperextensible skin, joint hypermobility, and vascular fragility, whereas this patient's acquired cutis laxa showed loose skin with decreased recoil and no vascular fragility.
Pseudoxanthoma elasticum (PXE) was excluded because it typically presents with yellow papules and calcified elastic fibers, neither of which were present clinically or histologically in this patient.

Surgical reconstruction (excision, rhytidectomy, blepharoplasty, or flap reconstruction) has provided the most consistent cosmetic benefit for cutis laxa across reported cases, though recurrence requiring revision surgery has been noted in some patients.
Medical therapies including vitamin E supplementation and topical emollients have shown minimal or no sustained benefit in reported cases of acquired cutis laxa.
Botulinum toxin has been proposed as a less invasive treatment approach for cutis laxa, but supporting evidence remains limited and long-term outcomes are unclear.
Mean age at genetic diagnosis of VEDS did not differ significantly between male and female patients.

Male VEDS patients showed a non-significant trend toward increased aortic-related mortality compared to female patients.
