The patient scored 7/9 on the Beighton hypermobility scale, three points above her age-specific threshold, indicating generalized joint hypermobility.
The patient was found to have aortic root dilation of 3.8 cm on transesophageal echocardiography, a cardiovascular finding consistent with connective tissue involvement.
Cardiac rhythm monitoring revealed atrial fibrillation in this patient with the ATR variant and Marfanoid phenotype.

Electromyography/nerve conduction studies demonstrated widespread sensory peripheral neuropathy in the bilateral upper and lower extremities, correlating with the patient's dysesthesia and decreased sensation.
Incidental protein electrophoresis revealed a small M spike leading to a diagnosis of monoclonal gammopathy of undetermined significance in this patient.

The patient experienced a six-year delay before whole exome sequencing identified the causative ATR variant, despite repeated presentations to emergency, urgent care, and primary care settings without diagnosis.
The patient repeatedly presented with generalized abdominal pain, migratory arthralgias of small, medium, and large joints, easy bruising, and poor wound healing over four years without diagnosis.
The patient later developed tension headaches, migraine with aura, and unintentional weight loss of 43 pounds over nine months during follow-up.
The patient's adult medical history included Raynaud phenomenon alongside palpitations, malignant melanoma, and insomnia.

Patients with syndromic genetic aortopathy undergoing TEVAR had similar odds of 30-day mortality and major postoperative complications (stroke, spinal cord ischemia, MI, CHF, respiratory complications) compared to those without SGA, after adjusting for confounders.
Three-year survival after TEVAR was not significantly different between patients with SGA and those without (73.7% vs. 63.1%, log-rank P = 0.11).

After adjusting for confounders using Cox proportional hazards models, there were no significant differences between SGA and non-SGA patients in 3-year overall mortality, reinterventions, or aortic rupture rates.
There were no significant differences between SGA and non-SGA groups in overall mortality and reinterventions within the first year of follow-up after TEVAR.

Typically developing children scored significantly higher than both mild-to-moderate and severe ASD groups across all MABC-2 domains (manual dexterity, aiming and catching, balance).

A fetus with lethal osteogenesis imperfecta type II carried a heterozygous in-frame deletion of COL1A2 exons 4-17.

Breakpoint analysis of the maternal exon 12-17 deletion revealed a complex rearrangement involving insertion of an inverted duplicated segment of exon 3 and intron 3 at the deletion junction, suggesting genomic instability.

Despite carrying two distinct COL1A2 in-frame deletions, the mother displayed only joint hypermobility and a family history of osteoporosis, without overt features of osteogenesis imperfecta, illustrating variable expressivity.
The authors conclude that N-terminal in-frame COL1A2 deletions show variable expressivity ranging from mild connective tissue features to perinatal lethality.

Hypermobility spectrum disorders were identified as the second most common hereditary bleeding disorder underlying heavy menstrual bleeding, affecting 6 of the 31 HBD patients.
Medical treatment for HMB significantly reduced menstrual blood loss as measured by PBAC score at 6 months.
Physical health-related quality of life (SF-12 PCS) significantly improved after 6 months of HMB treatment.
Mental health-related quality of life (SF-12 MCS) significantly improved after 6 months of HMB treatment.
Anxiety and depression scores on the EQ-5D-3L significantly improved after 6 months of HMB treatment.
Overall EQ-5D utility index improved significantly after 6 months of HMB treatment.
Menstrual Bleeding Questionnaire (MBQ) scores decreased significantly after 6 months of treatment, indicating reduced impact of HMB on HRQoL.
SAMANTA questionnaire scores decreased significantly after 6 months of treatment, indicating reduced HMB severity/impact.

Women with a hereditary bleeding disorder had significantly greater residual bleeding burden (higher PBAC and MBQ scores) at 6 months than non-HBD women.
SAMANTA scores were numerically higher in the HBD group at 6 months but did not reach statistical significance after adjustment.
The authors propose that in hypermobility spectrum disorders, unaddressed musculoskeletal symptoms such as joint pain and fatigue may limit HRQoL improvement after HMB treatment.
The authors propose that in platelet dysfunction, hormonal therapy fails to correct the underlying hemostatic defect, resulting in persistent bleeding despite treatment.
Prior literature cited indicates hemostatic disorders may be present in 5-36% of women with heavy menstrual bleeding.

Genotyping of 854 IBD biobank DNA samples found that 4.2% carried hereditary α-tryptasemia (HαT).

Among IBD subtypes with known classification, HαT was roughly twice as frequent in ulcerative colitis (13/196) as in Crohn's disease (8/237), though neither showed true enrichment above population baseline.
Spatial transcriptomics of descending colon biopsies showed higher numbers of mast cells in HαT samples compared with non-HαT IBD samples.
MRGPRX2 expression was notably higher specifically within mast cells of HαT colon samples, indicating increased transcription rather than simply more mast cells.
MRGPRX2 transcripts were detected outside of mast cell clusters, suggesting other intestinal mucosal cell types may also express MRGPRX2.
ddPCR validation on matched descending colon samples confirmed significantly elevated MRGPRX2 mRNA in HαT compared with non-HαT IBD tissue.
Pseudobulk differential expression analysis of spatial transcriptomics data showed globally increased MRGPRX2 expression in HαT samples regardless of cell source.

In CyTOF analysis of small intestinal biopsies, MRGPRX2+ mast cells showed higher expression of activation markers CD63, CD203c, LAMP1, and SIGLEC8 than MRGPRX2− mast cells, across both HαT and non-HαT groups.
When examining the overall mast cell compartment independent of MRGPRX2 status, no significant differences in CD63, CD203c, or LAMP1 expression were observed between HαT and non-HαT participants.

Kounis syndrome pathophysiology involves IgE-mediated or alternative mast cell activation releasing histamine, platelet-activating factor, proteases, and leukotrienes that induce coronary spasm, destabilize plaque, and promote thrombosis.

Kounis syndrome type III, defined by coronary thrombosis with eosinophil and mast cell infiltration (including peri-stent tissue in prior stent recipients), is rare, comprising only 5.1%-8.9% of reported KS cases.

In a 69-year-old female with prior metal allergy, KS type III was confirmed via eosinophil infiltration in aspirated thrombus and strongly positive patch tests for nickel and cobalt (core stent components), after excluding malapposition, thrombophilia, and heparin-induced thrombocytopenia.
Genetic testing in the same patient identified an intermediate metabolizer status for clopidogrel (CYP2C19 *1/*3 genotype), prompting a switch to prasugrel.

An 85-year-old male developed recurrent stent thrombosis, coronary aneurysm formation, generalized rash, and marked eosinophilia (2500/µL), with skin patch testing later revealing hypersensitivity to nickel, manganese, titanium, vanadium, and zinc used in the implanted stents.

A 52-year-old male with recurrent in-stent restenosis showed strong vanadium hypersensitivity on patch and lymphocyte transformation testing; trace vanadium (0.1%) was subsequently confirmed in the stent alloy despite not being a listed component.

A 65-year-old female developed very late stent thrombosis 36 months after sirolimus-eluting stent implantation, with histologically confirmed eosinophil/neutrophil infiltration and subsequent coronary aneurysm formation at both stent edges.

A 67-year-old male developed generalized urticaria followed by acute chest pain and stent thrombosis 14 years after sirolimus-eluting stent implantation, representing the longest documented latency for KS post-implantation, with alternative causes systematically excluded.

In 4 of the 6 reviewed cases, patients exhibited no classical cutaneous or systemic signs of allergy during the acute KS episode, with the allergic reaction manifesting instead as coronary complications (thrombosis, restenosis, aneurysm, or evagination).

In 50% of patients (3/6 cases), Kounis syndrome type III manifested as coronary aneurysms or vessel evaginations, attributed to extracellular matrix degradation by mast cell mediators (histamine, tryptase) and eosinophil mediators (major basic protein, matrix metalloproteinases).

Only 2 of 6 patients (33%) exhibited cutaneous symptoms such as rash, and only 2/6 (33%) had histopathological confirmation of eosinophil/mast cell infiltration; the remainder relied on clinical suspicion.

The paper notes that tryptase levels typically peak around 30 minutes post-reaction and decline by 120 minutes, while histamine has a very short half-life requiring measurement within 10 minutes of symptom onset, limiting biomarker-based diagnosis of KS.

Across the 6 reviewed cases, 5 of 6 patients had favorable clinical outcomes while 1 patient died as a consequence of Kounis syndrome type III, following management with reperfusion therapies, antiplatelet agents, and corticosteroids.

In 5 of the 6 cases the cause of KS type III was attributed to stent metals and/or polymeric materials, while in 1 case sirolimus (the drug eluted from the stent) was the suspected allergen; three of six patients had documented atopy.
A Danish population-based cohort found a modest but significant overall increase in cancer risk after chronic urticaria diagnosis, with the highest risk in the first year.
A Taiwanese population-based cohort of 12,720 CU patients found an overall cancer SIR of 2.2 and hematologic malignancy SIR of 4.1, with highest risk in ages 20-39.
An Italian study of 1493 consecutive CU patients found a very low malignancy risk (0.007%), confirming the rarity of the CU-cancer association.
A Swedish study of 1155 CU patients found no statistically significant association between chronic urticaria and malignancy overall.
Chen et al. reported a substantially elevated risk of non-Hodgkin lymphoma among CU patients (SIR 4.4).
Sorensen et al. also reported an elevated risk of non-Hodgkin lymphoma in urticaria patients (SIR 2.91).
CU patients with MGUS had a substantially higher rate of hematologic malignancy compared with CU patients without MGUS.
Patients presenting with new-onset CU at older age (>56 years) were more likely to have associated underlying MGUS.
A study found significantly higher PD-1 expression in CSU patients compared with healthy controls, with PD-1 positively correlating with TGF-β and disease activity.

IgE autoantibodies against IL-24 were detected in all CSU patients studied, with blood levels correlating with disease activity.

Total IgE level patterns distinguish CSU autoimmune subtypes and predict treatment response: elevated IgE suggests type I autoallergic CSU with better omalizumab response, while low IgE suggests type IIb autoimmune CSU with better cyclosporine response.
Very low circulating IgE levels may be associated with impaired anti-tumor immune surveillance and could represent an unexpected marker of higher cancer risk.
Histamine released by mast cells can induce tumor cell proliferation by acting on H1 receptors expressed on tumor cell surfaces.

Case series data across multiple small cohorts show variable malignancy prevalence in CU patients, ranging from 2% to 25% depending on the population studied.
Colonic and jejunal eosinophil numbers were increased in BBDP-N rats compared to controls.
Mast cell numbers were increased in the intestinal mucosa of BBDP-N rats compared to controls, though mast cell activation was not significantly different.

Treatment with oral local budesonide (0.5 mg/kg/day for 28 days) decreased eosinophil and mast cell infiltration in the intestinal mucosa of BBDP-N rats.
Colonic sensitivity increased over time in untreated BBDP-N rats, consistent with visceral hypersensitivity development.
Budesonide treatment prevented the increase in colonic sensitivity seen over time in BBDP-N rats.
Budesonide treatment had only a limited effect on intestinal permeability in BBDP-N rats.
Diabetes is described as an established cause of small fiber neuropathy (SFN), with the diagnosis based on fasting plasma glucose, HbA1C, or 2-hour OGTT glucose thresholds.
There is ongoing controversy over whether prediabetes carries a higher prevalence of SFN compared to normoglycemia.
Hypertriglyceridemia is supported by sufficient literature as a relevant factor to screen for in the etiological diagnosis of SFN.
Insulin resistance, assessed via surrogate indices (TyG, AIP, METS-IR, HOMA-IR, QUICKI), is strongly suspected as a contributor to autonomic SFN beyond metabolic syndrome per se.
Hyperuricemia has been significantly associated with neuropathy risk in diabetic patients, although a direct causal role remains uncertain.
Vitamin B6 intoxication is reported as a cause of SFN, diagnosed via serum/plasma pyridoxal 5-phosphate level.

Vitamin B12 deficiency is associated with SFN, though total circulating B12 may be an unreliable marker of neural tissue B12 status, requiring second-line tests when the value is borderline (180-350 pg/mL).
Chronic kidney disease is described as a well-known cause of neuropathy, including SFN, diagnosed via serum creatinine and eGFR.
SFN can be linked to chronic liver disease/dysfunction, including MASLD, suspected via indices such as the fatty liver index combining BMI, waist circumference, TG, and GGT.
Chronic alcohol abuse is a possible cause of SFN, suggested by elevated GGT, AST/ALT ratio >2, and elevated MCV.
Hereditary hemochromatosis, mainly involving HFE gene mutation, is a possible and possibly underestimated cause of SFN, suggested by elevated transferrin saturation, ferritin, and MCV.
Sarcoidosis is established as a main cause of SFN, with liver function test abnormalities observed in 20-40% of sarcoidosis patients (mainly ALP and GGT elevation).
Hypothyroidism, diagnosed via elevated TSH, is a possible cause of SFN, although prevalence and mechanism remain unclear.
Positive ANA was reported in 27.5% of SFN patients in the Lang et al. series, supporting autoimmune connective tissue disorders (Sjögren's syndrome, SLE) as a leading identifiable cause of SFN.
Anti-tTG IgA is the first-line test for celiac disease diagnosis (a possible SFN cause) with reported sensitivity of 89-93% and specificity of 98%.

Serum free light chain assay is recommended alongside SPEP and SIFE as first-line workup for monoclonal gammopathy/AL amyloidosis in SFN, since monoclonal peaks may be too weak to detect on SPEP alone.
HCV infection is one of the main viral infections causing SFN and should be screened for serologically in first-line workup.
HIV infection is one of the main viral infections causing SFN and should be screened for serologically in first-line workup.
Serum ACE testing for sarcoidosis screening was found to be insensitive and nonspecific, with its elevation too frequent and clinically meaningless in a large SFN patient series.
Elevated serum chitotriosidase correlates with sarcoidosis disease activity and multi-organ dissemination, with diagnostic sensitivity up to 89%.

Newly discovered antibodies (anti-Caspr2, anti-LGI1, anti-FGFR3, anti-TS-HDS, anti-plexin D1) are proposed for advanced etiological workup of painful or acute-onset SFN, though their pathogenicity remains unestablished.
TTR gene mutation testing is recommended when SFN presents with dysautonomia, cardiomyopathy, or rapidly evolving distal polyneuropathy suggestive of familial amyloidosis.

Serum lyso-Gb3 level is used to screen men and GLA gene mutation testing is used for women with suspected Fabry disease presenting with childhood-onset painful acroparesthesia, cardiomyopathy, or proteinuria as a cause of SFN.
Gain-of-function mutations in sodium channel genes (SCN9A, SCN10A, SCN11A) or TRPA1 are implicated in child-onset or familial paroxysmal painful acroparesthesia or erythermalgia presenting as SFN.
COL6A5 gene mutation testing is recommended for familial neuropathic itch presenting as SFN.

Mutations in at least 12 different genes cause hereditary sensory and autonomic neuropathies (HSANs), presenting with prominent sensory loss, ulcerative mutilations, and variable autonomic disturbances.
Despite comprehensive etiological screening, no cause is identified in approximately half of SFN cases, which remain classified as idiopathic.
Rheumatoid arthritis and systemic sclerosis are other autoimmune connective tissue disorders possibly associated with increased prevalence of SFN.

ANCA and cryoglobulinemia testing are recommended in acute, painful, asymmetrical (mononeuropathy multiplex-pattern) SFN presentations suggestive of vasculitis, as these have been associated with small nerve fiber involvement in some cases.
TTR gene mutation testing is recommended when clinical features (dysautonomia, cardiomyopathy, rapidly evolving distal neuropathy) suggest hereditary transthyretin amyloidosis as a cause of SFN.

Serum lyso-Gb3 level is recommended for men and GLA gene mutation testing for women suspected of Fabry disease presenting with paroxysmal painful acroparesthesia, cardiomyopathy, proteinuria, or angiokeratoma.
Genetic testing of SCN9A, SCN10A, SCN11A, and TRPA1 is recommended for suspected gain-of-function channelopathies in familial or child-onset paroxysmal painful acroparesthesia or erythermalgia.
COL6A5 gene mutation testing is recommended for familial neuropathic itch as a cause of SFN.

Hereditary sensory and autonomic neuropathy (HSAN), involving mutations in at least 12 different genes, should be considered in patients with prominent sensory loss, ulcerative mutilations, and variable autonomic disturbances.

Newly discovered antibodies (anti-Caspr2, anti-LGI1, anti-FGFR3, anti-TS-HDS, anti-plexin D1) are associated with sensory neuropathies including painful or acute-onset SFN, though their pathogenicity is not yet established.
Serum chitotriosidase (CTO) level correlates with sarcoidosis disease activity and multi-organ dissemination, with diagnostic sensitivity of up to 89%.

Elevated serum 1,25-dihydroxy vitamin D is associated with sarcoidosis disease activity and has diagnostic utility particularly for extrapulmonary sarcoidosis, associated with hypercalcemia and hypercalciuria.
Serum soluble IL-2 receptor (sIL-2R) is elevated in sarcoidosis and other immunological diseases (SLE, RA, ANCA-associated vasculitis) that may be associated with SFN.
Minor salivary gland biopsy is the most relevant laboratory (histological) test in etiological work-up of SFN, useful for diagnosing primary Sjögren's syndrome, sarcoidosis, and amyloidosis.
Abdominal fat tissue aspirate or biopsy detects AL amyloidosis deposits in 70-90% of cases, higher than for hereditary (67%) or wild-type (14%) TTR amyloidosis.
Chest X-ray or CT scan is abnormal in 85-90% of patients with sarcoidosis, supporting imaging as the best diagnostic approach given the predominance of pulmonary forms.
Despite comprehensive etiological screening, many SFN cases remain idiopathic, probably in about half of patients.
The authors recommend repeating etiological testing at 1 year after initial evaluation if SFN symptoms persist and no cause was found, guided also by new clinical signs.
The authors caution that MGUS prevalence increases with age independent of neuropathy, so its detection in an SFN patient may reflect a coincidental association rather than a causal one.
ANCA testing or cryoglobulinemia testing should be performed for vasculitic mechanisms of SFN, which typically present as an acute, painful, distal, asymmetrical mononeuropathy multiplex pattern.
Both LFM and BBH016 significantly reduced fecal pellet output in males following water-avoidance stress, with a weaker effect in females.
Colonic mast cell infiltration was significantly reduced by both LFM and BBH016 treatment in males, with less pronounced effects in females.
Gut microbiota composition showed sex-dependent responses with distinct microbial trajectories in each treatment group.
Linear discriminant analysis effect size (LEfSe) identified seven key bacterial taxa showing treatment- or sex-specific enrichment.

In male rats, specific gut bacterial taxa were enriched following both LFM and probiotic treatment, reflecting sex-specific microbial responses to therapy.

Functional (KEGG-based) prediction analysis showed enrichment of estrogen signaling and bile acid metabolism pathways in male rats following LFM treatment.
In female rats, LFM treatment was associated with attenuation of proinflammatory microbial functional pathways.
Correlations between gut microbial taxa and host physiological outcomes were predominantly observed in male rats, suggesting stronger microbiome-host coupling in males than females.

For ME/CFS and long/post-COVID patients without postexertional malaise, several guidelines explicitly endorse moderate, individually adapted physical activation.
Pacing strategies are highlighted across guidelines as a central concept of activity management for long/post-COVID and ME/CFS.

Purified IgG entered HUVECs but not human foreskin fibroblasts, indicating cell-type-specific IgG uptake, with no difference between disease groups in entry or degradation kinetics.
IgG from ME/CFS and PCS-CFS, but not MS, patients induced significant mitochondrial fragmentation (reduced mitochondrial surface area) in HUVECs.

Gender-stratified analysis showed IgG from female ME/CFS and PCS-CFS patients induced significantly more mitochondrial fragmentation than IgG from male patients, whose effect was not statistically significant.

Multiple linear regression found no significant association between disease severity (Bell score) and IgG-induced mitochondrial surface area in ME/CFS or PCS-CFS, whereas severity was significantly predictive of mitochondrial surface area changes in MS patients.

IgG from ME/CFS and PCS-CFS patients significantly decreased protein levels of Drp1, mitofilin, Miga1, and PLD6 in HUVECs, suggesting mitochondrial protein destabilization rather than classical Drp1-mediated fission.
LC3β, a mitophagy marker, showed a non-significant trend toward decreased levels in HUVECs exposed to ME/CFS and PCS-CFS IgG.
Both Fab and Fc fragments entered HUVECs with efficiency similar to intact IgG, but neither fragment reproduced the mitochondrial fragmentation induced by intact ME/CFS IgG.

HUVECs exposed to IgG from ME/CFS patients showing the mitochondrial fragmentation phenotype exhibited significantly increased spare respiratory capacity and a non-significant trend toward higher basal respiration, unlike IgG from HD, PCS-CFS, or MS.
ECAR (glycolytic activity) patterns and total, mitochondrial, and glycolytic ATP levels showed no significant differences across HD, ME/CFS, PCS-CFS, and MS IgG-exposed HUVECs.

When cells were forced to rely on OXPHOS by substituting galactose for glucose, the ME/CFS IgG-induced increase in spare respiratory capacity disappeared, suggesting glycolytic compensation rather than enhanced OXPHOS underlies the metabolic effect.

Fab fragments from ME/CFS patients reproduced the increased HUVEC respiration seen with intact ME/CFS IgG, while Fc fragments from healthy controls (not ME/CFS) induced an overall increase in metabolic respiration rate.
IgG from a subset of ME/CFS patients induced secretion of IL-1β significantly, with non-significant trends toward increased IFNγ, TNFα, and IL-6 in healthy donor PBMCs.
IgG from MS patients significantly induced secretion of IL-5, IL-10, and TNFβ and reduced TGFα levels in PBMCs, a pattern not observed with ME/CFS IgG.
IgG from PCS-CFS patients showed a cytokine induction trend similar to MS, with a significant increase in TNFβ compared to healthy controls, unlike ME/CFS IgG which had no effect.

IGHV3-16 was enriched within the immune complex of multiple sclerosis (MS) patients compared to controls.

AZU1, which showed reduced presence within immune complexes across all three disease groups, exhibited a non-significant trend toward increased serum levels in PCS-CFS patients.
Total serum VWF levels showed a non-significant trend toward increase in PCS-CFS patients, contrasting with the significant decrease observed within immune complexes.

FCN2 and serotransferrin (TF), which were detected in reduced amounts within immune complexes of all three disease groups, showed significantly increased serum levels in ME/CFS, PCS-CFS, systemic sclerosis, and MS patients.

Gene Ontology analysis of the immune proteome showed a decreased response to bacterial infection in PCS-CFS patients compared with ME/CFS patients.

GSEA Reactome analysis revealed increased hemostasis, platelet activation and signaling, platelet-derived cytosolic Ca2+ response, and fibrin clot formation pathways in the immune proteome of PCS-CFS patients compared to ME/CFS patients.
Mass spectrometry analysis of the immune complex proteome did not detect any EBV or HHV-6A protein signatures in any of the disease groups.

IgM antibody levels against fibronectin were negatively associated with disease severity in the ME/CFS autoantigen microarray cohort.
A similar analysis of IgG levels against the 120-autoantigen panel failed to differentiate ME/CFS cases from healthy controls, unlike the IgM-based analysis.

Multiple linear regression combining Bell disability score, gender, and average mitochondrial surface area found no significant association between disease severity and IgG-induced mitochondrial fragmentation in ME/CFS or PCS-CFS, whereas disease severity significantly predicted mitochondrial surface area in MS patients.

In Case 1 (16-year-old male with ME/CFS, NMH, and MCAS), escalating continuous oral cromolyn from 800 to 1600-2000 mg/day produced marked functional improvement, raising his wellness score from 20/100 to 70/100.
Reducing Case 1's cromolyn dose to 400-800 mg/day during a manufacturing shortage caused a marked worsening of symptoms, supporting a dose-dependent therapeutic effect.

Case 1's serum tryptase levels (1.3 and 1.9 mcg/L) were within normal range despite a clinical diagnosis of MCAS, illustrating that normal mediator levels do not exclude the diagnosis under Consensus-2 criteria.
In Case 2, intranasal cromolyn (Nasalcrom) improved skin erythema, headache, diarrhea, brain fog, anxiety, and depression before oral cromolyn was even introduced.

In Case 2, escalating oral cromolyn to 1600 mg/day along with adjunct topical forms (eye drops, nasal rinse, vaginal application) stabilized all MCAS symptoms and raised her wellness score from 26/100 to 61/100.

Topical ophthalmic cromolyn (Opticrom) resolved eye grittiness and conjunctival erythema in Case 2, previously misdiagnosed as dry eye syndrome, and eyelid swelling and cheek rashes fully resolved at a higher drop dose.
Case 3's plasma histamine level was markedly elevated relative to the reference range, supporting a biochemical mast cell activation abnormality alongside his clinical MCAS diagnosis.
In Case 3, escalating oral cromolyn from 800 to 1600 mg/day fully resolved facial flushing, rashes, and hives and raised his wellness score from 30/100 to 70-80/100 over 12 months.

In Case 4, oral cromolyn dose escalation from 400 to 1600 mg/day produced progressive improvements in orthostatic intolerance, fatigue, brain fog, temperature regulation, flushing, and complete resolution of rashes/hives/headaches, raising her wellness score from 60/100 to 86/100.

Case 5 developed ME/CFS, MCAS, and Long COVID after a probable SARS-CoV-2 infection, presenting with profound fatigue, orthostatic intolerance, cognitive fogginess, and post-exertional malaise that left her housebound and requiring a wheelchair.

In Case 5, oral cromolyn at 800-2400 mg/day improved gastrointestinal symptoms, fatigue, and brain fog, and increased daily step tolerance without provoking post-exertional malaise; a dose reduction during a shortage caused a marked functional decline that was reversed only by increasing the dose above the prior 1600 mg/day level.
Rohrhofer and colleagues estimated that up to 25.3% of ME/CFS patients meet criteria for MCAS, supporting substantial overlap between the two conditions.

All five patients required doses above the standard 800 mg/day (1600-2400 mg/day) to achieve optimal benefit, and these higher doses were well tolerated with no reported side effects, remaining within the FDA-approved maximum of 40 mg/kg/day.
PCS patients had significantly longer reaction times than the CTRL group in both the Flanker and N-back cognitive tasks, while CAD patients performed comparably to CTRL.
PCS patients showed significantly lower accuracy than CAD patients in the Flanker task and lower accuracy than CTRL in the N-back task, with CAD showing intermediate accuracy.
PCS patients showed the most pronounced increase in self-reported sleepiness after cognitive tasks compared with CAD and CTRL groups, indicating greater cognitive load/fatigability.

PCS patients showed lower temporal sample entropy of cerebral blood flow (more rigid, less intermittent blood flow regulation) in the dorsolateral prefrontal cortex, particularly during the N-back working memory task, compared with CAD and CTRL groups.

PCS patients displayed higher spatial variability (coefficient of variation of sample entropy across channels) of cerebral blood flow regulation compared to CAD and CTRL groups, especially during the N-back task.
A significant difference in sample entropy was also found between CAD and CTRL groups in the Flanker task.
Spatial variability of blood flow regulation (CV(SampEn)) during the N-back task decreased from PCS to CAD to CTRL, with a statistically significant difference between PCS and CTRL.
Higher spatial variability of blood flow regulation (CV(SampEn)) in the N-back task was significantly associated with longer reaction times and reduced accuracy across participants.
Regression analyses showed neither sex nor the sex-by-age interaction significantly influenced sample entropy values of cerebral blood flow.
In PCS patients, sample entropy in the Flanker task decreased with increasing age (uncorrected P = 0.025), but this association did not survive Bonferroni correction.

Among PCS patients, cognitive dysfunction was reported as a lead symptom in 75%, fatigue/exercise intolerance in 83%, and shortness of breath in 100%.
PCS patients had high fatigue scores on the Multidimensional Fatigue Inventory (mean 81.5±8.2), objectively confirming fatigue as a prominent symptom.

Citing prior literature, the authors note that SARS-CoV-2 infection causes pericyte-mediated capillary constriction that reduces cerebral cortical blood flow by approximately 17%, contributing to attentional deficits.
The CFS model group showed significantly reduced body weight, swimming time, and open-field standing duration and grid crossings compared with the control group, confirming the fatigue phenotype.
ULK1 mRNA expression and the p-ULK1/ULK1 protein ratio were significantly increased in skeletal muscle of the CFS model group compared with control.
LC3 mRNA expression was significantly increased in skeletal muscle of CFS model rats compared with control rats.

Both WNM and coenzyme Q10 treatment significantly upregulated AMPK mRNA expression in skeletal muscle compared with the untreated model group.
WNM and coenzyme Q10 both significantly upregulated ULK1 mRNA and the p-ULK1/ULK1 ratio compared with the untreated model group.
Warming needle moxibustion significantly upregulated ULK1 mRNA expression in skeletal muscle compared with the model group.

Children and adolescents with chronic physical health conditions overall showed higher internalizing, externalizing, and total behavior problems than peers without such conditions or test norms.
Among the chronic physical health conditions examined, chronic fatigue syndrome showed the largest elevations in internalizing problems (e.g., anxiety/depression) relative to comparison groups.
Thalassemia showed the largest elevations in total behavior problems and externalizing problems among the chronic physical health conditions studied.
Effect sizes for behavioral/emotional problems tended to be larger when derived from parent reports compared to adolescent self-reports.
The elevation of total behavior problems in children with chronic physical health conditions was larger in this updated meta-analysis than in the prior meta-analysis it updates.
10.7% of HSD/hEDS patients with headache/migraine had unruptured intracranial aneurysms on neuroimaging, a rate comparable to or higher than reported in vascular EDS/general EDS cohorts.
4.8% of HSD/hEDS patients with headache/migraine were diagnosed with spontaneous cervical artery dissection (SCeAD), a higher rate than previously reported in HSD/hEDS cohorts.
5.8% of HSD/hEDS patients with headache/migraine had fibromuscular dysplasia of head/neck vessels, all female, predominantly with HSD.
88.3% of HSD/hEDS patients in this headache-clinic cohort had a history of migraine, confirming previously documented high migraine prevalence in hypermobile populations.
There was no statistically significant difference in sex distribution, with 96.1% female across the HSD/hEDS cohort, reflecting the known strong female predominance of these conditions.
There was no statistically significant difference in the rate of UIA development between HSD and hEDS diagnostic groups.
There was no statistically significant difference in the rate of SCeAD between HSD and hEDS diagnostic groups.
There was no statistically significant difference in the rate of FMD between HSD and hEDS diagnostic groups, though most FMD patients had HSD.
Slightly more than half of HSD/hEDS patients with UIA had a history of migraine with aura, suggesting a possible link between aura and aneurysm development in this population.
All HSD/hEDS patients diagnosed with spontaneous cervical artery dissection had a history of migraine, suggesting migraine as a potential co-risk factor for SCeAD in this population.
Five of six HSD/hEDS patients with fibromuscular dysplasia had a history of migraine with aura, and all had a migraine history, suggesting migraine with aura as a possible co-risk factor for FMD.

In an exploratory non-hypermobile comparison group of 13 headache patients matched for imaging, none developed UIA, SCeAD, or FMD, supporting hypermobility (rather than migraine alone) as the relevant risk factor.

Vertebral artery involvement predominated in SCeAD among HSD/hEDS patients (especially females with HSD), which the authors suggest may be distinct from the general population's typical carotid artery predominance.
Carotid artery involvement predominated in FMD among HSD/hEDS patients, all diagnosed with mild disease without significant stenosis.
UIA diagnoses occurred at a relatively young age (<50 years in 10/11 patients) with small aneurysm sizes (mean 3.8 mm, median 3 mm), mostly saccular and located in the anterior/carotid circulation.

Beighton score, a standard measure of joint hypermobility, did not differ significantly between autistic, high-AQ, and non-autistic groups with hEDS/HSD, despite autistic people reporting more associated symptoms.
Non-autistic participants with hEDS/HSD experienced significantly longer delays between symptom onset and diagnosis than autistic participants.

Autistic participants with hEDS/HSD were significantly more likely to report dermatological, orthopaedic, and pain symptoms than non-autistic participants, while high-AQ and non-autistic groups did not differ on any symptom.
Autistic participants with hEDS/HSD were more likely to report abnormal scarring than the high-AQ group.
Autistic people with hEDS/HSD were more likely to have co-existing cardiological, neurological, and immune system conditions, and sleep disturbances, than non-autistic and high-AQ groups.
Autistic respondents with hEDS/HSD were more likely to have been diagnosed with dysautonomia/POTS, chronic fatigue/ME, and mast cell activation syndrome (MCAS) than non-autistic respondents.

Autistic participants with hEDS/HSD were more likely to be diagnosed with other neurodivergent conditions (ADHD, dyspraxia, dyslexia, dyscalculia) and mental health conditions (anxiety, depression) compared with the other groups, and high-AQ participants were more likely than non-autistic participants to be diagnosed with anxiety and depression.
Both autistic and high-AQ groups had significantly higher PHQ-4 scores (poorer mental health) than the non-autistic group, with no significant difference between autistic and high-AQ groups.
Self-rated physical health (EQ-5D-5L) was significantly lower in the autistic and high-AQ groups compared to the non-autistic group, with no difference between autistic and high-AQ groups.

Autistic participants with hEDS/HSD were significantly more likely than non-autistic and high-AQ participants to have been referred to nearly all clinical specialties in the past 5 years, including cardiology, gastroenterology, neurology, occupational therapy, pain management, physiotherapy, rheumatology, and urology.
Autistic and high-AQ participants with hEDS/HSD were significantly more likely to receive carer support than non-autistic participants.
Autistic participants with hEDS/HSD were significantly less likely to be in employment than both the high-AQ and non-autistic groups.

Autistic participants with hEDS/HSD were significantly more likely to receive disability benefits than the high-AQ and non-autistic groups, and high-AQ participants were more likely than non-autistic participants to receive benefits.
In a beta-regression model, lower self-reported physical health scores in hEDS/HSD patients were predicted by greater limitations in usual activities, mobility problems, and anxiety/depression.
The negative impact of difficulty carrying out usual activities on physical health scores was significantly stronger for non-autistic participants than for autistic participants with hEDS/HSD.

In a linear regression, PHQ-4 (mental health) scores among hEDS/HSD patients were predicted by younger age, male gender, GP-initiated care steps (lower scores), and difficulty with self-care and usual activities (higher scores).

The negative impact of self-care difficulty on PHQ-4 mental health scores was significantly stronger in non-autistic participants than autistic participants, whereas the negative impact of usual-activity difficulty on PHQ-4 scores was significantly stronger in autistic participants than non-autistic participants.
Within the high-AQ group, females had substantially higher PHQ-4 scores (poorer mental health) than other genders, a gender difference significantly larger than seen in the non-autistic group.

Rare variants in collagen biosynthesis pathway genes, predominantly COL5A1, COL18A1, COL17A1, and post-translational modification enzymes, were significantly enriched in hEDS subjects compared to unaffected controls.
Rare variants in HLA and adaptive immune axis genes, including HLA-A, HLA-B, HLA-C, and TAP transporters, were significantly enriched in hEDS subjects versus unaffected controls.
Rare variants in mitochondrial respiratory chain genes were significantly enriched in hEDS subjects compared to unaffected controls.
Mitochondrial respiratory chain variant enrichment was 4.2-fold greater in a pediatric fracture subgroup of hEDS patients compared with controls.
Genome-wide analysis identified seven genes, all encoding structural or cytoskeletal proteins, that achieved Bonferroni-corrected genome-wide significance for association with hEDS.
A machine learning model using subject-stratified cross-validation to prevent data leakage achieved 80% accuracy in classifying hEDS status based on rare genetic variants.
The vEDS patient's dermal fibroblasts, and the iPSC line reprogrammed from them, carry a pathogenic COL3A1 c.755G>T variant, which was corrected via CRISPR/Cas9 to generate an isogenic control line.

Vascular smooth muscle cells differentiated from the vEDS patient's iPSCs showed cytoskeletal differences compared to those derived from the isogenic gene-corrected control line, supporting the line's utility for studying disease mechanisms.

Both tendon-targeted (developmental) and tamoxifen-inducible (adult) Cre models produced dose-dependent reductions in Col5a1 expression in insertion and midsubstance regions relative to wild-type tendons.
Developmental collagen V knockout (TEN-KO) tendons had reduced whole-tendon cross-sectional area compared to TEN-HET and wild-type tendons.
Developmental collagen V deficiency and knockout produced dose-dependent reductions in max load, linear stiffness, and max stress of supraspinatus tendons.

TEN-KO tendons showed increased stress relaxation, reduced dynamic modulus, and increased phase shift relative to WT and TEN-HET tendons, indicating altered viscoelastic behavior with developmental collagen V loss.

Acute (inducible, adult) collagen V knockdown did not alter whole-tendon elastic (max load, stiffness) or viscoelastic (percent relaxation, dynamic modulus, phase shift) properties relative to wild-type controls.
Both developmental (TEN-KO) and acute adult (I-NULL) collagen V loss reduced regional modulus at the insertion and midsubstance, though effect was more pronounced in the developmental model.

Collagen fiber realignment under load was impaired (increased circular variance) in both developmental (TEN-HET/TEN-KO) and, to a lesser extent, inducible (I-HET/I-NULL) collagen V-deficient tendons in insertion and midsubstance regions.

Atomic force microscopy revealed no differences in fibril-level d-period strain, local variance, or global variance between WT, TEN-KO, and I-NULL tendons at any applied strain level in either region, indicating preserved nanoscale fibril mechanical behavior despite collagen V loss.

Tenocyte cell density was unchanged across genotypes in both insertion and midsubstance regions, but TEN-KO tendons showed decreased nuclear aspect ratio (more rounded nuclei) in the insertion region compared to WT.

TEM showed developmental collagen V-deficient (TEN-HET, insertion) and knockout (TEN-KO, insertion and midsubstance) tendons had shifts toward larger-diameter collagen fibrils compared to WT, consistent with collagen V's role in capping/limiting fibril growth during development.

Inducible adult collagen V knockdown (I-HET, I-NULL) produced only subtle shifts toward larger-diameter collagen fibrils in insertion and midsubstance regions relative to WT, less pronounced than in the developmental model.

Developmental collagen V knockout (TEN-KO) tendons showed upregulation of matrix-remodeling enzymes Mmp2, Mmp13, Mmp14, and the MMP-inhibitor Timp1 in insertion and midsubstance regions, suggesting a sustained catabolic/remodeling state.

TEN-KO tendons showed upregulation of matricellular proteins (Postn, Fap, Fn1, Spp1, Tnc, Lum) and tendon-related collagens (Col1a1, Col3a1) in insertion and midsubstance regions relative to WT/TEN-HET.

TEN-KO tendons showed elevated Lox, Loxl1, Loxl2 (collagen crosslinking enzymes), Casp3, Igf1, and Cdh11, suggesting increased crosslinking activity likely reinforcing structurally compromised fibrils.
TEN-KO tendons showed downregulation of Bmp4, Ltbp4 (TGF-β bioavailability regulator), and Vegfb (angiogenesis/metabolic support), potentially limiting regenerative and signaling capacity.
TNF-α was downregulated in the insertion region of TEN-HET (collagen V heterozygous) tendons relative to WT, though overall gene expression differences between WT and TEN-HET were minimal.

In the inducible model, Aspn was upregulated in the insertion region of I-NULL tendons relative to WT/I-HET, and Postn was upregulated in I-HET tendons relative to WT in both insertion and midsubstance regions, but overall gene expression changes with acute collagen V loss were minor.

The authors propose that in classic Ehlers-Danlos syndrome, where COL5A1 haploinsufficiency is common, tendon-related symptoms (joint hypermobility, tendon laxity) may arise primarily from developmental failures in matrix organization rather than ongoing adult matrix instability, implying developmentally-timed therapeutic windows.

The MRI-derived tibial spino-meniscal clearance distance was markedly smaller in patients with arthroscopically confirmed hypermobile lateral meniscus (HML) compared with those with stable posterior horns.
TSMC showed strong diagnostic accuracy for detecting HML on ROC analysis, with an optimal cutoff below 1.2 mm.
At the <1.2 mm cutoff, TSMC yielded high sensitivity and specificity for HML with a diagnostic odds ratio of 37.1.
TSMC measurement demonstrated excellent intraobserver and interobserver reliability among radiologists and an orthopaedic surgeon.

In multivariable logistic regression adjusting for age, sex, tibial plateau width, posterior tibial slope and MRI field strength, each 0.1-mm reduction in TSMC independently increased the odds of HML.

Posterior tibial slope and tibial plateau width showed no correlation with TSMC, indicating TSMC reflects a specific posterior horn-tibial spine spatial relationship rather than general knee morphology.
Nearly one-third of the arthroscopy cohort (164 patients with heterogeneous knee symptoms) had arthroscopically confirmed hypermobile lateral meniscus.

While patients with HML reported more lateral mechanical symptoms, joint-line tenderness and higher pain scores, none of these clinical variables independently predicted hypermobility once TSMC was included in the multivariable model.
In the Pilates group, Bristol Impact of Hypermobility (BIoH) total scores significantly decreased (improved) from baseline to 8 weeks.
There was a significant group-by-time interaction for BIoH, indicating that the Pilates group improved significantly more than the waitlist control group over the 8-week period.

Tampa Scale of Kinesiophobia (TSK-11) scores decreased significantly over time overall, but the group-by-time interaction was not statistically significant and the mean change (1.5 points) did not reach the minimum clinically meaningful change threshold of 4 points.
Body Awareness Rating Questionnaire (BARQ) scores improved significantly more in the Pilates group than in the waitlist control group, with a large effect size.
Physical activity levels, measured by log-transformed IPAQ MET scores, did not change significantly over 8 weeks in either the Pilates or waitlist control group.
Improvements in BIoH, TSK-11, and BARQ observed at 8 weeks in the Pilates group were maintained at 6-month follow-up.
Physical activity (IPAQ) decreased at 6 months compared to baseline and 8-week levels in the Pilates group.

About 17% of participants who completed the 8-week Pilates program reported some increase in pain or exacerbation of pre-existing problems attributed to the Pilates exercises, with about half describing the discomfort as transient or resolvable through modification.

Among participants who completed 8 weeks of the Pilates program, 88.2% reported they were 'Likely' or 'Very Likely' to recommend the program to others, indicating high acceptability despite modest measured effect sizes.

The observed 25.4-point improvement in BIoH score was slightly below the previously proposed 30-point threshold for clinically meaningful change, and smaller than the 31.7-point change reported in a prior small BIoH intervention study.

Pilates participants reported completing an average of 2.3 Pilates sessions per week (33.5% completed 3 days/week, 27.6% completed 2 days/week), with 71% able to complete the full 25-minute sessions Usually or Always.
Among the 40 EDS-related TikTok videos analyzed, quality scores differed significantly by creator type on both the Global Quality Scale (GQS) and modified DISCERN (mDISCERN).

Across the full sample of 184 rare-disease videos (including EDS), physician- and medical professional-created videos had significantly higher GQS and mDISCERN quality scores than influencer- and patient-created videos.

Post hoc pairwise testing confirmed physician-created videos scored significantly higher than influencer and patient videos on both quality instruments, and non-physician medical professional content also outperformed influencer content.
Despite lower measured content quality, influencer- and patient-created videos accounted for the large majority of total views across the 184 rare-disease videos.
Physician-created videos generated substantially higher normalized engagement (interactions per 1000 views) than videos from all other creator types, despite reaching smaller total audiences.

Across all creator types and rare diseases, citation of peer-reviewed literature or clinical guidelines in TikTok videos was extremely rare, and citation rates did not differ significantly by creator type.
Patient-created content represented the largest proportion of videos across most of the rare genetic diseases studied, including EDS.

The study identified a mismatch between content quality and viewer engagement, with high-quality physician content underviewed relative to lower-quality but more popular influencer and patient content, echoing patterns reported for other health topics on TikTok.
Loss-of-function mutations in SLC2A10 impair GLUT10 function, disrupting reactive oxygen species handling and elastin-collagen maturation, leading to arterial tortuosity in ATS.

SLC2A10 mutation leads to decreased transcription of decorin, an inhibitor of TGF-β, causing disinhibition of TGF-β signaling and impaired extracellular matrix formation contributing to arterial tortuosity.
Unlike ATS, autosomal recessive cutis laxa type 1b (FBLN4 mutation) and autosomal dominant Loeys-Dietz syndrome are characterized by upregulation of TGF-β signaling rather than disinhibition.

The patient presented with grossly dilated ascending aorta (56 mm), dilated aortic annulus (16 mm), moderate aortic insufficiency, coarctation of the aorta, and concentric left ventricular hypertrophy.

CT imaging showed severe coarctation, gross tortuosity of the aorta and left common carotid/subclavian arteries, and tracheobronchial compression, consistent with suspected arterial tortuosity syndrome.
Unlike other heritable arteriopathies, arterial dissection has rarely or never been unequivocally recorded in ATS despite its progressive nature.
Older studies reported 40% mortality before age 4 years in ATS, whereas newer studies show improved prognosis.

Regular echocardiographic surveillance is recommended at least every 3 months until age 5, then tailored but at least annually thereafter, due to potential rapid or later progressive aortic dilatation.

Given the low dissection risk and amenability to vascular surgery, an aggressive surgical approach may not be indicated for slowly progressive aortic root dilatation in ATS, with management guidelines similar to Marfan syndrome suggested as appropriate.
Patients with ATS show a slight male predominance and a commonly present history of consanguinity.
Joint hypermobility (JHM) was present in 42.3% of the enrolled health science students.
Female students had significantly higher Beighton scores than males, indicating greater joint hypermobility.
Among students with joint hypermobility, 95 reported chronic musculoskeletal pain while 40 reported acute musculoskeletal pain, showing pain is common in this group.
Chronic musculoskeletal pain was significantly higher among students with mild joint hypermobility (Beighton score cut-off 4-6/9).
Chronic and acute musculoskeletal pain followed a descending anatomical gradient, being highest at the neck and lowest at the knees.
Adolescents with idiopathic scoliosis showed a median Beighton score of 6, indicating generalized joint hypermobility in this cohort.

Despite high prevalence of generalized joint hypermobility in the cohort, joint hypermobility did not significantly contribute to variance in AIS-related quality of life in the multiple regression model.
Back pain intensity was strongly and negatively correlated with quality of life in adolescents with idiopathic scoliosis.
Habitual physical activity level showed a weak but significant positive correlation with quality of life in adolescents with idiopathic scoliosis.

In stepwise multiple linear regression, pain intensity and physical activity were the only variables significantly associated with quality of life, together explaining 35.8% of variance in QoL scores (adjusted R2 = 33.9%).
Psychological distress variables (stress, anxiety, depression) did not significantly contribute to variance in quality of life among adolescents with AIS, contrasting with some prior studies.

Thoracic and thoracolumbar/lumbar Cobb angles (spinal curvature severity) were not significantly associated with quality of life, contrasting with prior research linking greater curvature to lower QoL.
Age, BMI, and time since diagnosis were not significant predictors of quality of life in the regression model.
Involvement in habitual physical activity was very low among adolescents with AIS, with only 17.4% reporting routine weekly physical activity.
Adolescents with AIS reported moderate back pain intensity overall, with a median NRS score of 5.
Lateral meniscus posterior root injuries occur in 12-15% of patients undergoing ACL reconstruction and carry significant biomechanical implications.
The deep lateral femoral notch sign has an almost 40% prevalence in patients who have both ACL tears and concomitant lateral meniscus posterior root tears.
Congenital deficiency or traumatic injury to the popliteomeniscal fascicles can produce a hypermobile lateral meniscus, which may be associated with knee pain and locking.
Meniscofemoral ligaments stabilize the lateral meniscus in the setting of posterior root tears and act as secondary restraints against posterior tibial translation in PCL-deficient knees.
Injuries to the anterior lateral meniscus often lack clinical significance and may represent pseudotears rather than true tears.
Among classifications of lateral meniscus posterior root tears, LMORT Type 4 represents the most common tear pattern.

Specific MRI signs (coronal cleft, sagittal ghost, axial radial defect, and sagittal truncated triangle) aid detection of lateral meniscus posterior root tears, which require a high index of suspicion to diagnose.

A de novo missense variant in DNMT3A (c.1585G>A, p.D529N) affecting a highly conserved aspartate in the ADD domain was identified in both twins and reclassified as likely pathogenic, establishing the diagnosis of Tatton-Brown-Rahman syndrome (TBRS).

Both twins displayed joint hypermobility (Beighton scores 6/9 and 5/9), and one had a history of joint dislocations, skin striae, and easy bruising, indicating a connective tissue phenotype accompanying TBRS.

One twin had a mildly dilated aortic root (3.7 cm) with impaired left ventricular function, and the other had moderate left ventricular impairment with a normal aortic root, indicating cardiac involvement in this TBRS family.

Genome-wide methylation profiling showed that both twins and a third TBRS patient with a loss-of-function DNMT3A variant exhibited genome-wide hypomethylation relative to 64 normal controls, consistent with impaired DNMT3A function.

The authors propose that tall stature combined with connective tissue hypermobility increases apical lung tension, promoting alveolar distension and subpleural bleb formation, a mechanism analogous to that proposed for Marfan, Loeys-Dietz and vascular Ehlers-Danlos syndromes.
Only about 10% of patients with Marfan syndrome develop pneumothorax, illustrating that pneumothorax affects a minority even in monogenic connective tissue disorders known to predispose to it.

A previously reported father-son pair with TBRS caused by a different pathogenic DNMT3A variant (p.R736C) also had pneumothorax in the son, supporting an association between DNMT3A-related TBRS and pneumothorax.

Approximately 75% of patients with familial pneumothorax remain genetically unclassified even after assessment by a dedicated pneumothorax genetics multidisciplinary team, indicating additional causal genes remain to be discovered.

The p.D529N variant is present at very low frequency in gnomAD (4 heterozygotes, allele frequency 2.478×10^-6), which the authors note could reflect somatic clonal haematopoiesis rather than germline occurrence, given DNMT3A's known association with this phenomenon.
The proband carries a heterozygous 2.492 Mb duplication spanning nearly all of PAR1 at Xp22.33, currently classified as a variant of uncertain significance.
Duplications encompassing the full SHOX coding sequence and its regulatory enhancers are linked to overexpression (triplosensitivity) and tall stature, as observed in this proband.
On examination the proband showed generalized obesity, proportionate tall stature, short toes, and joint hypermobility.
Hypotonia noted in early childhood improved over time, but joint hypermobility persisted through the most recent assessment.

The authors propose that DHRSX dysregulation may impair dolichol-dependent glycoprotein processing and autophagic homeostasis during neural development, potentially contributing to the proband's neurodevelopmental phenotype.

Biallelic missense variants in DHRSX have previously been reported in association with global developmental delay, intellectual disability, ASD, seizures, hypotonia, craniofacial dysmorphism, and obesity, overlapping with the proband's phenotype.
ASMT variants and reduced melatonin-synthesizing enzyme activity have been associated with ASD and intellectual disability in multiple prior cohorts.
ASMTL was identified as a gene within the Autism Spliceform Interaction Network and a genetic risk factor for autism, interacting with the autism candidate gene TDO2.
A previously reported smaller 270 kb duplication at Xp22.33 encompassing CRLF2, CSF2RA, SLC25A6, and ASMTL has been associated with ASD.
Dysregulation of CSF2RA, which encodes a receptor binding CSF2 on hematopoietic lineages, can cause excessive pulmonary surfactant accumulation and pulmonary alveolar proteinosis.
Dysregulation of SLC25A6 and CD99, both located within PAR1, has been linked to Klinefelter syndrome traits such as cardiac abnormalities, intellectual disability, and autoimmune disease.
EEG at 19 months in the proband showed intermittent slowing in the left temporo-parietal region.
Brain MRI at 22 months showed periventricular white matter T2 FLAIR hyperintensities, mild splenial atrophy, and a choroid plexus cyst, but these were considered nonspecific and age-appropriate.

Applying ACMG/ClinGen technical scoring, the Xp22.33 duplication totaled only 0.6 points, below the 0.9-point threshold for a likely pathogenic call, largely because SHOX has a ClinGen triplosensitivity score of 0 and the region contains fewer than 35 genes.

ClinVar querying for X-chromosomal copy number gains similar to the proband's duplication identified 394 variants (67 pathogenic, 5 likely pathogenic, 322 VUS), with only one (ClinVar 1808677) closely matching in size and location.

Both full siblings of the proband have neurodevelopmental diagnoses (ASD in the 17-year-old brother, autistic features in the 16-year-old sister), suggesting a possible familial genotype-phenotype correlation that could not be confirmed due to unavailable testing.

The authors note that recent large cohort data suggest a potentially increased risk of early childhood neurodevelopmental diagnoses following prenatal SARS-CoV-2 infection, particularly with third-trimester exposure, relevant given the proband's mother had third-trimester COVID-19.

Other prospective studies using validated developmental screening tools did not find significant associations between prenatal SARS-CoV-2 exposure and neurodevelopmental outcomes through two years of age, contrasting with the large-cohort finding cited above.

PAR1 copy number variants in sex chromosome aneuploidies (Klinefelter syndrome, Jacob/XYY syndrome, and higher-grade aneuploidies) are associated with overlapping neurodevelopmental traits including delayed speech/language, ADHD, intellectual disability, and ASD.

Generalised joint hypermobility was ranked the #1 priority condition by an Australian Delphi panel of healthcare professionals for development of clinical practice guidelines addressing chronic lower limb musculoskeletal pain in children and adolescents.
All 16 parents/caregivers surveyed (100%) rated development of a clinical practice guideline for generalised joint hypermobility as appropriate or very appropriate.
Growing pains was ranked the #2 priority condition overall for clinical practice guideline development, despite existing diagnostic coding, due to variability in diagnosis and treatment.
Joint instability of the lower limb was ranked #4 overall priority condition, common across all healthcare professional groups (general practitioners, paediatric specialists, allied health).
Juvenile idiopathic arthritis was ranked #5 (unweighted) among the top 10 priority conditions, common across two of the three professional groups.

Of 81 grey- and peer-reviewed literature documents identified covering 77 of 124 scoped lower-limb pain conditions, only four (2 adult, 2 paediatric) contained information specifically relating to chronic pain management, highlighting a major evidence and guideline gap.
Meta-analysis found no significant difference between female and male ballet dancers in the prevalence of overuse injuries.
No significant sex difference was found in the incidence of overuse injuries among ballet dancers.
No significant sex difference was found in the anatomical location of overuse injuries in ballet dancers.
The foot and ankle complex was identified as the most commonly affected anatomical region for overuse injuries in both male and female ballet dancers.
Only two studies assessed severity of overuse injuries between sexes and their findings contrasted with one another, limiting conclusions on sex-based severity differences.
After propensity score matching, greater rectocele degree was independently associated with increased odds of constipation in multivariate logistic regression.
Lower uterine position relative to the pubic symphysis at maximal Valsalva maneuver was independently associated with higher odds of constipation.
Uterine prolapse was significantly more prevalent among women with constipation than those without.
Patients with chronic constipation showed significantly greater levator ani hiatal ballooning and increased hiatal area compared to non-constipated individuals.

No significant intergroup difference was found in perineal hypermobility between constipated and non-constipated women, consistent with prior literature that it is not an independent predictor of obstructed defecation.

No significant differences were observed between constipation and non-constipation groups in bladder neck mobility or cystocele, or bladder position relative to the pubic symphysis at rest or maximal Valsalva maneuver.
Worsening constipation symptoms correlated with marked descent of bladder position during maximal Valsalva maneuver and a significant increase in vesicocele incidence.
Non-constipated patients showed no significant changes in pelvic floor anatomy over a median 2.25-year follow-up interval, indicating structural stability without constipation.

In constipated patients, serial ultrasound examinations approximately 2.5 years apart showed progressive descent of the bladder and rectal ampulla relative to the pubic symphysis at maximal Valsalva maneuver, increased bladder mobility, and enlargement of the levator ani hiatus area.
A higher proportion of constipated patients exhibited vesicocele, uterine prolapse, and perineal hypermobility at the subsequent ultrasound examination compared to the prior examination.
Cerebrospinal fluid IL-8 concentrations are consistently reported as increased in fibromyalgia patients and are linked to glial activation and nociceptive transmission.
Elevated CSF glutamate concentrations have been reported in fibromyalgia, consistent with heightened excitatory neurotransmission and impaired inhibitory pain modulation.

CSF proteomic profiling has identified differential expression of proteins including apolipoprotein C-III, galectin-3-binding protein, malate dehydrogenase, and proSAAS-derived peptides in fibromyalgia.
Neurofilament light chain, a marker of subtle neuronal injury, may be altered in fibromyalgia patients though this remains under investigation.
Peripheral blood pro-inflammatory cytokines IL-6, IL-8, TNF-α, and IFN-γ are elevated in fibromyalgia patients, reflecting systemic low-grade inflammation.
CRP, an acute-phase reactant, is increased in several fibromyalgia patients, reinforcing a chronic low-intensity inflammation model.
Peripheral blood B-cell transcriptomic analyses show upregulation of interferon-regulated and inflammation-associated genes (S100A8, S100A9, VCAM1, CD163, SERPINA1, ANXA1) in fibromyalgia.
Serum proteomic platforms identify elevated immune-modulatory proteins (AXIN1, STAMBP, SIRT2) and chemokines (CCL2, CCL17, CXCL9, CXCL11) associated with symptom severity in fibromyalgia.
Serum BDNF is frequently elevated in fibromyalgia and has been associated with intensified pain sensitivity and cognitive symptoms.

Correlations between peripheral inflammatory markers and CSF cytokine concentrations are generally weak in fibromyalgia, suggesting peripheral biomarkers only partly reflect central neuroinflammation.
Fibromyalgia patients show flattened diurnal cortisol rhythms with reduced morning cortisol, blunted cortisol awakening response, and reduced circadian amplitude, indicating HPA axis dysregulation.
Some fibromyalgia patients show elevated CSF CRH concentrations despite normal or reduced peripheral cortisol, suggesting impaired downstream HPA signaling or adrenal insensitivity.
Polymorphisms and epigenetic modifications (DNA methylation) in NR3C1, encoding the glucocorticoid receptor, have been linked to fibromyalgia symptom severity and stress reactivity.
Fibromyalgia patients show consistently reduced overall HRV, decreased high-frequency components, and elevated LF/HF ratio, reflecting reduced vagal tone and sympathetic predominance.

Genetic polymorphisms in COMT are among the most robustly replicated genetic associations in fibromyalgia, linking impaired catecholamine metabolism with heightened pain sensitivity and stress vulnerability.
Abnormal nocturnal melatonin secretion patterns occur in fibromyalgia alongside non-restorative sleep, circadian disturbances, and increased pain sensitivity.
Metabolomic profiling shows frequently elevated BCAAs (leucine, isoleucine, valine) in fibromyalgia, implicating disrupted muscle energy metabolism and mTOR signaling.

Tryptophan metabolism is significantly dysregulated in fibromyalgia, with increased kynurenine pathway metabolites and reduced serotonin/melatonin precursors, indicating neuroinflammation and NMDA-mediated excitotoxicity.

Lipidomic alterations including elevated ceramides, sphingomyelins, LPCs, and PCs suggest dysregulated sphingolipid/glycerophospholipid metabolism affecting apoptosis, neuroinflammation, and membrane fluidity in fibromyalgia.

Fibromyalgia patients showed significantly increased oxidative stress markers (TOS, TAS, MDA, OSI) compared with healthy controls, indicating oxidative lipid damage and deficient anti-inflammatory regulation.
PBMC transcriptomes in fibromyalgia consistently show upregulation of proinflammatory cytokine/chemokine genes and downregulation of anti-inflammatory mediator genes.
TLR signaling genes TLR2, TLR4, and MyD88 are upregulated in fibromyalgia, suggesting an activated innate immune response.
Decreased expression of the inhibitory neurotransmission gene GABRB3 is reported in fibromyalgia, consistent with a central excitatory-inhibitory imbalance underlying hyperalgesia and allodynia.

fMRI studies show hyperactivation of the insula and anterior cingulate cortex during nociceptive processing, alongside hypoactivation of the prefrontal cortex and periaqueductal gray, indicating impaired descending pain inhibition in fibromyalgia.

Resting-state fMRI shows increased DMN connectivity with pain-processing regions (insula, ACC) linked to pain rumination, and reduced DMN-executive network connectivity correlating with cognitive impairment in fibromyalgia.

Voxel-based morphometry studies report reduced gray matter volume in pain- and affect-processing regions (ACC, insula, thalamus, prefrontal cortices) in fibromyalgia, interpreted as maladaptive neuroplastic adaptation.
Magnetic resonance spectroscopy shows elevated glutamate in the insula and decreased GABA in prefrontal regions in fibromyalgia, indicating region-specific neurotransmitter imbalance.
PET imaging shows altered μ-opioid receptor availability in the ACC, PFC, and amygdala in fibromyalgia, supporting impaired endogenous analgesic mechanisms.

Low-dose naltrexone is proposed as a novel pharmacologic approach for fibromyalgia, acting by attenuating microglial activation and neuroinflammatory cascades in patients with heightened central immune signaling.

fMRI studies show hyperactivation of the anterior insula and anterior cingulate cortex in fibromyalgia patients during nociceptive stimulation, reflecting heightened interoceptive, affective, and salience processing of pain.
Reduced activation/modulation within the prefrontal cortex and periaqueductal gray suggests impaired top-down descending pain inhibition in fibromyalgia.

Resting-state fMRI shows increased DMN connectivity with pain-processing regions (insula, ACC) linked to pain rumination, and reduced DMN-executive network connectivity correlating with cognitive impairments.
Voxel-based morphometry studies report reduced gray matter volume in the ACC, insula, thalamus, and prefrontal cortices of fibromyalgia patients, interpreted as maladaptive neuroplastic changes.

Diffusion tensor imaging identifies microstructural white matter alterations connecting the PFC, limbic system, and somatosensory regions, implicating disrupted top-down pain and affective modulation circuits.
Magnetic resonance spectroscopy shows region-specific neurotransmitter imbalances in fibromyalgia, with elevated glutamate in the insula and decreased GABA in prefrontal regions.
PET imaging demonstrates altered mu-opioid receptor availability in the ACC, PFC, and amygdala of fibromyalgia patients, supporting impaired endogenous analgesic mechanisms.

Wearable accelerometry and gyroscopic sensors enable objective, continuous quantification of low-level activity fluctuations and fatigue accumulation in fibromyalgia that are missed by retrospective self-report.

Wearable sleep-monitoring devices combining actigraphy, photoplethysmography, skin temperature, and electrodermal activity capture sleep onset latency, awakenings, fragmentation, and sleep-stage distribution relevant to central sensitization in fibromyalgia.

Wearable autonomic monitoring (HRV, skin conductance, temperature, respiratory rate) reveals reduced HRV, heightened sympathetic tone, and blunted parasympathetic responses correlating with pain, stress resilience, and sleep quality in fibromyalgia.

Ecological Momentary Assessment reveals diurnal symptom patterns in fibromyalgia, including morning stiffness, transient mid-day symptom relief, and evening symptom worsening, masked by daily/weekly summary measures.

EMA-derived indices of moment-to-moment symptom volatility are more closely associated with disability, perceived lack of control, and reduced quality of life than mean symptom intensity in fibromyalgia.

EMA combined with wearable sensors shows activity-symptom relationships in fibromyalgia are highly context-dependent, influenced by baseline fatigue, emotional state, prior sleep, and pacing strategies.

Unsupervised machine learning (k-means, hierarchical clustering, Gaussian mixture models) consistently demonstrates that fibromyalgia encompasses heterogeneous phenotypes differing in pain intensity, fatigue, sleep, mood, and functional impairment, often independent of demographic variables.
Predictive modeling approaches (random forests, gradient boosting, neural networks) permit prediction of symptom severity, loss of function, quality of life, and treatment response in fibromyalgia.

SNRIs such as duloxetine and milnacipran modulate descending inhibitory pain pathways and show enhanced efficacy in fibromyalgia patients exhibiting prominent affective dysregulation and central sensitization.
Gabapentinoids (pregabalin, gabapentin) regulate voltage-gated calcium channels to attenuate excitatory neurotransmission, showing benefit in fibromyalgia patients with hyperalgesia or allodynia.
Tricyclic antidepressants provide analgesic and sleep-modulatory effects in fibromyalgia, but their anticholinergic profile can limit tolerability, particularly in older adults.

Low-dose naltrexone acts by attenuating microglial activation and neuroinflammatory cascades, offering a potential therapeutic avenue for fibromyalgia patients with heightened central immune signaling.
Mindfulness-based stress reduction interventions potentiate parasympathetic tone, emotional resilience, and attentional control in fibromyalgia patients.
Graded exercise programs use dose titration tailored to baseline fatigue, pain sensitivity, and cardiovascular function to maximize benefit while minimizing symptom exacerbation in fibromyalgia.
Neurofeedback and other neuromodulation techniques aim to normalize aberrant cortical network activity associated with central pain processing and emotional regulation in fibromyalgia.

Adjunctive neuromodulation strategies including transcranial magnetic stimulation, transcutaneous electrical nerve stimulation, and vagus nerve stimulation support mechanistically informed approaches to restore central pain circuitry and autonomic function in fibromyalgia.

Biomarker-guided enrichment strategies can identify mechanistically homogeneous fibromyalgia patient cohorts, improving signal detection in clinical trials and supporting mechanistic validation of novel interventions.
The Turkish version of COMPASS-31 demonstrated good test-retest reliability with an overall intraclass correlation coefficient of 0.838 in fibromyalgia patients retested after one week.
Subdomain test-retest reliability of the Turkish COMPASS-31 ranged from 0.646 (bladder) to 0.886 (gastrointestinal), indicating variable but generally acceptable stability across domains.
The Turkish COMPASS-31 showed high internal consistency with a total Cronbach's alpha of 0.912, and subdomain alphas ranging from 0.785 to 0.940.
Question 8 of the COMPASS-31 showed a low corrected item-total correlation (0.115) compared to other items, suggesting weaker contribution to the overall scale, along with Questions 12 and 24.

A statistically significant positive correlation was found between total COMPASS-31 scores and total FIQR scores, indicating that greater autonomic symptom burden is associated with greater fibromyalgia-related disability.

Total COMPASS-31 scores showed a strong negative correlation with SF-36 general health perception, indicating that greater autonomic dysfunction is associated with lower health-related quality of life.
COMPASS-31 total score correlated negatively with SF-36 vitality and mental health subscales, supporting convergent validity of the scale.

Consistent with known fibromyalgia epidemiology, the study population was overwhelmingly female (96.6%) and centered in the fourth to fifth decade of life (mean age 43 years), matching reported sex and age distribution of fibromyalgia.

Fibromyalgia is a chronic pain syndrome with widespread musculoskeletal pain, fatigue, non-restorative sleep, and cognitive impairment ('fibro-fog') with a worldwide prevalence of 0.2–6.6% predominating in women.
Neuroimaging in FM has traditionally shown reduced gray matter in cingulate, insula, and prefrontal cortices, with altered connectivity in salience and default mode networks.

In FM, structural and functional cerebellar abnormalities—including lobular atrophy and hypertrophy, disrupted peduncular integrity, and altered connectivity with prefrontal and temporal cortices—correlate with pain sensitivity, affective symptoms, and cognitive dysfunction.

The authors hypothesize that the cerebellum contributes to chronic pain in FM through generation of persistent prediction errors, causing a chronic mismatch between sensorimotor inputs and expected outcomes that disrupts error-based learning and drives maladaptive plasticity.

Animal studies show cerebellar stimulation elevates nociceptive thresholds, morphine injection into anterior cerebellar cortex induces analgesia, and fastigial nucleus modulation reduces visceral reflexes, indicating a bidirectional cerebellar role in pain modulation.
Voxel-based morphometry studies in FM consistently report gray matter reductions in cerebellar lobules IV-V (correlating with disease duration) and lobules VI and VIII.
In contrast to sensorimotor lobule atrophy, gray matter volume increases have been observed in posterior cerebellar regions such as Crus II and VIIb in FM.
Diffusion tensor imaging studies indicate altered microstructural integrity in the cerebellar peduncles and other white matter tracts in FM, suggesting disrupted cerebellar output.

Patients with FM show cerebellar hyperactivation during nociceptive stimulation and at rest, involving sensorimotor lobules VI-VIII and cognitive-affective regions such as Crus I/II and VIIb, with abnormal activity observed at both pain onset and offset.

Connectivity analyses indicate atypical interactions between cerebellar lobules IV-VI, Crus I, and the vermis with medial prefrontal, orbitofrontal, and temporal cortices, correlating with depressive symptoms, cognitive impairment, and increased experimental pain sensitivity.
Human neuroimaging shows increased activity in cerebellar lobule VI and Crus I during pain anticipation, supporting a predictive role of the cerebellum in pain processing.

The authors propose that inhibitory non-invasive brain stimulation protocols (cathodal tDCS or low-frequency rTMS) applied to the posterior cerebellum (Crus II/VIIb) may reduce maladaptive prediction-error signaling, and note early evidence that cerebellar tDCS can alter pain thresholds, though targeted clinical trials are still needed.
The first dedicated study of nociplastic (fibromyalgia-like) pain in multiple sclerosis estimated its prevalence at approximately 17%.
More recent work found that about one-quarter of people with MS who experience chronic pain meet criteria for nociplastic pain, with a further subgroup showing mixed neuropathic-nociplastic features.
MS patients with nociplastic pain tend to report higher pain intensity, more coexisting pain conditions, and greater quality-of-life impairment than those without.
A large US survey linked widespread nociplastic pain in people with MS to reduced physical activity and poorer overall functioning.
Physical activity appears beneficial not only for nociceptive but also for neuropathic and nociplastic pain in MS, mechanisms for which pharmacological options are limited.
