For nociplastic (fibromyalgia-like) pain in MS, NSAIDs and especially opioid therapy should be avoided because efficacy is poor and risks of central sensitization and cognitive side effects are increased.
The prevalence of several headache types, most prominently migraine, is higher in people with MS compared with the general population.
A temporal association between migraine attacks and MS relapses has been discussed, though underlying mechanisms remain incompletely understood.
SIBO prevalence was reported to be as high as 60-100% among patients with bronchial asthma.
SIBO prevalence was reported at 50-87.5% among patients with food allergies.
SIBO prevalence was reported at 30.9% among patients with mast cell activation syndrome.
SIBO prevalence was reported at 27.9% among patients with chronic spontaneous urticaria.
Treating SIBO improved symptoms of bronchial asthma according to the reviewed literature.
Treating SIBO improved symptoms of mast cell activation syndrome according to the reviewed literature.
Unlike in BA and MCAS, treating SIBO did not improve symptoms in patients with chronic spontaneous urticaria.
SIBO is proposed to trigger a Th2-skewed immune response through mucosal pathway activation and low-grade endotoxemia.
SIBO-associated Th2 activation is linked to increased synthesis of IL-4, an interleukin involved in allergic reactions.
SIBO-associated Th2 activation is linked to increased synthesis of IL-5, an interleukin involved in allergic reactions.
SIBO-associated Th2 activation is linked to increased synthesis of IL-13, an interleukin involved in allergic reactions.
Across the reviewed studies, SIBO diagnosis was established using lactulose or glucose hydrogen breath testing.
The authors suggest a 'gut-allergy axis' linking SIBO and atopic disease could offer new therapeutic options and potentially improve quality of life in atopic patients.
Pluviatolide showed no cytotoxicity toward BMMCs at concentrations ranging from 25 to 100 µM as measured by CCK-8 assay.

Pluviatolide inhibited IgE-antigen-induced β-hexosaminidase release (a marker of mast cell degranulation) from BMMCs and RBL-2H3 cells in a concentration-dependent manner with an IC50 of approximately 35.06 µM.

The inhibitory effect of pluviatolide on degranulation was completely reversed after repeated washing steps, with degranulation returning to levels seen in antigen-stimulated controls, indicating a reversible, presence-dependent mechanism of action.
Pluviatolide reduced ionomycin-induced β-hexosaminidase release by 33% at 100 µM compared to DMSO control, indicating inhibition of calcium-dependent, receptor-independent mast cell activation.

Pluviatolide reduced thapsigargin-induced β-hexosaminidase release by 41% at 100 µM compared to DMSO control, further supporting inhibition of receptor-independent, ER Ca2+-ATPase-mediated mast cell activation.
Pluviatolide caused a concentration-dependent reduction in Tnfa and Il6 transcript levels in antigen-stimulated BMMCs as measured by qRT-PCR.
Pluviatolide reduced secretion of TNF-α and IL-6 protein from antigen-stimulated BMMCs as measured by ELISA, corresponding with reduced transcript levels.
Pluviatolide reduced phosphorylation of the proximal FcεRI signaling tyrosine kinases Lyn and Syk in antigen-stimulated BMMCs.
Pluviatolide reduced phosphorylation of the downstream adaptor proteins LAT and PLCγ1 in antigen-stimulated BMMCs.
Pluviatolide reduced antigen-induced activation (phosphorylation) of MAPKs ERK1/2, JNK, and p38 in BMMCs.
Pluviatolide decreased phosphorylation of NF-κB p65 in antigen-stimulated BMMCs, a key regulator of inflammatory cytokine expression.
Oral administration of pluviatolide (20 mg/kg) significantly reduced antigen-induced vascular permeability (Evans blue extravasation) in a passive cutaneous anaphylaxis (PCA) mouse model.
Histological analysis showed a marked reduction in ear tissue mast cell degranulation in pluviatolide-treated mice compared to vehicle controls in the PCA model.
In a preliminary dose-finding pilot experiment, only the 20 mg/kg oral dose of pluviatolide produced a reproducible reduction in PCA responses, while 1 and 5 mg/kg did not (data not shown).
Inotodiol reduces HMGCR protein expression exclusively via ubiquitin-mediated proteasomal degradation, without altering SREBP-dependent transcriptional activity.
Unlike inotodiol, lanosterol reduces HMGCR expression through a mechanism involving SREBP-regulated transcriptional activity, in addition to any post-translational effects.
Both inotodiol and lanosterol suppressed FcεRI-induced mast cell activation, reducing secretory granule release and TNF-α production.
Mast cell stabilization by inotodiol/lanosterol was mechanistically attributed to compromised cortical actin dynamics resulting from impaired actin remodeling and turnover.
Impaired cortical actin dynamics prevented assembly of the LAT signalosome, blocking PLC-γ1 activation that is essential for calcium-dependent mast cell activation.

Co-treatment with mevalonolactone, farnesol, or geranylgeraniol reversed the mast cell-stabilizing effects of both inotodiol and lanosterol, indicating these effects depend on depletion of downstream mevalonate pathway isoprenoids.

Unlike mevalonolactone, farnesol, and geranylgeraniol, squalene did not reverse the mast cell-stabilizing effects of inotodiol and lanosterol, supporting that non-sterol isoprenoids rather than sterol synthesis intermediates mediate the effect.

Because inotodiol downregulates HMGCR solely via ubiquitin-mediated protein degradation without altering SREBP-driven transcription, the authors propose it as a potentially safer anti-allergic therapeutic candidate that avoids the broader transcriptional reprogramming of SREBP-regulated genes seen with lanosterol and statins.

Mast cell activation test (MAT) using free amoxicillin to stimulate CD34+-derived mast cells sensitized with patient sera showed 53.57% sensitivity and 100% specificity for detecting amoxicillin allergy.
MAT using dendrimeric amoxicilloyl conjugates (G4-AXO/G5-AXO) as stimuli achieved 46.43% sensitivity with 100% specificity for amoxicillin allergy diagnosis.
Combining free amoxicillin and dendrimeric conjugate stimuli in the mast cell activation test increased overall sensitivity to 75% while fully preserving 100% specificity.
The mast cell activation test identified positive results among patients classified as basophil activation test (BAT) non-releasers, who would otherwise be missed by conventional BAT diagnosis.
The mast cell activation test detected allergic sensitization in patients with undetectable specific IgE (sIgE) by ImmunoCAP, suggesting greater sensitivity than serological testing in some patients.

Across the entire cohort, prenatal exposure to any disease-modifying therapy for MS was not associated with a difference in cumulative incidence of neurodevelopmental disorders compared with no exposure.

In both univariate and multivariate (adjusted) models, none of the individual DMT classes (interferon-β, glatiramer, monoclonal antibodies, fumarates, or S1PR modulators) were associated with increased risk of neurodevelopmental disorders, with consistent results in a sensitivity analysis limited to pregnancy-only exposure.
Overall, 3.99% of children in the cohort (followed to age 2) had a major congenital anomaly, with no significant difference in most DMT-exposed groups compared with unexposed children.
In the main analysis, prenatal exposure to S1PR modulators showed a non-significant trend toward higher risk of major congenital anomalies compared with unexposed children.

In a sensitivity analysis counting only exposure occurring between conception and birth (excluding the 6-month washout period), prenatal S1PR modulator exposure was significantly associated with increased risk of major congenital anomalies, an association that remained significant after adjustment and in a further sensitivity analysis restricting controls to the same birth year.

The authors propose, based on prior mechanistic literature, that S1P/S1PR signaling is critical to embryonic cardiac and CNS development (e.g., neural tube closure, atrioventricular canal formation), offering a plausible mechanism for the teratogenic signal observed with S1PR modulators.
Daidzein pretreatment reduced allergic manifestations and mast-cell activation in an OVA-induced murine food allergy model.
Daidzein shifted the immune response toward a Th1-biased profile, effectively reducing Th2- and Th17-associated cytokines in the food allergy model.
Daidzein strengthened intestinal barrier integrity by upregulating Claudin-1 expression in the food allergy model.
Daidzein strengthened intestinal barrier integrity by upregulating ZO-1 expression in the food allergy model.
Daidzein remodeled the gut microbial community by enriching butyrate-producing genera such as Roseburia in the food allergy model.
Elevated fecal butyrate levels in daidzein-treated mice were positively associated with enrichment of butyrate-producing Roseburia.
PEA stabilizes mast cells and prevents their degranulation as part of its pleiotropic anti-inflammatory function.
A clinical trial reported efficacy of ultramicronized PEA for migraine prophylaxis in children.
In 24 migraine patients, plasma PEA levels significantly increased 120 minutes after nitroglycerin administration used to experimentally trigger a migraine attack.
In an open-label study of 25 adult migraine patients, PEA taken every 12 hours for 3 months reduced monthly attack frequency, intensity, and improved sleep quality.
A single-blind study of 20 adult patients with migraine with aura found statistically significant pain relief after 60 days of umPEA 1200 mg/day given for 90 days.
In a rat model of sciatic nerve constriction, PEA levels significantly decreased in the spinal cord 3 days after injury and in the dorsal raphe and rostral ventral medulla 7 days after injury.
PEA was suggested to help manage autism-spectrum-disorder symptoms, potentially via mucin-degrading gut bacteria (Akkermansia, Ruminococcus) modulating endocannabinoidome mediator levels.

Perinatal non-allergic activation of mast cells by infections or stress-related triggers may cause in utero brain inflammation, potentially inducing preterm labor and increasing future risk of autism spectrum disorder.
PEA showed higher treatment success rates for fibromyalgia pain compared with duloxetine or pregabalin.

A meta-analysis of double-blind RCTs found PEA (300-1200 mg/day for 8-12 weeks) increased quality of life and improved sleep while reducing symptom severity versus placebo across neurological, gynecological, musculoskeletal, and irritable bowel syndrome patients.
Using genetically and pharmacologically mast-cell-deficient mice, Nautiyal et al. showed brain mast cell numbers fluctuate under stress and influence propensity to develop anxiety-like behaviors.
Mast-cell-derived IL-4 and IL-13 promote Th2 cell differentiation, while TNF-α and tryptase promote dendritic cell maturation and IL-12 production, facilitating Th1 polarization.

Mast-cell-derived IL-4 activates STAT6 signaling in dendritic cells, upregulating CCL17 and CCL22 chemokines that recruit Th2 cells and promote a microglial switch toward a pro-inflammatory phenotype.
PEA administration has been used to enhance innate immunity responses and regulate mast cell degranulation in patients with SARS-CoV-2 infection.
Tussilagone significantly reduced Tween 80- and substance P-induced systemic pseudo-allergic reactions in vivo.
Tussilagone attenuated passive cutaneous anaphylaxis (PCA) reactions in the animal model.
Tussilagone suppressed degranulation of LAD2 mast cells in vitro.
Tussilagone decreased production of the inflammatory cytokines TNF-alpha, IL-8, and MCP-1 from activated mast cells.
Tussilagone suppressed Tween 80- and substance P-induced calcium influx in MRGPRX2-expressing HEK293 cells.

Tussilagone inhibited tolimidone-induced Lyn kinase activation and suppressed substance P- and Tween 80-induced beta-hexosaminidase release, with an inhibitory profile comparable to the Lyn/Btk antagonist bosutinib.
Tussilagone suppressed Tween 80- and substance P-induced calcium influx in HEK293 cells expressing MRGPRX2.
Tussilagone inhibited tolimidone-induced activation of Lyn kinase, showing an inhibitory effect comparable to the Lyn/Btk antagonist bosutinib.
Tussilagone suppressed substance P- and Tween 80-induced β-hexosaminidase release from mast cells, with an inhibitory profile similar to bosutinib.
Tussilagone reduced phosphorylation of the MRGPRX2 downstream signaling molecules Btk, PLCγ1, PKC, p38 MAPK, IκB-α, and NF-κB p65.
Prior studies cited show that intraepithelial nerve fiber density in the tongue is reduced by 30-60% in patients with BMS, indicating peripheral trigeminal small fiber neuropathy.
TRPV1 receptor is upregulated in affected oral tissues of BMS patients, supporting a peripheral nociceptive component.
P2X3 purinergic receptor is upregulated in affected oral tissues of BMS patients, supporting a peripheral nociceptive component.
Neurophysiological and functional imaging studies cited show deficient pain-inhibitory mechanisms, altered brainstem reflexes, and abnormal central processing of pain and taste in BMS.
BMS has an estimated general population prevalence of ~0.7% but affects up to 10-15% of postmenopausal women.
Randomized trials cited have shown that topical clonazepam and capsaicin provide benefit for BMS symptoms.

Serial bilateral greater and lesser occipital nerve blocks (lidocaine plus betamethasone) produced progressive relief in a case of refractory BMS, with 50% improvement after the first block, 80% after the second, and complete remission after the third, sustained at 24-month follow-up.
Initial treatment with low-dose amitriptyline (25 mg) and gabapentin (900 mg/day) produced approximately 30% improvement in pain intensity after two months, but relief remained incomplete.

A prior study (Grémeau-Richard et al. 2010) found that lingual nerve block with lidocaine transiently abolished pain in about half of BMS patients, but pain promptly recurred once the anesthetic wore off.

A prior case report (Walega et al. 2014) demonstrated significant, sustained relief in a patient with recalcitrant BMS using bilateral stellate ganglion block, suggesting a role for sympathetic nervous system involvement.

Approximately 12 months after achieving remission, the patient experienced a mild relapse of burning sensation (about 20% of original pain level), which was again fully resolved with a fourth occipital nerve block.

The authors hypothesize that pain relief from occipital nerve block in BMS occurs via inhibition of afferent traffic into the trigeminal nucleus caudalis through the trigeminocervical complex, thereby quieting central sensitization driving oral burning pain.

The authors identify seven clinical features (bilateral distribution, absence of local triggers, constant burning pattern, associated dysgeusia, partial response to systemic neuromodulators, stress-related exacerbation, and normal peripheral exam) that together support classifying this patient's BMS as centrally mediated.
Bortezomib-treated mice fed standard chow developed mechanical allodynia beginning on day 3 that persisted for the remainder of the study.
A ketogenic diet prevented development of bortezomib-induced mechanical allodynia, keeping mechanical thresholds similar to vehicle-treated chow-fed controls.

Bortezomib-treated groups showed a significant increase in cold-evoked nociceptive behaviors (biting, licking, favoring) compared with vehicle groups, and cold sensitivity developed in both chow- and KD-fed BTZ mice, though KD-fed mice recovered during washout while chow-fed mice worsened.
Bortezomib-treated chow-fed mice had significantly decreased intraepidermal nerve fiber density compared with all other groups, and this reduction was prevented by a ketogenic diet.
Vehicle-treated ketogenic diet-fed animals had a significantly increased neurite outgrowth (total square-to-cell-body ratio) from harvested DRG compared with chow-fed groups.
Lower IENFD significantly correlated with worse (higher) mechanical sensitivity thresholds across mice.
Lower IENFD significantly correlated with worse (higher) cold sensitivity response frequency across mice.
In vivo circulating blood ketone levels significantly correlated with subsequent in vitro DRG neurite outgrowth, suggesting a metabolic memory effect of ketosis on neurons.
Bortezomib-treated chow-fed DRG neurons showed a significant increase in maximum and spare glycolytic capacity (ECAR) compared with all other groups, an effect prevented by ketogenic diet.

Baseline mitochondrial respiration (OCR) did not differ significantly between groups, though BTZ-treated chow-fed animals differed from vehicle-treated chow-fed animals after FCCP injection; specific mitochondrial respiration measures showed no significant group differences.
Exogenous ketone pretreatment in vitro significantly mitigated bortezomib-induced neurite degeneration in DRG neurons, though not fully to control levels.
Mice fed a ketogenic diet had significantly elevated blood beta-hydroxybutyrate levels confirming entry into ketosis, regardless of bortezomib treatment.
Genetically predicted higher circulating fractalkine (CX3CL1) levels were associated with a reduced risk of glossopharyngeal nerve disease.
Genetically predicted higher circulating SLAMF1 levels were associated with a reduced risk of glossopharyngeal nerve disease.
Genetically predicted higher circulating TNF levels were associated with a reduced risk of glossopharyngeal nerve disease.
Genetically predicted higher circulating TNFRSF9 levels were associated with a reduced risk of glossopharyngeal nerve disease.
Genetically predicted higher circulating matrix metalloproteinase-1 (MMP-1) levels were associated with an increased risk of glossopharyngeal nerve disease.
In reverse-direction MR, genetic liability to glossopharyngeal nerve disease was associated with decreased circulating neurotrophin-3 (NT-3) levels.
Genetically predicted higher circulating FGF21 levels were associated with an increased risk of phantom limb syndrome with pain.
Genetically predicted higher circulating osteoprotegerin levels were associated with an increased risk of phantom limb syndrome with pain.
Genetic liability to phantom limb syndrome with pain was associated with reduced circulating IL-10RA levels in reverse-direction MR.
Genetic liability to phantom limb syndrome with pain was associated with reduced circulating IL-17A levels in reverse-direction MR.
Genetic liability to phantom limb syndrome with pain was associated with reduced circulating TNFSF12 levels in reverse-direction MR.
Genetically predicted higher circulating CD40 ligand levels were associated with a lower risk of small fiber neuropathy.
Genetically predicted higher circulating CCL8 levels were associated with a lower risk of small fiber neuropathy.
Genetically predicted higher circulating oncostatin M levels were associated with a lower risk of small fiber neuropathy.
Genetically predicted higher circulating IL-20RA levels were associated with an increased risk of small fiber neuropathy.
Genetically predicted higher circulating IL-24 levels were associated with an increased risk of small fiber neuropathy.
Genetic liability to small fiber neuropathy was associated with reduced circulating IL-2RB levels in reverse-direction MR.
Genetic liability to small fiber neuropathy was associated with reduced circulating IL-5 levels in reverse-direction MR.
Lower genetically predicted circulating SIRT2 levels were associated with an increased risk of unspecified neuralgia or neuritis, suggesting a protective role.
Higher genetically predicted levels of CCL28, CD244, FGF23, FGF5, IL-12B, and CCL3 were each associated with elevated risk of unspecified neuralgia or neuritis.
Genetic liability to unspecified neuralgia or neuritis was associated with reduced circulating CCL23 levels in reverse-direction MR.
Genetically predicted higher circulating FGF23 levels were associated with increased risk of unspecified neuralgia or neuritis.
Genetically predicted higher circulating FGF5 levels were associated with increased risk of unspecified neuralgia or neuritis.
Genetically predicted higher circulating IL-12B levels were associated with increased risk of unspecified neuralgia or neuritis.

Genetically predicted higher circulating CCL3 levels were associated with increased risk of unspecified neuralgia or neuritis, consistent with prior evidence implicating CCL3 in monocyte recruitment and macrophage activation in neuropathic pain models.
In reverse-direction MR, genetic liability to neuralgia or neuritis was associated with decreased circulating CCL23 levels.
In reverse-direction MR, genetic liability to neuralgia or neuritis was associated with increased circulating CXCL5 levels, suggesting a bidirectional interaction between CXCL5 and neuropathic pain.
IC/BPS was strongly associated with a comorbid diagnosis of irritable bowel syndrome in a phenome-wide analysis of the eMERGE-III cohort.
Dysuria was strongly associated with IC/BPS diagnosis, validating the phenotyping approach.
Polyuria was strongly associated with IC/BPS diagnosis in the phenome-wide analysis.
IC/BPS was associated with gastroesophageal reflux disease and oesophagitis, supporting a shared epithelial dysfunction mechanism.
IC/BPS was associated with allergic rhinitis in the phenome-wide comorbidity analysis.
A novel comorbidity signal was identified between IC/BPS and anaphylactic shock.
IC/BPS was associated with intervertebral disc disorders.
IC/BPS was associated with laxity of ligament or hypermobility syndrome in the phenome-wide analysis.
Chronic pain and anxiety showed suggestive (sub-Bonferroni-significance) associations with IC/BPS.
In a more conservative secondary comorbidity analysis, IC/BPS was newly associated with Barrett's esophagus and osteoarthrosis/osteoarthritis.
DNAAF4 (DYX1C1) was the top gene in ultra-rare damaging variant gene-burden collapsing analysis, with 3 case carriers and no control carriers, though not study-wide significant.
HTR7, a serotonin receptor gene implicated in visceral hypersensitivity in IBS, was highlighted as having multiple case carriers of qualifying ultra-rare damaging variants and no control carriers.
The 5-gene Mendelian-disorder gene-set containing ATP2A2 and ATP2C1 showed significant enrichment of ultra-rare damaging variants in IC/BPS cases, replicating a prior association.
Network-based heterogeneity clustering identified a gene cluster (including SMAD3) enriched for the anaphase-promoting complex-dependent catabolic process pathway among IC/BPS cases.
A gene cluster including EGF and PIK3R3 was enriched for positive regulation of the MAPK cascade pathway among IC/BPS cases.
Integrin/focal adhesion network genes were enriched in an NHC gene cluster among IC/BPS cases, implicating mechanotransduction signaling.

Fast preranked gene-set enrichment analysis (fGSEA) of ultra-rare variant burden found significant enrichment of the 'Transport of small molecules' pathway (including ATP2C1, ATP2A2, and multiple SLC genes) in IC/BPS cases, robust across 1000 permutation runs.
A synonymous SLC9A5 variant showed the strongest single-variant (ExWAS) association with IC/BPS, but its low TraP score suggests it is likely benign rather than a true risk variant.

A synonymous CD68 variant was the second most significant ExWAS association with IC/BPS, but is likely benign given its low TraP score; CD68 encodes a scavenger receptor downregulated in Hunner lesions.

A rare segregating missense PIEZO2 variant was identified via family-based analysis in a family with multiple affected members; PIEZO2 encodes a mechanosensitive ion channel implicated in bladder micturition control and visceral hypersensitivity in IBS.

A de novo PLXNA4 variant was identified in one of 13 IC/BPS trios; PLXNA4 marks a sentinel urothelial cell subtype involved in immune signalling and wound repair, suggesting a plausible mechanism for defective epithelial repair in IC/BPS.
One IC/BPS-affected individual carried a pathogenic 16p11.2 duplication CNV, previously also identified in congenital anomalies of the kidney and urinary tract.
The HLA-DQ2.5 haplotype (DQA1*05:01 and DQB1*02:01) was associated with Hunner lesion status among IC/BPS patients, suggesting a mucosal autoimmune contribution.
Superficial retinal vessel density (whole, foveal, and parafoveal) measured by OCT-A was significantly reduced in MCTD patients compared with healthy controls.
Deep vascular plexus densities (DWD and DPFD) were significantly reduced in MCTD patients compared with healthy controls.
Perifoveal vessel density in both superficial and deep vascular plexi was significantly decreased in MCTD patients compared with healthy controls.
Foveal avascular zone area did not differ between MCTD patients and healthy controls.
Structural OCT retinal thickness (foveal and parafoveal) was similar between MCTD patients and healthy controls.
In MCTD patients, older age was inversely correlated with both superficial and deep retinal vessel density.
In healthy controls, older age was also inversely correlated with superficial and deep retinal vessel density.
No difference in retinal vessel density was found between elderly (≥65y) and non-elderly subjects, suggesting disease duration rather than chronological age may drive vascular changes.
Longer MCTD disease duration was positively correlated with higher plasma creatinine levels.
Longer MCTD disease duration was inversely correlated with deep whole retinal vessel density (DWD).
Estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR) was positively correlated with deep whole retinal vessel density (DWD) in MCTD patients.
Serum complement C3 levels were positively correlated with patient age in the MCTD cohort.

Serum complement C3 levels correlated with superficial parafoveal retinal vessel density (SPFD) in MCTD patients; the authors interpreted higher C3 (complement activation) as linked to vascular changes, though the discussion described this as an inverse relationship despite a positive correlation coefficient being reported.
No difference in OCT-A retinal vessel density measurements was found between MCTD patients on steroids versus those not on steroids.
Nailfold videocapillaroscopy showed non-specific microvascular abnormalities in 60% of MCTD patients and scleroderma-like patterns in 40%.
No significant correlation was found between OCT-A retinal vessel density and nailfold videocapillaroscopy pattern (non-specific vs scleroderma-like) in MCTD patients.
No difference in OCT-A retinal vessel density was found between MCTD patients with versus without lung involvement (UIP, GGO, NSIP).
Anti-U1-RNP antibodies, a defining serologic marker of MCTD, were detected in 100% of the study patients.
Raynaud's phenomenon was present in the entire MCTD study population.
Among 221 hospital employees previously surveyed, 11.8% reported persistent fatigue when recontacted at reassessment following mild SARS-CoV-2 infection.

Applying the Canadian Consensus Criteria, at least 3.2% of the 221-employee cohort fulfilled diagnostic criteria for ME/CFS approximately 21 months after SARS-CoV-2 infection, with the estimate potentially ranging up to 9.0% under alternative assumptions.

All 19 assessed hospital employees were classified as having post-COVID-19 syndrome (PCS), with no alternative explanation found for their symptoms; of these, 36.8% met ME/CFS criteria (PCS-ME/CFS) and 63.2% did not (PCS-non-ME/CFS).
Functional impairment measured by the Bell disability score was similar between subgroups, with a median of 60/100 overall (60 for PCS-ME/CFS, 65 for PCS-non-ME/CFS).

Fatigue and insomnia were universally reported (19/19), with concentration disorders and palpitations in 94.7% and memory disorders, breathlessness, limb weakness and anxiety in 84.2%, persisting for a median of at least 550 days.
In the orthostatic test, 1 of 19 hospital employees was diagnosed with POTS (heart rate increase >30 bpm or standing HR >120 bpm).
Orthostatic hypotension was found in 21.0% (4/19) of participants in the orthostatic test.

Cognitive testing with the MoCA showed a mean score below normal (25.63/30), with 42.1% of participants scoring below the cutoff for normal cognition; ME/CFS patients scored lower on average than non-ME/CFS patients.

Exploratory small fiber neuropathy screening (burning pain, sensory disorders, sleep disorders due to pain, nocturnal pain, hyperesthesia) was positive in a substantial proportion, with ME/CFS participants reporting more positive items on average than non-ME/CFS participants (3.29 vs 1.08).
Acute phase reactant abnormalities were seen in a subset of participants, with increased fibrinogen and factor VIII in 16.7% each and decreased antithrombin in 11.1%.
Von Willebrand factor was elevated in a third of participants, with the highest proportion of abnormal values among all coagulation markers assessed, suggesting a shift toward thrombogenic activity.
Homocysteine concentration was elevated above the reference threshold (<10 μmol/L) in the majority of participants tested, with a median of 13.0 μmol/L.
IgG autoantibodies against the M3 muscarinic acetylcholine receptor were increased in the large majority of participants tested.
IgG autoantibodies against the ß2-adrenergic receptor were increased in two-thirds of participants tested.

IgG autoantibodies against M4 muscarinic receptor and angiotensin II type 1 receptor were each elevated in about one-fifth of participants tested, and combined GPCR autoantibody levels were low-grade increased in 44.4% and increased in 22.2% of participants overall.
Serological evidence consistent with possible EBV reactivation (positive IgG or IgM against early/immediate-early antigens) was found in the large majority of tested participants.

IgG antibodies against EBNA1 and p18/p23 VCA were positive in nearly all/all tested participants, and IgM against VCA and ZEBRA IEA were all negative, indicating prior primary EBV infection rather than acute infection in this cohort.
Increased monocyte counts, supportive of EBV reactivation, were found in 40.0% of participants tested.

Vitamin D-25-OH levels were markedly decreased in the large majority of participants, an unexpectedly low finding compared to prior PCS/ME-CFS studies where levels were within normal range; the authors caution this finding is not disease-specific or causal.
Metabolic abnormalities included increased total cholesterol, increased triglycerides, low HDL-cholesterol, and increased LDL-cholesterol in a substantial minority to majority of tested participants.
Thrombelastography (ROTEM) and routine coagulation markers (Quick/INR, thrombin time) showed no major coagulopathies or abnormalities despite altered acute phase reactants.
Among 216 post-COVID-19 syndrome rehabilitation outpatients, 15 (6.9%) met Canadian Consensus Criteria for ME/CFS.
PCS patients meeting ME/CFS criteria were significantly younger than those without the ME/CFS phenotype.
Female sex was significantly more common among PCS patients meeting ME/CFS criteria compared to those without the phenotype.
Baseline fatigue severity, measured by the Fatigue Assessment Scale, was significantly higher in the ME/CFS phenotype group than in the non-ME/CFS group.
Fatigue scores failed to improve with rehabilitation in the ME/CFS phenotype group, in contrast to significant improvement in the non-ME/CFS group.
Baseline six-minute walk test distance was significantly lower in the ME/CFS phenotype group compared with the non-ME/CFS group.
Both ME/CFS and non-ME/CFS groups improved on the six-minute walk test over the course of rehabilitation, with no significant difference in the magnitude of improvement between groups.
During fMRI, people with CFS showed higher BOLD signal in the right rostral caudate than healthy controls specifically while suppressing anger-related memories.
CFS participants showed higher BOLD signal in the left rostral caudate than controls specifically during suppression of fatigue-related memories.
There was only a nonsignificant trend toward lower BOLD signal in the posterior putamen in CFS versus controls during anger suppression, though task-dependent group differences were observed.
CFS patients showed significantly higher BOLD signal in the left posterior insula than controls while actively recalling both anger and fatigue-related memories.
Voxel-based morphometry found no significant whole-brain grey matter volume differences between CFS patients and healthy controls.
During the in-scanner tasks, people with CFS reported significantly higher fatigue ratings than healthy controls across conditions.
CFS participants reported significantly higher distress ratings than controls after completing the memory tasks.
Despite neural differences, CFS and control groups did not differ in self-reported task adherence, including memory vividness, suppression effort, success at suppression, or time spent counting.
In controls, left caudate BOLD signal during fatigue suppression correlated significantly with post-scenario fatigue ratings, but this brain-behaviour relationship was absent in CFS patients.

Across both groups combined, greater left insula BOLD signal while thinking about anger was associated with lower subsequent distress ratings, with controls showing the strongest effect and CFS showing only a nonsignificant trend.

CFS participants had significantly higher self-reported anxiety and depression symptoms than controls despite exclusion of current psychiatric conditions, consistent with known comorbidity between CFS and mood/anxiety disorders.

Pre-treatment with Diosgenin (10, 20, and 40 mg/kg, i.p.) for 21 days significantly reduced immobility duration in forced swim and tail suspension tests in an LPS-induced mouse model of chronic fatigue syndrome.
Diosgenin treatment improved anxiety-like behavior, thermal hyperalgesia, locomotor activity, and grip strength deficits induced by LPS.
Diosgenin reduced LPS-induced elevation of nitrite (total nitric oxide) levels in brain homogenate.
Diosgenin decreased LPS-induced lipid peroxidation in brain tissue.
Diosgenin restored/increased the activity of antioxidant enzymes (SOD, catalase) and reduced glutathione levels that were depleted by LPS.
Diosgenin reduced LPS-induced elevated levels of tumor necrosis factor-alpha (TNF-α) in brain tissue.

A patient with persistent fatigue, intermittent fever, anorexia, and weight loss was initially given a diagnosis of chronic fatigue syndrome after pulmonary, cardiac, and other organ workups were unremarkable, but her symptoms persisted and she was later found to have renal sarcoidosis on kidney biopsy.

Participants with chronic overlapping pain conditions reported an average of 4.40 distinct COPCs, with fibromyalgia, chronic low back pain, and chronic fatigue syndrome being the most commonly reported.
Most participants (72%) were currently receiving medical treatment for their COPCs, most frequently from primary care physicians.
Participants averaged 2.82 current health care providers and 4.28 past providers consulted for their pain conditions.
Despite extensive health care engagement, 77.7% of participants reported no improvement or worsening of their condition.
No significant associations were found between the number of health care providers or medications used and clinical pain or psychosocial outcomes.
In HEK293 cells with the MMTV promoter, MR rs5522 showed slightly higher EC50 (lower potency) than wild-type MR but similar fold-activation across all corticosteroids tested.
With the TAT3 promoter, MR rs5522 had a higher EC50 (lower affinity) and lower fold-activation for cortisol compared to wild-type MR.
With the TAT3 promoter, MR rs5522 showed slightly lower EC50 (higher affinity) and higher fold-activation for aldosterone and corticosterone compared to wild-type MR.

Spironolactone and progesterone showed similar antagonist activity against MR rs5522 and wild-type MR (Ile-180) in both MMTV and TAT3 promoter systems, suggesting these agents could be used to regulate brain MR rs5522 activity.
The mean diagnostic delay for hEDS/HSD in the UK survey population was 19.0-21.7 years.
Chronic pain was reported by 83.9% of survey respondents with hEDS/HSD.
Joint subluxations were reported by 73.8% of survey respondents with hEDS/HSD.
Gastrointestinal manifestations were reported by 66.3% of survey respondents with hEDS/HSD.
High rates of neurodivergence were observed among survey respondents with hEDS/HSD, suggesting comorbidity with autism spectrum and related conditions.
Unemployment was reported by 45.6% of survey respondents with hEDS/HSD.
Disrupted education was reported by 55.9% of survey respondents with hEDS/HSD.
Benefit dependence was reported by 47.9% of survey respondents with hEDS/HSD.
Regional differences in access to care and heavy reliance on private healthcare were noted among UK respondents with hEDS/HSD.
The survey identified regional differences in access to diagnosis and care for hEDS/HSD across the United Kingdom.
Respondents reported heavy reliance on private healthcare for diagnosis and management of hEDS/HSD.
Nearly all patients (98.8%) had an increased C6-atlas interval (>10 mm), a radiographic measure of forward head posture, with a cohort mean of 39.12 mm.
96.4% of patients showed ligamentous cervical instability (facet joint translation >2 mm) at C1-C2 in lateral flexion, with a mean total translation of 7.84 mm.
94.9% of patients had decreased depth of cervical lordotic curve (normal 7-10mm), with a cohort mean of only 1.58 mm.
Multidirectional ligamentous instability was found in the lower cervical spine, with mean flexion instability of 5.29 mm and extension instability of 4.41 mm (both above the 4 mm normal cutoff).
Optic nerve sheath diameter (a marker of intracranial pressure) was elevated in 87.9% (left) and 80.7% (right) of patients, with cohort means of 7.28 mm and 7.17 mm, well above normal (<5.0-5.4mm).

95.2% of patients had slightly elevated pupil diameters bilaterally (>4mm), with bilateral total mean of 10.83mm and elevated percent light constriction (74.9% vs normal 30-60%), suggestive of a sympathetic-dominant state.
Vagus nerve cross-sectional area was reduced in 98.8% (right) and 91.7% (left) of patients relative to normative values, with cohort means of 1.22mm2 (right) and 1.34mm2 (left).

Internal jugular vein cross-sectional area at C1 (supine) was below normal (<90mm2) in 91.7% (left) and 95.2% (right) of patients, with cohort means of 40.97mm2 and 39.94mm2 respectively, indicating compression at the atlas.

Vagus nerve cross-sectional area was significantly smaller in hEDS patients (mean 2.55mm2 total) compared to healthy controls from a prior study (mean 4.00mm2), a very large effect (Cohen's d = -2.20).
Lying on a Denneroll cervical extension traction device significantly increased IJV cross-sectional area at C1 compared to supine positioning without the device (105.1mm2 vs 80.4mm2).

IJV cross-sectional area at C1 was significantly smaller than at C4-C5 in the supine position, indicating that compression is concentrated at the level of the atlas and could be missed with standard mid-neck ultrasound evaluation.

The most frequently reported symptoms at initial presentation were brain fog (95%), fatigue (94%), headaches (93%), concentration difficulty (92%), and neck pain (92%), each far exceeding general population prevalence.
83.1% of the cohort self-reported experiencing more than 20 symptoms at initial intake, underscoring the multisystem burden of hEDS.
75% of the cohort had a prior diagnosis of dysautonomia, consistent with the broad reported range (31-94%) in the hEDS literature.
34.5% of patients had ocular hypertension (IOP >42.0 mmHg), with a mean bilateral total IOP of 38.34 mmHg and no significant left-right difference.

Whole-exome sequencing identified a novel heterozygous deep intronic COL5A1 variant (c.1774-95C>T) in the proband that segregated with classical EDS features in the family and was prioritized based on strong phenotype-genotype concordance.

Minigene splicing assay showed the mutant COL5A1 construct produced an aberrant transcript containing a 139-bp pseudoexon insertion from intron 15, in addition to the normal transcript, whereas the wild-type construct produced only the expected exon 15-17 transcript.

The aberrantly spliced transcript is predicted to introduce a premature termination codon shortly downstream of the pseudoexon, producing a truncated protein consistent with a loss-of-function/haploinsufficiency mechanism.
Following functional splicing evidence, the variant was reclassified from a variant of uncertain significance (VUS) to likely pathogenic under ACMG criteria.

The proband presented with multiple atrophic scars, widespread bruising, soft and hyperextensible velvety skin, and hypermobile finger joints, with a history of fragile skin, frequent injuries, and slow wound healing since childhood, consistent with classical EDS.

The proband's father, presumed variant carrier, showed a milder phenotype (skin laxity and mild dysmorphic craniofacial features), while the mother showed no abnormal features, suggesting variable expressivity within the family.

The authors propose that antisense oligonucleotides (ASOs) targeting the cryptic splice site activated by c.1774-95C>T could, in principle, restore normal COL5A1 splicing as a future personalized therapy, though this was not experimentally tested.

A patient with a clinical phenotype consistent with periodontal Ehlers-Danlos syndrome did not carry variants in C1R or C1S, the genes typically implicated in this EDS subtype, suggesting additional genetic causes exist.
The title indicates a case report describing a novel variant of Ehlers-Danlos syndrome linked to a mutation in the COL1A2 gene; no further detail is available from title alone.
All 11 patients across the six identified EDS subtypes presented with joint hypermobility and skin hyperextensibility as shared core features.

Genetic testing (whole-exome sequencing, clinical exome sequencing, and Sanger sequencing) identified six distinct EDS subtypes among the 11 patients: cardiac valvular EDS, dermatosparaxis EDS, musculocontractural EDS type 1, combined osteogenesis imperfecta/EDS type 2, brittle cornea syndrome type 2, and kyphoscoliotic EDS types 1 and 2.
Eight distinct variants were detected across the cohort, including two novel variants, expanding the known molecular spectrum of EDS.
Molecular diagnosis of cardiac valvular EDS prompted implementation of subtype-specific cardiologic monitoring for affected patients.
Molecular diagnosis of brittle cornea syndrome type 2 enabled early ophthalmologic intervention in affected patients.
Molecular diagnosis of dermatosparaxis EDS guided avoidance of invasive procedures due to tissue fragility risk.
Molecular diagnosis of combined osteogenesis imperfecta/EDS type 2 led to implementation of fracture-preventive measures.
One patient was diagnosed with musculocontractural EDS type 1, a subtype identified among the cohort of 11 patients.
Patients with combined osteogenesis imperfecta/EDS type 2 were identified, and molecular diagnosis led to implementation of fracture-preventive measures.
Kyphoscoliotic EDS types 1 and 2 were among the six subtypes molecularly diagnosed in this cohort.
Two novel pathogenic variants were identified among the eight variants detected across the cohort, expanding the known molecular spectrum of EDS.
The study noted intrafamilial variability in clinical presentation among EDS patients from the same families.
The authors highlight the need to consider possible dual diagnoses of EDS subtypes, particularly in consanguineous families.
Molecular diagnosis was reported to improve surgical risk management across all EDS subtypes in the cohort.
Patient 1 was found to carry compound heterozygous TNXB variants (c.7222C>T and c.8780T>C) located in trans on non-homologous exons, confirming a molecular diagnosis of classical-like EDS.
Patient 2 carried compound heterozygous TNXB variants (a novel frameshift c.5947_5948delinsTT and a missense c.8300C>T) in trans, confirming a molecular diagnosis of classical-like EDS.

The authors hypothesize that the c.5947_5948delinsTT frameshift variant produces a truncated protein likely subject to nonsense-mediated mRNA decay (NMD), a mechanism previously linked to more severe clEDS phenotypes.
Both parents of Patient 1, each heterozygous carriers of a single TNXB missense variant, were clinically asymptomatic for clEDS.

The mother and maternal grandfather of Patient 2, both heterozygous carriers of the frameshift TNXB variant c.5947_5948delinsTT, presented with mild joint hypermobility, suggesting possible haploinsufficiency.

Patient 1 exhibited multiple extra-EDS comorbidities including inflammatory bowel disease, multiple food intolerances, tachycardia, microalbuminuria, suspected (unconfirmed) mast cell activation syndrome, and asthma.
Patient 2, in addition to clEDS features, was diagnosed with ADHD and autism spectrum disorder.

Because the identified TNXB variants in both patients were located in exons non-homologous to the TNXA pseudogene, the risk of diagnostic misinterpretation from TNXA-TNXB sequence homology was minimised.
MLPA analysis of the TNXB gene detected no structural (copy number) variants in either patient.
The identified TNXB variants (in this and prior published clEDS cohorts) were all previously unreported and did not cluster into recurrent, population-specific hotspots.
Vascular Ehlers-Danlos syndrome is caused by pathogenic variants in COL3A1 leading to abnormal type III collagen and high risk of arterial dissection and rupture.
Genetic testing for COL3A1 variants enables cascade screening of relatives and informs prognosis through genotype-phenotype correlations.

Medical management of VEDS emphasizes strict blood pressure control typically using beta-blockers and angiotensin receptor blockers, along with lifestyle modification and avoidance of high-risk medications.

Both open and endovascular surgical interventions are increasingly feasible in VEDS patients with careful selection and technique, though iatrogenic injury and device-related complication risks remain substantial.
Pregnancy in VEDS patients carries significant maternal risk, necessitating specialized management.
Vascular Ehlers-Danlos syndrome is caused by mutations in the COL3A1 gene, which encodes type III collagen, leading to arterial fragility and joint hypermobility.
Internal carotid artery dissection occurs at higher rates in individuals with vEDS compared to those without, particularly following Valsalva maneuvers or physical exertion.

A 22-week structured, moderate-intensity progressive aerobic and resistance exercise training program via cardiac rehabilitation increased 6-minute walk test distance by 58% (417 m to 658 m) in a patient with vEDS after two carotid artery dissections.
Following the structured exercise program, the patient's depression severity (PHQ-9) decreased from a score of 4 to 2, and he discontinued benzodiazepine use.
Health-related quality of life improved after the exercise program, with the Dartmouth Co-Operative Charts score decreasing (improving) from 21 to 15.

One month after completing cardiac rehabilitation, repeat MR angiography showed no evidence of new vascular pathology and confirmed stable vascular status, with the pre-existing left ICA pseudoaneurysm remaining stable, indicating the structured exercise program did not provoke vascular complications.

The patient experienced kinesiophobia (fear of exercise/movement) after his arterial dissection, which the authors note is common in similar individuals and required management through shared decision-making during rehabilitation.

Prior to structured exercise intervention, exercise restriction and fear of recurrent dissection led to a sedentary lifestyle with significant deconditioning, 11-kg weight loss, anxiety requiring benzodiazepine treatment, and medical withdrawal from college.
Vascular Ehlers-Danlos syndrome is an autosomal dominant disorder caused by pathogenic variants in the COL3A1 gene encoding collagen type III alpha-1 chain.
Pulmonary complications of vEDS include cavitary lesions, cysts, bullae, fibrous nodules, pneumothorax, hemopneumothorax, and pulmonary hemorrhage.
Spontaneous pneumothorax can be an early presenting sign of vEDS, sometimes occurring before intestinal or vascular complications appear.
Pneumothorax or hemopneumothorax is listed as one of the formal diagnostic criteria for vascular Ehlers-Danlos syndrome.

Deficiency of type III collagen in pulmonary tissue in vEDS weakens the pulmonary parenchyma and subpleural supporting structures, predisposing to bullae/subpleural emphysema formation and subsequent pneumothorax on rupture.
A multi-institutional study by Shalhub et al. found the prevalence of spontaneous pneumothorax/hemothorax among patients diagnosed with vEDS to be 8.7%.

Boussouar et al. found that 12.5% of a large vEDS cohort with long-term CT follow-up had a history of spontaneous pneumothorax, with emphysema (32.3%), linear opacities (20.5%), calcified nodule clusters (6.6%), and cavitary nodules (2.9%) being the most common CT abnormalities.
Boussouar et al. found that although COL3A1 variant type significantly influences arterial and digestive complications and mortality in vEDS, it did not significantly influence lung CT abnormalities.
There is currently no cure for vEDS, but standard pneumothorax treatment has been reported to be effective in this population.
Unlike classic and vascular EDS subtypes, the hypermobile EDS subtype lacks a confirmed identified causative gene, limiting genetic differentiation from other EDS subtypes.
Mutations in ADAMTS2 cause a form of Ehlers-Danlos syndrome with distinct clinical features affecting connective tissue.
Mutations in ADAMTSL2 cause Geleophysic Dysplasia, a connective tissue disorder with distinct clinical characteristics.
Mutations in ADAMTS10 cause Weill-Marchesani Syndrome, a connective tissue disorder with distinct clinical features.
Mutations in ADAMTS17 also cause Weill-Marchesani Syndrome, a connective tissue disorder with distinct clinical features.
Mutations in ADAMTSL4 cause Ectopia lentis, a connective tissue-related ocular disorder.
Mutations in ADAMTSL6 cause thoracic aortic aneurysms and dissection, a connective tissue-related cardiovascular disorder.
Mutations in ADAMTS19 are associated with valvular disease, a connective tissue-related cardiovascular abnormality.
Mutations in ADAMTS6 are associated with a further, distinct connective tissue disorder.
Female sex was significantly associated with smaller unassisted maximum mouth opening compared to males.
Female sex was significantly associated with smaller assisted maximum mouth opening compared to males.
A greater superior condylar distance relative to the articular eminence was significantly associated with larger assisted maximum mouth opening.
Higher age was significantly associated with lower odds of a TMJ subluxation diagnosis, suggesting a protective effect of increasing age against subluxation.

The overall logistic regression model (age, sex, superior condylar distance, Boering classification, condylar angle) significantly predicted TMJ subluxation diagnosis, though with modest explanatory power.

The multinomial regression model using age, sex, and tomographic predictors did not significantly explain open-locking history, indicating imaging parameters had limited predictive value for this outcome.
Right and left TMJ tomographic measures (condylar angle, anterior distance, superior distance) did not differ significantly, confirming bilateral symmetry.

Homologous right and left tomographic measures were strongly correlated, as were anterior and superior condylar distances and condylar angle with anterior distance, leading to exclusion of redundant variables from regression models.
The Boering classification of condylar translation was not a significant predictor of unassisted or assisted maximum mouth opening or of TMJ subluxation diagnosis.
In this cross-sectional sample, a DC/TMD diagnosis of TMJ subluxation was present in 16.7% of participants, and 45.3% reported at least one lifetime open-locking episode.
The pooled prevalence of joint hypermobility syndrome across included studies was estimated at 17.2%.
JHS prevalence was higher in girls (24.2%) compared with boys (17.9%).
JHS was associated with several orthopedic disorders including scoliosis, knee injuries, hip dysfunction, jaw dysfunction, and shoulder dysfunction.
Digestive disorders were identified as one of the main non-orthopedic conditions underlying or associated with JHS.
Vesicoureteral reflux was identified as one of the main non-orthopedic conditions associated with JHS.
Orthostatic tachycardia syndrome (POTS) was identified as one of the main non-orthopedic conditions associated with JHS.
Anxiety disorders were identified as one of the main non-orthopedic conditions associated with JHS.

Multimodal supportive treatments (education, mindfulness/body-stability training, exercise/physical therapy, psychological counseling, occupational therapy, TENS, splinting, and foot orthosis) showed promise for managing musculoskeletal symptoms and psychological comorbidities of JHS, but evidence for extra-articular systemic symptoms was limited.

Whole-genome sequencing identified a previously undescribed hemizygous missense variant in exon 4 of NKAP (c.612A>C, p.Arg204Ser) in a 12-year-old male proband with Marfanoid phenotype and intellectual disability.
Sanger sequencing confirmed the same NKAP hemizygous variant in the proband's affected younger brother and heterozygous carrier status in the unaffected mother, consistent with X-linked inheritance.

The proband exhibited joint hypermobility, habitual dislocation of the right shoulder joint, and arachnodactyly, overlapping with hypermobility spectrum/Ehlers-Danlos-type features but occurring within a Marfanoid/HDDS phenotype.
The proband developed childhood absence epilepsy at age 5, shortly after a vaccination and febrile viral illness, a feature not previously reported in NKAP-related HDDS.

At age 3, following tonsillitis, the proband developed knee pain and ankle joint swelling initially diagnosed as juvenile arthritis, later withdrawn as non-inflammatory; this arthropathy of unknown origin had not been previously linked to HDDS.
Echocardiography revealed a mild mitral valve prolapse (3 mm) with mild mitral regurgitation in the proband, consistent with connective-tissue involvement seen in some HDDS patients.

In the original Fiordaliso et al. cohort of 10 HDDS patients, five distinct missense mutations clustered in exons 8-9 (encoding the NKAP C-terminal domain) were found to produce a truncated protein and severe developmental defects, with c.998G>A (p.Arg333Gln) being most common.
The C-terminal domain of NKAP binds histone deacetylase 3 (HDAC3), implicating chromatin modification in NKAP's transcriptional regulatory function.

NKAP interacts with CIR (CBF1-interacting corepressor) within the Notch signaling corepressor complex, and NKAP mutations are proposed to indirectly affect TGF-β signaling and extracellular matrix gene expression, providing a candidate mechanism for the connective tissue phenotype.

Despite prominent joint hypermobility, neither the proband nor previously reported HDDS patients showed the skin hyperextensibility and vascular/tissue fragility characteristic of Ehlers-Danlos syndrome, supporting differentiation of HDDS from EDS.

HDDS differs clinically from Marfan syndrome by the involvement of the central nervous system, absence of lens subluxation, and lack of severe aortic damage, with only one of ten previously reported patients showing moderate aortic root dilatation.
The proband's IQ score was 75, corresponding to borderline intellectual development on the Wechsler scale.
Radiographic assessment showed a bone age delay of 2-2.5 years in the proband, while bone mineral density (Z-score) was normal.

Xu et al. (2024) reported prenatal diagnosis of severe congenital heart defects (ventricular septal defect, pulmonary stenosis, aortic dextraposition) and brain abnormalities in two male fetal siblings carrying the NKAP c.988C>T (p.Arg330Cys) variant, inherited from carrier female maternal relatives; both pregnancies were terminated.
Strong familial aggregation was found across studies, supporting a hereditary component in the development of hallux abducto valgus.
Variants in collagen- and extracellular matrix-related genes were identified as potential hereditary determinants of hallux abducto valgus.
First-ray hypermobility was one of the most consistent biomechanical factors associated with hallux abducto valgus development.
Abnormal foot pronation was identified as a recurring biomechanical factor linked to hallux abducto valgus.
Reduced activity of the abductor hallucis muscle was consistently associated with hallux abducto valgus.
Female sex was identified as a recurring predictive risk factor for hallux abducto valgus.
Older age was identified as a recurring predictive risk factor for hallux abducto valgus.
Prolonged use of narrow or inadequate footwear was identified as a recurring predictive extrinsic risk factor for hallux abducto valgus.
Gymnastics training in prepubertal athletes was found to positively impact bone health, especially at weight-bearing skeletal sites.
Around puberty, risk of bone health-related injury increases, possibly due to later menarche, lower bone age, and nutritional deficiencies.
Dance-specific studies showed mixed results regarding bone health outcomes.

Anthropometric and biomechanical factors including shorter stature, joint hypermobility, scoliosis, and flexibility-strength imbalances may influence injury risk, particularly in association with being prepubescent.

Later menarche, inadequate energy intake, and discipline-specific bone development may contribute to tendon injuries, bone stress, and overuse injuries in post-pubertal aesthetic and acrobatic athletes.
Regular pre-pubertal gymnastics training supports superior balance development.
Training intensity can influence psychological stress and illness, particularly pre-menarche, and male athletes respond differently to training than females during growth and maturation.
Energy availability, along with psychological and behavioural factors, may further affect injury, illness and performance outcomes in these athletes.
Females with scoliosis had approximately 3 times higher odds of also having hallux valgus compared to those without scoliosis.
Overall, scoliosis was present in 22.3% of participants and hallux valgus in 74.8%.
Females with scoliosis were significantly younger than those without scoliosis.
No significant difference in height was found between the groups with and without scoliosis.
Weight and BMI were significantly lower in females with scoliosis compared to those without.
The orientation of the scoliosis apex and the side of hallux valgus showed no significant difference, suggesting similar lateralization.

All 17 skin biopsy studies reviewed reported decreased intraepidermal nerve fiber density (IENFD) in fibromyalgia patients compared to healthy controls, with reported prevalence of reduced IENFD ranging from about 30% to 85%.
A non-length-dependent pattern of nerve fiber loss was more common than length-dependent loss, with 85% of FMS patients showing reduced IENFD at the thigh versus about 12% at the distal leg.
A length-dependent pattern of nerve fiber loss, with greater loss distally, was observed in only a minority of FMS cases.
About 15% of FMS patients showed a generalized pattern of nerve fiber loss, with significant reductions at both distal and proximal biopsy sites.
In adolescents with juvenile fibromyalgia, 53% had significantly reduced IENFD compared to only 4% of age-matched healthy controls.
FMS patients with generalized IENFD reduction had a more severe clinical profile, with higher pain intensity and greater functional impairment than those with preserved innervation.
In an 18-month observational study, FMS patients with reduced IENFD at both distal and proximal sites experienced more severe symptoms and poorer treatment outcomes than those without such reduction.
Over the 18-month observation period, IENFD reduction in FMS patients did not progress over time.

Aberrant expression of microRNAs, particularly miR-let-7d, was found in white blood cells and skin biopsies of FMS patients and correlated with reduced IENFD, along with aberrant IGF-1 receptor expression.

FMS patients showed a significant reduction in the length of dermal nerve fibers associated with blood vessels compared to healthy controls, whereas overall dermal PGP 9.5-immunoreactive nerve fiber length did not differ.

A study of hypothenar arteriole-venule shunt (AVS) innervation found significantly increased peptidergic sensory nerve fibers within AVS in FMS patients, suggested to dysregulate blood flow and contribute to widespread pain.

In an exclusively male FMS cohort, 83% of participants had reduced IENFD in at least one biopsy site, with more than 50% showing a generalized reduction pattern and proximal-only reduction being rare, differing from patterns seen in women.

Direct comparison of 158 women with FMS and 53 with SFN found FMS and SFN to be distinct clinical entities: FMS patients had reduced IENFD in 66.2% of cases predominantly at proximal sites, contrasting with more distal denervation in SFN, along with differing clinical profiles.

FMS patients had earlier symptom onset (~10 years younger), more intense/widespread pain, comorbid IBS and sleep disturbance, and family history of chronic pain/mood disorders, whereas SFN patients more often had localized neuropathic symptoms, impaired glucose metabolism, and family history of neurological disease.

One study found an increase in papillary dermal mast cells in FMS patients (5–14 per field) compared to controls (0–1 per field), with strong α1-antitrypsin positivity and overexpression of proteinase-activated receptor 2.
In the same skin biopsy study, expression of monocyte chemoattractant protein-1 (MCP-1) and vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF) was significantly lower in FMS patients compared to controls.
A small study demonstrated up-regulation of δ- and κ-opioid receptors in the skin of FMS patients, the first study investigating these receptors outside the CNS.
Skin expression of pro-inflammatory cytokines (IL-1β, IL-6, IL-8, TNF-α) in FMS patients yielded conflicting results across studies.
Electron microscopy revealed unusual unmyelinated fiber morphology, including 'ballooned' Schwann cell sheaths around C-fibers, in a subset of FMS patients compared to controls.
Skin biopsies from FMS patients showed evidence of oxidative stress and mitochondrial dysfunction.
A pilot study reported that intravenous immunoglobulin (IVIG) treatment improved nerve fiber density in a small group of patients with coexisting FMS and SFN.

An 18-month supervised, home-based multicomponent physical activity program significantly increased IENFD at both proximal and distal skin biopsy sites in FMS patients, and this small fiber regeneration correlated with clinical improvement on the Fibromyalgia Impact Questionnaire.
Genetic predisposition is implicated in FMS development, with polymorphisms in genes such as SLC6A4 and COMT associated with altered pain perception and neurotransmitter metabolism.
Inflammatory processes in FMS pathophysiology are supported by elevated cytokine levels, including IL-6 and IL-8, and immune cell activation.

The earliest skin biopsy studies in FMS (mid-1980s), using immunofluorescence, revealed deposits of immunoglobulins, particularly IgG, at the dermal-epidermal junction, raising the possibility of an immune-mediated mechanism.
Fibromyalgia affects an estimated 2-8% of the global population, predominantly women, and causes chronic widespread pain, fatigue and disability.
Eating disorders affect approximately 9% of individuals over the lifespan, show female predominance, and are associated with substantial morbidity and mortality.
Fibromyalgia and obesity co-occur in an estimated 40-70% of cases, suggesting bidirectional interactions between pain, metabolism and eating pathology.
Individuals with fibromyalgia show low resilience to stressors and elevated rates of disordered eating behaviors such as emotional eating, food avoidance and body image preoccupation.
Individuals with eating disorders show a higher prevalence of chronic pain conditions, including fibromyalgia.
Fibromyalgia patients frequently show HPA axis dysregulation with hypocortisolism and blunted cortisol responses to stress, contributing to fatigue and reduced stress resilience.
Fibromyalgia patients show autonomic imbalance with sympathetic hyperactivity and parasympathetic hypoactivity that correlates with sleep disturbances and orthostatic intolerance.
Up to 60-80% of fibromyalgia patients have comorbid depression, anxiety disorders, PTSD or other mood disturbances.
In contrast to fibromyalgia, anorexia nervosa is associated with CRH-mediated hypercortisolism driven by severe caloric restriction, which suppresses appetite and disrupts energy homeostasis.
Elevated pro-inflammatory cytokines (IL-6, IL-8, TNF-alpha) and central neuroimmune activation have been documented in fibromyalgia.
Gut-brain axis disruption, including intestinal dysbiosis and impaired enteroendocrine signalling, is implicated in central pain sensitization in fibromyalgia.
Fibromyalgia patients show elevated lipid peroxidation products (malondialdehyde and 4-hydroxynonenal) and reduced antioxidant capacity.
Fibromyalgia patients show decreased levels of coenzyme Q10, SOD, catalase and glutathione peroxidase, which correlate inversely with FIQ scores, pain and anxiety levels.
Mitochondrial dysfunction is a key feature of fibromyalgia pathophysiology, potentially contributing to both oxidative stress and characteristic fatigue.
Systematic reviews show fibromyalgia involves elevated total oxidative stress, reduced total antioxidant status and increased oxidative stress index correlating with pain intensity and disability.
Individuals with anorexia nervosa exhibit altered mitochondrial function and increased oxidative stress in leukocytes, with evidence of mitochondrial complex I inhibition.
Nrf2 activity appears impaired in fibromyalgia, contributing to oxidative damage and neuroinflammation.
In migraine models, a condition frequently comorbid with fibromyalgia, Nrf2 pathway activation reduced oxidative stress and neuroinflammation in the trigeminal system and alleviated pain behaviors.
Interventions enhancing Nrf2 activity, such as coenzyme Q10 supplementation, have shown promise in improving pain and fatigue in fibromyalgia, though robust RCTs are still needed.
Moderate-intensity exercise induces transient ROS increases that activate Nrf2, upregulating antioxidant genes including SOD, catalase, GPx and HO-1.
Excessive endurance exercise or exercise to exhaustion can paradoxically suppress Nrf2 activity and increase oxidative damage, unlike appropriately dosed exercise.
Broccoli sprout extract sulforaphane consumption significantly upregulates NQO1, GST and HO-1 expression in humans, with effects persisting several days.
Curcumin supplementation (500-2000 mg/day) reduces markers of oxidative stress and inflammation in chronic pain populations, though direct evidence in fibromyalgia-specific cohorts remains limited.
Consumption of 400-800 mg green tea catechins daily can enhance antioxidant capacity and reduce oxidative stress markers in humans.
A pilot interventional study found that 12 weeks of Mediterranean diet adherence reduced oxidative stress markers and improved functional capacity in fibromyalgia patients.

An EAT-26 total score of 20 or higher, or high dieting/bulimia subscale scores, should prompt further clinical assessment and possible referral to eating disorder specialists in fibromyalgia patients.
A German validation of the Central Sensitization Inventory found markedly higher mean CSI scores in fibromyalgia patients than in healthy controls.
In a large clinical cohort of 562 fibromyalgia patients, over a third had CSI scores ≥40, which correlated moderately-to-strongly with established fibromyalgia severity indices.
A multicenter Chinese study found extremely low fibromyalgia prevalence and milder clinical impact, suggesting cultural under-recognition of central sensitization symptoms.

Clinically relevant CSI scores (≥40) are also found in a substantial minority of people with chronic musculoskeletal pain who do not have a fibromyalgia diagnosis, suggesting a broader central sensitization spectrum.

Portuguese and Brazilian fibromyalgia cohorts showed similar pain intensity but significantly different levels of fatigue, emotional distress, and cognitive symptoms, illustrating sociocultural modulation of the clinical phenotype.
A prospective cohort study found that higher baseline central sensitization scores preceded and predicted the later onset of chronic musculoskeletal pain, supporting a temporal/causal role for CS.
Fibromyalgia prevalence varies substantially by region, averaging about 2.64% in Europe, 2.41% in North America, and up to 1.62% in parts of Asia.
Pooled international data estimate global fibromyalgia prevalence at roughly 3.98% in women versus 2.40% in men, a statistically significant sex difference.

Passive transfer of IgG from fibromyalgia patients, but not controls, into mice induced pain hypersensitivity via sensitization of nociceptive afferent neurons in the dorsal root ganglia, implicating autoantibodies in FM pathogenesis.

Task-based fMRI in fibromyalgia shows abnormal salience attribution and disproportionate cortical activation relative to stimulus intensity, consistent with lowered central pain thresholds and amplified nociceptive gain.
Resting-state fMRI in fibromyalgia shows increased functional connectivity between the default mode network and insular cortex, with magnitude tracking clinical pain intensity.

Spinal cord fMRI during temporal summation paradigms shows enhanced dorsal horn and ascending spinal pathway activity in fibromyalgia patients compared with healthy controls, indicating early spinal-level amplification of nociceptive signaling.
In osteoarthritis, fMRI shows altered activation of the insula, ACC, and sensorimotor cortex reflecting central pain amplification that correlates only weakly with structural joint damage.

In rheumatoid arthritis, fMRI reveals altered pain processing in insular, limbic, and prefrontal regions particularly in patients with pain despite low inflammatory activity or clinical remission, supporting a role for central sensitization in residual non-inflammatory pain.

In a substantial proportion of RA patients, pain flares did not temporally coincide with increases in DAS28, and conversely DAS28 increases were often not accompanied by pain intensification, showing dissociation between inflammatory activity and pain.
Nearly 12% of RA patients meeting DAS28 remission criteria continue to experience clinically significant persistent pain, indicating additional non-inflammatory nociceptive/nociplastic mechanisms.

A substantial proportion of RA patients exhibit neuropathic pain features, ranging from 17% to 36% depending on assessment instrument, indicating neuropathic pain can emerge even with controlled inflammation.
Patients with comorbid RA and OA show a substantially higher proportion of chronic refractory pain than those with RA alone, even without objective signs of inflammation.

A systematic review found that a substantial proportion of patients report unsatisfactory long-term pain outcomes after large-joint arthroplasty, supporting a role for central sensitization beyond structural joint damage.
Fibromyalgia prevalence in RA patients ranges from 4.9% to 52.4%, markedly exceeding the general population prevalence of 1-5%, indicating a strong comorbid relationship.
Fibromyalgia prevalence in psoriatic arthritis patients ranges from 9.3% to 38.3%, versus about 1.78% in individuals without inflammatory rheumatic disease.
Patients with RA show markedly higher multimorbidity prevalence (31-86%) compared with individuals without RA (18-71%).

Treat-to-target DMARD/biologic strategies achieve remission or low disease activity in 40-60% of RA/PsA patients, but persistent pain despite adequate inflammatory control occurs in about 20-30%, increasingly attributed to central sensitization unresponsive to further immunosuppression.
The modified painDETECT questionnaire in knee osteoarthritis shows higher scores correlating with quantitative sensory testing findings consistent with central sensitization.

Blockade of the fractalkine receptor CX3CR1 attenuates mechanical allodynia, and mechanical allodynia is abolished in Cx3cr1 knockout animal models, implicating microglial fractalkine signaling in central sensitization.

Elevated glutamate levels correlate with fibromyalgia severity, while reduced GABA correlates with pain intensity, supporting an excitatory-inhibitory neurotransmitter imbalance underlying central sensitization.

Serotonin-norepinephrine reuptake inhibitors (duloxetine, milnacipran) and the anticonvulsant pregabalin have shown promising results reducing pain, alleviating fatigue, and improving quality of life in fibromyalgia patients.
Intermittent cold stress (ICS) induced significant mechanical hypersensitivity in mice, lowering paw withdrawal thresholds from baseline.
ICS also induced thermal hyperalgesia in FM mice that persisted over two days.
2 Hz electroacupuncture at ST36 significantly reversed mechanical and thermal hyperalgesia in FM mice.
Intracerebroventricular (ICV) injection of PD-L1 reversed both mechanical and thermal hyperalgesia in FM mice similarly to EA.
Trpv1−/− mice did not develop thermal hyperalgesia after ICS induction, indicating TRPV1 is required for FM-associated thermal pain.
PD-1 protein expression was significantly reduced in the CB5 cerebellar region of ICS-induced FM mice compared to normal mice.
EA, ICV PD-L1 injection, and Trpv1 deletion all significantly restored PD-1 protein levels in the CB5 cerebellar region of FM mice.
TRPV1 protein concentration in the CB5 cerebellar region was significantly increased in FM mice, and this was inhibited by EA and PD-L1 injection.
Downstream PI3K/Akt/mTOR phosphorylation was significantly increased in the cerebellum of FM mice and was reduced by EA, PD-L1 injection, and Trpv1 deletion.
MAPK pathway activation (pERK, pp38, pJNK) was increased in the cerebellum of FM mice and was reduced by EA and PD-L1 injection, while Trpv1−/− mice showed normal MAPK levels.
Transcription factors pNFκB and pCREB were significantly increased in the cerebellum of FM mice and were reduced by EA, PD-L1 injection, and Trpv1 deletion.
Nociceptive sodium channels Nav1.7 and Nav1.8 showed higher activity in FM mice cerebellum, which was reduced by EA, PD-L1 injection, and Trpv1 deletion.
PD-1 expression was also decreased in the CB6 and CB7 cerebellar regions of FM mice, and this was reversed by EA, PD-L1 injection, and Trpv1 deletion.
TRPV1 expression was significantly increased in CB6 and CB7 regions of FM mice, and this increase was attenuated by EA and PD-L1 injection, while being absent in Trpv1−/− mice.
ICV injection of a PD-L1-neutralizing antibody significantly attenuated the analgesic effect of EA on both mechanical and thermal hyperalgesia in FM mice.
PD-L1-neutralizing antibody injection also diminished the analgesic effect of ICV PD-L1 injection on mechanical and thermal pain in FM mice.

Concurrent PD-L1-neutralizing antibody administration blocked the molecular restoration of PD-1 expression normally induced by EA or PD-L1 injection in the CB5-7 cerebellar regions, confirming PD-L1/PD-1 as the mediator of EA's molecular analgesic mechanism.

With PD-L1-neutralizing antibody co-administration, TRPV1 and its downstream pPI3K/pAkt/pmTOR, pERK/pp38/pJNK, pNFκB/pCREB, and Nav1.7/1.8 signaling remained elevated in the CB5-7 regions despite EA or PD-L1 treatment, indicating loss of the treatments' molecular antinociceptive effect.
The review notes that some studies suggest craniosacral therapy may provide therapeutic benefit for fibromyalgia among other conditions such as migraine, low back pain, depression, and anxiety.
MRI studies have shown that intracranial and spinal CSF circulation is pulsatile, occurring at approximately 6 to 12 cycles per minute, consistent with the proposed craniosacral rhythm.
New basic research shows that in migraine models, trigeminal ganglion neurons are directly activated by CSF influx.
Meningeal lymphatic CGRP signaling has been implicated in pain induction via CSF efflux and associated neuroinflammation.
Fibromyalgia affects 2% to 3% of individuals in the United States, with the highest prevalence occurring among females aged 20 to 55.
Fibromyalgia patients experience altered pain perception and sensory processing due to central nervous system changes triggered by infections, emotional trauma, and other factors.
No single gene has been identified that predisposes individuals to fibromyalgia, but having a first-degree relative with fibromyalgia increases the likelihood of developing the disease.
Aerobic exercise reduced pain, fatigue, and depression in patients with fibromyalgia.
Strength training led to improvements in physical function and well-being in patients with fibromyalgia.
Mixed exercise training (aerobic plus strength) led to less pain and better physical function in fibromyalgia patients, despite persistence of central sensitization.
Land-based therapeutic exercise focused on strengthening, joint range of motion, and neuromuscular control improved pain and quality of life in osteoarthritis patients.
Manual therapy added to a supervised exercise program further improved pain, stiffness, and function in osteoarthritis patients and delayed the need for surgery.
Occupational therapy reduced feelings of helplessness, increased confidence in managing symptoms, facilitated re-engagement with family and work, and lowered mental fatigue in chronic pain patients.
A randomized clinical trial found that mindfulness-based stress reduction prevented patients with chronic pain from overusing opioids and improved chronic pain symptoms.
Patients undergoing multidisciplinary biopsychosocial rehabilitation had higher odds of returning to work at 1 year than patients treated with physical therapy alone.

In Long et al.'s study, patients whose exercise program matched their directional preference showed significantly greater improvement in pain, disability, medication use, activity interference, and depression scores than those given mismatched or non-directional exercises.
Failure to centralize symptoms during MDT assessment is a strong prognostic indicator of higher disability, poorer outcomes, and increased psychosocial distress.

MDT produced statistically significant reductions in pain and disability at 1 week compared with passive therapies, but did not outperform strengthening, flexion exercises, or other active interventions in chronic low back pain.

A review of randomized clinical trials found insufficient evidence to support mechanical cervical traction as a stand-alone treatment for neck pain, though some trials showed benefit when combined with other interventions.
