A systematic review found a small but statistically significant improvement in pain of all severities with MDT compared with control methods, but no improvement in disability; effects were clinically and statistically significant for moderate-to-severe pain but only statistically significant for mild-to-moderate pain.

A 2014 RCT by Rosedale et al. found that knee osteoarthritis patients receiving MDT directional-preference exercises had significantly improved pain and physical function scores at 2 weeks and 3 months compared with controls.

A 2022 case report described a 41-year-old female with osteoarthritis whose knee pain, range of motion, muscle strength, and performance improved after MDT used as adjuvant therapy alongside electrotherapy, soft tissue approaches, and therapeutic training.

The core MDT principles of directional preference and symptom centralization are not appropriate for treating fibromyalgia because its pain is non-mechanical and not influenced by specific movement directions.

In an RCT by Long et al., patients performing MDT exercises matched to directional preference had greater reductions in pain and disability than those receiving spinal manipulation or non-specific exercises.

Peterson et al. reported that patients treated with MDT required fewer treatment sessions to return to normal function than those treated with alternative methods, resulting in lower healthcare costs.
An RCT found that MDT produced short-term improvements in pain and disability similar to manual therapy, but MDT sustained these functional improvements over a longer period.

Patients with low back pain who displayed a directional preference had better outcomes with MDT exercises than with non-specific exercise programs, whereas those without a directional preference had comparable improvements regardless of treatment modality.
A systematic review found that MDT produced a small but statistically significant reduction in neck pain of all severities compared with control interventions.
The same systematic review found that MDT did not significantly improve disability outcomes for neck pain compared with control methods.

A 2014 RCT by Rosedale et al. found that directional-preference MDT exercises significantly improved pain and physical function scores in knee osteoarthritis patients at 2 weeks and 3 months compared with controls.

A 2022 case report described a 41-year-old female with osteoarthritis whose knee pain decreased and range of motion, muscle strength, and performance improved after adjuvant MDT combined with electrotherapy and soft tissue therapy.

Because fibromyalgia symptoms are non-mechanical and not influenced by specific movement directions, the core MDT principles of directional preference and symptom centralization are considered inappropriate for treating its underlying pathophysiology.

In a randomized controlled trial by Long et al., patients who performed MDT exercises matched to their directional preference showed greater reductions in pain and disability than those who received spinal manipulation or non-specific exercises.

Peterson et al. reported that patients treated with MDT required fewer treatment sessions to return to normal function than those treated with alternative methods, resulting in lower healthcare costs.
A randomized controlled trial found that MDT produced short-term improvements in pain and disability comparable to manual therapy, but MDT sustained these functional improvements over a longer term.

A study found that patients with low back pain who displayed a directional preference had better outcomes with MDT exercises than with non-specific exercise programs, whereas patients without a directional preference showed comparable improvement regardless of treatment modality.

Lower pain catastrophizing was correlated with improvements in disability, pain intensity, and depression at 6 and 12 months, and cognitive-behavioral therapy aimed at reducing catastrophizing improved coping through cognitive restructuring.

Occupational therapy interventions such as energy conservation strategies, activity pacing, and task simplification help limit symptom aggravation and translate MDT-driven symptom improvements into functional gains.
Functional emphasis is important in chronic pain populations because improvements in pain or movement capacity do not necessarily translate into better quality of life.
Yildiz et al found that HBOT (2.4 ATA, 15 sessions) reduced mean VAS pain intensity by 3.31 points, though the between-group difference vs sham was not significant.

Two Izquierdo-Alventosa et al trials using a lower-pressure HBOT protocol (1.45 ATA, 40 sessions) each found a 2.47-point reduction in VAS pain with large within-group effect sizes, but no formal between-group comparison was reported.
Ablin et al found HBOT (2.0 ATA, 60 sessions) produced a significantly greater VAS pain reduction than pharmacological treatment (duloxetine or pregabalin), by 2.31 points with a large effect size.
In post-traumatic CRPS, Kiralp et al found HBOT (2.4 ATA, 15 sessions) reduced VAS pain by 3.1 points, an effect persisting 45 days and significantly greater than minimal changes seen with sham.
In idiopathic trigeminal neuralgia, Gu et al found HBOT produced a clinically meaningful VAS reduction (≥2 points) in 60-75% of patients vs 20-30% with sham, with effects persisting up to six months.
Pritchard et al found no statistically significant reduction in pain scores over 12-month follow-up in patients with radiation-induced brachial plexopathy treated with HBOT.
Hadanny et al found HBOT reduced fibromyalgia Widespread Pain Index scores by 3.7±3.0 points with a large within-group effect, replicated in the crossover phase.
Boussi-Gross et al found HBOT reduced fibromyalgia WPI scores by 4.5±5.9 points, with significant superiority over pharmacological treatment and a large effect size.
Ablin et al found a smaller WPI reduction (2.4±5.9 points) with HBOT that did not reach significance versus pharmacological treatment.

Efrati et al found HBOT reduced fibromyalgia tender point counts by 8.46 points (primary group) and 11.54 points (crossover group), with very large effect sizes and significant between-group differences.
Multiple fibromyalgia trials found HBOT increased pressure pain thresholds (dolorimetry) with generally medium effect sizes; one trial correlated PPT changes with reduction in pain indices.
Across three fibromyalgia trials, 29% to 53.3% of HBOT-treated participants no longer met fibromyalgia diagnostic criteria post-treatment, versus only 0 to 6.7% in control groups.
Boussi-Gross et al found HBOT increased SF-36 Physical Component Summary by 24.1±17.9 points and Mental Component Summary by 24.3±20.8 points, with significant between-group differences.

Curtis et al found HBOT reduced total FIQR (Fibromyalgia Impact Questionnaire Revised) scores by 33.8 points, significantly greater than controls, with the control group showing similar gains after crossover.

In one fibromyalgia trial, HBOT increased 6-minute walk test distance by 49.5 m and improved induced fatigue by 1.18 points, with no relevant improvement in controls; an exercise comparator showed smaller gains.
In CRPS, HBOT was associated with improved wrist joint mobility (+19.3° flexion) and reduced edema (wrist circumference decreased 1.9 cm).
Two fibromyalgia trials found HBOT significantly improved sleep disturbances on the MOS Sleep Problems Index and Jenkins Sleep Scale.

Boussi-Gross et al found HBOT produced large improvements in PTSD severity and somatization, and moderate improvements in general psychological distress and depression in fibromyalgia patients with a history of trauma.
Gu et al found HBOT reduced daily carbamazepine requirements by 60-70% in trigeminal neuralgia patients compared to 15-20% in controls, with effects evident within one day and lasting up to 60 days.

Four fibromyalgia trials using SPECT found HBOT was associated with significant increases in brain activity and cerebral perfusion in multiple Brodmann areas within prefrontal and temporal cortices, with correlations to clinical outcomes in three studies.

HBOT was generally well tolerated across trials with no serious, life-threatening, or permanent adverse events reported; mild middle-ear barotrauma was the most common adverse event, occurring in 12-40% of participants.
Meta-analysis found low-certainty evidence that MBSR improved quality of life at short term follow up compared with active control groups in people with fibromyalgia.
MBSR also improved quality of life at long term follow up versus active control, though with a smaller effect than at short term.
MBSR improved pain catastrophising at short term follow up versus active control with moderate certainty evidence.
MBSR improved pain catastrophising at long term follow up versus active control with moderate certainty evidence.
MBSR showed no significant pooled effect on depression versus active control at short or long term follow up, with low to very low certainty evidence.

MBSR showed no significant pooled effect on pain severity versus active control at short or long term follow up, with low to very low certainty evidence, not supporting MBSR for pain intensity reduction.
MBSR had a small significant benefit on pain severity at short term follow up compared with waiting list control.
MBSR showed no significant effect on pain severity at long term follow up versus waiting list control.
MBSR showed a significant improvement in depression at short term follow up compared with waiting list control.
MBSR did not show a significant improvement in depression at long term follow up versus waiting list control.
One included trial (Pérez-Aranda et al. 2019) found MBSR was cost effective, producing improved quality adjusted life years and lower costs versus active control and treatment as usual.

One included trial (Fjorback et al. 2013) found MBSR was associated with healthcare cost savings and reduced disability pension claims, despite the intervention itself costing five to six times more than usual care.
Extensive enzymatic hydrolysis of ovalbumin maximally reduced antigenicity but failed to induce oral tolerance in a murine model.
Partial hydrolysis of ovalbumin by papain prevented allergic diarrhea and systemic anaphylaxis in mice, comparable to intact ovalbumin.
Protection by partially hydrolyzed ovalbumin was associated with preservation of CD103+ dendritic cells in the gut.
Preservation of CD103+ dendritic cells by partial hydrolysis suppressed Th2 polarization in the gut.
Partial hydrolysis-induced tolerance suppressed mast cell activation in the gut, mediated via preserved CD103+ dendritic cells.
Partial hydrolysis-induced tolerance suppressed aberrant overexpression of Gsdmc (gasdermin C) family genes in the gut.

Six weeks of intranasal HDM sensitization increased chymase (mast cell degranulation marker) immunoreactivity in the anterior cingulate cortex, dorsal striatum, and amygdala compared to PBS-treated control mice.
Quantitative immunofluorescence confirmed a significantly larger chymase-positive area in the ACC of HDM-sensitized mice compared with PBS controls.
Concomitant intraperitoneal cromolyn sodium administration during HDM sensitization significantly reduced the HDM-induced increase in chymase-positive area in the ACC.
Total DAPI-positive cell number in the ACC did not differ between HDM-sensitized and PBS control mice.
No difference was found in the number of c-Fos-positive cells in the ACC between HDM-sensitized and PBS control mice, despite a prior finding of increased c-Fos protein in whole brain homogenates.
GFAP-positive area (reactive astrocyte marker) was increased in the ACC of HDM-sensitized mice compared with PBS controls.
Cromolyn sodium co-administration during HDM sensitization significantly reduced the HDM-induced increase in ACC GFAP-positive area.
Iba1-positive area (microglial marker) was significantly increased in the ACC of HDM-sensitized mice compared with PBS controls.
Cromolyn sodium co-administration significantly reduced the HDM-induced increase in ACC Iba1-positive area.
In vivo two-photon calcium imaging showed a decreased frequency of somatic calcium activity in ACC pyramidal neurons of HDM-sensitized mice, with no change in the auditory cortex control region.
Cromolyn sodium co-administration during HDM sensitization prevented the HDM-induced reduction in ACC pyramidal neuron somatic calcium activity frequency.
Peak amplitude of somatic calcium transients was decreased in ACC pyramidal neurons of HDM-sensitized mice compared with PBS controls.
Cromolyn sodium administration during HDM sensitization attenuated the HDM-induced decrease in peak amplitude of ACC pyramidal neuron calcium transients.
HDM-sensitized mice failed to show the normal habituation-related reduction in open field ambulatory distance seen upon repeated testing, unlike PBS control mice.
Cromolyn sodium co-administration during HDM sensitization restored the normal habituation pattern (reduction in ambulatory distance) in the open field test.
HDM-sensitized mice lost the typical rodent aversion to bright light in the light-dark transition test, spending more time in the light zone than PBS controls.
Cromolyn sodium co-administration during HDM sensitization reversed the atypical loss of light aversion, restoring typical dark-chamber preference similar to PBS controls.
HDM-sensitized mice showed significantly reduced sucrose consumption in the sucrose preference test, indicating anhedonia/depressive-like behavior compared to PBS controls.
Cromolyn sodium co-administration during HDM sensitization prevented the reduction in sucrose preference, with the HDM+Cromolyn group showing similar sucrose preference to PBS controls.
BAL total cell counts and protein concentration were increased in HDM-sensitized mice compared to PBS controls, reflecting allergic lung inflammation.
Intraperitoneal cromolyn sodium administration during HDM sensitization significantly reduced BAL cell counts and protein concentration, attenuating lung inflammation.
IgG autoantibodies against the FcεRIα subunit are detectable in a substantial proportion of CSU patients, and most of these are functionally capable of triggering basophil histamine release.
CSU can be classified into type I (autoallergic) and type IIb (autoimmune) endotypes based on autoantibody profiles, with type I more common than type IIb and substantial overlap between them.
Type IIb CSU is characterized by elevated CRP and anti-TPO-IgG with lower total IgE, and reduced blood eosinophil and basophil counts, distinguishing it from type I CSU.
A cross-sectional analysis found higher rates of comorbid allergic diseases (asthma, atopic dermatitis, allergic rhinitis) in CSU patients compared with control individuals.
Increased serum total IgE levels are seen in a wide proportion of CSU patients, especially those with atopic dermatitis or type I autoallergy, and are associated with longer disease duration.
NSAIDs are the most common medications that exacerbate CSU symptoms, termed NSAID-exacerbated cutaneous disease, affecting up to 30% of patients.
About 28% of type IIb CSU patients have at least one comorbid autoimmune disease, most commonly Hashimoto's thyroiditis.
Treating comorbid autoimmune thyroid disease with thyroid hormones has been reported to significantly improve urticaria symptoms in CSU patients.
Up to 60% of patients with chronic urticaria show insufficient response to first-line second-generation H1-antihistamines, requiring increased doses.

A meta-analysis found that cyclosporine combined with antihistamines led to response in 73% of CSU patients at low-to-moderate doses by week 12, with dose-dependent adverse events in over half of patients.
Approximately 30% of CSU patients remain symptomatic at the licensed omalizumab dose over a 6-month period, but updosing to 600 mg improves symptom control with complete response in up to 60%.

A retrospective cohort of 386 sgH1AH-refractory CSU patients found that high initial omalizumab dose, elevated basophil counts, low platelet-to-lymphocyte ratio, and higher IgE levels predicted early treatment response.
Two phase 3 trials comparing ligelizumab (higher IgE affinity anti-IgE) with omalizumab in sgH1AH-refractory CSU failed to demonstrate superiority of ligelizumab.

Dupilumab (anti-IL-4Rα) showed significant improvement in itch/hives and higher clinical remission rates versus placebo in omalizumab-naïve CSU patients (CUPID A), but low efficacy in omalizumab-intolerant/incomplete responders (CUPID B).
In the CUPID C study, 30% of dupilumab-treated omalizumab-naïve CSU patients achieved complete response at 24 weeks, similar to CUPID A results.

A phase 2 trial of fenebrutinib (BTK inhibitor) in 93 sgH1AH-refractory CSU patients showed rapid improvement in disease activity regardless of type IIb autoimmunity status, but development was stopped due to transient transaminase elevations.

Two phase 3 trials (REMIX-1, REMIX-2) of remibrutinib in sgH1AH-refractory CSU patients showed significantly greater symptom improvement and higher complete/well-controlled rates than placebo, leading to FDA approval.

A phase 2 trial found rilzabrutinib (1200 mg/day) produced significant symptom improvement at week 12 with rapid onset by week 1, with particularly favorable effects in patients with low IgE/eosinophils, positive basophil histamine release assay, and angioedema.
A phase 1b study of barzolvolimab (anti-KIT antibody) in 45 CSU patients showed rapid symptom reduction within 1 week, sustained for 12 weeks, well tolerated regardless of prior omalizumab treatment.
Gene expression and serum levels of MRGPRX2 are elevated in CSU patients and correlate with disease severity, supporting it as a potential drug target.

A phase 2a study of lirentelimab (anti-Siglec-8) showed high complete response rates in omalizumab-naïve and refractory CSU patients, but a subsequent phase 2 trial (NCT05528861) failed to meet its primary endpoints.
Increased serum levels of TSLP, an epithelial-derived type 2 cytokine, were noted in CSU patients compared with controls.

A phase 2b trial of a TSLP-targeting agent in 183 CSU patients (with or without omalizumab) showed no significant symptom improvement at week 16, though omalizumab-naïve patients had delayed, sustained improvement post-treatment.
Elevated C5a levels in CSU patients enhance histamine release induced by IgG-mediated cross-linking of FcεRI, linking complement activation to mast cell activation.

A phase 1 trial of YH35324, a long-acting IgE-Trap-Fc fusion protein, demonstrated greater and longer suppression of serum-free IgE levels in a dose-dependent manner compared with omalizumab, with a favorable safety profile and no serious adverse events.
XBS treatment (low/medium/high dose) alleviated OVA-induced lung histopathological damage and significantly reduced lung injury scores compared with the OVA group.
OVA-challenged mice showed markedly elevated serum IgE levels compared to control, which XBS administration lowered at all doses.
OVA challenge increased pro-inflammatory cytokines TNF-α, IL-1β and IL-6 in lung tissue, along with increased peripheral WBC, NEUT%, MONO% and EO%, all of which were reversed by XBS treatment.

Tail-vein injection of compound 48/80, a classic mast cell degranulator, induced acute lung injury with inflammatory infiltration and proteinaceous exudates, together with elevated serum histamine and lung IL-6/TNF-α, which XBS treatment attenuated.
XBS effectively suppressed IL-6 and TNF-α expression in lung tissue and lowered serum histamine at all tested doses in the compound 48/80 acute mast cell-mediated model, in a dose-dependent fashion.

Network pharmacology identified core AA-metabolism enzymes among XBS's predicted 32 core targets, including ALOX5 (5-LOX), PLA2G2A/PLA2G10 (secretory PLA2s), PTGS1 (COX-1), and MAPK14/MAPK1/MAPK8, linking XBS action to arachidonic acid metabolic pathway regulation.

OVA challenge significantly increased lung leukotriene B4, thromboxane B2, 15(S)-HpETE and 12-OxoETE compared with control, indicating activation of leukotriene synthesis and oxidative lipid mediator production in chronic allergic inflammation.
XBS-M treatment markedly reduced OVA-elevated LTB4, TXB2, 15(S)-HpETE and 12-OxoETE, suggesting preferential targeting of LOX-mediated AA metabolism under chronic inflammatory conditions.

Compound 48/80 stimulation predominantly activated the COX pathway, significantly increasing TXB2, PGD2, PGJ2, 15-keto-PGF2α and free arachidonic acid, indicating rapid enzymatic conversion of AA into prostaglandins during acute mast-cell driven inflammation.

XBS-M treatment markedly attenuated compound 48/80-induced elevations in TXB2, PGD2, PGJ2, 15-keto-PGF2α, and free AA, indicating suppression of both AA release and downstream prostaglandin production.

In the OVA model, phospho-p38/p38 ratio and 15-LOX expression were markedly increased, consistent with the leukotriene- and HETE-dominant metabolic profile; XBS significantly attenuated p38 MAPK activation and suppressed 15-LOX expression.

In the compound 48/80 acute model, rapid activation of p38 MAPK together with marked COX-2 induction reflected the prostaglandin-driven acute response of mast-cell degranulation; XBS markedly reduced phospho-p38/p38 ratio and downregulated COX-2 expression.

UHPLC-QTOF-MS chemical profiling identified five major bioactive compounds in Xiebai San: glycyrrhizic acid, liquiritin, chlorogenic acid, kukoamine B, and mulberroside A, which may contribute to therapeutic effects through intestinal metabolism or direct local action.

Single-cell RNA sequencing of one ESCC patient showed the proportion of mast cells among immune cells increased from 4% pre-treatment to 12% post-treatment following neoadjuvant anti-angiogenic plus chemotherapy, despite an absolute decrease in mast cell number.
Post-treatment tumor-infiltrating mast cells showed increased expression of pro-inflammatory cytokines (IL1B, IL18, TNF) and chemokines (CCL3, CCL4, CCL2, CXCL2, CXCL8) compared to pre-treatment.
In 68 treatment-naïve ESCC patients, tumor-infiltrating mast cell density was negatively correlated with maximum tumor diameter.
Mast cell density showed a weak, non-significant negative correlation with pathological T stage in ESCC.
Patients with higher tumor mast cell density (MC-high) had significantly longer overall survival than those with lower density (MC-low).
Tumor-infiltrating macrophages and CD8+ T cells were more abundant in tumor than normal tissue but their density did not correlate with tumor diameter or overall survival, unlike mast cells.
Expression of the mast cell marker gene KIT was significantly lower in ESCC tumor tissue compared to normal esophageal samples in the TCGA-ESCA cohort.
Expression of the mast cell marker gene FCER1A was significantly lower in ESCC tumor tissue compared to normal esophageal samples in the TCGA-ESCA cohort.
Genes differentially expressed between KIT/FCER1A high- and low-expression groups in TCGA-ESCA were enriched for extracellular region and vascular smooth muscle contraction pathways.
Desmoplasia grade alone did not stratify survival, but among patients with mature/mild desmoplasia, high mast cell density was associated with significantly better overall survival than low density.
Stromal fibrosis grade alone did not affect survival, but among patients with mild fibrosis, high mast cell density was associated with significantly better overall survival than low density.
The majority of tumor-infiltrating and normal-tissue mast cells retained tryptase within their cytoplasm, indicating a predominantly non-degranulated phenotype.

LPS stimulation of the human mast cell line HMC-1 caused dose-dependent upregulation of chemokine genes CCL19, CCL21, and CXCL8, with increased CCL19 and CXCL8 protein secretion confirmed by immunofluorescence.
LPS was detected by immunofluorescence in the tumor stroma of 32 of 68 (47.1%) ESCC patients, with a distribution pattern similar to mast cells, but was undetectable in normal esophageal mucosa.
In mast cell-deficient rats, TNBS failed to induce visceral hypersensitivity that occurred in control rats, showing mast cells are required for TNBS-induced VH.
The literature contains contradictory statistical data regarding whether colonic mast cell numbers are altered in IBS patients.
IBS patients show significantly increased levels of IgG antibodies against specific foods, and dietary avoidance reduces discomfort, implicating IgG-food complexes in mast cell activation and VH.

Colonic mast cells from IBS patients express higher numbers of MRGPRX2 receptors than healthy people, enabling non-IgE-mediated pseudo-allergic activation by spicy foods, medications, and substance P.
Intestinal infections can induce local (non-systemic) IgE production against specific food antigens, triggering mast cell degranulation and sensitizing TRPV1 channels.
Confocal laser endoscopy showed that IBS patients exhibit immediate widening of epithelial gaps and immune cell recruitment in the intestinal mucosa upon antigen exposure.
Psychological stress activates CRF-R1 receptors on mast cells, directly inducing rapid degranulation and release of tryptase.

The mechanosensitive ion channel Piezo1 responds to intestinal mechanical traction, and IL-33 heightens Piezo1 sensitivity, triggering mast cell degranulation even during normal physiological traction.

microRNA-199 is reduced in IBS colon tissue, and since it normally inhibits TRPV1 production, its reduction leads to excessive TRPV1 accumulation in sensory neurons and pain.

Polymorphism of the serotonin transporter gene SLC6A4 was associated with abnormal SERT function in IBS-D patients compared with healthy controls.

ME/CFS onset age distribution in Norway and across Europe shows two distinct incidence peaks, one in adolescence and one in middle age.
Gaussian mixture modelling estimated early onset ME/CFS peak at a mean age of ~16.0 years (SD 4.3) and late onset peak at ~36.6 years (SD 10.5) using combined EMEA data from all countries.
Infectious mononucleosis/glandular fever as a trigger was more strongly associated with early onset ME/CFS relative to other infection or no infection triggers in the DecodeME subcohort.

Trigger type frequency differed significantly between early and late onset ME/CFS groups in the EMEA cohort, with infectious and vaccination triggers more common in early onset, and accident/injury/surgery, no particular event, and pregnancy/birth more common in late onset.
Early onset ME/CFS was associated with greater odds of more severe disease (moderate, severe or very severe) compared to late onset ME/CFS.
Early onset ME/CFS was associated with much greater odds of being severe or very severely affected compared to moderate or milder disease, relative to late onset ME/CFS.
Early onset ME/CFS was associated with markedly greater odds of being very severely affected compared to severe or milder disease.
Illness duration only modestly and inconsistently associated with disease severity, indicating that the greater severity in early onset ME/CFS is not primarily explained by longer illness duration.
There was no significant difference in the proportion of males and females between early and late onset ME/CFS groups.
Respondents with a first-degree relative with ME/CFS were more likely to belong to the early onset group compared to the late onset group.
A peak in new ME/CFS onset cases occurred in 2009 and 2010, coinciding with the 2009 H1N1 swine flu pandemic.
Adolescents with ME/CFS scored significantly worse (higher) on the Wood Mental Fatigue Inventory than healthy controls, with a large effect size.
Adolescents with ME/CFS scored significantly worse (lower, indicating more fatigue) on the PedsQL MFS cognitive fatigue subscale than healthy controls, with a large effect size.

The PedsQL MFS cognitive fatigue subscale discriminated ME/CFS cases from healthy controls with an AUC of 0.914; a cut-off score of <65 yielded 67% sensitivity and 96% specificity, with a positive likelihood ratio of 18.5.

At baseline, WMFI and PedsQL MFS cognitive fatigue subscale scores were significantly and strongly negatively correlated in both ME/CFS cases and healthy controls, supporting construct validity of the WMFI.

The WMFI and PedsQL MFS cognitive subscale were both significantly correlated with the Functional Disability Inventory and PedsQL total score, indicating satisfactory construct validity against general functional/quality-of-life measures.
Both the WMFI and PedsQL MFS cognitive fatigue subscale showed moderate responsiveness to change in ME/CFS patients over 24 months of multi-modal treatment.

At 24-month follow-up, WMFI and PedsQL MFS cognitive fatigue subscale scores remained strongly negatively correlated in ME/CFS patients, with both measures shifting to reflect general improvement in cognitive symptoms over time.

In prior published work cited by the authors, persistent chronic fatigue syndrome patients had significantly higher (worse) WMFI mean scores than patients who had recovered from chronic fatigue syndrome.

Prior literature cited by the authors reports strong internal consistency of the WMFI (Cronbach's alpha 0.85 in non-clinical controls, 0.93 in fatigued patients) and excellent test-retest reliability (r = 0.89 over two days).

The Long COVID group's overall symptom burden was intermediate, lower than the Severe ME/CFS group but higher than the Moderate ME/CFS group.

The study framework treats ME/CFS following infectious mononucleosis and Long COVID following SARS-CoV-2 infection as comparable examples of post-infectious chronic illness, enabling direct behavioral and pathophysiological comparison.
Analysis of biobanked muscle biopsies revealed specific oxidative damage in ME/CFS skeletal muscle that differed from both healthy controls and fibromyalgia patients.
Subcellular fractionation and biochemical assays showed that oxidative imbalance in ME/CFS muscle produced direct functional consequences on the sarcoplasmic reticulum and mitochondrial compartments.

Lymphocyte analyses from Stanford confirmed oxidative stress as a shared feature of ME/CFS and Long COVID, with 20 Long COVID patients and 27 ME/CFS patients showing oxidative imbalance relative to 25 controls, though with distinct molecular signatures between the two conditions.
Studies demonstrated mitochondrial RNA dysregulation and altered β-oxidation pathways in ME/CFS skeletal muscle.
Quadriceps femoris biopsies from ME/CFS patients showed compromised oxidative phosphorylation and progressive mitochondrial morphological abnormalities.
Earlier electron microscopy studies found no major structural mitochondrial defects in ME/CFS muscle, though functional anomalies were present, an observation later corroborated by molecular studies.

Oxidative stress-induced mitochondrial dysfunction is proposed to impair subsarcolemmal calcium homeostasis, causing elevated intracellular sodium and reduced handgrip strength as markers of systemic fatigue.

Transcriptomic analyses of ME/CFS muscle showed differential expression of genes related to mitochondrial bioenergetics, oxidative balance, energy metabolism and muscle trophism, including reduced transcription of the gene encoding the nicotinic acetylcholine receptor binding site.

Vastus lateralis biopsies in ME/CFS showed a shift toward fast-fatiguing type 2X myosin heavy-chain fibers with high ATP consumption and low endurance, while single-fiber contractile capacity was preserved.
Handgrip strength studies show a strong inverse correlation between muscle fatigue and overall ME/CFS disease severity, suggesting mitochondrial impairment extends across multiple muscle groups.
IL-6 is a dual-function myokine that has anti-inflammatory/metabolic effects when transiently released during contraction but contributes to systemic low-grade inflammation under chronic conditions.

In women with ME/CFS, serum extracellular vesicle proteomic profiles before and after maximal exercise showed altered proteins linked to muscle contraction, immune activation, and brain signaling, correlating with disease severity.

In male ME/CFS patients, plasma extracellular vesicle proteomic analysis post-exercise showed alterations in immune-related proteins and proteins controlling sleep/wake cycle, proportional to disease severity, replicating the pattern seen in women.
Magnetic resonance spectroscopy during repeated exercise showed excessive lactic acid accumulation in muscle and slowed phosphocreatine recovery in ME/CFS patients.
Brenu et al. (2011) first described altered cytokine profiles in ME/CFS, with increased pro-inflammatory cytokines (IL-1β, IL-6, TNF-α) and reduced anti-inflammatory cytokine IL-10.

miRNA analyses of ME/CFS muscle biopsies showed differential expression of miRNAs regulating mitochondrial biogenesis, calcium homeostasis, and oxidative stress responses; several of these miRNAs are also dysregulated in Long COVID, suggesting convergent post-viral fatigue mechanisms.

Large-scale trials of therapies directly targeting the oxidative stress/energy production vicious cycle, such as CoQ10, NADH, or antioxidants, have generally shown only modest effects in ME/CFS.

A large comparative analysis of ME/CFS versus Long COVID patients (Eckey et al.) concluded there are no specific therapy recommendations yet, but patient-reported experience data provide urgently needed real-world evidence for future targeted care and trials.
Not all Long COVID cases progress to ME/CFS, indicating incomplete overlap between the two post-viral conditions.

MRI-based comparison confirmed that fatigue-related findings are similar between Long COVID and ME/CFS.

The magnitude of loading-related extrusion change (Δ bipedal-sitting and Δ unipedal-sitting) was larger in the hypermobile group than the non-hypermobile group in unadjusted comparisons.
Patellar tendon stiffness measured by shear-wave elastography was significantly lower in the hypermobile group compared with the non-hypermobile group.

A subset of 24 patients with bilateral Grade 2 hypermobility were mainly younger (mean age 36), predominantly male (18/24), and often had high BMI, suggesting a possible underlying connective tissue predisposition to nerve instability.
Male patients had a significantly higher likelihood of confirmed UNE than females.
Sedentary/desk-based employment was significantly more common among confirmed UNE patients than non-UNE patients.
Prevalence of diabetes mellitus did not differ significantly between UNE and non-UNE patients.
Thyroid dysfunction (predominantly hypothyroidism) was found in 7 patients (6 with UNE) without a significant association with UNE.
A history of prior elbow trauma was present in a minority of patients, and the majority of confirmed UNE cases appeared idiopathic or related to repetitive use rather than acute injury.
Obesity was numerically more common among non-UNE patients but the difference in BMI between UNE and non-UNE groups was not statistically significant.
Regular weightlifting was not a statistically significant risk factor for UNE, with prevalence comparable to the overall cohort.

Bilateral disease was common among confirmed UNE patients, and a substantial minority of unilaterally symptomatic patients showed objective contralateral abnormalities on imaging/electrodiagnostics despite clinical silence, suggesting a subclinical pre-symptomatic stage.

Ultrasound was positive (CSA enlargement and/or hypermobility) in 82% of confirmed UNE cases, with substantial overlap between static compression (CSA enlargement) and dynamic instability (hypermobility) findings.

Ultrasound demonstrated higher sensitivity than EDX for confirmed UNE, while EDX had slightly higher specificity, and the two modalities showed only moderate concordance, supporting a complementary multimodal diagnostic approach.

The authors propose a novel multimodal composite scoring system (C-UNE) integrating clinical, ultrasound, electrodiagnostic, and occupational/contextual domains (total 17 points) to stratify likelihood of clinically significant UNE, though it remains unvalidated.

Local anesthetic resistance, where standard doses fail to provide adequate analgesia, has been observed in patients with Ehlers–Danlos syndrome, certain muscular dystrophies, and hypermobility disorders.
True pharmacologic resistance to local anesthetics is exceedingly rare and may involve alterations in voltage-gated sodium channels, though genetic contributions remain incompletely understood.

Most cases of apparent local anesthetic failure are due to technical factors such as poor procedural technique, suboptimal dosing, medication errors, or inadequate spread to target nerves, rather than true pharmacologic resistance.

Clinical consequences of local anesthetic resistance include inadequate postoperative pain control, increased opioid consumption, prolonged post-anesthesia care unit stays, unplanned hospital admissions, and reduced patient satisfaction.
Among 270 patients referred to orthopedic rehabilitation, 57 (21.1%) met the 2017 diagnostic criteria for hypermobility spectrum disorders.
HSD frequency was markedly higher in women (31.7%) than in men (4.7%) among screened orthopedic rehabilitation patients.
Patients diagnosed with HSD had a mean age of 39.4 years, were predominantly female (91.2%), and 68.4% were Kuwaiti nationals.
Among HSD patients, 63.2% were classified as generalized HSD, 26.3% as localized HSD, and 10.5% as peripheral HSD according to the 2017 classification framework.
The median Beighton score among HSD patients was 4.0 (IQR 3-5), ranging from 1 to 9.
The most frequently positive Beighton maneuver was passive apposition of the left thumb to the forearm (58.5%), while the least frequent was active right elbow hyperextension >10° (30.2%).
The knee was the most frequent site of primary orthopedic diagnosis or injury among HSD patients (45.3%), with knee osteoarthritis (27.7%), ACL tear (8.8%) and meniscal tear (7.0%) most common.

The hand and the foot/ankle were each involved in 19.4% of primary orthopedic diagnoses, with De Quervain's syndrome, flexor tendon injury, hand fracture and TFCC tear each accounting for 3.5%, and ankle fractures (10.5%) and pes planus (5.3%) most common in the foot/ankle.
Secondary orthopedic diagnoses or injuries occurred in 32 HSD patients, most frequently at the knee (40.6%) and foot/ankle (28.1%).
Tertiary orthopedic diagnoses or injuries occurred in 10 HSD patients, most frequently at the knee (50.0%) and spine (20.0%).
Among HSD patients, 80% required surgical intervention as primary orthopedic management.
For secondary management, 67.7% of HSD patients required surgical procedures, and for tertiary management, 40% required surgery, most often conservative management (60%) directed at the knee (40%).

Knee-directed procedures were the most common orthopedic management approach among HSD patients (45.7%), including total knee arthroplasty (20.0%), ACL reconstruction (10.9%), knee arthroscopy (7.5%) and meniscectomy (7.3%).
Anesthesia data available for 42 HSD patients showed general anesthesia in 81.0%, spinal in 16.7%, and local in 2.4%, with mean postoperative hospitalization of 7.9 ± 6.6 days (range 1-20).
Higher Beighton scores were significantly correlated with greater primary orthopedic diagnosis/injury burden among HSD patients.
Higher Beighton scores were significantly correlated with greater need for secondary orthopedic management among HSD patients.
Higher Beighton scores were strongly correlated with the need for tertiary orthopedic management among HSD patients.
Older age was inversely correlated with secondary orthopedic diagnosis or injury burden in HSD patients.
Older age was inversely correlated with need for primary orthopedic management in HSD patients.
Older age was strongly inversely correlated with need for secondary orthopedic management in HSD patients.
Higher patient body weight was significantly correlated with greater primary orthopedic diagnosis/injury burden among HSD patients.

HSD classification (generalized vs localized/peripheral) was significantly associated with secondary orthopedic management burden, with generalized HSD patients showing higher secondary management burden.

Among 29 patients with connective tissue disease (Marfan, Loeys-Dietz, or Ehlers-Danlos syndrome) undergoing mitral valve repair, 83% had less than trivial mitral regurgitation immediately after repair.
There was no significant difference in 30-day survival after mitral valve repair between patients with connective tissue disease and those with degenerative mitral regurgitation.
Intermediate-term survival after mitral valve repair did not differ significantly between patients with connective tissue disease and those with degenerative mitral regurgitation.
Among CTD patients followed for a median of 3.5 years after mitral valve repair, none required mitral valve reintervention or experienced recurrence of significant mitral regurgitation.
Of 3210 patients who underwent penile prosthesis insertion between 2012-2024, 40 (1.25%) developed real glans hypermobility requiring glanspexy.
Glanspexy was performed at the time of primary implantation in 22.5% of patients and as a secondary procedure in 77.5%.
67.65% of patients who underwent glanspexy reported being satisfied with the procedure.
77.78% of patients felt their erection shape was better after glanspexy.
76.47% of patients felt that glanspexy treatment met their expectations.
94.12% of patients agreed they would still choose to undergo glanspexy surgery again.
Glanspexy performed as a secondary procedure, in comorbid patients, after multiple implant revisions or genital/pelvic surgeries was associated with lower patient satisfaction.
A female patient homozygous for a COL1A1 glycine substitution (c.1012G>A; p.(Gly338Ser)) presented with severe OI resembling type III/IV.
A second female patient homozygous for a COL1A2 glycine substitution (c.1730G>C; p.(Gly577Ala)) also presented with severe OI resembling type III/IV.
Heterozygous parents carrying the COL1A1 glycine substitution were phenotypically asymptomatic, unlike their homozygous affected child.
Heterozygous parents carrying the COL1A2 glycine substitution had OI type I, a milder phenotype than their homozygous affected child.
Population-level analysis of gnomAD 4.1 showed that glycine residues near the N-terminal region of the COL1A1 triple-helix domain are more tolerant of substitutions in unaffected individuals.
In contrast to COL1A1, COL1A2 triple-helix glycine residues did not show a similarly tolerant region in unaffected individuals in gnomAD.

The patient's short stature, cachexia, micrognathia, and a large visceral arterial aneurysm at a young age raised clinical suspicion for an underlying connective tissue disorder, most likely vascular Ehlers-Danlos syndrome (vEDS) or a related vasculopathy.
Patients with vascular Ehlers-Danlos syndrome (vEDS) have inherent arterial fragility due to COL3A1 gene mutations, resulting in high rates of spontaneous dissections, aneurysms, and ruptures.

Because of suspected vEDS, the procedural team used a gentle, low-pressure, minimal-instrumentation strategy with balloon-assisted flow control to reduce the risk of vascular rupture during catheter manipulation.

A large proximal splenic artery aneurysm coexisting with a high-flow splenic arteriovenous fistula was successfully treated using dual-balloon-assisted (arterial inflow and venous outflow control) dense coil packing followed by NBCA-Lipiodol glue embolisation.
At 15-day follow-up, CECT confirmed successful fistula closure with normal hepatic/portal venous opacification and preserved viable enhancement in the superior pole of the spleen.
Endovascular treatment of SAVF has been reported to provide comparable technical success to surgery but with lower mortality (0% vs >4%) and faster recovery.
A prior reported case using coils and NBCA to treat SAVF achieved durable occlusion but resulted in splenic infarct as a complication.
Das et al. encountered coil migration during SAVF embolisation, highlighting inadequate flow control, and subsequently adopted arterial balloon occlusion to prevent this.

Coexistence of splenic artery aneurysm and arteriovenous fistula, often due to aneurysmal rupture into the splenic vein, can result in portal hypertension, splenomegaly, and high-output cardiac failure.

Whole-exome sequencing and Sanger validation identified a homozygous pathogenic NEPRO variant (c.280C>T; p.Arg94Cys) segregating with disease in an Iranian consanguineous family, establishing the molecular diagnosis of anauxetic dysplasia type 3 (ANXD3).
Joint hypermobility/laxity of the fingers, toes, and other joints was a recurring clinical feature across affected family members with ANXD3 due to the NEPRO variant.
The study expands the ANXD3 phenotypic spectrum by reporting previously infrequent or unreported systemic features including microcephaly, clubfoot, cataracts, urolithiasis, and hearing impairment.
Recurrent urolithiasis in one patient is a novel, previously unreported feature possibly indicating renal involvement in ANXD3, though noted with caution given the small number of cases.

Comparison across ANXD3 cohorts showed head circumference heterogeneity: Iranian patients presented with microcephaly, whereas previously reported patients (Narayanan et al., Remmelzwaal et al.) had macrocephaly.
Severe short stature, brachydactyly, and thoracolumbar kyphoscoliosis were consistently observed across all reported ANXD3 patients, supporting these as core disease features.
Neurodevelopmental outcomes varied among ANXD3 cases: cognitive and motor delays were present in the Iranian patients and in the Remmelzwaal et al. case, but not in the Narayanan et al. patient.

NEPRO encodes a protein implicated in ribosomal RNA processing via the RNase MRP complex, and the p.Arg94Cys substitution is predicted to interfere with this process, potentially explaining the skeletal abnormalities of ANXD3.
Trio exome sequencing identified a de novo pathogenic SMARCA4 variant (c.3315G>T) confirming the diagnosis of Coffin-Siris syndrome in the patient.
This case reports congenital hypothyroidism as a novel comorbid feature in SMARCA4-related Coffin-Siris syndrome, not previously described in the literature.

The patient lacked the classic fifth-digit hypoplasia/aplasia and coarse facial features typically used as diagnostic clues for Coffin-Siris syndrome, illustrating phenotypic variability in SMARCA4-related cases.

A variant of uncertain significance in the X-linked gene AP1S2 (linked to neurodevelopmental disorders) was also detected by trio exome sequencing and may contribute to the patient's neurobehavioral phenotype in an oligogenic manner alongside the SMARCA4 variant.
Fluoxetine was introduced to treat the patient's severe anxiety as part of multidisciplinary management.
Levothyroxine replacement therapy for congenital hypothyroidism has been stable since infancy with good adherence and no reported issues.
Cleft palate repair surgeries, including a revision at age 10, improved feeding and reflux symptoms although speech therapy remained necessary.
The patient exhibited proportionate growth restriction with height, weight, and head circumference below the 2nd percentile, consistent with short stature and microcephaly.

A proteomic comparison of PBMCs from fibromyalgia patients versus controls identified 251 quantified proteins, of which 47 were differentially expressed and proposed as potential biomarkers of fibromyalgia.
Repeated reserpine administration produced comparable mechanical allodynia (reduced von Frey withdrawal threshold) in both male and female mice from day 7 through day 28.
Reserpine reduced paw withdrawal latency to radiant heat (thermal hyperalgesia) comparably in male and female mice from day 7 through day 28.
Reserpine induced cold allodynia with a sex-dependent temporal profile, emerging earlier in females (day 7) than males (day 14) and persisting through day 28 in both sexes.
Reserpine significantly increased immobility time in both male and female mice in the tail suspension test and forced swimming test, indicating depressive-like behavior.
Intraperitoneal HRW (0.3 mM, once daily for 6 days) progressively reversed reserpine-induced mechanical allodynia, achieving complete reversal within four days in both male and female mice.
HRW reversed thermal hyperalgesia with a sex-dependent time course, achieving full reversal after 3 days in males and 4 days in females.
A single day of HRW treatment abolished reserpine-induced cold allodynia in both sexes, with greater inhibition in females (61.5%) than males (48.9%).
Six days of HRW treatment normalized reserpine-induced increases in immobility time in both the tail suspension test and forced swimming test in both sexes, with no effect in vehicle-treated mice.
Reserpine increased spinal cord 4-HNE (lipid peroxidation marker) in both male and female mice, and this increase was normalized by HRW treatment.

Reserpine increased spinal cord NLRP3 inflammasome protein levels in both sexes, and these elevated levels persisted despite HRW treatment, indicating HRW's analgesic effect does not require spinal NLRP3 suppression.
Reserpine increased phosphorylated ERK1/2 in the spinal cord of both sexes, reflecting maladaptive synaptic plasticity, and HRW normalized this increase.

In the spinal cord, HRW selectively increased HO-1 expression in male but not female mice, revealing a sex-specific antioxidant enzyme response, while reserpine itself did not alter HO-1 in either sex.
In the spinal cord, HRW selectively increased NQO1 expression in female but not male mice, complementary to the male-specific HO-1 response, while reserpine alone did not alter NQO1 in either sex.
Reserpine reduced spinal cord SOD-1 expression in both sexes, and HRW treatment normalized this downregulation equally in males and females, representing a shared antioxidant mechanism.
Unlike the spinal cord, reserpine and HRW had no significant effect on 4-HNE or p-ERK1/2 protein levels in the amygdala of either sex.
Reserpine increased NLRP3 protein levels in the amygdala of both male and female mice, and HRW treatment reversed this increase in both sexes, unlike the persistent elevation seen in the spinal cord.
Reserpine reduced HO-1 expression in the amygdala of both sexes, indicating supraspinal oxidative stress/impaired antioxidant defense, and HRW treatment reversed this decrease in both sexes.
Reserpine did not significantly alter NQO1 or SOD-1 protein levels in the amygdala of either male or female mice.
Serum GRIN1 protein levels were significantly higher in fibromyalgia patients than in healthy controls.
Serum P2RX1 protein levels were significantly higher in fibromyalgia patients than in healthy controls.
Serum P2RY2 protein levels were significantly higher in fibromyalgia patients than in healthy controls.
A moderate, statistically significant positive correlation (r = 0.61) was found between serum GRIN1 and P2RX1 levels in FM patients.
A moderate-to-strong statistically significant positive correlation (r = 0.70) was found between serum GRIN1 and P2RY2 levels in FM patients.
A moderate statistically significant positive correlation (r = 0.63) was found between serum P2RX1 and P2RY2 levels in FM patients.
ROC curve analysis showed serum GRIN1 had good diagnostic performance for FM with AUC 0.817 (95% CI 0.750–0.884), sensitivity 91.4%, specificity 72.0%.
ROC curve analysis showed serum P2RX1 had good diagnostic performance for FM with AUC 0.778 (95% CI 0.707–0.849), sensitivity 78.5%, specificity 75.3%.
ROC curve analysis showed serum P2RY2 had the highest diagnostic performance among the three markers for FM, with AUC 0.842 (95% CI 0.776–0.908), sensitivity 92.5%, specificity 80.6%.

FM patients showed significantly higher rates of sleep disturbance, fatigue, headache, morning fatigue, dry mouth, leg numbness, dry eyes, difficulty concentrating, feeling of swelling in soft tissues, and family history of FMS compared with healthy controls.
Morning fatigue was a significant predictor of fibromyalgia, with FM patients 4.78 times more likely to experience it than controls.
Dry mouth was a significant predictor of fibromyalgia, with FM patients 2.56 times more likely to experience it than controls.
Leg numbness was a significant predictor of fibromyalgia, with FM patients 3.80 times more likely to experience it than controls.
Difficulty concentrating was a significant predictor of fibromyalgia, with FM patients 5.06 times more likely to experience it than controls.
Feeling of swelling in soft tissues was a significant predictor of fibromyalgia, with FM patients 2.45 times more likely to experience it than controls.
Headache was identified by multivariate logistic regression as a significant predictor of fibromyalgia, though no specific odds ratio value was reported in the text.

The review reports that butyrate-producing bacteria such as Faecalibacterium prausnitzii and Roseburia spp. are decreased in fibromyalgia patients, potentially compromising intestinal barrier integrity.

Pro-inflammatory bacteria such as Bacteroides and Escherichia species, which produce endotoxins like LPS, are reported to be increased in fibromyalgia and may activate TLR4 leading to systemic and neuroimmune inflammation.

Altered microbial diversity and shifts in the Firmicutes-to-Bacteroidetes ratio are reported in FM, a change previously associated with metabolic dysfunction and immune dysregulation in other chronic pain conditions.

Systemic immune activation via LPS interacting with TLR4 on immune cells is proposed to trigger pro-inflammatory mediator release and chronic low-grade inflammation contributing to pain sensitivity and fatigue in FM.
Elevated levels of pro-inflammatory cytokines TNF-alpha, IL-6, and IL-1 beta are reported in FM and correlate with pain hypersensitivity, neuroinflammation, and central sensitization.
Disruption of tight junction proteins such as ZO-1 and occludin is described as compromising gut barrier integrity, leading to influx of microbial antigens and immune dysregulation in FM.

Microglial activation in the CNS, potentially driven by peripheral inflammatory signals from gut-derived endotoxins, is proposed to enhance pain processing and contribute to cognitive dysfunction ("fibro fog") in FM.

Since approximately 90% of serotonin is synthesized in the gut, reduced gut-derived serotonin due to dysbiosis may contribute to mood disorders, sleep disturbances, and heightened pain sensitivity in FM.
Gut microbiota-regulated imbalance between inhibitory GABA and excitatory glutamate signaling is proposed to contribute to hyperalgesia, anxiety, and impaired pain modulation in FM.

Reduced levels of neuroactive SCFAs such as butyrate may contribute to neuroinflammation and altered central pain processing in FM, as butyrate normally helps maintain blood-brain barrier integrity and modulate glial activation.

Altered microbial composition and metabolite production may disrupt vagal signaling along the gut-brain axis, contributing to autonomic dysfunction, mood disturbances, and pain hypersensitivity in FM.
Gut microbiota-mediated disruption of cortisol production via the HPA axis may lead to an exaggerated stress response, contributing to symptom exacerbation in FM.
Gut bacteria-mediated metabolism of tryptophan into serotonin and kynurenine may be dysregulated in FM, potentially contributing to neuroinflammation, mood disturbances, and central sensitization.
Altered bile acid metabolism, which acts as a signaling pathway in gut-liver-brain communication, may disrupt immune homeostasis and perpetuate chronic pain and fatigue in FM patients.
Mast cell counts in GI lamina propria were elevated in systemic mastocytosis, MCAS, and inflammatory disorders compared to healthy tissue.
The tryptase depletion index (TDI) did not differ significantly among SM, MCAS, inflammatory disorder, and healthy control groups, with observed fluctuations attributable to measurement noise.
ROC analysis showed that both TDI and mast cell enumeration have low sensitivity and specificity for diagnosing MCAS.
Atypical, CD25-positive mast cell infiltrates were confirmed as a diagnostic feature of systemic mastocytosis.
KIT D816V mutation testing, along with CD25/CD30 markers, can substantiate a diagnosis of systemic mastocytosis, in contrast to mast cell counting which showed limited diagnostic utility.
Peritoneal lavage tryptase activity, a marker of mast cell degranulation, was significantly increased at 0.5h, 1h, and 1.5h after intestinal manipulation compared to laparotomy controls.
Mesenteric connective tissue mast cells degranulated rapidly (0.5h, 1h, 3h) after intestinal manipulation, whereas gastric and other GI-tract mast cells did not.
Unlike mesenteric mast cells, gastric mast cells did not show increased degranulation after intestinal manipulation.

Depletion of peritoneal macrophages with clodronate liposomes prior to intestinal manipulation did not alter mesenteric mast cell degranulation, indicating a macrophage-independent activation mechanism.
Ex vivo mechanical manipulation of explanted mesenteric tissue did not induce mast cell degranulation, suggesting mechanical stress alone is not sufficient to trigger degranulation.

Cervical vagotomy performed before intestinal manipulation significantly reduced IM-induced mesenteric mast cell degranulation compared to sham-vagotomized animals, indicating a vagal-dependent activation mechanism.
Ex vivo incubation of mesenteric tissue with the muscarinic agonist bethanechol induced significant, dose-dependent mast cell degranulation, unlike substance P or nicotine.
The muscarinic antagonist atropine blocked bethanechol-induced mesenteric mast cell degranulation, confirming a muscarinic receptor-mediated mechanism.
Neither substance P (neurokinin receptor agonist) nor nicotine (nicotinic acetylcholine receptor agonist) induced significant mesenteric mast cell degranulation ex vivo.
Mast cell-deficient KitW-sh/W-sh mice did not show reduced GI transit after intestinal manipulation, unlike wildtype Bl6 mice which showed significantly pronounced dysmotility.
KitW-sh/W-sh mice showed reduced leukocyte (MPO+ cell) infiltration into the muscularis externa after intestinal manipulation compared to wildtype Bl6 mice.

Selective depletion of connective tissue mast cells in Mcpt5-Cre/DTRfl/fl mice did not alter IM-induced MPO+ cell infiltration into the muscularis externa or GI-transit times compared to Mcpt5-Cre control mice, indicating connective tissue mast cells are not required for postoperative ileus.
Basophils are the rarest granulocyte, comprising approximately 1% of peripheral blood leukocytes in healthy individuals, and are involved in IgE- and non-IgE-mediated hypersensitivity.
SCF binding to c-kit does not by itself trigger mast cell degranulation, but it significantly enhances mast cell activation and mediator production by facilitating FcεRI crosslinking.
IL-3 is identified as the most potent differentiation factor for human basophils, acting through its highly expressed surface receptor CD123.
The BAT is a flow cytometric assay measuring upregulation of CD63 and CD203c on basophils after ex vivo allergen incubation, used to predict type I hypersensitivity reactions.
Basophils from cancer patients retained their capacity to be activated by IgE- and non-IgE-mediated triggers regardless of prior chemotherapy, targeted treatment, or biologics exposure.
BAT evaluation demonstrated that IgE-based anti-cancer immunotherapeutics can be administered to most patients with cancer, with likely fewer than 5% potentially hypersensitive.
The MAT is a novel flow cytometric assay for exploring mast cell reactivity, currently used to assess allergen responses, but less developed than the BAT with potential future applications in cancer.
Basophil infiltration was identified in human non-small cell lung cancer, accounting for 0.4% of tumor leukocytes by flow cytometry.

Histamine binding to HRH1 receptors within the tumor microenvironment suppresses CD8+ T cell activity, promoting tumor growth and treatment resistance, and HRH1 antagonists can restore CD8+ T cell function.

A retrospective cohort of stage IV lung cancer patients receiving H1 antihistamines alongside immune checkpoint inhibitors showed significantly improved overall survival and progression-free survival compared to ICI alone.

In a humanized melanoma xenograft model, tumor-infiltrating mast cells clustered in micro-regions unresponsive to anti-PD-1 therapy, co-localizing with FOXP3+ Tregs and reduced CD8+/granzyme B+ T cell infiltration and reduced HLA class I expression.

Combining anti-PD-1 treatment with c-Kit inhibitors sunitinib or imatinib, which deplete mast cells, restored CD8+ T cell activity and enabled complete tumor regression in the melanoma xenograft model.

The proportion of basophils in tumor-draining lymph nodes was an independent negative prognostic factor after surgery in pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma, recruited via CCL7/MCP-3 and activated by T cell-derived IL-3 to release IL-4.
Therapeutic or genetic depletion of mast cells in experimental PDAC models reduced tumor growth and enhanced survival outcomes.
Galectin-3 secreted by lung adenocarcinoma cells activates basophils in an antigen-independent manner, enhancing their production of IL-4 and IL-13.

Lung cancer-derived exosomes containing SCF activate mast cells via SCF-Kit signaling, inducing tryptase release that reinforces pro-angiogenic and pro-metastatic remodeling, and other exosomes shift mast cells toward pro-coagulant/thrombosis-associated mediator profiles.

In 102 gastric cancer patients, the average number of mast cells and blood vessels was significantly higher than in normal gastric tissue, and tryptase-positive mast cells correlated with increased angiogenesis and lymph node metastasis.
Stage I gastric cancer patients with higher tumor tissue tryptase expression had superior overall survival and progression-free survival, indicating tryptase as a positive prognostic marker.

Lower circulating basophil blood counts correlate with advanced tumor (T) stage, higher lymph node (N) stage, increased venous and perineural invasion, and poorer overall survival in colorectal cancer.
Higher mast cell infiltration was reported as a predictor of poorer response to anti-PD-1 immune checkpoint blockade in patients with melanoma.
A subpopulation of intestinal ILC2 expresses the immune checkpoint molecule CD160 in mice infected with the parasitic nematode Strongyloides ratti.

CD160+ ILC2 represent a distinct ST2-IL-17RB+Ki-67+ subset that expands in vivo during S. ratti infection, whereas CD160- ILC2 are ST2+IL-17RB-Ki-67- and are the dominant producers of type 2 cytokines.
Upon in vitro stimulation, sorted CD160+ ILC2 progressively lose CD160 expression while gaining cytokine-producing capacity, suggesting CD160 marks an immature or checkpoint-restrained ILC2 state.
CD160-competent RAG KO mice efficiently controlled S. ratti infection, with less than 1% of the infective dose remaining by day 10 post-infection.
CD160-deficient RAG KO mice failed to expand intestinal ILC2 and failed to activate mucosal mast cells, resulting in persistently high intestinal worm burden for nearly 100 days.
Adoptive transfer of CD160-competent ILC2 into S. ratti-infected CD160-deficient RAG KO mice partially restored mast cell activation and reduced intestinal worm burden by 50%.

Intra-observer reliability of intraepidermal nerve fiber density (IENFD) measurement was excellent (ICC>0.9) whether comparing two conventional visual readings or comparing visual reading to Innerve-assisted reading.
Innerve-assisted reading improved interobserver reliability of IENFD determination compared with conventional visual reading, raising ICC from 0.88 and 0.87 (visual readings) to 0.93.
Innerve-assisted reading nearly halved reading time for the observer familiar with the interface but was slightly slower for the second, less-trained observer.
Bland-Altman analysis showed lower dispersion (better agreement) of intra- and inter-observer IENFD values at lower fiber densities, consistent with fewer fibers to count.
For an observer less familiar with Innerve, reading time on high-density slides decreased with practice across the study, suggesting a training/learning bias affecting interface use.

The study cohort's IENFD values (assessed by observer 2's first visual reading) were evenly distributed across severity categories from poor (<3/mm) to near/above normal (>9/mm), providing a balanced representation of SFN severity for algorithm testing.
Mendelian randomization suggested that genetically higher circulating MCP2 levels are associated with a lower risk of small fiber neuropathy.
Mendelian randomization suggested that genetically higher circulating CCL11 levels are associated with an increased risk of small fiber neuropathy.
Mendelian randomization suggested that genetically higher circulating IL18R1 levels are associated with an increased risk of small fiber neuropathy.
Reverse Mendelian randomization indicated that genetic liability to SFN decreases circulating CD6 levels, with no significant reverse effect on the other 90 inflammatory proteins.
Bayesian colocalization analysis showed moderate evidence (PPH4=0.612) that CCL11 and SFN share a common causal genetic variant.
Colocalization support was weak for IL18R1 (PPH4=0.100) and MCP2 (PPH4=0.251), limiting evidence for a shared causal variant with SFN.

PheWAS using the AstraZeneca PheWAS Portal (UK Biobank exome data) found no significant genetic associations between the three prioritized proteins and other disease traits, arguing against major horizontal pleiotropy or safety liabilities.
Protein-protein interaction network analysis (STRING/Cytoscape) showed that CCL11 has significant interactions with therapeutic targets associated with SFN retrieved from GeneCards.

Paclitaxel-treated mice developed persistent mechanical allodynia on days 3, 5, and 7 after the first injection compared with controls, confirming induction of chemotherapy-induced peripheral/small fiber neuropathy.
Paclitaxel-treated mice showed significantly reduced intraepidermal nerve fiber density (IENFD) in hind paw skin compared with controls, confirming small fiber neuropathy in the model.

In the paclitaxel-induced mouse SFN model, CCL11 was significantly elevated in serum, dorsal root ganglia, and spinal cord compared with controls, directionally consistent with its MR-based risk association.

In the paclitaxel-induced mouse SFN model, IL18R1 was significantly elevated in serum, dorsal root ganglia, and spinal cord compared with controls, directionally consistent with its MR-based risk association.

In the paclitaxel-induced mouse SFN model, MCP2 was significantly elevated in serum, dorsal root ganglia, and spinal cord compared with controls, which is discordant with its suggestive protective association in the MR analysis.
Deep learning-based virtual screening (TransformerCPI2.0) identified top-ranked candidate small molecules with predicted interaction scores greater than 0.97 against CCL11, IL18R1, and MCP2.

Molecular docking showed Dracorhodin perchlorate and Pseudolaric acid A-O-b-D-glucopyranoside had the strongest predicted binding affinities to IL18R1, both below the -7.0 kcal/mol threshold for strong binding.
Molecular docking showed Dehydrocostus lactone had notable binding activity to CCL11.
Molecular docking showed Vasicine hydrochloride had binding capability to both CCL11 and MCP2, suggesting potential for multi-target engagement.
Molecular docking showed Raspberry ketone glucoside exhibited stable binding activity to both IL18R1 and MCP2.

Prior studies analyzing leukocyte protein expression in SFN patients found elevated systemic levels of IL-8, IL-2, and TNF compared with healthy controls, cited as evidence that inflammation contributes to SFN.
Biallelic RFC1 AAGGG repeat expansions were significantly more common in patients with idiopathic peripheral neuropathy than in controls.
Biallelic RFC1 expansions were found in 6.9% of patients with pure sensory neuropathy, the highest prevalence among the neuropathy subtypes examined.
Biallelic RFC1 expansions were found in 1.1% of patients with pure small fiber neuropathy, indicating a modest but present contribution in this subgroup.
Monoallelic RFC1 expansions were nominally more frequent in patients with idiopathic peripheral neuropathy than controls, but the difference was not statistically significant.
No second mutations or second-allele expansions were found among monoallelic RFC1 expansion carriers, suggesting no evidence of compound heterozygosity explaining disease in this group.

An integrative computational pipeline combining ExpansionHunter Denovo and ExpansionHunter with unsupervised clustering achieved 97.2% concordance with repeat-primed PCR for detecting and genotyping RFC1 expansions from short-read whole-genome sequencing data.

A 32-year-old man with a 13-year history of treatment-refractory diarrhea-predominant IBS was found intraoperatively to have vertebral artery compression of the vagus nerve (CN X), and microvascular decompression produced immediate and sustained resolution of his GI symptoms.
Vascular compression of the CN VII/VIII complex by a looping posterior inferior cerebellar artery (PICA) causing hemifacial spasm resolved almost completely after microvascular decompression.

A previously published case (ref. 7) described a 58-year-old woman with nausea, vomiting, and diarrhea plus glossopharyngeal-type throat/cheek pain due to PICA compression of the CN IX/X complex on the same laterality as the current case, who became symptom-free at 1-year follow-up after MVD.

The authors propose that surgical vagotomy is known to cause gastroparesis (reduced motility), suggesting by analogy that intermittent vagal overactivity (vagus rhizopathy) could cause the opposite effect—hyperperistalsis with abdominal pain—as a mechanism for GI distress from vagal compression.
Vagal nerve injury (e.g., from surgical vagotomy historically used for peptic ulcer disease) has been strongly associated with GI dysfunction, most notably gastroparesis.

Glossopharyngeal neuralgia has rarely been associated with cardioinhibitory syncope, proposed to result from aberrant glossopharyngeal afferent activity reflexively increasing vagal efferent outflow causing bradycardia and hypotension.
A meta-analysis of eight international studies estimated the worldwide prevalence of irritable bowel syndrome at approximately 11%, a diagnosis typically made by exclusion.
The paper cites prior HRV studies showing consistently reduced parasympathetic/vagal activity in IBS patients compared to healthy controls.
Only 4.4% of the cohort had an official IBS diagnosis, whereas 47.8% met criteria for a broader IBS-compatible symptom cluster, yielding an underdiagnosis ratio of 10.8.
Neuro-vegetative symptoms (sweating, palpitations, dizziness) were more prevalent than any single transit symptom, with sweating being the most common complaint at 19.1%.
Among transit symptoms, bloating (11.8%) and constipation (10.3%) were the most common.
Constipation was reported approximately four times more frequently than diarrhea, indicating a predominance of a slow-transit phenotype.
Maladaptive eating behaviors were highly prevalent: distracted eating 50.0%, hurried eating 27.2%, irregular meal schedules 73.5%, and regular snacking 65.4%.
Diagnosed food-related conditions in the cohort included lactose intolerance and celiac disease (each 8.1%), gluten intolerance (5.1%), and Crohn's disease (2.2%).
Patients with the functional DGBI phenotype had significantly higher BMI (28.15 kg/m2, overweight-to-obese range) than asymptomatic controls (24.47 kg/m2).
DGBI cases were significantly less likely to report regular snacking than controls, suggesting adaptive avoidance behavior.
In a logistic regression model of DGBI ~ Age + Sex + BMI + Snacking, BMI remained a significant, robust predictor of DGBI status after adjustment.

A sensitivity analysis excluding participants with CRP >10 mg/L (n=98) showed results consistent with the primary analysis for neuro-vegetative features, transit symptoms, IBS diagnosis, and IBS-compatible cluster, indicating low-grade inflammation did not bias the findings.
No direct statistical association was identified between individual eating behaviors and specific gastrointestinal symptoms, despite the high prevalence of maladaptive eating patterns.
In a mouse model of Long COVID, nasal anti-CD3 antibody treatment increased brain FoxP3+ IL-10+ regulatory T cells.
Nasal anti-CD3 mAb treatment reduced microglial and astrocytic gliosis in the white matter and hippocampus of Long COVID model mice.
Nasal anti-CD3 mAb treatment restored hippocampal neurogenesis in mice with post-COVID neuroinflammation.
Nasal anti-CD3 mAb treatment improved short-term memory in the Long COVID mouse model.
Nasal anti-CD3 mAb reprogrammed microglia away from an antigen-presenting, NF-κB-driven inflammatory state toward a chemokine signaling, phagosome, and TGF-β-related regulatory phenotype.
Patients with Long COVID who had neurological symptoms showed lower circulating regulatory T cell populations compared to others.

In a series of 98 patients with systemic nickel allergy syndrome undergoing oral nickel sulfate challenge, gastrointestinal symptoms were common, led by meteorism and bloating, followed by heartburn, abdominal pain, diarrhea, and constipation.
A patient with dermatologic nickel allergy who was diagnosed with irritable bowel syndrome had her intestinal and extraintestinal symptoms resolve or improve after starting a low-nickel diet.
SNAS patients had a much higher rate of positive lactose breath tests than healthy controls, suggesting nickel-induced inflammation may cause secondary hypolactasia.
Nickel sensitivity is more prevalent among individuals with gastroesophageal reflux disease than in non-GERD individuals, suggesting nickel-induced immune activation may contribute to GI symptoms.

Dermatologic manifestations of SNAS in the Ricciardi cohort included exacerbation of allergic contact dermatitis in a third of patients, systemic contact dermatitis in about 15%, and urticaria/angioedema in roughly a quarter.
In the Ricciardi cohort, headache was the most common neurologic symptom of SNAS, with migraine headache occurring in about 7% of patients.

Headache, dizziness, and fatigue reported by patients after nickel-rich meals could not be reproduced by oral nickel challenge, the diagnostic gold standard, calling into question their specific attribution to nickel.
A case of severe migraine associated with nickel allergy required surgical removal of an atrial septal defect closure device.

All 15 fibromyalgia patients studied had at least one metal allergy (nickel most common) versus none of 10 controls, and reducing metal exposure resolved symptoms in 70% of patients at 5-year follow-up.
Self-reported nickel allergy was associated with wheezing and asthma in a cohort of young German adults.
Nickel allergy was more common in overweight/obese outpatients and was associated with worse metabolic parameters and impaired growth hormone secretion.
Nickel allergy prevalence was markedly higher among overweight women than the general population.
Over half of overweight women with nickel allergy had a significant reduction in BMI after 24 weeks on a low-nickel diet.

Among obese subjects, those with nickel allergy showed greater GH-IGF1 axis impairment, higher prevalence of empty sella, reduced pituitary volume, and higher normalized T2 pituitary intensity compared with non-allergic subjects.
SNAS patients have a higher prevalence of thyroid autoimmune markers, potentially increasing risk for autoimmune thyroid disease such as Hashimoto thyroiditis.
A study of nearly 5000 women found that nickel allergy was associated with a 2.47-fold increased odds of endometriosis, potentially reflecting estrogenic properties of nickel.

Patients with nickel allergy had a 10.5-fold increased risk of adverse effects (most commonly new-onset/worsening migraine and palpitations) after patent foramen ovale closure with a nitinol device, though no deaths, bleeding, TIA, or stroke occurred within 90 days.

A case of ASIA syndrome (autoimmune/autoinflammatory syndrome induced by adjuvants) developed one year after nickel-titanium chin implant placement, with fever, fatigue, cytopenias, organomegaly, proteinuria, elevated ferritin, and low-positive ANA that resolved after implant removal.

In obese individuals patch-tested for nickel allergy, those with nickel allergy showed greater GH-IGF1 axis impairment, higher prevalence of empty sella, reduced pituitary volume, and higher normalized T2 pituitary intensity than nonallergic individuals.
SNAS patients were found to have a higher prevalence of thyroid autoimmune markers, potentially increasing risk of autoimmune thyroid disorders such as Hashimoto thyroiditis.
In a study of 4985 women, nickel allergy was associated with a 2.47-fold increased odds of having endometriosis, possibly related to estrogenic properties of nickel.

In a double-blind study, patients with nickel hypersensitivity had significantly more adverse effects following PFO closure with nitinol devices than those without nickel allergy, most commonly new-onset/worsening migraines and palpitations, with a 10.5-fold increased risk overall, though no serious events (death, bleeding, TIA, stroke) occurred within 90 days.
A case report described a systemic allergic reaction to a nickel-containing atrial septal defect closure device that required surgical removal.
A case report described nickel-induced systemic dermatitis triggered by a sacral neurostimulator.
Metal allergy, including nickel allergy, can precipitate Kounis syndrome (acute coronary syndrome from hypersensitivity reaction) in patients with coronary stents or atrial septal occluder devices.
A 60-day low-nickel diet decreased cutaneous and extracutaneous symptoms in SNAS patients, with symptoms recurring upon nickel reintroduction while those remaining on the diet continued to improve.
A low-nickel diet produced marked improvement in 20 IBS patients with suspected SNAS.

SNAS patients who received telehealth nutritional counseling with individualized diet plans and video consultations showed improved quality of life and greater adherence to the low-nickel diet after 30 days.
A clinical trial found that hydroponic-cultivated (low-nickel) tomato sauce combined with a low-nickel diet improved quality of life and gastrointestinal symptoms in SNAS patients.

In a randomized controlled trial of 112 SNAS patients, oral nickel hyposensitization with gradually increasing microdoses (up to 1.5 µg/week) over 1 year significantly improved cutaneous and gastrointestinal symptoms and tolerance of dietary nickel reintroduction compared to placebo.

In a randomized trial of 23 nickel-allergic patients receiving oral immunotherapy vs 12 placebo patients, IFN-γ, IL-13, and IL-5 levels significantly decreased in treated patients compared to placebo, and 20/23 OIT patients tolerated dietary nickel reintroduction versus none in placebo.
A 2006 study found that disulfiram combined with a low-nickel diet resulted in complete resolution of hand eczema in 10 of 11 patients.
