In vivo knockdown of MDK reduced pancreatic stellate cell and mast cell infiltration/activation, alleviating pancreatic damage and fibrosis in the chronic pancreatitis mouse model.
In vivo knockdown of NCL reduced pancreatic stellate cell and mast cell infiltration/activation, alleviating pancreatic damage and fibrosis in the chronic pancreatitis mouse model.
Antibody-mediated depletion of γδ T cells significantly reduced hindlimb perfusion recovery on day 7 after femoral artery ligation compared with wildtype and isotype-treated control mice.
γδ T cell depletion significantly reduced vascular cell proliferation (BrdU+ endothelial and smooth muscle cells) and resulted in smaller collateral lumen diameters compared to control groups.

TCRα knockout mice, lacking conventional αβ T cells, showed no impairment in perfusion recovery or vascular cell proliferation/lumen diameter compared with wildtype mice, indicating αβ T cells do not contribute to arteriogenesis in this model.
γδ T cell depletion significantly reduced the number of perivascular M2-like (MRC1+) macrophages without altering total macrophage numbers or M1-like macrophage counts.

γδ T cell depletion significantly reduced perivascular mast cell degranulation on day 1 after femoral artery ligation while total mast cell numbers/recruitment remained unchanged, indicating γδ T cells regulate mast cell activation rather than recruitment.
γδ T cell depletion did not affect platelet-neutrophil or monocyte-platelet aggregate formation, nor the proportions of circulating neutrophils or monocytes on day 1 after arterial ligation.
γδ T cell depletion did not alter perivascular neutrophil infiltration (MPO+ cells) around growing collaterals on day 1 after ligation.
Ifng mRNA expression was increased in γδ T cells of wildtype mice following induction of arteriogenesis by femoral artery ligation, compared to sham-operated controls.

Exogenous IFNγ administration rescued the mast cell degranulation deficit in γδ T cell-depleted mice back to isotype control levels, without significantly changing total perivascular mast cell numbers.

Systemic blockade of the IFNγ receptor completely inhibited mast cell degranulation in wildtype mice without affecting mast cell recruitment, confirming a requirement for IFNγ signaling in mast cell activation during arteriogenesis.

Daily IFNγ administration further reduced the number of M2-like (MRC1+) perivascular macrophages on day 7 in both γδ T cell-depleted and isotype mice, indicating a pro-inflammatory bias that impairs late-phase resolution.

γδ T cell subset composition reprogrammed over time after arterial ligation: CD27+/CD39− (IFNγ-associated) γδ T cells predominated on day 1, while CD39+ (IL-10-associated/regulatory) subsets increased by day 3, with total γδ T cell proportion unchanged.

IL-10 administration on day 3 after ligation promoted perivascular macrophage polarization toward the M2-like phenotype and reduced M1-like macrophages in both γδ T cell-depleted and isotype mice, without changing total macrophage numbers.
IL-10 treatment improved hindlimb perfusion recovery by day 7 after arterial ligation in both γδ T cell-depleted and isotype control mice compared with saline treatment.
Exogenous IL-10 rescued vascular cell proliferation and collateral lumen diameter in γδ T cell-depleted mice, restoring them toward levels seen in isotype controls.

Among adults selected for escalated work-up, the diagnostic yield of a clonal mast cell disorder was far lower in those with an MCA/anaphylaxis index presentation than in those with a non-MCA (hematology-first) index presentation.
KIT D816V was detected in the majority of systemic mastocytosis patients and in none of the idiopathic or secondary anaphylaxis cases.
TET2 was the most frequently mutated gene overall and was enriched in the systemic mastocytosis subgroup compared with idiopathic anaphylaxis.
SRSF2 P95 hotspot mutations clustered specifically within the systemic mastocytosis cohort and were part of the high-risk S/A/R genotype in advanced disease.
DNMT3A mutations, including the R882H clonal hematopoiesis hotspot, were observed in SM and CM patients but not in IA or secondary anaphylaxis.
Patients with mastocytosis (SM+CM) were significantly older than those without mastocytosis (IA or secondary anaphylaxis).
Mastocytosis patients were predominantly male compared with non-mastocytosis patients.
Mediator-related symptoms at presentation were far less common in mastocytosis (largely detected via hematology pathway) than in the non-mastocytosis (IA/secondary anaphylaxis) group.
Platelet counts were lower in patients with mastocytosis than in those without mastocytosis.
Basal serum tryptase was significantly higher in mastocytosis patients than in non-mastocytosis patients, and levels above 20 ng/mL occurred exclusively in the mastocytosis group.
Urticaria pigmentosa, present in a fifth of the cohort, was strongly associated with a final diagnosis of cutaneous mastocytosis.

MPL mutations, at non-canonical loci distinct from the classic W515 hotspot, were detected exclusively in idiopathic anaphylaxis patients and in none of the mastocytosis cases, raising the possibility of incidental clonal hematopoiesis or occult myeloproliferative neoplasm.

The high-risk SRSF2/ASXL1/RUNX1 (S/A/R) co-mutation genotype, previously linked to inferior survival in Western advanced systemic mastocytosis cohorts, was identified among this Southeast Asian cohort's advanced SM patients, confirming conservation of this adverse molecular architecture.

A single idiopathic anaphylaxis patient carried a TET2 variant without KIT D816V or other mast cell-specific drivers, most likely representing incidental age-related clonal hematopoiesis rather than true mast cell clonality.

Some KIT-negative cutaneous mastocytosis cases nonetheless carried myeloid co-mutations (TET2, DNMT3A), suggesting overlap between clonal hematopoiesis and mast cell disease independent of KIT status.
Overall, half of the sequenced cohort harbored at least one pathogenic or likely pathogenic myeloid variant, with a much higher proportion in the non-MCA pathway than the MCA/anaphylaxis pathway.

Among the 24 sequenced adults, final multidisciplinary diagnoses were idiopathic anaphylaxis in 45.8%, systemic mastocytosis in 29.2%, cutaneous mastocytosis in 16.7%, and secondary anaphylaxis in 8.3%, with no cases meeting criteria for MMAS.

Among mastocytosis patients, the only identified anaphylaxis trigger was a honeybee sting in one indolent systemic mastocytosis patient who experienced severe anaphylaxis; no other food/drug triggers were identified in the remaining mastocytosis patients.

The 7.1% diagnostic yield of CMCD among this Thai clinician-escalated MCA/anaphylaxis subgroup contrasts markedly with the ~47% yield reported in Western cohorts of unexplained anaphylaxis without cutaneous mastocytosis, likely reflecting differences in referral pathways and screening approaches rather than true biological difference.
Skin mast cells from CSU patients show significantly upregulated MRGPRX2 expression, contributing to heightened mast cell sensitivity.

A gain-of-function MRGPRX2 mutation (185A>G) found in a subset of CSU patients increases degranulation, calcium influx, and ERK phosphorylation, and correlates with significantly higher disease activity scores (UAS7).
CSU patients unresponsive to loratadine had significantly lower baseline serum NGF levels than responders or healthy controls, and symptom improvement correlated with rising NGF levels.
Serum ET-1 levels are significantly elevated in CSU patients, particularly those resistant to antihistamine therapy, positioning ET-1 as a potential predictor of therapeutic refractoriness.
Elevated serum and cutaneous BDNF levels have been observed in CSU patients compared to healthy or non-allergic individuals, with eosinophils and TNF-α-stimulated keratinocytes as likely sources.
Mast cell-derived IL-33 markedly enhances histamine-induced itch through an IL-13-dependent mechanism, driving an immune-nerve signal amplification loop that sustains pruritus.
Intradermal SP administration induces more pronounced and persistent wheals, flares, itching, and granulocyte infiltration in CSU patients compared to controls.
Both SP and NK1R expression are markedly upregulated on basophils of CSU patients, and SP stimulates basophils to release histamine at levels comparable to anti-IgE and fMLP.
CGRP injection studies show enhanced wheal and erythema responses in patients with chronic idiopathic urticaria and delayed pressure urticaria.
CSU patients exhibit increased wheal responses to intradermal VIP injections and a non-significant trend toward elevated serum VIP levels.

Elevated serum IL-31 levels in CSU correlate positively with itch severity, disease activity, and impaired quality of life; levels are higher in antihistamine nonresponders and decrease following successful omalizumab treatment.
The dermis of CSU patients shows increased numbers of TSLP+ and IL-33+ cells (endothelial cells, fibroblasts, macrophages, mast cells), along with elevated serum TSLP and IL-33.
IL-33 gene single nucleotide polymorphisms have been linked to susceptibility to chronic spontaneous urticaria.

In randomized, placebo-controlled phase 3 trials, dupilumab significantly reduced disease activity scores (ISS7, UAS7, HSS7) and total serum IgE in omalizumab-naïve, H1-antihistamine-refractory CSU patients, though the magnitude of IgE reduction correlated only weakly with clinical improvement.
An open-label pilot study and case series demonstrated that oral tofacitinib elicits rapid, profound clinical responses in patients resistant to maximally dosed antihistamines.
In a multicenter, double-blind, randomized, placebo-controlled phase II trial, tezepelumab failed to achieve the primary endpoint at week 16 in the overall CSU cohort.

In omalizumab-naïve participants, tezepelumab produced a statistically significant and clinically meaningful reduction in UAS7 versus placebo, with benefit persisting up to 32 weeks after treatment cessation, most evident in patients with low baseline IgE and longer disease duration.
The selective MRGPRX2 antagonist EP262 abolished agonist-evoked cutaneous mast-cell degranulation in MRGPRX2-knock-in mice, supporting advancement into phase II trials for CIndU and CSU.

fMRI studies in CSU patients show enhanced functional connectivity between the left inferior orbitofrontal gyrus and the caudate nucleus that correlates positively with itch severity, while reduced connectivity with the hippocampus is inversely associated with anxiety levels.
Among CSU patients categorized by basophil responsiveness to IgE stimulation (responders, non-responders, basopenics), basopenic patients exhibited the highest pruritus intensity scores.
Serum eosinophil granule protein levels correlate positively with urticaria severity.

In the dermis of CSU patients, the MCTC mast cell subset (co-expressing tryptase and chymase) constitutes over 99% of the mast cell population, positioning it as the key effector cell under neurogenic regulation.

119 of 170 Fabry disease patients (70%) had reduced intraepidermal nerve fiber density on skin punch biopsy.
Patients with reduced IENFD were more often male (68% vs 26%) and older (48±13 vs 39±15 years) compared to those with preserved IENFD.
Cardiac, renal, and cerebrovascular manifestations were significantly more frequent in Fabry patients with reduced IENFD than those with preserved IENFD.
Patient-reported peripheral nervous system symptoms, including FD-associated pain, hyperhidrosis, and hypo-/anhidrosis, did not differ significantly between patients with reduced vs preserved IENFD.
Quantitative sensory testing showed significantly worse cold detection thresholds in patients with reduced IENFD compared to those with preserved IENFD.
Interventricular septal thickness and diastolic myocardial mass were significantly higher in Fabry patients with reduced IENFD.
Plasma lyso-Gb3 was higher and alpha-galactosidase-A enzyme activity was lower in Fabry patients with reduced IENFD compared to those with preserved IENFD.
Renal function was more impaired and cardiac biomarkers (hs-Troponin, NTproBNP) were higher in Fabry patients with reduced IENFD.

Carriers of the late-onset GLA p.N215S variant had a milder neurological phenotype with less frequent renal, cerebrovascular, GI and ENT involvement, and better preserved CDT, but showed similar cardiac involvement and no difference in IENFD compared with classical FD variants.
IENFD was consistently lower in male than female Fabry patients across all ages, and decreased with age at a similar rate in both sexes, with strong effect sizes.
An IENFD threshold of 4.2 fibers/mm best predicted subsequent development of late gadolinium enhancement on cardiac MRI, with an AUC of 0.74.
An IENFD threshold of 1.0 fiber/mm best predicted subsequent cardiac device (ICD/pacemaker) implantation, with an AUC of 0.7.
In multivariable Cox regression adjusted for age and sex, IENFD < 4.2 fibers/mm was an independent predictor of developing myocardial LGE, conferring a 5.26-fold higher risk.
In multivariable Cox regression adjusted for age and sex, IENFD < 1.0 fiber/mm was an independent predictor of subsequent cardiac device implantation, conferring a 3.72-fold higher risk.

Fabry patients excluded from LGE analysis due to pre-existing cardiac device implantation or severe renal impairment (the most severely affected patients) also showed markedly reduced IENFD, supporting the association between low IENFD and severe organ involvement.

IENFD differed by indication for cardiac device implantation: patients with symptomatic ventricular tachycardia had the lowest IENFD, followed by bradycardia, while patients receiving prophylactic ICDs had comparatively higher IENFD.

QST cold detection threshold was associated with LGE development but was less informative than IENFD in nested model comparisons, and was not significantly associated with cardiac device implantation, so it was excluded as a covariate from the primary models.
In a cohort of 14 men with wild-type transthyretin amyloidosis, 92.9% showed objective clinical signs of neuropathy on neurological examination.
Electrophysiological testing showed evidence of neuropathy in 71.4% of patients, predominantly axonal and sensorimotor in pattern.
Patients had a median Neuropathy Impairment Score of 8 (IQR 8), indicating a mild to moderate degree of large-fiber neuropathy impairment.

Disability staging using the Familial Amyloid Polyneuropathy and Polyneuropathy Disability score was low, with a median stage of 1, suggesting mild functional disability despite high neuropathy prevalence.
Electrochemical skin conductance, a measure of small-fiber/sudomotor function, was abnormal in 64.3% of patients, indicating high prevalence of small-fiber neuropathy.
Despite frequent small-fiber neuropathy signs, autonomic symptom burden was limited, with a median COMPASS-31 score of 12, indicating only mild autonomic symptomatology.
Autonomic symptom burden assessed by the Survey of Autonomic Symptoms was also low, with a median score of 7.5.
A majority of patients (69.2%) reported decreased quality of life on the Norfolk Quality of Life scale, indicating that neuropathy meaningfully affects daily life despite mild clinical scores.

The study concludes that both large- and small-fiber neuropathy are highly prevalent in wild-type transthyretin amyloidosis, and although their clinical/functional impact is mild to moderate, they still reduce patients' quality of life, suggesting new therapeutic avenues could be relevant.

The authors note that ATTRwt amyloidosis has traditionally been considered a purely cardiological condition, but recent studies and this study's findings suggest neurological involvement is more significant than previously believed.

Both BEA and SNS significantly reduced visceral hypersensitivity, measured as electromyographic responses to colorectal distension, in a neonatal acetic acid IBS rat model.
BEA and SNS improved intestinal epithelial barrier integrity, as evidenced by transepithelial electrical resistance and tight junction protein expression.
Circulating norepinephrine levels, dysregulated in the IBS model, were normalized following BEA/SNS treatment, indicating restoration of autonomic balance.

Pancreatic polypeptide levels, dysregulated in the IBS model, were normalized after treatment, with females showing a greater degree of PP modulation than males, suggesting sex-dependent autonomic response to neurostimulation.
BEA and SNS increased acetylcholine release, consistent with activation of the cholinergic anti-inflammatory pathway.
BEA and SNS reduced tumor necrosis factor-alpha (TNF-α) levels, suggesting suppression of inflammation via the cholinergic anti-inflammatory pathway.

At baseline, SHR females had significantly higher systolic, diastolic, and mean arterial pressure but lower heart rate than Wistar females.
Intravenous ethyl ferulate at 15 mg/kg and 30 mg/kg, but not 7.5 mg/kg, significantly reduced MAP and HR compared with vehicle and the lower dose in Wistar females.
Ethyl ferulate at 15 mg/kg and 30 mg/kg markedly decreased MAP and HR in hypertensive SHR females compared with vehicle and 7.5 mg/kg.
Pretreatment with the muscarinic antagonist atropine completely prevented ethyl ferulate-induced hypotension and bradycardia in Wistar females.

In SHR females, atropine fully abolished ethyl ferulate-induced bradycardia but only partially prevented the hypotensive response, suggesting an additional non-muscarinic mechanism in hypertensive animals.

β1-adrenergic blockade with atenolol did not prevent ethyl ferulate-induced MAP reduction in either Wistar or SHR females, indicating the cardiac adrenergic pathway is not involved in the hypotensive effect.

In SHR females, β1-adrenergic blockade abolished ethyl ferulate-induced bradycardia while leaving the hypotensive effect intact, indicating cardiac adrenergic contribution to the chronotropic but not the hypotensive response in hypertension.

Ganglionic blockade with hexamethonium prevented ethyl ferulate-induced hypotension and bradycardia at 7.5 and 15 mg/kg in Wistar females, indicating a nicotinic/ganglionic contribution in normotensive animals.

In SHR females, ganglionic blockade with hexamethonium amplified the ethyl ferulate-induced MAP reduction at all doses but completely prevented the bradycardic response, suggesting loss of nicotinic receptor contribution to hypotension with hypertension progression.
Inhibition of nitric oxide synthase with L-NAME did not prevent ethyl ferulate-induced hypotension or bradycardia in SHR females, indicating the NO pathway is not involved in these acute effects.
The patient's chronic abdominal pain and diarrhea were initially diagnosed as IBS after IBD and celiac disease were excluded, prior to the later diagnosis of collagenous colitis.
Before the eventual diagnosis of spondyloarthritis, the patient's diffuse polyarthralgia with normal imaging led to a working diagnosis of fibromyalgia.
Many patients with microscopic colitis, including collagenous colitis, are initially misdiagnosed with IBS due to overlapping symptomatology.
A large proportion (20%-60%) of collagenous colitis patients present with at least one additional autoimmune disorder, supporting an immune-mediated pathogenesis.
Colonic tissue in collagenous colitis shows a proinflammatory cytokine profile with overexpression of IFN-γ, TNF-α, IL-1β, and IL-6, along with increased nitric oxide and prostaglandin production.
Histology in collagenous colitis shows diffuse lymphocytic infiltration dominated by CD4+ lymphocytes in the lamina propria and CD8+ lymphocytes intraepithelially, contributing to epithelial injury.
Genetic predisposition to collagenous colitis is suggested by association with HLA-DQ2 and HLA-A2 haplotypes, which are also linked to celiac disease, autoimmune thyroiditis, and type 1 diabetes.
Smoking is a well-documented risk factor for collagenous colitis, associated with earlier onset (about 10 years) and a three- to fourfold increased relative risk.
NSAIDs are the most frequently implicated drug class in collagenous colitis, acting via prostaglandin inhibition leading to mucosal barrier disruption and local immune activation.
Budesonide is the treatment of choice for inducing and maintaining remission in collagenous colitis, achieving clinical remission in 80%-88% of patients with rapid quality-of-life improvement.
Sulfasalazine, used empirically based on classic IBD treatment models, induces clinical improvement in 40%-50% of collagenous colitis patients.
